source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Wuqubʼ Kaqix simply adorns himself shiny silver and sparkling jewels; resplendent jade and celestial turquoise; bright feathers and superlative exclamations and sublime elocutions of a shameless braggarts boasting to then pronounce: “look at me I am the Light of the Sun; my resplendence shines as bright as the Great Star;  my Silver Nose is like that of Moon…” This is the way of the Dark Twin, Tezcatlipoca yet our text expects us to know this and now we do.

This way of Wuqubʼ Kaqix will not do for the noble ethics of the Maize People and their New Sun and Moon under which Noble Lords must prove themselves through hard work and ritual sacrifice; the keeping of the days in the Sacred Calendar, blood-letting and the bleeding of oneself; abstention from the ʼgood-lifeʼ through fasting and long pilgrimages, all which manifest the true mark of a Noble Ruler of the People who over time becomes a Great Lord of the Pueblo. Merit, not material wealth is the way a Noble Ruler should be chosen. And this is where we find ourselves in this story that we enter En Media res, which is to be dropped in to a drama that is in full swing.

In fact we have entered the mythic narrative of the Wooden People; the mythic plot of the mythic narrative we just saw the very end of with the destruction of the Wooden People. But now, here, we are about to find out what that Sun of the Wooden People was like, in order to obtain an idea of what it takes to be and become a Cultural Hero.

Here Begins the Story of Wuqubʼ Kaqix and Chimalmat; their Sons Sipakna and Kabʼraqan; and, the Hero Twins: Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej

This then is where the story begins of Wuqubʼ Kaqix and his wife Chimalmat that tells of their two sons: Sipakna, Kabʼraqan.

Here then begins the story of their defeat by the Boys; the Sons; the Twins: Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

Not yet was there the Sun, but there was One who puffed himself up ʼas ifʼ he were the Sun; the puffed-up One who saw himself as the Sun was known as Wuqubʼ Kaqix; Seven Scarlet Macaw was his name.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
It was just ʼself-aggrandizement-nimarisaj ribʼ that created his conceit and it was just his self-aggrandizing conceit that caused him to think upon himself as the ʼBig Man-Nimalaj Achi-Nimaʼ Winaqʼ.

This was the arrogant one known as Seven Red Feathers-Wuqubʼ Kaq Kʼix spoken of as Seven Macaw: Wuqubʼ Kaqix. Wuqubʼ Kaqix saw himself as a Great Lord that shone like the calm white light; the soft white light, the quite white light-saqnatanoj that shone like rich radiant remembrance of the Sun and Moon; saqnatanoj as the ʼfirst rays of sunʼ are known, for they are said to be the remembrance of the Sunriseʼs even warmth and the Moonlightʼs balanced perfection: saqnatanoj.

Saqnatanoj

This, then, was when soft white light enveloped the Sky-Earth in the calm quiet glow of Dawn; its luminous warmth of smooth golden light blanketed the Face of the Earth in an ancient, ancestral remembrance recalling the moment when the Ancient Ones, the Divine Ancestors watched and waited for the First Dawn; a memory of an Age; a recollection of a Sun that had come and gone.

Saqnatanoj:  the time, the place; the moment; the space just before the arrival of the shimmering, shining, sparkle of the bright white light of Dawn: Saqnatanoj.

Saqnatanoj: embodiment, ensoulment of the resplendent recollection and remembrance, the radiant recuerdo y recolección of the first rays of sunlight of Sunrise; the glistening gleam of the glossy glow of Dawn, just named, just known as: Saqnatanoj.

Saqnatanoj:  an all-embracing divine white light that envelops the Sky-Earth in the Pre-dawn hour on the Pre-dawn horizon before the Sunrise erupts to shed its brilliant bright light on the Face of the Earth: Saqnatanoj.

Saqnatanoj is the nostalgic remembrance of the origins of Kaj-Ulew in the pre-dawn hour just before the ʼsprouting forth of the Sunʼ showers its brilliant heat across the Lake-Sea; Earth-Sky illuminating the Sacred World-Santo Mundo-Saq Ulew with essence that emanates from the dim white light of Saqnatanoj to bring forth Nawal Intuition; Ancestral Genius; Primordial Intelligence-Saq Naʼoj; Divine Remembrance-Saq Natbʼal that radiate from Saqnatanoj.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This is the time and place when and where Day-keepers and Prayer-makers wake to call-out in order to cry-out their prayers and petitions when and where they beg and beseech the Dawning Sun as the entering ʼFace of Day; Face of the Sun; Kinich Ajawʼ the ʼSun-Faced Lordʼ as the Sun was invoked at the ʼBreak-of-Dayʼ by the Rulers of the ʼMountain-Plain; Juyubʼ Taqʼajʼ who were the Lords of the ʼFace of the Earth-Rajawal Uwach Ulew.ʼ

Here we are presented with this heartfelt mythic image that feeds as it sustains the Maya Soul with a profound sense of hope inherent to the rebirth and renewal of lifeʼs possibilities with each New Day; an image known to you well as the Sowing and the Dawning; Ewaxibʼal, Saqiribʼal that sprout forth to then rise and climb up upon the Face of the Sky-Earth; Kaj-Ulew: the World.

So here we are at the beginning of our New Narrative where Wuqubʼ Kaqix has come to meet the Dawn a perfect metaphor to begin the telling of a New Story in the light of a New Day.

There was the First Sky-Earth; Nabʼe Kaj-Ulew but the light of the Sun and Moon was still quite dim. And so it was Lord Seven Macaw-Ajaw Wuqubʼ Kaqix who spoke forth when he saw himself as the bright light-saqetal-white light of the Wooden People; for Wuqubʼ Kaqix-Seven Macaw saw himself as the ʼdivine sign-saqetal-sacred exampleʼ that he wanted; that he wished; that he willed the Wooden People to follow; for Seven Macaw saw himself as the ʼperfect path-saqetal-sacred wayʼ to take; the perfect path to be taken-up; the divine example to be taken-after for those who survived the Great Flood-Nim Bʼutik.

He just acted as if he were of the same essence as the Ancient Transforming Ones-Nawal Winaq who were the Magical Transforming Ancestors-Nawal Winaq; known as those who were the ʼFirst-born Ones-Nawales-First-sprouted Onesʼ that were the First Magical Ancestors known as Nawal Winaq also spoken of as Nawinaq.

And so it was and so it would come to be that these ʼFirst-born Onesʼ who were the ʼFirst-sprouted Ancestorsʼ were endowed with the magical power of  transformation; thus were they named Nawal Winaq: Mythical Ancestors of Magical Transformation.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Saqetal was the Perfect Path; Perfect Way that Wuqubʼ Kaqix formed and shaped by molding and modeling his perfect ways-saqetal to make himself out to be of the same being and condition-kʼojeʼik-nature and essence as Nawal Winaq, so that he as the Perfect Path, Perfect Way would be followed as a Nawal Winaq who would be the perfect Saqetal for the Wooden Beings to follow wherever they went when they wandered across the Sky-Earth and Lake-Sea; Kaj-Ulew; Cho-Palo.

This is what led Wuqubʼ Kaqix to say what he was led to say as the One-Jun who said that he was indeed a  Nawal Winaq who must be followed as their Nim Ajaw-Great Lord who would serve perfectly as the Saqetal of the Wooden People as their Nim Ajaw.

And so it was that Lord Seven Macaw; Wuqubʼ Kaqix said: “My nature, my essence shall shine forth over the Formed People, the Shaped People. For I am their Sun; I am their Light; I their Moon; I their Reflection and their Sustenance; for it is they who look to me for their light; for their warmth!”

“So be it! Ta Chuxoq! May it come to be! Great is my perfection, great is my reflection; great is my resplendence; great is my resemblance to the light of the Sun; to light of the Moon.”

“For I am the walkway of the People; and, I too am the pathway of the Pueblo!” In bʼinibʼal winaq; In pu chakabʼal rumal winaq!

“For my eyes are of pure silver, they just shimmer, they just shine with the resplendence of emeralds, brilliant and bright; like the glittering gleam of  precious gemstones; katiltotik chi yamanik, like the sparkling splendor of imperial green of jade; raxa kuwal for they shine resplendent from my divine countenance.”

“My teeth sparkle just the same, as they are formed from precious stone, bright and blue; these precious turquoise stones reflect the Sea and the Face of the Sky. This is the essence of my bedazzling, burnished teeth that shimmer, as they shine forth from my memorable majestic mouth of a regal, royal Lord.”

“And with regard to my fine noble nose; oh, my refined noble nose, my fine refined divine noble nose gleams and glimmers with a glint so bright that its shimmering shine reaches as far as the bejeweled light of the Moon.”

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
“Silver then is my noble throne; my sacred silver throne that illuminates the Face of the Earth every time I fly from that bright shining perch of mine.”

“This makes my essence the very same as the divine light of the Sun; and Moon. For I am the sacred light of the Divine Daughters of the Dawn; the Sacred Sons of the Sun; those Born in the Light; Begotten in the Light; Daughters of the Moon, Sons of the Sun: Saqil Al, Saqil Kʼajol; Beloved Vassals, Precious Subjects of Noble Lords.”

“And so it is that I am the Sun; I too am the Moon of those who are the Divine Daughters-Venerable Vassals of this Noble Realm; I am the bright light of the Sun; I too am the bright light of the Moon; the Sun and Moon of those who are the Sublime Subjects-Sacred Sons of this Noble Realm; Saqil Al, Saqil Kʼajol; Divine Descendants, Sacred Subjects; Devout Daughters of the Regal Realm; Loyal Sons of this noble Kingdom; those Precious Replacements borne and begotten in the bright light of the Eternal Sun; conceived and engendered in the luminous light of the transforming Moon.”

“So be it! Ta Chuxoq! May it come forth so; may it come to be! For I am truly divine; for truly sacred am I; my divine light; my radiance is that of a Noble Lord; a Noble Lord whose noble splendor reaches far,” said Wuqubʼ Kaqix.

But it was not true that Wuqubʼ Kaqix was the Sun. It was just his conceit; it was just his arrogance that brought forth his puffed-up sort of stuffed-up sense of self importance.

He thought himself to be just like the Sun because of his fiery red feathers that burned in a bright blaze as he made his way across the great green canopy of the Jungle Forest where he was truly the Lord Seven Scarlet Macaw.

The bright countenance of the Wuqubʼ Kaqix shone only as the pale dim light that his bright red-feathers reflected when he took to flight; so that his whitish moonlit sort of washed-out light only reached as far as where he walked around and flew about.

For truly, his resplendent face did not illumine all that lay beneath the Sky; and so it was that his radiance didnʼt lighten-up all there was to be brighten-up there below the Sky.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This was before the Face of the Sun, Moon, and Great Star could be seen in the Sky. For the Sun had not yet dawned; the Moon had not yet risen; and the Great Star did not yet shine in the sky; not yet, but still Wuqubʼ Kaqix wished to be revered as if he were the very light of the Sun and Moon.

He wished to be named as a Noble Lord; to be known as an Entitled Ruler; to be addressed as a Sovereign Ruler by being given noble entitlement-kukobʼisaj-noble investiture that named him as the direct descendant of the Sun; that named him the direct descendant of the Moon.

The light of the Sun, the light of the Moon had not yet become visible; not yet had the divine light of Sun and Moon shown their radiance; not yet had the Sun and the Moon revealed themselves to be the Replacements who were the Descendants of  the Sunʼs golden radiance; of the Moonʼs bright silver light.

For the truth was that Wuqubʼ Kaqix desired only to be named a Noble Lord; he hungered only to be the One whose grandeur surpassed all others; the One who wished to be named by titles of noble entitlement; the One who wished to be provided with tribute in accord with his noble position. For it was he, Wuqubʼ Kaqix who wished to be recognized as the One who had earned the right to be sustained because of his royal rank and noble status.

This is when a great deluge was made fall; when the great flood came to pass, the flood that was created to destroy the careless, heartless Wooden People; Tree Beings, Reed Beings, the ones known as Poy, Ajam Cheʼ; those who were just dressed up and adorned Doll People-Poy; those who were they bedecked in shimmering shining finery; just bejeweled Puppet People; these who were those Ancient Ancestral Beings; Wooden Men whittled from Wood; just the Tzʼite Tree;  and the Women formed and shaped from the bundled and bound Reeds, Rushes thick with abundance, rich with sustenance were they; those who were of Tzʼiteʼ and Sibʼaq from which were carved and crafted Wooden Men of Tzʼiteʼ; Reed Women of Sibʼaq; fashioned swiftly to be finished fast these Formed Being; these Shaped Beings were never made to last.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
These were those that were Wooden People whoʼs language and looks; speech and appearance were lost forever when they were transformed into Spider Monkeys-Kʼoy who swung through the treetops speaking their ancestral animal speech; acting in their ancient animal ways. They just spoke and acted as they were molded and modeled to speak and act which meant they were just another flawed and failed fallen attempt to form and shape formed and shaped people on the Face of the Earth.

AND SO WE SHALL TELL NEXT, we shall tell further, of when Wuqubʼ Kaqix died; when he was defeated; when Formed Beings, Shaped Beings were formed and shaped by AjTzʼaq, AjBʼit; the Former, the Shaper, known as Molder-Modeler; those who created, those who crafted; those who formed and fashioned the Formed Beings they finished when they were there to bring them forth; when they were there to bring them out as that which was known as the Formation; to be seen as the Generation of what is invoked to be remembered as the Creation of life that led naturally to the Peopling; the Populating of the Face of the Earth: utzʼuquxik, uwinaqirik kʼaslem, winaqirem Uwach Ulew.

This, then, is the origin, the root, the very beginning of Ancient Word that tells of the defeat and fall of Wuqubʼ Kaqix by the Two Boys, the Two Sons: Kaʼibʼ Kʼajolabʼ.

Junajpu is the name of the First-Jun; Ixbʼalamkej is the name of the Second-Kabʼ. They were just divinities: e Kabʼawil.

It was the Two Boys-ri Kʼajolabʼ-Two Sons Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej who saw evil in the self-magnifying ways that Wuqubʼ Kaqix acted before the Heart of the Sky: Ukʼuʼx Kaj.

This then was when the Sons-ri Kʼajolabʼ-the Boys; said to each other: “This is just no good, no good at all. Surely, the way things are, is not the way they should be.”

“So then, what would it be but a chance;  just a try; an attempt nothing more, to take a shot at him when he lands upon his throne at the top of his Nance Tree where he takes his mid-day meal of golden yellow fruit that is his food-echa.”

“Let us just fire a ball-jun abʼaj-a stone with our blowgun when heʼs perched up in his Tapʼal Tree. Letʼs just shoot one shot at him nothing more.”

body:
“In this way perhaps we might wound him, causing him illness, causing him sickness, leading to his death and defeat.”

“This way we might just finish off his wealth that is his jade, his silver, his jewels, his precious stones with which he adorns himself for his own glorification; his pride, his vanity, his arrogance.”

“If not this is the way everyone will come to act in the world where silver mustnʼt be the source of power and authority; sovereignty and rule!”

“So be it; Chuxoq bʼa la na! May it come to pass!”

This is what these companions said as the two of them took up the road each one of them shouldering his blowguns: ubʼ.

Now this Wuqubʼ Kaqix had Two Sons: the First Son went by the name of Sipakna, the Smoking One, Volcano Boy; he who was known as the Spiny-Backed One, Caiman Boy. Sipakna was the “Maker of Mountains” who was the First One; the First Son of Seven Scarlet Macaw: Wuqubʼ Kaqix.

The Second Son-ukabʼ kʼajolabʼ went by the name of Kabʼraqan; Two-Footed One, Earthquake Boy. It was he who shook the Sky for he was the Quaker of Earth; Shaker of the Sky.

Kʼabʼraqan was the Second Son who was the Destructive One; the One whose destiny it was to make the Sky shake for what was his in life was to make the Earth quake: this Two-Footed One-Kabʼ Raqan was known as the “Destroyer of Big Mountains-Leveler of Small Mountains” thus he was named: Kabʼraqan; Earthquake.

Chimalmat then was the name of their Mother, the Woman who was the Wife of Wuqubʼ Kaqix; Shield-bearer; Chimalmat was her name.

Chimalmat then was the name of the Mother of Sipakna and Kabʼraqan; the Woman-the Wife of Wuqubʼ Kaqix; Shield-bearer; Chimalmat was her name.

Chimalmat-Shield-bearer

Chimalmat-Shield-bearer-she who is the shield of her Pueblo; from chimalli-shield, something laid out flat, like the open hand of divination; chimala. Wuqubʼ Kaqix will fall over backwards from the top of his tree to fall flat on his back or chimalmat; chimalmat then means ʼone who is laid-out flat on the backʼ which is a play on the name of his Nahua Woman Chimalmat which is her name, a name that comes from the Nahuatl speaking people of the North.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This is where larger estuaries fed by rivers of sweet water created the perfect environment for Pacific Caiman-Crocodiles to thrive off the abundance of marine life that grew and multiplied there in mangroves. It is from down there beside the water that one can look to the East from the Ocean Shore to look-up upon the Spiny Back-Bone of the Volcanic Cordillera of El Salvador, Guatemala, and Chiapas all of which was once imagined to be just One Great Cipacatli; One Great Caiman; One Great Crocodile.

And then there was Kabʼraqan who moved the mountains. He just shook them causing the Face of the Earth to shake and shutter; quiver and quake so that with the tap, tap, tapping of the two feet of Kabʼraqan was enough to create an earthquake.

This Kabʼraqan was a real destroyer; for it was he who was the leveler of mountains. The Small Mountains, the Great Mountains-Chʼuti Juyubʼ, Nimaʼ Juyubʼ, they just quivered; they just quaked; to shiver and shake so that in no time these Small Mountains; Great Mountains were leveled to the ground; demolished, destroyed; and so it was that the Mountains were brought down to the ground by the Two-Footed One; to Number Two Son known and named: Kʼabʼraqan.

It was they, Sipakna and Kabʼraqan, who made themselves out to be the Big Ones, the Great Ones. That is what the two sons of Wuqubʼ Kaqix did. They just did what their Father showed them to do by making a great big deal out of themselves.

This was the direct result of them following the fine example of their Fatherʼs self-aggrandizing ways; to then take-up his path of arrogance and conceit that led to them becoming bragging and boastful all of which resulted in all of their  proud and arrogant ways. This was how they came to exist in the World of the Sky-Earth: Kaj-Ulew.

“Look at me, Iʼm the Sun,” boasted Wuqubʼ Kaqix.

“Look at me, Iʼm the Maker of the Earth,” erupted Sipakna.

“Look at me I shake the Sky; I level the Earth,” quaked Kabʼraqan.

body:
They were just-xa the Sons of their Father, Wuqubʼ Kaqix. It was just from him that they brought forth their self-aggrandizement-nimarisaj ribʼ, in order to manifest their own arrogance and conceit; pride and vanity as they followed in the footsteps of their Father-kikajaw on the path of their Lord-kikajaw: Wuqubʼ Kaqix, Lord Seven Scarlet Macaw.

Meanwhile, the other Boys, the other Sons-ri Kʼajolabʼ, on the other hand, clearly saw their ways as being ugly-itzel; they saw the wicked-itzel ways of Sipakna and Kabʼraqan with their self-aggrandizing speech and arrogant actions as                        a direct confrontation, a challenge to the ways of Heart of the Sky, Heart of the Earth; Ukʼuʼx Kaj, Ukʼuʼx Ulew.

This was long before the forming and shaping of Our First Mother, Our First Father; this was long before the First Ancestors had been formed and shaped by the Former, the Shaper; Tzʼaqol, Bʼitol.

So this then was when they thought about the death-kamik and disappearance-sachik of the three arrogant ones, the three of them were to be finished off by the Boys, the Sons, ri Kʼajolabʼ.

They just planned to ʼdisappearʼ them from the Face of the Earth-dead and gone-once and for all was what the Boys wanted; was what the Boys wished for those who knew not how to respect the ancestral ways of the Sky and the Earth known as the Sky-Earth; Kaj-Ulew.

SO HERE IT IS; THIS IS IT; this is just-xa the Ancient Ancestral Account of the Boys blowgunning down Ajaw Wuqubʼ Kaqix, spoken of as Lord Seven Scarlet Macaw, Siete Guacamayo; Seven Papagayo.

This is the telling of how they, the Boys, took him down out of his Tajpal Tree; this is the Original Account of Seven Scarlet Macaw being shot down out of this throne that was found perched high-up in the forest canopy by those known as One Hunter-Junajpu-Blow-gun Boy and his twin brother; Jaguar-Moon, known near and far as Little Jaguar-Deer: Ixbʼalamkej.

body:
The Two Boys, the Two Sons, Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej; they just did it; they just did it with their power of transformation; they just did it with the Nawal power of their breath and the magical way they blew through their blowgun; the way they just ʼpuffedʼ on their blowgun; the blowgun they always shouldered on their shoulder wherever they went.

And so, now it was that they headed out walking; walking in the direction of the Great Tajpal Tree shouldering their blowgun on their shoulder; bearing the burden of their thoughts within; determined to do what was theirs to do as divine twins.

We shall tell all three stories of each one of their defeats; each story of each defeat of each one of all three rivals, three enemies, three adversaries. For all three fell one at a time to the Nawal Ways of Two Boys, Two Sons who were Nawal Winaq.

Now this Wuqubʼ Kaqix had his One Big Tree; Jun Nima Cheʼ, where he found his sustenance; rechaʼ.

This One Great Big Tree was the Nance tree known as a Tapaʼl. Tapaʼl was the proper Kʼicheʼ name given to the Nance tree, just as Tapaʼl was the proper Kʼicheʼ name given to the plentiful yellow fruit that grew on this massive coastal tree that grew up and out of the Earth like a World of its own; a World that provided  Wuqubʼ Kaqix with his secure sense of affluence in a World that he ruled over from up above with great confidence because of the way his Tapaʼl Tree provided for Seven Scarlet Macaw who was sustained by the sweet and sour sustenance that he devoured day after day beneath the Noon-day Sun when Wuqubʼ Kaqix could always be found on his Great Throne: Nim Qʼalibʼal.

And so it was that Wuqubʼ Kaqix landed high up in his Tapaʼl tree to feed on and off its great abundance. He just suckled the tart fruit that grew there, the yellow fruit of the Nance tree, Tapaʼl, as it is named; as it is known to be the food he ate each and every day to then sit back on his throne to look out upon his regal realm of the Jungle Forest.

body:
This rich golden fruit was the very reason Wuqubʼ Kaqix landed atop this One Big Tree where every day he climbed all about its crown to feed off of its fruit that was his favored most food making it his sacred most sustenance.

And so it was that Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej saw that this was the feeding place of this Great Big Bird, Seven Scarlet Macaw: Wuqubʼ Kaqix. The Twins saw him move in about its leaves to then wander out and about its limbs; the limbs; the leaves of his Tapaʼl tree.

He suckled one round golden fruit of the Tapaʼl after the next, picking one after the other; selecting one after the other; never stopping his feeding, as he ate and ate these bite-sized little yellow fruit that were as sour as they were sweet.

Indeed, the Two Boys just hid out there waiting and watching, the two of them, in the branches of the Great Tapʼal Tree, sneaking about there in the leaves; moving about there in its limbs.

This then was when Wuqubʼ Kaqix arrived there up in his perch, settling down atop his golden sustenance, the yellow fruit of this tremendous tree. It was there that he devoured as he suckled the Tapaʼl fruit of the Tapaʼl tree.

Jun Junajpu enters the Ancestral Soul of the Descendant Junajpu:

To ensoul and to inspire the Descendant through the Knowing Remembrance of the Divine Ancestor;  Maya sense and experience Transcendence through the remembrance of the Transcendent Soul and Spirit of Divinity-Humanity.

This ʼmagical storyʼ relates an ancestral form of ʼsympathetic magicʼ by naming the first son Junajpu by the name of his father: Jun Junajpu. And so it is that our magically transforming narrative begins to speak of Junajpu as his Father Jun Junajpu which is the Maya way of being and becoming in the World known as becoming the Nawal or Ancestral Replacement of whoever or whatever is needed to bring oneʼs work to fruition. The Nawal nature and condition of Junajpu is to become his Father Jun Junajpu whose power and strength; seeing and knowing; capacities and capabilities ʼenter intoʼ his Junajpu.

body:
We know this is not a ʼscribal errorʼ because the name of the Father is done with the ʼperfect consistencyʼ of a Day-keeper naming the name of Jun Junajpu exactly ʼseven timeʼ as an invocation of Wuqubʼ Junajpu-Seven Junajpu  which is exactly what is expected of this performative tradition of ʼkeeping and countingʼ the days to ʼname and numberʼ their ʼNawalʼ ways according to the sacred count of days which is the way the Maya speak of the 260 Divinatory Calendar. In this way the Father and Uncle of Junajpu, IxBʼalamkej are made present through the incantation of their names in a magical sort of mythical kind of mystical way.

The Maya Scribes call us to participate with them in this magical performance and nawal experience of ancestral transformation through this ritual drama of the ʼhuntʼ of the Blowgunner; AjPubʼ and its incantation of the ancestral name of the ʼFirst Hunter-Jun-Junajpuʼ whose ancestral soul, nawal spirit will enter his son Junajpu. This might be called participatory mystique because of the way the text enchants us so much so that we want to play along in the mythical action and speech of the Hero Twins: Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej. These Maya Scribes want us to participate in their recitation of the Ancient Word of the Ancestral Account as ritual participants who enter fully in their sacred incantation through the nawal experience of invocation that calls upon the ancestral powers of transformation that is embodied and ensouled in this nawal act of performative speech that brings forth the magical naming the Son by the ancestral name of the Father: Jun JunAjPu.

We know the Boys  are grown-up and old enough to begin doing the work of performing the tasks of Cultural Heroes of ʼtaking-up the burdenʼ of their Father Jun Junajpu and Uncle Wuqubʼ Junajpu who are already dead for some twenty years or so.

And so it is that we know Jun Junajpu is dead by the fact that his ʼengendered sonsʼ are alive to complete his work in the world of the Sky-Earth. Jun Junajpu was decapitated long ago yet his ancestral soul survives as the guide and protector of his ʼreplacementʼ or ʼkʼexelʼ who we know as Junajpu.

The Seven Names of the Name Jun Junajpu

body:
In the Toppling of Wuqubʼ Kaqix

And so it was that Jun Junajpu (1) puffed when he blew hard; when he shot his blowgun ball sending it flying just as he planned to do so that it hit Wuqubʼ Kaqix right smack on his jaw.

Wuqubʼ Kaqix cried out as he fell from his perch; flying backwards he ended up landing all sprawled out-chimalmat-flat on his back, down on the ground beneath the Tapaʼl where he was caught off-guard; the Tapaʼlʼ where he was surprised at his mid-day meal way up high in the crown of his tree.

Quickly, Jun Junajpu (2) ran to grab hold of Wuqubʼ Kaqix. But it was the arm of Jun Junajpu (3) that was torn off quick like a stick by Wuqubʼ Kaqix who snatched it up like a limb; to then tear it away like a branch torn from a tree.

Wuqubʼ Kaqix quickly picked it up, to then double it over his shoulder before carrying it away like a bent-over stalk; like broken cane of maize.

It was only by losing his arm that Jun Junajpu (4) let go of the tight grip he had on Wuqubʼ Kaqix, allowing the Big Bright Bird to make his escape.

Nevertheless, the Two Boys, the Two Sons, ri Kaʼibʼ Kʼajolabʼ had done well for themselves; they were not at first defeated by Wuqubʼ Kaqix.

It was then that the arm of Jun Junajpu (5) was carried away by Wuqubʼ Kaqix as he made his way back home holding his broken jaw. He arrived back home with it just cradled in his hand.

“What have you brought back with you there?” asked Chimalmat, the wife, the woman of Wuqubʼ Kaqix.

“Indeed, what could it be? Those two tricksters; kaʼibʼ kʼaxtokʼ just shot me with their blowgun ball, dislocating my jaw as you can see. Now all my teeth are loose causing me this aching pain from which I now suffer so terribly,” said Wuqubʼ Kaqix before Chimalmat, to then continue as he did speaking while holding his broken jaw.

“First, this arm here that I carry must be hung over the hearth. Just tie it up there with a lasso; just bind it up there over the fire until they come for it. We will see then if those two really are the tricksters they appear to be,” said Wuqubʼ Kaqix.

It was then that Chimalmat hung the arm of Jun Junajpu (6) over the embers of her three-stone hearth.

body:
So this then was when they thought it over again, Jun Junajpu (7), Ixbʼalamkej.

Here ends the passage of the ʼSeven Blowgun Hunter-Wuqubʼ Junajpu naming of the names of the Father-Jun Junajpu and the Son Junajpu as a magnificent invocation of the Nawal Powers of Transformation of the Junajpu Lineage and its continuance as Life-Loving Line of the Living Light whose essence is embodied and ensouled in the Eternal Return.

This is when they spoke there to an ancient-looking Grandfather. Truly white-haired was the head of this Old Man, he was there alongside the ancient-looking Grandmother. Truly humble was the Grandmother.

They were just bent over like corn stalks, just doubled over were they like maize; like broken canes were those who had lived to see so many days. They were just bent down low because of their age; truly ancestral looking were these elderly old people indeed, and that is just how these two Ancient Ones appeared when they, the Boys, addressed them with great reverence and regard.

Saqi Nim Aq was the name of the Grandfather. Saqi Nima Sis  was the name of the Grandmother.

It was then that the Two Boys, the Two Sons, spoke with them as their Grandmother; when they spoke with them as their Grandfather; the Two Boys address to the Old Woman, the Old Man when they greeted them there beside the road, beneath the tree. And this is what they said:

“We wish you would accompany us when we go over there to bring back our arm that is hanging there upon the hearth of Chimalmat; the fire that burns alongside Wuqubʼ Kaqix. We shall just follow along behind you there so we can bring back what is ours; ours that is now theirs; ours that is theirs hanging over their fire,” said the Boys before continuing on in their reverent way:

body:
“Perhaps you will say: ʼThese here are our Grandsons who accompany us; dead is their Mother; dead is their Father; these Two Boys just tag along with us, they circle around us all day, they just run around us as they play while we make our way down the road looking for where our luck might lay. We might just give them away to someone else since our work every day is nothing more than removing worms-chikopil-animalitos from peopleʼs teeth; people who are those that have nothing to pay. This is what we do; this is our work; this our lifeʼs way,ʼ this is what you will say,” said the Boys to their Ancient Ancestors; Saqinim Aq, Saqinimʼa Sis.

“You must say this as though we were mere children, as if we were just Young Boys in the eyes of Wuqubʼ Kaqix. We will tell you what you need to know so you know just what to do when the time comes to do what you need to do. Donʼt worry, we will help you; we will tell you just what you need to say so you know just what to do,” said the Two Sons, the Two Boys when they gave their instructions to the Old Woman, the Old Man.

“Utz bʼa la! Very well, then,” they said.

So this then was when they went over to where Wuqubʼ Kaqix was lying on his ʼside-tzamalʼ, right there before his throne; uqʼalibʼal.

This is when the Old Grandmother, Old Grandfather who were spoken of as Atiʼt, Mamaʼ came passing by on the road. Just playing along behind them were the Two Boys. Just following Mamaʼ, Atiʼt, were the Two Sons running about as grandchildren always do when circling around behind their Grandfather, Grandmother.

The text reverses the traditional order of the naming the women first, man second; Grandmother, Grandfather; Atiʼt, Mamaʼ; Mamaʼ, Atiʼt which is significant because these two Saqinim Aq, Saqinimʼa Sis are traditionally known as Ancestral Grandmothers: Ratiʼt Qʼij, Ratiʼt Saq. Remember, they are the Seers; the Diviners; the Matriarchs of the Animal Tribes of the Jungle Forest.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This spreads a sense of reversal over this ancestral enchantment of this Ancient Account of Trickster-Kʼaxtoqʼ and his use of deception; his beguiling spell; his charming trickery; his nawal power of reversal go get his work done here; here in this delightful incantation of the Ancient Ones who show the way of the Trickster to their Grandsons who are born into the Sky-Earth as the Replacements-Kʼexel of those who were tricked into the hands of Death through deceit and its deceptions. This is the story of trickery we can all learn from to rise-up above all the rest to become the Sun and the Moon that move across the Earth as the very Heart of the Sky.

That was when they passed right below the House of the Noble Lord-Rochoch Ajaw where the Great Chief was laying on his side.  Just then, the one named Wuqubʼ Kaqix cried out, he just howled in pain, all because of his loose teeth were so loose where he was hit in the jaw by the blow-gun ball.

It was right then when Wuqubʼ Kaqix saw the Grandfather, the Grandmother, Mamaʼ, Atiʼt accompanying one-an-other on the road while their Grandsons circled around them like little birds as they played about them; now in front, now behind; round and round the Boys swirled as they twirled around them as they whirled about them; circling them as they played about ʼas ifʼ they were nothing more than children.

“Where are you coming from Our Grandfather-Qamam?” asked he who was seen to be a Noble Lord-Jun Ajaw.

“We are just out searching for what is ours-xa oj tzuqubʼey qibʼ; we are just out looking about for our sustenance,” they said.

“What then is your sustenance? Who, then, are your providers? Are not these children here that accompany you the ones who sustain you?” asked Wuqubʼ Kaqix.

“No, no, not at all, it is not that way, you Our Noble Lord-Lal Ajaw; these Boys here are just our Grandsons-Qamam. It is we who take pity on them. It is we who provide for their needs.  We are those who give them a portion of what is given to us, oh Noble Lord, Lal Ajaw,” said the Grandmother, the Grandfather; Atiʼt, Mamaʼ.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Wuqubʼ Kaqix was truly finished off by the great pain he received from his loose teeth and so it was that only with great pain that he spoke:

“I would like to ask a favor from you; for you to take pity on me; please, that you might show me a kindness.  What sort of medicine do you make; what poison to you cure? What illness do you treat; what sickness do you heal!” asked Wuqubʼ Kaqix.

“Just worms do we take from peopleʼs teeth; little animalitos are all that we pull from peopleʼs teeth-xa chikopil eyaj chiqelesaj; that is what is ours. Just eyes do we heal, just sight do we cure. Just bones do we set, you, oh Noble Lord, Lal Ajaw, this is what we do; this is what is ours,” said the Old Man, the Old Woman.

“Utz bʼa la! Very well, very well indeed, would you not do that for me; maybe just cure my teeth a little? Truly, they just ache all day; truly unbearable is the pain they give me.  I donʼt get any sleep because of them; because of them and my eyes. The little bastards, they shot me with their blowgun; those tricksters they hit me here on my jaw. Ever since it began, I havenʼt eaten a thing. So please, do me the favor and show me a kindness!  My loose teeth; they are truly a torment for me.”

“Very well, Lal Ajaw, it is just the little worms, those tiny little worms that eat away at your teeth. They are those that are there to cause you pain. It is just replacements that must go in, since your teeth must come out,” they said; those who are known as the Old Woman, the Old Man.

Healers of eyes, curers of teeth; bone-setters, just ancient old healers were they, specialists is what they were; spider bite and scorpion bite were what was theirs to cure; snake bite and poisonous spines and infectious thorns that is what they healed. They were real specialist just Curanderos; Hueseros were who they were.

They just worked for what the People could give them; their food; their sustenance; nothing more; the Pueblo had no more to give. Just feathers, jade beads, Tzʼite beans, pretty things, ancient clay figurines found buried in the ground beneath the earth dug-up there in the Milpa is what they received for their payment.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
These were the only things that most ailing people had to give; with cacao and maize is how they were paid; cacao and maize were the hard, hard beans and perfect, precious seeds with which they were paid; they were just given something in exchange for their work by the People of the Pueblo in the most generous way; by saying thanks; by showing gratitude with grace.

This is how they were paid when they were paid with ʼhard, hardʼ seeds and beans that they could use little by little as they made their way down the road watching and waiting to see what destiny provided for them in lives sustained by the misfortune of those who sought their special favors in the ancient art of healing that was the curing of illness brought on by accidents that were encountered as unfortunate incidents that were inevitably stumbled upon on the path of life.

“But it might not be so good that my teeth should be taken out. It is just because of them that I am a Lord-Jun Ajaw-a Ruler. It is because of my adorned eyes and adorned teeth of precious metal and shimmering silver that make me who I am; my adornment is what makes me a Noble Lord, Jun Ajaw,” cried Wuqubʼ Kaqix.

“Truly, my beauty, my finery, my elegance comes from the embellishment of my teeth and the adornment of my eyes. The source of my power and authority lies in my fine feathers, my resplendent jade necklace, my glittering emerald jewelry, my stunning turquoise mask are what make me who I am; a Big Man; a Great Chief; a Noble Lord,” confessed Wuqubʼ Kaqix.

“Donʼt worry; donʼt worry, we will put replacements in; replacements made of ground bone is what we will exchange them with, bright white bone is what we will put back in!” said the Old Ones, the Ancient Ones.

But the ground bone they said they would use as replacements was just white maize; finely ground white maize-saq ixim-was what they prepared to set in the mouth of Seven Macaw in exchange for the adorned teeth they pulled from his mouth.

“Very well, take them out! Just do what you have to do to cure me! Just help, just heal me if you will!” he then said when he spoke.

body:
This then was when the loose teeth of Wuqubʼ Kaqix came out. Just white maize was put back in to replace the teeth they pulled. And it was just those white kernels of maize that shown there bright in his mouth.

But then, suddenly, his face fell. No longer did he look like a Lord. No longer did he appear to be an Ajaw. This was when they finished taking out his jade teeth that once glittered and gleamed bright in his mouth, the resplendent jade mouth of Wuqubʼ Kaqix was no longer there where itʼd once been.

Then they turned to healing his eyes, the well adorned eyes of Wuqubʼ Kaqix. They just fixed his eyes by getting them back in order. This was when they took out the silver. They just extracted the precious metal without him feeling a thing.

This then was the beginning of the end of self-aggrandizement; the beginning of the end of self-magnification and its self-glorification that was stopped cold; none of it was allowed anymore.

It was just their ingenious thought; just their imaginative thinking; just their transformative kind of ancestral intelligence that was the root of their intuitive knowing known as ʼnaʼojʼ that let them know what they had to do and where they had to go no matter where they were or who they were with; it was just their nawal way of being that came from them; those who were known as Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej-xawi kinaʼoj, kinawal Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

This then was when he died, the one named Wuqubʼ Kaqix: Seven Macaw as he is known. It was then that Junajpu took back his arm and set it back in place.

Soon after that Chimalmat died, she was the woman; she was the wife of Wuqubʼ Kaqix she died too along with her man Seven Scarlet Macaw.

It was in this way that the wealth of Wuqubʼ Kaqix was lost. It was just a healer-AjKun-who took away the resplendent jade necklaces, precious jewelry, and prized gems.

All that made Wuqubʼ Kaqix the False-face Lord that made him who he was as the proud and arrogant ruler he became here on the Face of the Earth was given to an AjKun; Jun Curandero.

body:
Those who brought this about are named here as Nawal Atiʼt, Nawal Mamaʼ for it is they who accomplished it all; the Ancient Old Woman, the Ancient Old Man. They are those who did it with their Nawal powers of transformation; their miraculous powers of transformation that gave the Grandmother, Grandfather their magical powers of transformation; Nawal Atiʼt, Nawal Mamaʼ for they are those known as Nawal Winaq.

The Boys, the Sons had already taken back ʼtheirʼ arm to then plant it back in its place; the place from where it had been torn our and taken.

Their work had come out well; Junajpu could to do all that he had done before. They did what they did to bring about the death of Wuqubʼ Kaqix whoʼs proud and arrogant ways were seen to be so very wicked and evil to them; the Boys.

And so it was that the two of them walked on down the road; it was just the word of the Heart of the Sky-utzij Ukʼux Kaj that was their doing.

It was they who listened and heard the word of Heart of the Sky-Ukʼuʼx Kaj that was the calling of the Two Sons; that was the doing of the Two Boys-Kaʼibʼ Kʼajolabʼ those spoken of as Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

Now we shall talk of another arrogant one; Sipakna is his name; this then is the ancient ancestral account that tells of his death and defeat by the Two Boys; the death and defeat of Sipakna by Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej; their names.

These are the deeds; these are doings of Sipakna, the First born Son-Nabʼe Kʼajol of Wuqubʼ Kaqix.

“I am Maker of Mountains! In Bʼanol Juyubʼ!” says Sipakna.

“I am he: Maker of Mountains!”

This is what Sipakna said so let us tell his story of his work there with the Four Hundred Boys; Omuchʼ Kʼajolabʼ those who are known as the Four Hundred Sons.

Sipakna: Nabʼe Kʼajol-First Born Son of Wuqubʼ Kaqix; Caiman Son, Volcano Boy, the Spiny One; and, the Four Hundred Boys, Omuchʼ Kʼajolabʼ

Here then we shall tell of the deeds, the doing of the First-born Son; Nabʼe Kʼajol of Wuqubʼ Kaqix.

“In Bʼanol Juyubʼ! I am the Maker of Mountains,” said Sipakna.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
And so it was that Sipakna was bathing there in the Water on the bank of the River-chuchiʼ Jaʼ-he was just swimming along the edge of the River water  when the Four Hundred Boys came along with a Great Big Log.

Those Four Hundred Boys, Omuchʼ Kʼajolabʼ went along dragging their Great Log, a Great Tree that they needed for the Pillar-Raqan Kikabʼal-for the Post of their Hut-kikabʼal.

There were four hundred of them out walking along side the riverbank where Sipakna was taking his bath just swimming about in the River; in the water there.

They cut down another great tree; this one was for the Crossbeam of their Hut-uwapalil kikabʼal, the Hut of the Four Hundred Boys, the Hut they were making; the Hut they were building there.

So, then, Caiman Boy, Sipakna went over to where the Four Hundred Boys were standing beside their great log and when he arrived there amongst them Sipakna asked, “What are you doing, you Boys, you Sons, Ix Kʼajolab?”

“Itʼs this tree, this log. We just canʼt lift it; we just canʼt pick it up. We canʼt raise it to then shoulder it; so we canʼt shoulder it to carry it over there where it must go to build our hut,” said the Four Hundred Boys-Omuchʼ Kʼajolabʼ.

“I can shoulder it! I can carry it on my own,” boasted Caiman Boy, Sipakna. “Where does it go? What do you need for it?”

“Itʼs just the Crossbeam for Our Hut-xa uwapalil qakabʼal,” they said.

“Very well!” he said. So then right away Sipakna dragged the Great Big Tree-Nim Cheʼ  they had cut to where he could  lift it up to then bear it on his shoulder to where they were building their hut: the hut of the Four Hundred Sons; kikabʼal Omuch Kʼajolabʼ; the Four Hundred Boys.

“Just stay here with us, Son; you can stay right here, you Boy-at Kʼajol-you Son,” they said.

“Do you have a Mother, a Father?” they asked.

“There are none to speak of,” he said.

“Let us then press you into our service so that you might carry another post for us tomorrow. We need help with another one of our logs that we must raise up for the Center Post of our hut-raqan qakabʼal.”

“Fine!” he said.

body:
This then was when they decided it was best they talk it over; so the Four Hundred Boys took council with one another to gather together their thoughts in order to figure out what to do next:

“He is only a Boy! What should we do about him? Shouldnʼt we just kill him? For what he does is just no good. He alone lifts up these Great Big Wooden Posts of ours all by himself and he is just a Boy!” And so then it was that they quickly came up with a plan.

“Letʼs just dig a Deep Hole to then tell him: ʼGo down into the Hole and bring up the Earth,ʼ” said the Four Hundred Sons.

“Then, when he is bent over at work down in the Hole, we will throw the Great Wooden Post down upon him so that he dies in an instant down there, in the Hole,” said the Four Hundred Sons, the Four Hundred Boys: Omuch Kʼajolabʼ.

So they dug it out; they just carved it out; they dug One Big Hole that descended far down below. For truly, the hole they dug was a deep hole that went down deep below; deep down in the ground did their deep, deep hole go.

Then they asked Sipakna to do as they planned; when they planned to ask him to do what they wanted him to do, “We want you to keep going, keep digging down; just keep digging out the hole deeper down below; just go down as far as you can go. We just canʼt reach down any deeper. We just canʼt dig down any further; we just canʼt go any farther down below; we canʼt dig down any farther down; down in the ground below; but perhaps you can keep going, going down; down in the hole,” he was told.

“Call up to us when the rest of the dirt is dug out. When you have gone as far as you can go down below,” they instructed.

“Very well!” is all Sipakna said as he descended down into the hole; the hole they dug down deep below. But before going any deeper down into the hole they had begun digging for him he decided to dig out another hole to the side so that he could continue on down with their work of digging a very deep hole; the hole for the center post of their hut; the hut that they had been making all on their own.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
The hole that Sipakna now dug was just a side hole; a side hole that was his escape, his salvation; for the hole Sipakna dug was a safety  hole to save him from being killed by them, the Four Hundred Boys-Omuchʼ Kʼajolabʼ who only wanted death for him, the Boy, the Son, Sipakna.

He knew he was to be killed. So he dug a side shaft off to one side in order to form a second hole to escape from those up above who wanted to kill him down deep below in their hole they dug for his burial.

“Well, how far along are you?” asked the Four Hundred Boys as they ʼthrew down-ʼ their words to him down deep in the hole.

“I am still digging fast, Iʼll call up to you when itʼs finished being dug-out,” said Sipakna.

But he was not digging a hole in which he was to be buried; he was digging out his safety hole to the side, his means of escape; the cavern he was working on was to be his salvation.

So this, then, was when Sipakna called up to the Boys. He was already safely tucked away in the side hole heʼd made when he called up to them to tell them all they needed to know:

“Come on down so you can take away the last of the earth from the hole; it is all dug out; itʼs all ready to go. Truly, I have dug a deep, deep hole that goes deep down below. Canʼt you hear me calling out to you? As for your calls, they only sound like echoes, as if you were ʼone or two levelsʼ away,” cried Sipakna when he called up from below.

Sipakna, he was just hidden away in his hole, his way of escape, when he called up from down below where he waited in the cavern he dug out to the side of the deep, deep hole that descended deep down below.

Meanwhile, the Four Hundred Boys dragged their Great Big Tree-Ki-Nimaʼ Cheʼ-into place above the hole that was the opening of the hole where the Boy was waiting; just waiting far down below.

They, the Four-Hundred Boys, prepared themselves just right so they could throw down their Great-Big-Tree; Ki-Nimaʼ-Cheʼ with all their might; they wanted to send that Great Big Tree all at once so that it went straight down to the bottom of the hole.

They listened but they heard nothing, not a word, silence was all that came up from down below.

body:
“Be still. Quiet, donʼt speak. Letʼs listen for his cries when cries out when post hits and he dies,” they said to one another in a hush, just whispering to each other in a silent, sort of secretive way.

This then was when they covered their faces and threw their great big post down deep to the bottom of their deep, deep hole…

It was then that he called out, letting out a cry. Just one call is all they heard when they let it go; that great big tree was sent flying down; down to the bottom of their deep, dugout hole.

“Okʼa! It Entered! It Entered! Perfecto! Eso! We did it! Didnʼt we do well? Is he not just dead? Is he not finished?” they cheered.

“What was he up to? What was he doing; doing all that he did?”

“Who sent him here amongst us anyway?”

“It was just a sign; a sign, him and his doing; his doing all that he did!”

“What he was doing was just no good? So be it!” they said then there, there above the hole.

“To begin with it, it didnʼt start out well; it all began when he came here to get in between us; us, the Four Hundred Boys!” they said, contented now with what they had done to him, Sipakna-Caiman Boy-the Spiny One-the Smoking One: Cipacatli.

“Letʼs make our strong three day maguey drink; our three-day fermentation; our three day sweet drink; our Three Day Maguey-Oxij Ki as it is called; so we can celebrate and make a toast on the third day.”

“When those three days pass, we will toast; we will drink to ʼour hut-qakabʼal. This is what we will do, we who are ʼWeʼ we who are ʼUsʼ the Four Hundred Boys; la Oj Omuchʼ chi Kʼajolabʼ.”

“So, then, tomorrow we shall look; and the day after tomorrow we shall look too; to see if the ants donʼt just come up and out of the Earth. When we know he is rotten; when we see that he is decomposed then our hearts will be contented and our souls consoled.”

“Then we shall drink our sweet-ki-poison, our bitter-ki-cure; our three day sweet drink will be ours to share to make a toast and cheer a cheer,” they said as they planned their celebration of their ritual killing of Sipakna and the finishing of their hut.

body:
Every single word was heard by Sipakna from where he was safely sequestered in the side hole he had dug to the side. He listened to all that was said by the Four Hundred Boys. Their talk resounded down deep below where he waited for the days to pass so the Ants could perform their role.

This then was when Sipakna heard them talking, which was when he heard all they said; so that when he heard them say: “the next day” which he heard quite well he knew it was time to put his plan into action.

It was their words that he heard on the second day; the day that the Ants flooded up from below as a sign that signaled and then began to show to the Four Hundred Boys that Sipakna was dead down deep below in the this sacrificial hole.

The Ants swarmed over the pillar; they swarmed over the post; like a whirlwind this moving mass of ants swarmed over the great center post that the Four-Hundred Boys had sent to the bottom of hole just a few days ago.

Some of the Ants carried off his hair, some of them carried off his nails; the hair, the nails were carried up and out from below to pour out from where Sipakna now decomposed deep down below in the hole.

When the Four-Hundred Boys saw this they were overjoyed:

“Isnʼt that trickster-kʼaxtoqʼ-finished off now? Just look at the Ants. Havenʼt they already gathered together? Havenʼt they already swarmed all about? The Ants carry his hair; they carry his nails. Didnʼt we do right by him who wished to outdo us by doing that which we could do by ourselves!” And so it was that they congratulated one another on their defeat of Sipakna.

But Sipakna was still very much alive. He cut the hair from his head, he chewed his fingernails with his teeth, and then he gave the hair, the nails to the Ants so they could do what they did best which was to carry off what was so useful to them.

Sipakna did this so that his death would be known to them who waited up above for his death to flower up from deep down below. He did what he did with the Ants so that his dying would be felt in the hearts of the Four Hundred Boys, the Four Hundred Sons: Omuch Kʼajolabʼ.

body:
And when all of them were certain Sipakna was dead they began toasting with their ʼsweet drink-kikiʼ of the three days known as the Third Day: Roxij.

Roxij: the Third Day Drink that was ready to be drunk.  This was when the Four-Hundred Boys drank to drink their ritual drink until they were ritually intoxicated; divinely inebriated; ceremonially drunk.

The Four Hundred Sons; Omuch Kʼajolabʼ drank and drank until they were drunker than drunk; and so it was that they were so drunk that they didnʼt feel a thing when their fool-proof plan was flipped on its head; their devious plot to kill Sipakna suddenly wasnʼt going to their way when their Hut came crashing down on their head killing them all; leaving them deader dead.

Not even ʼone or twoʼ of the Four-Hundred survived, they were all killed by Sipakna; the Son of Wuqubʼ Kaqix.

This then was the death of the Four Hundred Boys who are said to have entered the Sky as the Stars-Chʼumilal known as Motz but that could be just a play on words: xa saqbʼal tzij-a play on words; xa tzaqbʼal tzij-words thrown into play; xa tzʼaqbʼal tzij-formed words better known as a lie!

Southern Quadrant of the Night Sky

Once again our Ancient Ancestral Account presents a lethal reversal of destiny that here in the case of the Four Hundred Boys, Four Hundred Sons means being undermined from deep down below in the hole while being hit from high up above. This shamanic reflection of the above and below is mirrored in their initiation hut being brought down on their head; the head, the skull of the Boys; of the Sons by the trickster son-Sipakna of a trickster father-Wuqubʼ Kaqix to up-end the fortune and fate of the Boys;  to flip the Sonsʼ destiny upside-down.

And so it was that they came to their inevitable end. This then is the revelation and recitation of the defeat and destruction; death and disappearance of the Four Hundred Boys, Four Hundred Sons: Omuchʼ Kʼajolabʼ.

body:
Which as we will come to see will have cosmic repercussions so that they end up in the  Southern Quadrant of the Night Sky where their Pillar and Crossbeams form the False Cross and Southern Cross where the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds cover the Southern Horizon of the South Sea.

This is where the Pacific Coast of Guatemala was once covered in Caiman and Sea-Turtles where early humans lived off of the estuaries teaming with shellfish to create purple dye for sacred cloth. This is where quantities and kinds of shrimp and crab, langoustine and mollusks, minnows and fish; sharks and rays; animals and birds of every species fed and clothed the early hunting and gathering; tuber planting and gourd growing matriarchal societies and cultures of the Pacific Littoral.

These are where the Boys, the Sons of the Great Mother gave sacrifice in rites of initiation from which they emerged as warriors of their Mothers and Grandmothers; keepers and caretakers of their hunting and gathering grounds on the Costa Sur, Boca Costa, and way up into the Highlands. This is where Great Ceiba Tree stood as Pillars; as Posts of the Sky-Earth.

These Giant Ceiba Trees of the Pacific Coast were where Early Mesoamericans lived in homes made among the massive buttress of the Ceiba Trees under palm frond roofs in rooms formed and shaped beneath these Pillars of the Heavens.

This is the remembrance of those mythic times and epic ancestral spaces.  It would be from these pillars that great dug-out canoes would be hued and burned into shape to then be dragged out into the Pacific upon which the Maya would paddle their way North and South; East and West in great paddling expeditions we no longer remember.

Saqbʼal tzij; Tzʼaqbʼal tzij; Tzaqbʼal tzij

body:
We know the Four-Hundred Boys enter the Night Sky as the Great Many Stars of the Southern Sphere of the Celestial Firmament when Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej enter the Sky as the Sun and the Moon so something is going on here that requires initiation by ʼentering the wordʼ with the Chuch-Qajaw Ojer Tzij; Mother-Fathers of the Ancient Word but until the Kʼicheʼ Maya are able to re-form and re-shape to re-create these folks we must attempt to understand what is happening through our own education in the field.

A great, great word play; a playful as words can be in a ʼword playʼ known as saqbʼal tzij heard also as tzʼaqbʼal tzij formed words that are lies; and, tzaqbʼal tzij thrown down words such as those thrown down by the Four Hundred Boys who threw them down the hole to Sipakna.

This is a play on play on a play on words-saqbʼal tzij; words thrown down like the rubber ball was thrown down into play; and, bone dice were thrown down in games of destiny that showed onesʼ connection with the Heart of the Sky; Trickster and Gamer who played with Destiny at the Crossroads of Life.

This Mocker of Men is said to live in the bounce of the ball; in the fall of the dice; in the drop of  a hat; in the path one chose at the Crossroads.  It is we who are his slaves; just as it is he who begrudgingly gives the gift of fortune that he then quickly takes away. This Lord of Crossroads, this Lord of the Rubberball and White Dice was there with every play of Fortune and Fame thrown down to make his presence known through the luck and the loss of each and every toss of each and every game of the Noble Lords and their playing and their playing and their playing of games.

These two noble games are played by the Fathers who are the Lords of the Twins.  Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu who play ball and dice all day; the ʼwhite-saq bone-baq dice gameʼ known as ʼsaqbʼalʼ that is one of the many games the Maya once played.

body:
When they played games that were play by throwing dice down into play; when they threw the rubberball down in the rubberball game where the ball was ʼthrown down into playʼ as you will most certainly see. The metaphor always that of being  ʼthrow down into playʼ whatever it is that is being throw-down into play; the decapitated heads of sacrificial victims heads being thrown down the temple stairs to roll out on to the plaza is very, very much included.

This was when Noble Lords played all-day long when playing dice and playing ball was what Noble Lords did when they lived out lives marked by and identified with serious play; in lives marked by tempting fate in order to play with destiny; the destiny of oneʼs life that was played out each and every day on the Sacrifice Ballcourt of Ballcourt Sacrifice or Sacrificial Ballcourt of Ballcourt Play: Pusbʼal Chaaj the name of the Ballcourt of Xibʼalbʼa; Pusbʼal Chaaj a name that is a metaphor that is word play that defies translation in playful sorts of playful kinds of ways; ways we will come to play with as we enter the Ballcourt where the ball will be ʼthrown down into playʼ as it is said; as they will come to say.

So yes saying the Four Hundred Boys is a Tzʼaqbʼal Tzij that is a lie that is a Saqbʼal Tzij that is a Play on Words that is a Tzaqbʼal Tzij a throwing down of words which is to say words are thrown down into play in order to make a challenge to play ball with and through word-play is the sort of serious play our Maya Scribes are engaged with here as they challenge us to play with them in serious play-serio ludare with the Ancient Word in this Ancient Ancestral Account.

This word play that is going on here is indeed is a very serious sort of play that is going on here with mythic words and mythic metaphors are grounded in word play that is founded in our playing with the ideas Mesoamerican Stargazers who took their play with both words and stars seriously; and what a play on words and with words this is! Someday we will understand this play or we already but have not agreed on what we understand for now it is enough to see the Mid-most Place in the Sky of Pleiades as the Heart of Sky.

body:
But here is the thing:  the Heart of the Sky is embodied by the Four Hundred Boys who are known as ʼWe who are the Vassals of Ukʼuʼx Kaj Jun Raqan; We who are the Boys of Heart of the Skyʼ so that the Four Hundred Boys who are the ʼHandful of Seeds or Motzʼ transform into the story just told of the Southern  Cross being raised up in the Southern Quadrant where the Twins take on the form of the Two of the Brightest Stars in the Sky: Alpha and Beta Centaur who are joined by their companions the Four Hundred Boys of Centaur and then Great Milky white atole of the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds of the Southern Quadrant with its False Cross and Southern Cross that Sipakna helps the Boys raise up to build their Initiation Hut known as Kabʼal  which might be a God House of Initiation as in Kabʼawil….but this is hard to know for certain.

This is the story that is being told through mythic metaphor in which the ʼhandful of seeds plantedʼ thrown down within the ʼheart of the Sky-heart of the Earthʼ which is say the seeds planted in Pleiades straight-up overhead in the Heart of the Sky at Mid-night known a ʼtikil aqʼabʼ or ʼplanted in the darkʼ as the seeds that are ʼthrown-down in the soil dug down in the Heart of the Earth to be sown at Mid-day known as ʼtikil qʼijʼ or ʼplanted in the sunʼ to form and shape a metaphor of planting above in the Middle of the Nightʼs dark to mirror the sowing below in the Middle of the Day in the light of the Sun.

This image of sowing and seeding; shooting and sprouting; growing and transforming to come to flowering and fruiting completion is the story being told here. This is the story that once fed and sustained the Soul of the Maize People who lived by its mythic metaphors in seamless soul sustaining ways known as Nawal Ways of being and becoming one with the Sacred Sustenance that formed and shaped Oneʼs body and soul. This is where we are moving as we make our way down the road on this mythic journey of el Pueblo de Maize.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This is the Sacred Narrative of the Moonʼs embrace and Sunʼs warm that nourish and nurture the ʼsprouting seeds of maizeʼ who as the Four Hundred Boys die to be planted in the Sky where they will come back to Life on the Face of the Earth where they will enter the ʼstruggleʼ as ʼhard, hardʼ seeds sown in the womb of the Earth to eventually flower out in the bright, light of the Sun at the Heart of the Sky in the Middle of the Day to be pulled up into Middle of the Night by the Moonlight whoʼs power and strength remind us: ʼas above so belowʼ the Sun and Moon of Night and Day tell us so. This is the Nawal Powers of the Hero Twins who as the Sun and Moon will guide and protect their People who as a Pueblo will grow and transform to become the Kʼicheʼ Maya People that prosper today like never before. This is their Ancient Ancestral Account that tells their story of changing and transforming ways of life, death, and rebirth of the Maize People and their Sacred Sustenance sown as seed in la Milpa.

Let us tell next of the defeat of Sipakna by Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej. Here then begins the story of the death and disappearance of Sipakna by the Twins; the story that tells of the First Son of Wuqubʼ Kaqix.

This is the story that tells of when Sipakna was defeated and destroyed by the Two Boys, the Two Sons known and named  Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej; for truly, it was a blow to their hearts that the Four Hundred Boys-Omuchʼ Kʼajolabʼ were killed by Sipakna.

For verily is must be told that those Boys, the Sons of Heart of the Sky known as Omuch Kʼajolabʼ were finished off-one and all-by Sipakna.

So let us tell then the story of Sipakna and how he was brought to an end by the clever, cunning genius of the Hero Twins who were Nawal Winaq in every way. This is it then; here it is; listen close to see all that shall come to pass.

Just fish, just crab-xa kar, xa tap-were what Sipakna hunted when he went wandering alongside the river where he made his way in search of prey; prey he sought throughout the day.

body:
Just these alone were his sustenance; just fish, just crab-xa kar, xa tap; just these alone were his quest and quarry; just these alone were what he ate every day; day after day. At Night he raised up Mountains; Mountain that climbed-up into the Sky.

This then was when a ʼlook-a-like replicaʼ of a great big crab was formed and shaped by Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej, who then brought that ʼlook-a-likeʼ crab to life.

They used the long shiny red flowers of the forest bromeliads known as turkey foot-raqan ekʼ to shape its claws. The Boys gathered the big red flowery ones, ʼpa jaqʼ the ʼopen onesʼ that they found growing bright red there in the forest.

These they fashioned ʼjust soʼ to form the claws of the crab, while they put into place the open shoots of bamboo grass to imitate the forearms of their decorated decoy so that when they were finished it looked just like a crab.

They used a round, stone-shaped gourd to replicate the clattering body armor of the crabʼs empty shell and underside; which, once they completed their work even they were taken back, surprised by how alive their formation felt; by how real their creation looked.

So this then was when they went to place their imitation crab there below the Cliff-Pek, below the Great Mountain-Nimaʼ Juyubʼ there in the West, known as Meʼawan: Bent-down Maize Plant.

Meʼawan is the name given to this place known as Meʼoj Awan; Doubled-Over Cane of Maize; Bent-Down Maize; Broken-over Maize Cane; just like the arm of Junajpu when it was hung over the embers burning in the hearth of Chimalmat; embers meant to dry-out the arm of the Maize Deity: Jun AjPu.

Meʼoj Awan is the last stage of the Lifecycle of Maize before the harvest of Maize in la Milpa. Meʼawan or Meʼoj Awan is the name of Bent-Down Maize whose cane is bent over in order that the head-aj of maize can dry downward so the birds canʼt peck at its grain and the rain canʼt feed the growth of deadly black spores of mold that ruin mazorca of maize-jal and cause death amongst the Maize People.

body:
Meʼawan is known as the Place of Origin of Maize thus in is seen as the Primordial Mountain of Maize where maize is said to originate above and below the great ravines and canyons that are shaped by the streams and rivers that course their way down the down this mountain that appears out of the clouds.

Meʼawan is the Mountain of Maize where Teocinte-Ajii is still found growing up and down the valley floor cut, carved, and crafted by the water winding its way down the ʼFlower-Suchitlʼ river known as the Suchiate that forms the border between Chiapas and Huehuetenango to shape the boundary line of Mexico and Guatemala.

Meʼawan was the name of the mountain where Sipakna would be defeated by the Two Boys, Two Sons; e Kaʼibʼ Kʼajolabʼ, JunAjPu, Ixbʼalamkej were their names.

This then was when the Boys, the Sons, met up with Sipakna by the waterʼs edge. There, beside the river they came upon Sipakna searching for his sustenance.

“Where are you going, you my Son, you my Boy-At Kʼajol?” the Two asked.

“I am not going anywhere; Iʼm just out searching for what is mine; my food; my sustenance, you, my Boys-Ix Kʼajolabʼ; you, my Sons-Ix Kʼajolabʼ,” said Sipakna.

“So, what then is yours-awech; what then is your sustenance-awechaʼ?” asked the Two who spoke as One.

“Just fish, just crab-xa kar, xa tap are what are mine; just fish; just crab are my sustenance that satisfy my hunger. But there are none to be found here so I havenʼt had a thing to eat, not one bite, nothing at all. There are no fish here to be caught; there is no crab to be had here either; so Iʼve had nothing to eat; nothing to eat at all,” said Sipakna. “The day before last is when I left off eating and I donʼt know how much longer I can endure my hunger,” said Sipakna to Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

“Well there is one real Big Crab down there in the canyon below. Truly, it is one Great Big Crab-Nimaʼ Tap. If itʼs your day, if itʼs your luck you might just catch him.”

“He just snapped at us when we tried to catch him. If he hasnʼt moved on you can grab him; surely someone as big as you can nab him,” said Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
“Take pity on me Boys; come along with me to show me the way. Show me nothing more than where he stays, Ix Kʼajolabʼ, you oh Sons. Surely you know where he lays and his crab-like ways so what would it be for you to join up with me to walk down the road and find him. What do you say; will you not show me the way?” pleaded Sipakna.

“No thanks, we donʼt want to; you can arrive there by yourself. Itʼs not such a lost place; itʼs not so very hidden away. Just follow along the ʼpathʼ of the water and you will find him there where he lies alongside the river. You will come upon this One Big Crab right there below the Great Mountain. Just listen to him clattering about there at the bottom of the ravine. Just get yourself going; youʼll arrive there just fine!” said Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

“Please, I beg of you, just help me this once! What if I donʼt find him, my Boys? Surely you can accompany me to show me where to go to show me where he is. Besides, there are plenty of birds for you to take down by the side of the road over there. Plenty of birds are to found up in the trees for you to test your luck with you blowguns, and I know just where you can find them,” said Sipakna.

His genuine humility and brutal hunger convinced the Boys to lead the way. And so they took off down the road together talking, as they liked to do and did so well. Sipakna didnʼt need to say another word to convince them of walking along with him.

Each one shouldered a blowgun; ever at the ready; ready to blow down the birds they found along the way. This is when they said what they had been waiting to say:

“You had better catch that Great Big Grab because that is the only reason we are going back there with you. We arenʼt going to try again to catch him because he bites; he just strikes out to then snap at you in a most vicious sort of violent kind of  way,” said the Boys before they continued talking as they accompanied Sipakna One to the left; One to the right; Sipakna in the middle with a Boy on either side.

They went on and on about this most precious prey; this quality quarry that lay in wait for Caiman Boy who was happy to be on his way.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
They never let up about how enormous this One Big Crab really was to whet the appetite of Sipakna as they honed their story just in case his hunger needed a bit more sharpening. They talked and talked about the Tap-Crab and their many attempts to catch him; all of their counsel was to provide him with the advice that would lead to their victory and his defeat.

“First we entered face-down-jupulik but that just frightened him away. Then we entered face-up-pakʼalik and almost got him, so perhaps you might begin by entering face-up-pakʼalik,” encouraging Sipakna whose hunger had got the best of him.

“Very well!” said Sipakna.

And so it was that the Boys, the Sons accompanied Sipakna. They walked until they arrived there at the bottom of the canyon.

There, lying out to one side-tzalam was the Crab-ri Top with its shiny red back glowing like a red hot ember down there at the bottom of the canyon-xe siwan.

Tzalam means to lay down on oneʼs side which is the way the Boys came upon Wuqubʼ Kaqix with his broken jaw and loose teeth. Tzalam or ʼto lay to oneʼs sideʼ is also the way ʼvictims of sacrificeʼ were placed on the Sacrificial Stone Altar of Sacrifice so that the ʼWhite Flint-Knife of Sacrificeʼ could open the space between the ribs to then reach in to grasp the palpitating heart with Jaguar Paws-Jaguar Claws; Eagle Talons-Eagle Claws grip to then rip the pounding heart from the human chest.

Imagine the predatorial strength a sacrificial act like that takes. Yet, this is the image suggested here through the evocative mythopoetic genius that says so much with so few words that leaves one wondering if that which is said to be ʼtzalamʼ is that which shall be sacrificed? The answer is yes for anybody who ends up on their side in the Popol Wuj is going to be sacrificed on their side: tzalam.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This beguiling, bewitching Crab formed from the mythic imagination; shaped by this poetic incantation of this enchanting sort of glossy scarlet shimmering shine so that it appeared to be alive and pulsating with life; you could see it down there below all aglow; crimson red, its living warmth pumping in the sun; its appetizing appeal; the beguiling grip of its grasp; the bewitching way it held oneʼs attention fast; those who gazed upon its enchanting charm, its captivating pull could not free themselves from the strength of its clasp; the crush of its clutch.

This pulsating red Crab grabbed hold of the attention of Sipakna and held it tight while focusing his resolve in the most enchanting way.

Sipakna now found he was grasped by the beguiling grip whoʼs grasp would not leave him be; bewitched now Sipakna knew that only by devouring the Crab would he be set free; he wished only to engulf his favored form of sustenance in order to conclude this strange play of predator and prey.

“Utz bʼa la! Very well!” cried Sipakna, who was now overjoyed; thankful for having finally found what heʼd been looking for, for so many days, he just wanted that crab in his mouth to swallow it whole, right then and there. For truly Sipakna was finished off by his hunger; just humbled, just humiliated by his insatiable appetite for fish and crab; crab and fish.

He wanted to enter face-down-jupunik at first, so he tried just that. But the crab rose face-up-pakʼal, so Sipakna came right back out yet determined to go right back in now that he had a feel for this place and its tight, tight space.

“You couldnʼt get him?” they asked.

“Not yet. He just rose-up coming at me face-up-xa pakʼalik kaqanik. I just missed him, but I almost gotʼim; I nearly caught him. Perhaps it would be better if I entered face-up-kipakʼeʼik kinok ubʼik” he said, reconsidering his position and perhaps remembering what they told him in the first place.

So then he entered face-up, little by little he made his way to where the Crab lay perfectly still; now it was just the two of them there at the bottom of the great canyon wall...
