source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
They screech-ketzitzotik; they shriek-ketzʼitilajik; as they bat their wings and fly around in a great swarm in their Bat House: Sotzʼi Ja.

In that Sotzʼi Ja that is a House of Bats is where Bats alone flitter and flutter all about in that closed-up, closed-off House of Bats where Bats and Bats alone are shut-up inside that place where Bats, and only Bats, are shut-up tight to fly around and around all night.

There is no place for them go; no place for them to hang, no place for them to hide; there is no way for them to get outside and fly away because those Bats are trapped so there is no way for them to get out.

These are just the flittering and fluttering Bats of Bat House whose obsidian-blade fangs grow out of their obsidian-blade snouts. There is no way for those Bats to escape that Bat House that is a House of Bats-Sotzʼi Ja with no way for anyone to ever get out!

The fifth house then is Chayim Ja-Obsidian Blade House is its name.  There are just perfectly ordered and perfectly aligned Obsidian Blades there inside Obsidian Blade House where the Obsidian Blades all look the same. They just resound off of one another as their sound resonates off the walls where they grind and grate as they scratch and scrape across the floor of the Obsidian Blade House; Chayim Ja: House of Obsidian Blades.

Many were the tests, many were the trials of Xibʼalbʼa, but Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu never ever even entered inside there; they never entered within these houses of tests and trials that we entered only by their names being named.

It was then that Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu presented themselves there before Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame; this was when they came forth before the Lords in the calm, dim light of Dawn: apanoq saqnatanoj.

“Where are my cigars of rolled tobacco? Where are my torch-pine torches that were left with you in the House of Dark-Qʼeqʼuma Ja-Dark House?” they were asked then.

“We finished them off-xqakʼiso, at Ajaw you Oh Lord, you Oh Father, At Ajaw,” they answered.

“Utz bʼa la! Very well then!” said Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
“So today then, your days are finished; your destiny has come to its end; now you shall die; now you shall be forgotten; your ancestral line; your ancestral lineage shall be cut-off at the trunk,” said Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame.

“Wakamik bʼa la xkʼis iqʼij, kixkamik, kixsachik, xkixqaqʼupix!”

“Here we shall end your days; here your existence shall be finished: for you will be sacrificed; your face lost, your countenance gone, vanished once and for all,” said Ajaw Jun Kame, Ajaw Wuqubʼ Kame-Lord One Death, Lord Seven Death.

Then they were sacrificed; then they were buried there in the place known as Sacrificial Ballcourt of Ballcourt Sacrifice-Pusbʼal Chaaj ubʼi xemuq wi.

Pusbʼal Chaaj is the name of the Sacrificial Ballcourt of Sacrifice is where they were buried; for it was they, Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu who were buried there beside Pusbʼal Chaaj.

They decapitated Jun Junajpu so that only his body-nimal; the body of Jun Junajpu, the Elder Brother-nimal was buried with the body of his Younger Brother which meant that just the body-nimal of the Older Brother-unimal-was buried with his Younger Brother-uchaqʼ.

They were buried beside Pusbʼal Chaaj there in Xibʼalbʼa.

“Go place his skull in the fork of the tree planted there standing beside the road,” said Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame: “Chiyaʼ ujolom xol cheʼ ri tikil pa bʼeʼ.”

When they went to leave the skull in the fork of the tree was when the tree began fruiting forth with heads of fruit; never had the tree fruited before the skull of Jun Junajpu had been placed in the fork of the treeʼs branches. And this is why we call this calabash gourd-tzima today the skull of Jun Junajpu as it is said; spoken of as ujolom Jun Junajpu; the skull-head-jolom of Jun Junajpu.

When they placed the skull in the fork of the tree, the tree fruited forth fully filling the limbs with perfectly round skull-like gourds-tzima that were a marvel to look upon.

Let us provide you with another translation of this bewildering mythopoetic passage of Maya-Mesoamerican Mythos in order that you might enjoy its wonder and awe in a slightly different way.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This is when they went over to place the skull of Jun Junajpu in fork of the tree; they placed it then there in its limbs; that is when the tree sprouted forth with fruit; fruit sprang forth from this tree; this tree that had never given fruit before.

This tree, with its branches and limbs, now sprouted forth with perfectly round gourds that looked like skulls; and it was these gourd-skulls or tzima-jolom that now completely covered the treeʼs limbs and branches; branches and limbs of a tree that had never given fruit before.

This Calabash Tree had never given fruit until the head-ujolom-the skull of Jun Junajpu was placed in the fork of the branches of this barren tree. The tree that is known as the Tzima, the Calabash, el Moro, el Guacal, the Gourd Tree; the gourd known of as the skull-jolom-head of Jun Junajpu; the One Ancient Blowgun Hunter; spoken of in Maya Kʼicheʼ as ujolom Jun Junajpu.

Then it was they, Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame who were left astonished; for it was they who were left astounded by what they saw sprouting forth from its branches; branches filled with gourds that left them bewildered.

They were just astounded by this gourd treeʼs skull-shaped fruit, for perfectly round was its appearance, there was no way of seeing which was the original skull of Jun Junajpu and which were all the other skull-like gourd-headed fruit that grew upon the limbs and branches of this most astounding; most astonishing tree whose fruit looked exactly the same as Jun Junajpuʼs skull that looked exactly like the tzima; like the gourds that now covered the tree.

All of Xibʼalbʼa saw its perfection when they came to look upon and marvel at the perfectly round shape of its fruit that now hung as gourd-skulls from its limbs; the branches of this most mysterious tree.

body:
And so they came to behold its magical essence for truly unbelievable was the identical shape of the perfectly round fruit of this enchanting tree; this tree that now revealed itself before those of Xibʼalbʼa; those who came to marvel at this tree and its transforming nature-kʼojeʼik that now appeared before them there-xux chi kikʼux-as its nawal essence sprouted forth before their hearts and souls as the wonder that it was.

The magical way its round skull-like gourds sprouted forth from its trunk and limbs caused both astonishment and awe in those who now gazed upon the perfect roundness of the great quantity of fruit that sprouted out of this tree now filled with gourds-tzel; this Gourd Tree; this Tzima as it is spoken of by all today.

The Tzima that now sprang forth with perfectly round fruit; the exact same size; the exact same shape of the head of Jun Junajpu; its fruit, its face mirrored reflections of one another; just perfect replacements of the twin skull-gourd; face-fruit-uwach-tzel of the jolom-calabash of Jun Junajpu that emerged from the branches when the head of Jun Junajpu was planted in the fork of the barren tree that stood beside the ballcourt; the Ballcourt of Xibʼalbʼa;  their Sacrificial Ballcourt of Ballcourt Sacrifice known as Pusbʼal Chaaj.

Truly marvelous was its nature; its wondrous nature; the magical, miraculous nature of this tree filled with gourds that sprouted forth before them there. Magnificent then was its nature because of what it had created when the skull-jolom-head of Jun Junajpu was placed in its branches. It was just its bringing forth of skull-like fruit that led those of Xibʼalbʼa to talk amongst one another about this astonishing Calabash Tree-Tzima saying:

body:
“It wouldnʼt be good if one was to pick its fruit. And it also would not be so good if one were to enter there; there beneath its fruiting limbs; the fruiting limbs and branches of this Calabash tree with all its skull-like gourds; its perfectly moon-shaped like fruit,” they said; holding themselves back from doing so, keeping themselves from going too close to where the tree grew; and, it grew where it stood; and, where its stood was where it was planted to stand-up straight there ʼbesideʼ the Ballcourt of Sacrifice: Pusbʼal Chaaj.

By now it was impossible to tell which skull-head-gourd was the original skull of Jun Junajpu for its fruit were just one and the same as all the other round gourds that sprouted forth from the limbs, from the branches, from the arms of this most magical tree spoken of as a ʼtzima or guacalʼ as it is known today.

All those of Xibʼalbʼa talked about its marvelous nature and how fruitful that marvelous nature was. That is how a Young Maiden-Jun Qʼapoj came to hear of it; when she heard her Father speak of it when he told of its wondrous ways.

Now we will tell of her arrival there to where the tree grew beside the ballcourt along the road; we will tell of the arrival of IxKikʼ there where the skull of Jun Junajpu was placed in the branches of the Tzima; in the limbs of the Calabash Gourd Tree.

IxKikʼ

Transforming Moon Maiden

One Maiden-Jun Qʼapoj

Moon Maiden-Blood Woman

Changing Moon Maiden

Transforming Month Maiden-Transforming Moon Maiden

The Story of the One Maiden

She of the Rubberball-She of the Changing Moon

She of Flowing Blood-She of Flowing Sap

She of Flowing Incense-She of Flowing Rubber

One Maiden-Jun Qʼapoj-IxKikʼ-She of the Blood Moon

Kuchumakikʼ-Blood Gatherer; Father of One Maiden-Jun Qʼapoj

Jun Qʼapoj-One Maiden IxKikʼ-Daughter of Blood Gatherer

Kuchumaʼ Kikʼ-Gatherer of Blood-Rubber-Sap

body:
The naming of the Father of the One Maiden-Jun Qʼapoj is named as One Lord-One Noble-Jun Ajaw. Jun Ajaw: One Lord; One Noble Lord is a name that tells us he is a Lord of Xibʼalbʼa; Lord of Darkness; Lord of the Night; Lord of Disease. The Father of IxKikʼ is named Kuchumakikʼ known as Blood Gatherer or Gatherer of Blood, Gatherer of Rubber he is the Lord-Qajaw-Father of the One Maiden-Jun Qʼapoj: IxKikʼ.

This then is the announcement that announces the noble entrance of IxKikʼ the Moon Maiden who will become the Moon Mother who is the Moon Goddess known as Saq Ixik the White Woman; Sacred Woman in the Codex Dresden.

And for those Nawal Descendants with the eyes to see; the ears to hear; the touch to feel; the taste to savor; the scent to smell; the intuition to perceive; and, the genius to know  this introduction of the IxKikʼ announces the novel forming and shaping of this new lineage of the Maize People.

These Peopleʼs lineage is founded in the Boys of IxKikʼ who are the Sons of IxKikʼ known as uKʼajolabʼ IxKikʼ: JunAjPu, IxBʼalamKiej. These are those who are brought into the Sky-Earth; Lake-Sea through the twin nature of their Nawal lineage; a Nawal lineage formed and shaped by their complementary and cooperative sense of duality that balances and harmonizes itself through the transformations of Life and Death; the movement of Night and Day; the ʼwalking and knowingʼ of the Sun and Moon.

This is harmonizing of the Divine Ancestors of Ixim Winaq comes about through the Hero Twins being ʼtwinned from withinʼ which is to say they are the Grandsons of their Lowland Grandfather of the Rubber Groves of the Cave World that is the Underworld of Xibʼalbʼa. The Sons of IxKikʼ are the Twin Grandsons of their Lowland Grandfather: Kuchumakikʼ or Gatherer of Blood, Gatherer of Rubber who is the Father-Ajaw of IxKikʼ or She of the Blood; She of the Rubber; She of the Moon; the Moon that changes and transforms to grow full to then pull on the sap that runs like blood from the cuts that are scored in the Rubber Trees.

One Maiden; Jun Qʼapoj

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
IxKikʼ, this One Maiden, will transform the world forever more as she stands up to her oppressors, to then defeat them through her ingenuity before climbing up and out of Xibʼalbʼa.

Without many words we are guided by the Owls up and out of the initiatory darkness of the underworld. This One Maiden; this Jun Qʼapoj named  IxKikʼ climbs up through the underworld to rise out of the archetypal hole of ʼemergenceʼ to sprout forth like a maize plant on the Face of the Earth.

Could this have been some sort of rite of initiation of Older Maidens on the path of becoming Young Women? Did Young Women enter a dark, cool place to gather their blood to be burnt over a fire with other flowers, herbs, tree sap, and incense?

Who knows but this text suggest such a possibility through this metaphor of IxKikʼ creating a replica of her own heart to outsmart the Lords of Death. By escaping death this One Maiden of One Father-One Lord-Jun Ajaw ascends into a New Life in a New World with New Obstacles and New Ordeals.

Certainly, this story tells of a rite of initiation that speaks to us through the symbolic language of mythic metaphor as this mythic Moon Maiden and Blood Gatherer have taken up the path of emergence to become the mythic Moon Mother and Goddess of Maize who will bring forth a Magical Harvest, as you will soon come to see, hear, and experience in this imaginal realm of myth-making created through these mythic words and their mythic metaphors.

This is to say the One Maiden of Maize will sprout out of the underworld darkness of death to begin her new life there on the Face of the Earth at first as a faint memory of the dim light that illuminates the Sky-Earth at the dawn of a new day, new life known as ʼsaqnatanojʼ to then enter the bright light in a completely new life of renewal and regeneration; a life filled with hope and possibility to live the out the ʼbright life-saq kʼaslem, winaqirem-peoplingʼ on the Face of the Earth.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This ʼsaq kʼaslem, winaqiremʼ or ʼbright life of creation and the peoplingʼ of the Face of the Earth is the direction the One Maiden-Jun Qʼapoj has taken. It is vitally important the reader understands this as IxKikʼ emerges from Xibʼalbʼa stronger than ever before for she has ʼentered the wordʼ by finding her own voice and creative expression as a maker of incense known as AjQʼol or a Person of Tree Resin which is and was a very important traditional art of ʼincense-makingʼ in the Maya-Mesoamerican world.

The text says, ʼXukiyaʼ aqʼanoq chi jul chuwi ulew-she grew up and out through the hole to climb up and out onto the earthʼ as it is said-chuchʼaxik. The text will continue to take on this metaphor of plant growth that speaks of the growth of the Moon Maiden become Moon Mother in this story of the Maize People that says:  as IxKikʼ grows so grow her Boys who will sprout forth on the Mountainside as two heads of maize sprouting forth from the ʼcane-bodyʼ of their Mother: IxKikʼ

So now IxKikʼ is no longer in the earth for she is above the earth just like the moon when rising full in the East when she comes up, out, above, and onto the Earth at the ʼComing Out Place of the Sunʼ known as the Relebʼal Qʼij.

The Full Moon rises full like IxKikʼ rises up and out of the hole at the Coming Out Place of the Sun with her full body completely filled out, completely round with two magical boys that will live their lives as one in and out of the womb.

The Moon acts like the Sun by rising as the Full Moon exactly where the Sun rises ʼfullʼ at his Coming Out Place of the Sun in the East on the Eastern Horizon where the hole of emergence opens for the Sun and Moon to rise up and out of the watery underworld there in the Caribbean Sea and Gulf of Mexico.

So here oneʼs imagination must fill out the suggestions and intimations of female initiation. Feminine genius comes to life here as this Young Woman overcomes the life and death ordeal she must face because of her own curiosity to know the unknown in the ʼface of the fruitʼ that hangs from the tree.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
IxKikʼ stands up for herself when challenged by her father and his generation of rulers. It is only her inventive and ingenious imagination that enables her to use the creative powers of making, modeling, and molding a solution for the life and death predicament she must overcome.

And so it comes to be that IxKikʼ overcomes death as she outwits the rigid authority embodied in the ʼblindʼ authoritarian ways of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa. She first deceives to then defeat these insensitive and closed minded Lords of Noble Rule and Authority and she accomplishes this through the use of her powerful intuitive capacities of a Nawal Ancestors; magical capacities of transformation that are alive and well in the ingenious powers flowing through her innovative fingers and imaginative hands.

This is the genius of Young Women and their creative powers that this ancient account speaks of in beautiful metaphorical speech and acts of creativity in search of transforming the world of the Sky-Earth. Truly, IxKikʼ is a trickster heroine herself and not ʼjustʼ the mother of trickster heroes.

IxKikʼs genius, her transformative magic comes from her nawal powers that enable her to imagine ingenious solutions to her apparently disastrous and deadly dilemma. By doing so she originates the ceremonial use of incense created from nodules of tree sap. After all, her name is IxKikʼ which means She of Blood, She of Sap, She of the Red Tree, She of Rubber, She of the Ballcourt-Sacrifice, She of the Moon, She of the Month, She of Menstruation.

Is it not the ancestral office of IxKikʼ the gathering of menstrual blood that is suggested in her gathering of the coagulated blood that forms her replica heart of sacrifice? Is not the first menstrual blood of a young woman the occasion to reflect upon a womanʼs change of heart in a womanʼs life that is indelibly ʼmarkedʼ by the first blood of menstruation?  This text does not speak of this in direct ways but it certainly suggests that IxKikʼ must gather her blood in order to mold and model a replacement heart she can use to defeat those of her fatherʼs generation; and, she succeeds at her task splendidly.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
IxKikʼ is a Blood Gatherer by tradition for she is a Gatherer of Blood; it is her cargo, her burden, her office this gathering of blood, sap, rubber and dye for she is a gatherer by name and lineage. IxKikʼ knows nothing of the ways of maize as the lineage of Jun Junajpu does. This is because IxKikʼ comes from the lineage of  archetypal Hunter-Gatherer of the Age or Sun before the Maize People which some say is the Age of the Gourd Head People: Tzuy-Wa Winaq.

One might say that as a Moon Maiden, Moon Mother IxKikʼ is a primordial being of the night and its darkness the time of hunters; meanwhile, the day and its sun light is the time of the gatherers, IxKikʼ has both of these elemental forces of nature pumping through her heart causing her blood to pulse within lunar tides as a being who is of the Moon and Night.

She emerges out of the Underworld carrying within her womb the Sun and Moon of the Age-Sun-Era-Epoca of the Maize People and their Night and Day; Light and Darkness. It is her power as the Ancestral Moon  that ʼpullsʼ sap-blood from those beings that bleed, maidens very much included.

But it will take maize beings who see themselves as the direct descendants of IxKikʼ and Jun Junajpu to continue her ancestral work of ʼgathering and collectingʼ the thick aromatic resins that flow so slow from scoured pine and copal trees as well as the thick latex tapped from the rubber tree. Was this work of collecting the gourds of the scoured and tapped trees the work of maidens in the past?

IxKikʼ embodies the power of transformation as she incarnates the continual movement and act of becoming other than that which one just was and is because IxKikʼ embodies the ways of the Moon and her constantly changing and transforming ways.

For IxKikʼ is just like the Moon for whom she is named, for she is the Female Lord or Ixoq Ajaw or Chuch-Qajaw known as the Mother-Father of all the dripping drops of sap, blood, resin, water, and rubber that transform the world once they are gathered together as the essence of Heart of the Earth; Heart of the Sky.

body:
It is this essence that is being gathered up to then be used as powerful forces of nature that in turn transform the Sky-Earth by calling upon Jun Raqan Kaqulja; Chʼipi Kaqulja; Raxa Kaqulja to form the clouds and shape the winds to bring the fog, mist, drizzle, and rain that is called upon through the use of the many forms of incense and rubber that Mesoamericans used to communicate with their Kabʼawil who gathered up their strength to deliver abundance and prosperity to their people who lived there on the Face of the Earth.

Oh, before we move up onto the Face of the Earth, it might be helpful to know that rubber was burnt in rituals of sacrifice to create black clouds of smoke to conjure up the dark black clouds that brought down the sustaining rains of the Maize People and their continual effort to bring forth their sacred sustenance: Maize.

Here then begins the Story of the One Maiden-Jun Qʼapoj

Here then is the story of One Maiden-Jun Qʼapoj, the Daughter of the One Lord-Jun Ajaw, his name is Blood Gatherer; Kuchumakikʼ ubʼi; Blood Gatherer is  his name: Kuchuma-Gatherer, Kikʼ-Blood, Rubber, Sap.

This was when Jun Qʼapoj, the One Maiden heard of it, the Daughter of one of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa, Blood Gatherer-Kuchumakikʼ is the name of this Lord of Xibʼalbʼa, Father of IxKikʼ the One Maiden-Jun Qʼapoj and it was her Father that told her about the perfectly round fruit of the tree that stood beside the ballcourt.

When this One Maiden-Jun Qʼapoj heard what was said about the fruit of the tree she became curious and thus excited by something that could be as marvelous as this enchanted tree could be; and so she began to think upon the marvelous way those of Xibʼalbʼa spoke about it.

This then was when she contemplated going to see this tree; an astounding tree, an astonishing tree covered in gourds; gourds as round as round could be.

body:
When its story-the story of this gourd tree-was told to this One Maiden-Jun Qʼapoj by her very own Father she was left amazed; just as she was left astonished by all that he had to say about this tree full of skull-like gourds; a tree that grew full with these skull-like fruit that were gourds that looked like skulls; a tree whose branches had sprung to life the moment the skull-head-jolom had been planted in the fork of the tree for all to see.

“Wouldnʼt it be good to go see this tree that everyone tells of with their story-telling speech; wouldnʼt it be good to go know what kind of fruit it really is? Is its fruit as sweet as they say it is; as sweet as I have heard it to be?” IxKikʼ said, curious to visit the tree after all she had heard people say as they spoke of this enchanted gourd-headed skull tree of Jun Junajpu.

So then she went off by herself; and, before long she arrived there beneath where the tree was planted; there beneath where the tree grew; there where the tree stood where it was planted to grow where it stood beside Pusbʼal Chaaj; beside the Place of Ballcourt Sacrifice is where it stood planted to grow forth just as wondrous as one could imagine an enchanted tree to be; a tree covered with perfectly round gourds; a tree studded with perfectly spherical gourd-like skulls for all to come and see.

“Jiyaʼ! Indeed! What sort of fruit is this that sprouts forth from the limbs of this tree?”

“Where does fruit such as this come; where does fruit such as this grow; fruit that sprouts forth from the arms of this tree that stands here planted?”

“Could it be that its fruit is so very sweet?” asked the Maiden; ri Qʼapoj.

“Would I die? Would I be lost; would I disappear? Would I end up ʼdead and goneʼ if I were to ʼpickʼ just one of its fruit?”

“Ma kikam taj, ma kisach taj, la kʼi ta xchinchʼup junoq?”  Xchaʼ kʼu ri Qʼapoj.

“Would I be a ʼgonerʼ if I took just one of them? Could it be? Would I really be ʼdone-forʼ if I were to ʼcutʼ just one of them?” asked the One Maiden-Jun Qʼapoja.

This was when it spoke up, the bone-ri bʼaq that was stuck there in the fork of the tree; this was when the bone spoke:

body:
“What do you want with just a bone; what do you want with just a round thing-kʼolokʼoxinaq-that sprouts forth from the branches of a tree-chu qʼabʼ taq cheʼ?” Asked the skull-jolom-head of Jun Junajpu when it spoke to the One Maiden-Jun Qʼapoj who stood there beneath its branches; there below its arms; beneath its arms-chu qʼabʼ, that is to say ʼbeneath the strength-chuqʼabʼ of the Calabash Tree: IxKikʼ is her name; the name of Jun Qʼapoj; One Maiden.

“Ma karayij? Do you really want it?” “Do you long for it?” “Is this then ʼnotʼ what you desire?” asked the skull speaking from the limb of the tree.

“Kanurayij! I do want it!” “Certainly I long for it!” “I do desire it; I do!” said the One Maiden when she spoke to the skull in the fork of the tree, the ʼround bone-like thing-kʼolokʼoxinaqʼ the sprout out from its limbs; that shot forth from its branches; that sprang from its arms.

“Utz bʼa la! So then, just extend your right hand so that I might see it,” said the Bone-Bʼaq; said the Skull-Jolom.

“We! Yes! Yes, Indeed!” said then the maiden as she extended her right hand up and out towards the face of the bone-xulikibʼa aqʼanoq uwikiqabʼ chuwach bʼaq.

So then it was when a shot-jun pitz-was made; a shot of spittle; a shot of saliva came shooting forth from the bone-uchubʼ bʼaq to land smack in the middle of the maidenʼs hand; in the palm of her hand; the palm of the maidenʼs right hand-uwikiqabʼ chuwach baqʼ.

Kʼate kʼut chi pitz kabʼan uchubʼ baq; ta xpetik taqal kʼut puqabʼ qʼapoj.

Then, when she looked at the palm of her hand, looking so very close, she saw that there was nothing left of the boneʼs saliva. It was then that the bone, the skull spoke to her beneath the tree.

“Just a sign-xa retal I have given you with my spittle-nuchubʼ, my saliva-nukʼaxaj. My head, my skull-nujolom is no longer useful, itʼs just bone; no longer is it covered with flesh,” said Jun Junajpu before he continued.

body:
“It is just like the head of a Great Lord-Nim Ajaw: only the flesh-uchʼaqʼ alone gives them their fine appearance. Then when they die, the people are frightened by their bones-their skeletons-their skulls,” said the ʼround-bone-like thingʼ that spoke to the One Maiden who listened intently to the Old Bone who spoke to IxKikʼ from the limb of the tree by saying:

“Similar to this and just like that are the descendants; the descendants of the Nim Ajaw are a Noble Lordʼs children; they are just like his saliva, his spittle; a Noble Lordʼs children embody as they ensoul the essence of the Noble Lord no matter if they are the sons of a ʼWise One-Naʼol-Sage or the sons of a Speaker-AjUchan-an Orator. They never disappear even after they are gone they will always be fulfilled; for they will never be forgotten even when their days are complete,” said Jun Junajpu.

“They will never be cut-off from the trunk of their lineage, nor will the memory of the Noble Lords be lost, nor shall be lost the Man of Knowledge-Achij Naʼol nor shall be lost the Man of Wisdom, or the Speaker-AjUchan-the Orator, the Master of the Ancient Word: AjUchan. Their children shall remain; their daughters, their sons shall remain as their replacements-kʼexel and so they will be remembered in the features of their descendants; their face with its mouth, its nose, and its eyes. Ta chuxoq! May it be so! May it come to pass!” said the Skull-Head speaking as the wise orator that he was.

“Ta chuxoq! So be it! This is just what I have done with you. That is why you must climb up onto the Face of the Earth. Mawi kakamik, katok pa tzij. You will not die, for you shall enter the word; you will not die, for you will enter the ancestral way of the ancestral word. You will not die for you will enter the ancestral tradition; you will not die, for you will enter the traditional way of the traditional life known to all as those who ʼenter the word-katok pa tzijʼ: Mawi kakamik: katok pa tzij! You will not die: enter then the word; enter the way; enter the truth; enter the tradition found in the Ancient Word.”

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
“Ta chuxoq! So be it! May it be so!” said the skull-head-xchaʼ ujolom of Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu the First Fathers of the Boys, the Sons: Kikʼajolabʼ Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej this is the story of their generation; their being engendered; their being begot; their conception; their creation.

It was just their genius-kinaʼoj that did it; it was just the word-utzij of Jun Raqan, Chʼipi Kaqulja, Raxa Kaqulja; the Heart of the Sky, Ukʼuʼx Kaj that brought it forth in and upon the Sky-Earth; Kaj-Ulew; the Mountain-Plain; Juyub-Taqʼaj; the Face of the Earth-Uwach Ulew.

Straight away her boys-ral, her sons-ukʼajol, her sprouts-ral began to grow as they sprouted forth-xwinaqir ral-as her boys, as her sprouts, as her sons that grew within her womb from the spittle-shot of pitz that landed in the palm of her right hand; the pitz from the chubʼ that was the kʼaxaj that caused the sprouting forth-kiwinaqirik of her two sons; the creation-kiwinaqirik of  her two boys: Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

So then the Maiden arrived home and after her completing six months, she was ʼknown-nawachil-divinedʼ by her Father; for truly this One Maiden was found out by her Father Blood-Gatherer who was the One known as Kuchumakikʼ-Gatherer of Blood, the name of her Father-Uqajaw.

It was only then that her Father remembered his Daughter when he saw that she was with child. This is to say: he remembered telling his Daughter about the marvelous tree that bore magical fruit on its bountiful boughs; abundant branches.

He remembered the prohibition regarding the picking of that round fruit and the way the Lords One Death; Seven Death forbid all those of Xibʼalbʼa from entering there beneath this enchanted treeʼs alluring limbs and beguiling branches covered with gourds filled with infinite encanto and endless enchantment.

This was when the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa gathered together their thoughts-kinaʼoj with Blood Gatherer-Kuchumakikʼ who then came together with Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame to say what they had to say in order to do what they had to do.

It was he, Blood Gatherer-Kuchumakikʼ, who now spoke first to One Death-Jun Kame while he addressed the assembly of Lords who gathered together in Council:

body:
“You, Oh Lords, Ix Ajawab, my daughter is with child. It is just her knee scraping-ujoxbʼal-just her lust that makes it so,” said Blood Gatherer-Kuchuma Kikʼ when he presented himself before the AjAwabʼ Xibʼalbʼa, the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa; Lords of Disease who were the Chief Judges, the Magistrates who were the Makers of Justice; it was they who were known to be the final measure of the word-qʼatabʼal tzij-those who weighed of the word of all the people of all the land.

“Utz bʼa la, Very well then, interrogate her, just chisel it out of her-chakʼoto uchiʼ-just carved it out of her mouth, if she doesnʼt confess with whom she was with then just sacrifice her; just take her to be sacrificed far from here,” said Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame when they spoke.

“Utz bʼa la, very well my Esteemed Lords; Alaq AjAwabʼ,” said Kuchuma Kikʼ when he took leave of the Noble Lords of Xibʼalbʼa those who weighed the word; they who were the final rule; final measure of the ancient way, ancient word. For there was no greater authority; nor was there a higher judge than that of the Lords Jun Kame; Wuqubʼ Kame with whom ended the supreme rulership of the Noble Lordsʼ noble judgment of the Lordsʼ noble word.

So then he, Kuchuma Kikʼ went there where she, IxKikʼ was waiting to be questioned as the Daughter of the Lord-Rumeʼal Ajawabʼ just as the Lords told him to do; and so the Lord Blood Gatherer; Ajaw Kuchuma Kikʼ did what he was told to do by asking what he was told to ask: “Who then is the father of the child that you carry in your womb, you, my daughter?” he asked.

“Child? What child? There is no child that you speak of, you my Father; you my Lord. There is no man whose face I know; for I know not the ʼface-uwachʼ of a manʼs ʼfruit-uwach,” she said when she answered her father, Kuchuma Kikʼ known as Blood Gatherer. “Maja bʼi wal, lal nuqajaw; maja bʼi achij, wetaʼm uwach,” xchaʼ kʼut.

“Fine then, it is true that you really are one for skinning knees, you knee-skinner, you; you, scrapper of knees!” said Kuchumakikʼ.

“Utz bʼa la! Utz bʼa la, qitzij wi chi at joxol cheʼk. Fine then, itʼs true-qitzij-you really are one for skinning knees-at joxol cheʼk!” said Blood Gatherer-Kuchumakikʼ.

body:
“Just go sacrifice her, you Messenger-Warriors of the Noble Reed Mat of the Council House-Ix AjPop Achij. Bring her heart back in your sacrificial gourd bowl-tzel-so the Lords may take it up in their hands to ʼroll it over; turn it aboutʼ so that it may be examined this very day,” he told the Owls-ri Tukur.

“Chipusu Ix AjPop Achij. Chikʼamaʼ uloq ri ukʼux chi upam tzel. Chikikʼololej Ajawabʼ wakamik,” xeʼuchax kʼut ri Tukur.

There were four of them when they flew off.  They gathered-up the gourd bowl of sacrifice-kitikʼem ri tzel ta xebʼek in their hands when they flew-up and away on their sacrificial burden of ritual sacrifice given to them to complete by the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

They cradled the maiden in their arms-kichʼelem ri qʼapoj, just as they bore their White Flint Blade of Sacrifice-Saqi Tokʼ Pusbʼal Re-known as their Sharp-edged White Flint Knife of Sacrifice.

This is when IxKikʼ spoke to the Owls with whom she was raised as a child of Xibʼalbʼa.

“You canʼt make good on those that are your orders to sacrifice me, you oh Messengers-Ix Samajel-you cannot bring to completion those instructions to kill me because there is no me ʼskinning my kneesʼ; mawi nujoxbʼal. What is mine; that which is within me; does not come from lustful acts-joxbʼal of longing and desire. Not me, itʼs just not my way, not ever, I am too clever for something as careless as ʼscrapping and skinning oneʼs knees,” she said finally, taking a chance to speak her truth.

“That which grows within me is just a making and manifestation of itself, it is just my going to marvel-numayjaj at the skull-head-jolom of Jun Junajpu; there on the skull-head-gourd tree known as the Tzima; the Calabash tree that stands beside Ballcourt of Xibʼalbʼa-Pusbʼal Chaaj-Sacrificial Ballcourt of Ballcourt Sacrifice.”

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
“Donʼt do it! Kʼekʼe ta kʼut! Donʼt you do it! Detain yourselves; restrain yourselves! Donʼt sacrifice me, you, oh, Envoy Owls-Ix Tukur-you, Emissary Owls;  fine companions of mine that you are; You, oh, Workers-Ix Samajel-You, oh, Messengers of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa,” said the Maiden when she spoke in her own defense; knowing what was the ʼrightʼ way to be taken up; and, what was wrong way to be  ʼleftʼ behind.

“What then should we place there as a replica, a replacement of your heart-ukʼexel riʼ kʼux-a replacement, replica of your heart?”

“Did your Father not tell us: ʼBring back her heart; that the Lords might turn it over in their hands making sure that it does not fall so that they might come to see what it is made of; so that they might roll it about in their hands so that can make certain it is formed like all the others. Quickly then, bring it back in the gourd bowl of sacrifice-pa tzel; just collect her heart, just gather it up by gathering it together at the bottom of your gourd bowl of sacrifice,ʼ” said the Owls speaking for their Lords.

These were the words; this was the message given to the Owls Messengers of Jun Kame; Wuqubʼ Kame; their Lords and Masters who sent the Owls out as their dutiful messenger; their obedient emissaries to comply and complete this deadly obligation that was now their burden to bear; this cruel cargo that was left for them to carry-out as the ritual sacrifice demanded of them on behalf of the Lords of Death; the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa. So then ri Tukur-the Owls spoke before the gathering silence of IxKikʼ who listened rapt to what the Owls said:

“Is that which we said not what we were told? What then will we place in the gourd bowl? What we want is that you should not be killed; what we desire for you is that you might then escape death; what we wish for you is that you should not be sacrificed so that you might live on the Face of the Earth,” said then the Emissary Owls; Envoys of Xibʼalbʼa-ri Tukur, AjSamajel Xibʼalbʼa; the Messenger Workers of Xibʼalbʼa.

“Utz bʼa la! That ʼthisʼ heart not be theirs! So be it! Ta chuxoq!” said the One Maiden; Jun Qʼapoja.

body:
And then she continued, when she spoke, speaking directly to the Owls-ri Tukur: “May this place here no longer be your abode; may this place no longer be your home; and, that you no longer force people to die a sacrificial death. So that in the future those who are true knee-scraping-fornicators will be yours to sacrifice as you see fit.”

And so it was that IxKikʼ spoke her mind as she gathered together the thoughts of her heart; the feelings of her soul that were hers to ponder and hers to contemplate; her heart and its thoughts that were hers to reflect upon, hers to consider; her heart, the seat of her soul; the resplendent soul of IxKikʼ that now shimmered and it shined forth as a luminous lunar reflection that mirrored her nawal thoughts and nocturnal images from within. IxKikʼ had spoken just as she would speak again.

“May it come to be that Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame receive sacrificial offerings of the sacrificial blood given as the blood offered through self-sacrifice.

And may they be given offerings of sacrifice of that which is known as the ʼresidue head of incense-jolomax-artificial blood formed from the head-jolom of those who make incenseʼ which is just the fuzzy head of foam known as jolomax that comes from the creation of incense. 	May this ʼfalse-bloodʼ be given to Xibʼalbʼa as that which is known as jolomax; jolomax the foamy head of fuzz that forms on top of boiling clay pot used to cook-up the gathered tree sap that is tapped from the Red Incense Tree-Kaq Cheʼ known as Cochineal,” said IxKikʼ who knew what she was talking about as she continued to specify how sacrifice would be apportioned to the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

“It is only this left-over fuzzy head of foam known as jolomax that forms as the head-jolom of the cooked-up concoctions of tree resin of the collected sap; the gathered blood of incense shall be theirs. Only these shall be the substitute sacrificial offerings of ʼblood sacrificeʼ and ʼfalse blood-jolomaxʼ that shall be given to the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa as burnt offerings of sacrifice; nothing more than this; not one more heart shall be sacrificed to them; those known as Jun Kame; Wuqubʼ Kame.”

body:
“May it come to be! Ta chuxoq! May this too come to pass!”

“May it only be the resin and sap of incense that smokes and smolders upon the sacrificial embers of the sacrificial fire set before them, in this way no longer will it be human hearts that will be offered up as burnt sacrificial offerings; offerings of sacrifice offered up to them on the burning embers of their altars of sacrifice: Ta chuxoq! So be it!” pronounced IxKikʼ as she affirmed her nawal powers of transformation that beat in her heart; the heart that was hers and not that which was to be sacrificed on the sacrificial fires of heart and blood sacrifice that blazed on the altars of sacrifice of Xibʼalbʼa. So be!

“Just use the resin that flows from the cuts that scores the bark, the husk, the face of trees-uwach cheʼ to tap the ʼresinʼ or ʼsapʼ that is the blood-kikʼ of these red incense trees; incense gathered up as sap-ukikʼ cheʼ for the making incense,” said the One Maiden: IxKikʼ.

And so it was that this One Maiden-Jun Qʼapoj made it so she could gather up the sticky red sap that oozed from the Red Tree-Kaq Cheʼ that she had tapped to cause it to flow with the pull of the moon that soon filled her ritual gourd bowl-tzel.

This red sap of incense soon coagulated as the thick red resin that clotted into a perfectly spherical shape at the bottom of the sacrificial gourd bowl-tzel; it just rounded itself out by taking the form of the sacrificial vessel in which it was gathered together as the precious red blood of IxKikʼ.

This was when the replacement heart, the substitute heart-ukʼexel ukʼux-was then squeezed together tight, the sap of the red tree-kaq cheʼ-ran like blood: kikʼ.

This was the work of IxKikʼ who was ʼShe of Sapʼ, ʼShe of Rubberʼ, ʼShe of Bloodʼ, ʼShe of the Changing, Transforming Moonʼ, who collected all that was to be gathered from all that flowed from the strength and through the pull of the Moon.  This was her domain; this was what was hers in life for she was a ʼgathererʼ as the Daughter of the Lord Blood Gatherer: Kuchuma-Kikʼ.

body:
This would make her a powerful presence on the Face of the Earth where she would be called to ʼgather-up the harvestʼ of her peopleʼs sacred sustenance; a gathering of sacred sustenance that was shown as a ʼsign and symbolʼ of her being and becoming the ancestral embodiment of her destiny as the Moon Mother of the Sacred Sons, Divine Twins of the Maize People; for indeed, IxKikʼ held the ancestral heroes of the Maize People in her Full Womb as the embodiment of the Full Moon: IxKikʼ.

This will be the sacred harvest held within the full moon-like womb of IxKikʼ; the full moon of IxKikʼ is her harvest net filled out with maize from within to form and shape the Maize Twins: Jun Ajpu Ixbʼalamkej. These are those Divine Twins who in the Classic Period were the sons of the Lord of Maize Jun Ixim whoʼs sons were known as Jun Ajaw, Yax Bʼalam; Jun Ixim who is similar if not equivalent to Jun Junajpu and Jun Ajaw, Yax Bʼalam being Classic Maya equivalents of Jun Ajpu Ixbʼalamkej or so it seems to be seen like this.

So this then was when the blood-red-sap of the bleeding Red Tree-Kaq Cheʼ was made to flow as imitation blood; imitation blood that IxKikʼ gathered together there in the gourd bowl of sacrifice; the gourd bowl of sacrifice brought by the Owls to gather-up the ʼheartʼ of IxKikʼ.

The blood, the sap of the Red Tree flowed forth just like blood; just like the substitute blood of the One Maiden who was there forming and shaping; molding and modeling her own substitute heart from the clotted, coagulated essence of substitute blood she used to form and shape; mold and model; craft and create a replacement heart; a replacement heart that was a replica heart; the replacement, replica heart of IxKikʼ: ukʼexel ukʼuʼx IxKikʼ.

Resplendent crimson-red blood was gathered in the gourd bowl-tzel. So then the tree was named by the maiden, Red Cochineal-Chʼuʼj Kaq Cheʼ-as it is called-chuchaʼxik: Sangre de Dragón is its name Croton sanguifluus.

body:
It was just because its bright blood-red sap formed a fuzzy head of sudsy foam known as a head or jolom when incense-makers and dye-makers cooked-up the blood-red sap into a refined blood-red dye. This then was when they came to call the ʼsuds or foamʼ that rose to the top of their work of decoction:  jolomax. This jolomax is that which they called ʼfalse blood-sangre falsa-kikʼ jolomaxʼ-as it is said-chuchaʼxik.

And then IxKikʼ spoke to the Tukur-Owls giving them their final instructions upon her taking leave of them and the underworld of Xibʼalbʼa.

This was just before this One Maiden climbed up and out through the opening between the two worlds; this is the opening that led up and out of the cave underworld to then move above watery limestone caverns that one climbed out of before moving up and out of the dark and into the light to make oneʼs way across the Face of the Earth guided and protected by the Sun, Moon, and Stars.

But before IxKikʼ could escape from Xibʼalbʼa she had to take leave of her allies the Owls, ri Tukur. This then is when IxKikʼ said what she said to ri Tukur, the Owls:

“Over there, on the other side, all of you will be well loved; there on the Face of the Earth you will find what is yours; you will find your luck and lot in life which will be the destiny that is yours and yours alone known to us as our Nawal; our Genius; our Way of Being and Becoming in the World of the Sky-Earth; Kaj-Ulew,” said IxKikʼ to the Owls-ri Tukur.

This then was when the Owls took leave of IxKikʼ giving her their last and final instruction before guiding and protecting her until she was safely up and out of the cavernous cave world of Xibʼalbʼa.

“Utz bʼa la, At Qʼapoj! Very well now, you our beloved Maiden!

Xqabʼe bʼa-Letʼs get ourselves going now

Qawabʼa aqʼanoq-We will guide you to where you can climb up above

Xa qabʼin apanoq- We must continue on our way

Oj na qayaʼixtaj uwa- to go leave the presence of the sustenance desired

Ukʼexewach akʼux- of your substitute heart, your surrogate heart

chi kiwach AjAwabʼ-before the faces, before the countenance of the Lords

Xechaʼ kʼut ri Samajel-Said then the Messenger-Workers of the Noble Lords

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Aj Samajel-AjAwabʼ Xibʼalbʼa-Messengers of the Lords of Death; Workers of Lords of Disease; Messenger-Workers of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa

“Utz bʼa la, At Qʼapoj! Very well then, you oh beloved Maiden!

“We are going to guide you to where you must continue up on your own; up, up, and upon the steep stairs that lead above. You must keep going by yourself from there, while we return to leave the imitation image of your substitute heart, a replica of your maiden heart. For it is us who must just present your mock heart before the presence of the Lords, the Rulers of Xibʼalbʼa,” said then the Ajsamajel Xibʼalbʼa; ri Tukur, the Worker Messengers of Xibʼalbʼa; the Owls.

When they arrived there before the Lords-Ajawabʼ it was those very same Lords who were there waiting with great expectations for the Owlsʼ to return with their sacrificial bowl; for it was Xibʼalbʼa who was there waiting for the return of the Owls-ri Tukur with their sacrificial gourd-tzel-ritual bowl that held the heart of the One Maiden: Jun Qʼapoj.

“Is it not finished?” asked then Jun Kame-One Death.

“Indeed, it is finished, you, oh Lords. Here then is her heart at the bottom of the gourd-tzel-bowl,” said the Tukur.

“Utz bʼa la! Letʼs have a look then,” said Jun Kame.

So then the Great Lord took up her heart in his hands; a deep resplendent red liquid dripped as it dropped just like blood when he held it up as the perfectly round spherical sacrificial heart they had longed for with all their heart and soul of Xibʼalbʼa.

“Stir up the coals, make them good and hot so we can place this, her heart, upon our fire; upon our embers; upon the coals of our sacrificial fire,” said Jun Kame.

And so they roasted it-the surrogate heart of sacrifice; the substitute sacrificial heart-they burnt it there on top of the red-hot fire burning in the sacrificial brazier of Xibʼalbʼaʼ.

Those of Xibʼalbʼa found it to be truly enchanting; they found its fragrance to be altogether captivating; fantastically fragrant did they sense its sweet seductive scent to be.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
They took in its rich aroma as they fell under the spell of its sumptuous scent; its sweet seductive smell; it was then when they came together closer to take in the sweet, sensuous seduction of this spellbinding scent; this enthralling aroma as best they could.

Before long they found themselves leaning in and over their sacrificial fire to take in the precious perfume of this enchanting incense and its beguiling bouquet that now completely captivated the underworld souls of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

Truly delicious did they find this otherworldly fragrance; the sweet-smelling smoke; the perfumed plumes that had grabbed hold of their senses and would no longer let them go now that they were caught in this smoking net rapture and its capture of their hunger for the sweet-smelling heart of this One Maiden; the replacement heart created and crafted by her forming and shaping of this sensuous substitute substance of their sacrificeʼs sacred sustenance: this sly, this smart looking surrogate heart; this clever, this cunning copy of ancestral abundance that now enveloped them in the rich sweet smoke of pure unadulterated enchantment.

And so they bent forward a little bit more as they were pulled ever closer to the potent perfection of this sweet smelling smoke that now took them in, to then place those of Xibʼalbʼa  under its spell-binding control.

It was then that the Owls, the Tukur flew off to guide the One Maiden-Jun Qʼapoj on her path of escape; her flight that took her up and away to never see or be seen again by those who were they of Xibʼalbʼa.

The Owls led IxKikʼ up and out through the hole that led up ever higher to where one stepped out from below and onto the Face of the Earth. Once IxKikʼ had risen up and out of the caverns below her guides returned in a hurry as feathery flurry to the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa whoʼs sight was left blurry which left them there where they were sitting on their heels. This is where they remained deep, deep down in thought; deep down below in the dark, dark underworld of paths and caves; caves and paths that formed as they shaped the entrails of the Earth.

The Great Reversal: Day and Night; Sun and Moon; Light and Dark

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Rain and Wind; Flood and Drought; Image and Reflection

The Great Reversal is now sown in IxKikʼ who is a curious Moon Maiden very much at home in the world. Her ʼround full-moon wombʼ will bring the Sowing and Dawning closer to fruition through her Sons who will face the tests, trials, and ordeals Houses of Xibʼalbʼa with their life and death struggles that the Boys of IxKikʼ will overcome and by doing so will change the Sky-Earth once and for all.

These Sons, who are Boys are Twins who are Heroes that will bring forth the powers of life and death; growth and decay; coming to light and falling into darkness; hiding in the shadows and shining in the light. This is the eternal challenge that is the never-ending competition between the light and the darkness; the Sun of Day versus the Moon, Stars, Constellation, and Planets of Night; the Windy Dryness of Day and Dewy Wetness of Night; the Malevolent Trickster Powers of Night and Benevolent Trickster Powers of Day all of which come together in the Boys, the Sons, the Twins where they will be engendered in Underworld Darkness of the Cold Lunar Night that is brought together with the Over-world Light and Warmth of the Sun of Day; IxKikʼ and Jun Junajpu; bear and beget the Nawal Essence of the Sacred Sons of the Sun and Divine Daughters of the Moon; Saqil Al, Saqil Kʼajol.

Above and below; night and day; light and darkness; rubber and blood; maize and humans; underworld and over-world; life and death; generative powers of creation-renewal and the deadly powers of death and disappearance; destruction and demise that are now brought together as the essence of the Sun and Moon; Day and Night; Life and Death to form and shape these ʼSupernaturalʼ Nawal Winaq-the Hero Twins-Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej. These are those who will transform the Face of the Earth by Peopling-Winaqarisajxik-Populating it with Maize People after the Boys transform into the Sun and Moon at the Dawning of the Sun and the Moon with their special sort of Era and Age that is peculiar to the Maize People.

body:
Remember that rubber smells like death and decay so that those who work with rubber are those who were associated with the transformative powers of death which, is to say the Nawal Essence of Death.  This is the Nawal essence of Kuchuma Kikʼ, Blood Gatherer and his daughter IxKikʼ if indeed they were seen as Rubber Gatherers as an aspect of being Blood Gatherers.  Remember that the Maya sense of Death is experienced as a very lively sort of alive and bouncy kind of Death filled with the lively sort of trickster spirit and soul of the Lords of Death.  These were those who were embodied in the Noble Lords and Rulers of the Lowland Rubber Groves where gourds where used to collect the rubber from the ʼtappedʼ rubber trees; rubber that smells just like the rotting flesh of death for rubber has a sweet-sour deathly smell; the smell of death.

This then is how the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa were defeated by the One Maiden-Jun Qʼapoj who through her creative cunning brought forth the crafting and creation of her enchanting incense that clouded over the eyes of Xibʼalbʼa leaving them ʼmisty-eyedʼ by her deception; which is to say all of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa-Rajawal Xibʼalbʼa were deceived by this One Maiden.

For it was they, the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa, who were left blind by the clever cunning of this most magical maiden, IxKikʼ who fooled her foe with her curious concoction brought forth through her inspired incantation that led to her ingenious invention that formed as it shaped the enchanting incense of her own forming and shaping; all of which brought about the defeat and destruction of those who wished to defeat and destroy her. This inventive work of crafted enchantment was something the Owls knew would lead to the defeat of the Lords of Death by the One Maiden: IxKikʼ.

body:
For it was she, IxKikʼ who blinded them all through her trickster powers of disruption that led to a deadly sort of deception whose sole purpose and intention was to bring about the decisive downfall of Xibʼalbʼa. All of which is just a masterful foreshadowing of what was to come through her Sons nawal powers of transformation and those nawal powersʼ eventual transformation of the Sky-Earth through the death, destruction, and disappearance of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

These are the Sons of IxKikʼ who are the Twins; the Boys that she now carried within her womb; Sons who continued to grow as she escaped from the clutches of the Lords of Death to emerge onto the Face of the Earth undeterred by their desire to sacrifice IxKikʼ to sever any hope of her Sons sprouting forth as the replacements-kʼexel of their Fatherʼs ancestral lineage of the life and light of the Maize People: Ixim Winaq.

This is where the Fathers of the  Boys, the Sons, the Twins had come from and where IxKikʼ was now ʼheadedʼ as she ʼreturned homeʼ with her ancestral harvest of descendants ripening in her womb to take their Ancestral Place on the Face of the Earth.

These were the Sons who would come to defeat and destroy the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa by bringing about their complete demise and utter downfall leading to their death, destruction, and disappearance.

This story we will tell when its time comes to fruition; but until then we will continue to tell of this One Maiden; Jun Qʼapoj: IxKikʼ is her name.

And so it was that the Mother of One Monkey, One Artisan was there at home when a Woman-Ixoq arrived; this Woman was known as IxKikʼ by name.  Are kʼute kʼo ri u-Chuch Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen ta xul ri Ixoq; IxKikʼ ubʼi.

When the Woman-ri Ixoq IxKikʼ arrived there with the Mother-Chuch of Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen she bore her beloved sons within her womb; it wouldnʼt be long now before the birth of her begotten sons who were her engendered sons of Jun JunAjPu; Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej were their names.

When the Woman-ri Ixoq arrived there with the Grandmother-ri Atiʼt; this then was when the Woman spoke then; when she spoke then with the Grandmother-ri Atiʼt-the Old Woman:

body:
“I have just arrived, I have just now come to you, Thou-Lal; you my revered Mother-Lal Chichuʼ; Thou-Lal, oh, Mother-in-law for it is I that am your Daughter-in-law-In Alibʼ La and I too am your child-In Alkʼwal La, you my revered Mother-Lal Chichuʼ,” she said when she entered there with the Grandmother-ri Atiʼt; the greatly esteemed Old Woman-ri Atiʼt who questioned her:

“Where is it that you come from? Could it be there that I have Sons-Wal? Did they not die in Xibʼalbʼa? These Two Boys here are their descendants, their Two Sons; they remain here as their ancestral remembrance-ketal-their familial recollection left as a ʼsignʼ of them, a ʼsignʼ of their descendencia-kitzijel for they remain as the spark, the flame, the fire that burns as the ember of the truth of their ancestry for they are the replacements-kʼexel of their Fatherʼs word and its way; the essence of their lineage, the inheritance of their ancestral family line. These Boys, their Sons, are their descendants, their remembrance, their ancestral inheritance: Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen; One Monkey, One Artisan are their names. So, yes indeed, if you saw where you came from? Go back that way!” Grandmother snarled at the Maiden-Qʼapoj who arrived there before her, the Old Woman-ri Atiʼt to present herself as the Mother of this Grandmotherʼs Grandsons; the Sons of Jun Junajpu.

“But it is true that I am your daughter-in-law-in Alibʼ la,” said IxKikʼ to save face; stating her case; resilient yet firm; beyond blame, resistant to shame, leaving her to say: “I was just as I continue to be: that which is of Jun Junajpu is that which grows within me; that which I carry here within my womb is that which is his; is that which is of him, Jun Junajpu; they are alive, your sons, for their essence lives within the Boys; that which is theirs, is that which lives within their sons that I carry within me!” she continued, now that she had the full attention of the Old Woman.

body:
“Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu are not dead; this is just a clear sign-ukʼutbʼal ribʼ saq-a lucid sort of  precious sign that is a perfect indication of their doing, of their making, You, oh, esteemed  Mother of mine; oh you, revered  Mother-in-law-Lal Walibʼ. You will see them in the beloved face of those that I bear within me,” she said to the Old Woman-Atiʼt-Grandmother, standing-up for herself as she was born to do as the Daughter of a Noble Lord; Jun u-Miʼal Ajaw.

The way IxKikʼ spoke and acted caused Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen to be filled with a ʼred-facedʼ sort of rage-keqʼaqʼal-they were just furious.

After all, it was they Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen who were left to warm the heart of their Grandmother; it was they who played flute like their Fathers had piped on their pipes; it was they who sang the way they sang; just painting, just writing; just carving, just sculpting the way they were taught by their Father; by their Uncle; Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu.

They were the replacements-kʼexel of their Fathers who taught them to paint, to write, to carve, to sculpt, to sing, to drum, to play on their flutes and now a second mother had arrived to replace not only them but their mother: IxBʼaqiyalo who as we know, has died; their Mother is dead and now another Mother of other Younger Brothers has come to take their place which was something that burned them up making them ʼred-facedʼ mad.

They, Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen were who they were because of who they came to be through their learning to do all they were taught to do and taught to be. It was they who came to work and play at everything they learned from them, their Father, their Uncle; Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu. All of this attention they gave to the artisansʼ and musiciansʼ ways of being and becoming were the artisans ways of their Fathersʼ lineage; which, were the very essence of what warmed their Grandmotherʼs heart each and every day.

These were the very things that made their Grandmotherʼs heart and soul content-Are kʼut kubʼul wi ukʼux ri Atiʼt-the Monkey Twinsʼ noble ways of being consoled the heart of IxMuqane who didnʼt want to live life any other way.

body:
So it was she, Grandmother-Chichu, who spoke; this is what the Old Woman-Atiʼt said: “I donʼt want you for my Daughter-in-law: Xmakawaj wi at ta Walibʼ. Xa ajoxbʼal ri kʼo chapam; ¡At Kʼaxtok!  That which you carry within, that which you bear there in your womb just comes from your scuffing and scraping your knees.”

“You, you are nothing but a trickster-¡at kʼaxtokʼ!-an imposter, a poser is what you are, a false-faced liar, is that not so? They died, the sons of mine you speak of, they are dead,” said the Old Woman-Atiʼt before she threw down an impossible challenge to IxKikʼ something she could not possibly accomplish if she did not bear the nawal essence of Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu within her.

“So letʼs just say it is true what you say. Utz bʼa la! Very well, so you are my Daughter-in-law; if that is what I hear you say. So then go! Jat bʼa la! Go bring back our sustenance; the sustenance that is ours; the sustenance that is ours to feed those who must be fed. Go bring back ʼOne Big Net of Our Maize; Our Sustenanceʼ-Ja jachʼa jun chi nima kʼat qajal; qechaʼ-that you might come back with here; since you are indeed ʼmyʼ Daughter-in-law-Walibʼ as I have heard you say-kanutaʼo,” she said to the Maiden-ri Qʼapoj.

“Utz bʼa la, Fine then!” she said. “Utz bʼa la,” was all there was to say.

And so it was that the Maiden went to the milpa-pa abʼix-where their maize grew. This is the milpa-pa abʼix-the cornfield of Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen. They cleared the way to their milpa-jokam ubʼeal kumal-it was an open path that led there; the Maiden simply followed the road-ubʼeʼl, she just followed the path that arrived there to the milpa-pa abʼix-where their maize grew.

There was just one head of maize in the milpa-xa kʼu ju wi ri abʼix-there wasnʼt two heads of maize, or three heads of maize; there was just one head of maize-xa ju wi ri abʼix-but this one head of maize was fruiting out as it ripened; so that it was found heading up as its kernels filled in and its face filled out as its hair grew long and fine to dry-up and turn dark brown-xuwachelaʼm wiʼ uwach chi ju wi.

body:
It should be ʼxa kʼo jun wi ri abʼix and xa jun wi ri abʼixʼ but the text is playing with an ancient ancestral accent meant to say something that this translator does not know other than we have returned to the ʼarchetypal imageʼ of ʼone head of maizeʼ growing on one cane of maize growing in the milpa of Jun Bʼatz, Jun Chowen that recalls the one tree planted beside the one ballcourt upon which the one skull of Jun Junajpu was placed in the fork of the tree: Jun Junajpu or One, One Blow-gun Man  in a world where One is Divine such as the One Maiden, Jun Qʼapoj; Jun Raqan Kaqulja and Jun AjPu…the One of Jun Kame is the One Celestial Sphere of the Sun, the Moon, and the One Great Star or Jun Nimaʼ Chumil known as Venus.

So the use of ʼju wi ri abʼixʼ instead of ʼjun wi ri abʼixʼ is a play on some sort of ancestral accent or some such idea as that being spoken of here: this One Head of Maize growing on One Cane of Maize in a Milpa with One and only One Cane of Maize: Jun Aj. Oh but what a play on words it is to call forth the great Maize Deity who will come and save the day of this one-jun Noble Lineage of Maize People.

This then was when the maiden lost heart which led her to say: “Just look at that; truly lost am I; what a loser, what a cheat am I; just a debtor, just a fraud, a failure, just fallen, failed; truly faulty, flawed am I, I am done for, done in; for I am a deceiver and deceived, thatʼs me. Where am I ever going to bring back one big harvest net filled with maize asked of me?” Mused the maiden who now wondered if indeed she could pull off this impossible task required from her by the Old Women-Atiʼt, the Grandmother-Iyom; her Mother-in-Law-Alibʼ.

“Kil la in makol, in kʼasbʼol! Apa xchinkʼam wi ri jun kʼat echaʼ kabʼixik?” xchaʼ kʼut. Oh, beloved readers what a marvelous play made on words to form a word-play beyond oneʼs imagination and expectations all which will not be taken up here because it is as sophisticated as it is complicated: kabʼixik-that which is asked of me and kabʼixik-that which comes from the milpa and Ixik-she of the moon; Kabʼ Ixik: Two that come from the Moon!

body:
But then an idea came to her and then another until she was doing what she was called to do and that was when she knelt down before the ʼone head of maizeʼ growing on the ʼone cane of maizeʼ where she invoked the names of the guardians of the milpa, the protectresses of the milpa through an invocation that cause the care-takers of all the sacred sustenance to come there to where IxKikʼ was in this milpa formed and shaped by the enchantment of these Divine Ancestors.

And so she summoned the guardians of grains and the keepers of the kernels of maize and cacao; she called out and upon the Goddesses of Sustenance as she sung out to the Protectresses of the Milpa.

Right there, before the One-Head of Maize of Jun Batzʼ, Jun Chowen IxKikʼ called out to the providers, the sustainers of the milpa petitioning them and pleading with them that they might provide her with that which would sustain her; that is to say, to provide and sustain them, her sons who were those that she was called upon ʼto feed those who must be fedʼ the sons of Jun Junajpu:

“Come, come down here; come, come down here where you are called; come, come down here; come, make your presence known where you are summonsed!”

“Ta tul wa uloq; Ta tul takʼaloq; Ta tul wa uloq; Ta tul takʼaloq; Ta tul wa uloq, ta tul takʼaloq IxToj; IxQʼanil; IxKakaw; IxPuTziYa! At chajal re kechaʼ Jun Bʼatzʼ Jun Chowen,” Xchaʼ ri Qʼapoj.

“Come, come down, come down here; Come; come where you are summonsed; come, come down to make your presence known; you who are known; you who are named: IxToj; IxQʼanil; IxKakaw; IxPuTziYa!”

“Come, come down, come down here; you who are the guardians; you who are care-takers of the sustenance of Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen; One Monkey, One Artisan as they are named; as they are known!”

IxToj; IxQʼanil; IxKakaw; IxPuTziYa

Mother Goddesses of Abundance; Maiden Goddesses of Prosperity

It is both important and necessary to open up this incantation and enchantment of the ʼMother Goddess Care-takers of the Milpa who are the Providers, Sustainers or Tzuqul, Kʼool of the Ixim Winaq.

body:
While stating that I have remained well within the limits of these dense embodiments of this Ancient Ancestral Names that tell of the day Toj that is Rain, Water, and Moon; the day Qʼanil Maize Seed and Mazorca; Hard seeds of Kakaw and Sustaining Chocolate; Alchemical Lime and Ash of the Nixtamal Tzi Ya. These are who are all of whom and through which provide and sustain the Maize People with their sacred sustenance as those who are they who feed those who must be fed.

Tzi Ya is the white-lime water of the nixtamal used to cook up the maize kernels through the process of nixtamalization which is the alchemical secret that completely forms and transforms the Mesoamerican Civilization by releasing all the vitamins and amino acids to transform Maize into Super-Sustenance. When this cooked and ground maize is combined with kakaw creates the essential factor that causes the Maya Mesoamerican Culture to People and Populate the Face of the Earth like never, ever before.

These are who IxKikʼ as the Moon Maiden; Moon Mother calls in to help her create the magical sustenance she needs to prove that her son; her beloved sons she bears in her womb are the engendered sons of Jun Junajpu, Wuqub Junajpu. The game is on an IxKikʼ refuses to sit down in the dust and cry and we know the reason why and that is she is One with Spirit in the Sky; Ukʼux Kaj Jun Raqan Kaqulja just as she is One with the Soul of the Earth; Ukʼuʼx Ulew IxMuqane and her allies IxToj; IxQʼanil; IxKakaw; IxPuTziYa.

This is the spinning movement that moves from the East Red to South Yellow to West Black to North White:

This then is the Cosmic Movement of Incantation that spins to the right to bring forth Sacred Sustenance out of the Night where the Full Moon rises in the East to pull on the powers of sustenance as IxKikʼ pulls on the ʼcorn silk of the golden locks of this One Head of Maizeʼ the One Magical Mystical Head of Maize that brings forth Her Sacred Sustenance that is His Sacred Sustenance from Dusk to Dawn throughout the Night.

body:
This is an invocation of this Maize Deity that is a Transgender Male Deity who is a Female Deity that is suggested here through these ancestral words with their mystical, magical, mythical powers to reveal the Ancestral Ways of these Ancestral Words; Ways and Words that are spoken to be heard here. And then the Daytime heat arrives through the Enchantment of the Warmth of the Sun from Dawn to Dusk as the Sunrises at Dawn just as the Full Moon rose from where the Sun rises at Dawn.

This is just one of the many secrets of the Day and Night Sky where and when Dusk and Dawn are both times of the day when the Moon and Sun rise from the Coming Out Place of the Sun: Relebʼal Qʼij as this sacred place is known. This is the Enchanting Movement suggested here as we open the road to abundance through IxKikʼ and her invocation of her allies; allies of the Moon: You, oh, Beloved IxKikʼ come, come down; come, come down here to fill our One Big Net with Maize...

“IxToj-XToj”: Goddess of Sacrifice, Goddess of the Moon, Rain, Water, Blood; “IxToj-XToj” You of the East, You of the Red Dawning Place; You of the Coming out Place of the Sun; Come, Come make your presences known that you might provide us with the Blood of Sacrifice; the Rain from the Sky; the Water from the Moon that which is Our Sustenance Provide for Us; to Sustain Us Here on the Face of the Earth. So then we may provide for you in order to sustain you as we wish as we must.

IxToj; XToj; this is why we call on you to come to us as the payment of blood sacrifice that is given with Maguey Thorns and Obsidian Blades to bleed the blood that drips as it drops like rain; the rain that falls to sustain us with your sustenance that will feed those who must be fed with the Maize and Cacao fed with our blood that takes the form of rain; the rain to sustain those who call out for their sustenance; sustenance provided by us to sustain you of IxToj with sacrifice so this reciprocal cycle never stops or becomes stuck by sustaining to be sustained; by providing to be provided for in the never ending spin of sacrifice given to call down the rain to call up the maize and cacao that feed and sustain again and again.

body:
“IxQʼanil; XQʼanil”: Goddess of Maize, Goddess of the Mazorca, Mother of the Milpa, Celestial Seed of the Morning Star, Bright Golden-Yellow Shimmering, Shinning Women, Mother Goddess of Maize. You of the Golden Warmth of the South; IxQʼanil Mother Goddess of Plenty; Mother Goddess of the Abundant Southern Quadrant and Corner; Southern Side of the Holy World, Sacred World Come, Come Down, Come to Us; Provide for Us with Your Sacred Sustenance; the Heat, the Light, the Sublime Warmth of the Sun.

You IxQʼanil; Come Sustain Us with Your Golden Wealth, Your Generous Prosperity; You the Golden Embodiment of Maize; Qʼanil; Come to Us; Provide for Us;  Sustain Us with One Big Net of Beautiful, Bountiful Maize; IxQʼanil; Precious, Perfect Heads of Maize: Qʼanil la Mazorca that Shines Resplendent like the Sun like the Nimaʼ Chumil: Venus.

“IxKakaw-XKakaw” Goddess of Cacao, Wealth of Merchants, Rich Abundance of Noble Lords, you who are the essence that binds the Woman-Cacao and Man-Maize at Marriage Feasts, you of the Fertile and Fecund Darkness of the Western Sky; Place of the Falling Down Place of the Sun of the Dark Night Sky.

You Mother Goddess of the West; Provide us with Your Rich Chocolate Gift of Sustenance; Sustain Us with your Wealth of Cacao that We may be Sustained with the divine drink sweetened with honey spiced with chili of your forming and shaping that is beat and blended into the rich frothy thickness that comes forth from your chocolate essence; chocolate essence taken from your breast-like pods of the tree cacao; her limbs, her arms, her branches hang heavy with sacred sustenance: IxKakaw.

body:
You, Mother Cacao; Mother Chocolate you who are ʼtwice hard or ka-kowfʼ; You who are known as Ka-Kaw-double hard for you are who are ground on the grinding stone known as Ka so that Ka…Ka…Wa is the Sustenance known as Kakawa, the sacred food to feed us all; Wa that must be Ground Twice; KaKa as it is said for it is you who are taken from the breast Ix-Im; you who taken as sacred sustenance; Ix-Im suckled from the nipple that nurtures; the nipple that nourish of the Divine Mother of Sustenance;  IxIm; come, come down, come to us; sustain us, provide for us now; you who are known as: IxKakaw.

“IxPuTziYa-XPuTziYa”-And You Goddess of Cooked Maize in Ash; you who are Transformed Maize boiled in White Lime: Nixtamal-Goddess of Transformation; Goddess of the Moon-Maize-Sustenance. Sustain us, Provide for us you of the White Lime of the Nixtamal; You of the Grey Ash of the White North Land of the Ancestors; Land of the Dead; You who are the Face of the Moon and her magical, mysterious, miraculous ways of transformation; ways of the Nixtamal that transforms rock hard kernels into a wealth of soft tasty nutrition.

You IxPuTziYa that cooks and soften to transform solid stone-like maize seeds into soft sacred sustenance filled with nourishing nutrients  because of you IxPuTziYa; may the heat of fire and alchemical life of water and lime; water and ash transform Maize into nourishing, nurturing sustenance to fed those who must be fed.

You IxPuTziYa; You the of the Nixtamal Water are the One who sustains and provides for us; come, come down, come, come where you are summonsed with us here in this magical Milpa with its One Cane-xa jun aj with just One Head of Maize; xa jun wi aj; just one head-xa jun uwi with flowing hair-wi aj of corn silk-tzamay from which to gather oneʼs destiny as the provider and sustainer of the sacred sustenance of the Maize People.

IxKikʼ; IxToj; IxQʼanil; IxKakaw; IxPuTziYa

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
“You, you Goddesses of Sustenance; you Caretakers; you Keepers of the Milpa of Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen come down here to provide us with your sustenance!” invoked the Maiden, IxKikʼ who was right there standing before the One Cane of the Milpa-Jun Aj rech Abʼix; there where she called upon them the Goddesses of Sustenance; those who are known as the Providers; those who are known as the Sustainers: Tzuqul; Kʼool.

IxKikʼ invoked the Guardians, Keepers, Care-takers of the Sacred Sustenance of One Monkey, One Artisan when she invoked the names; to then enchant the words: At chajal re kechaʼ Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen!”

This was when she called upon their Nawal powers of miraculous transformation that transformed maize growing in the Milpa of Jun Bʼatz, Jun Chowen as the ʼmountain food of the Animal People-Chikopil Winaqʼ into ʼsacred sustenance of the Maize People-Ixim Winaqʼ.

Maize People-Ixim Winaqʼ

These Ixim Winaq were those who suckled their sacred sustenance from the breast of their mother from-Ix the nipple-Im of the breast-tzʼum of their mother-uchuch who provided and sustained them with Ixim-Sustenance that ʼsprouted forth-tzuq-paʼ as the tendril hairs-wi of the hard seed-naqʼ to form and shape the Ixim Winaq: the People of Sustenance; the People of Cacao-Kakaw; the People of Maize-Qʼanil the Sacred Sustenance of the Ixim Winaq.

These are those who ʼshoot out-tzuq paʼ from the ʼtendril hairs-wi-tendril shootsʼ who sprout out of the seed that is sown-ewexibʼal in the earth; the sprouting forth of the sown seed hidden-ewabʼal beneath the ground to hide it from the Bird People like Wuqubʼ Kaqix and others such as the Grackle known as Chʼoʼk or Chʼaʼk.

This sacred narrative is also suckled as the sacred sustenance of the Ixim Winaq who imbibed it from-ix-its very nipple-im of their mother as the real and metaphorical essences that formed and framed, shaped and structured the Maya-Mesoamerican soul and spirit; body and mind as Ixim Winaq.

body:
This is then is the real and metaphorical essence of Ixim Winaq: Maize People the motherʼs milk of the Maize People formed and shaped from words and images; metaphors that awaken the imagination in order to create human consciousness and its hunger for stories of creation and destruction that bring about the formation and germination of life and its populating the Face of the Earth; stories of creation that warm the heart and sustain the soul.

These are Mother Goddesses, the Matriarchs of the Maize People who IxKikʼ enchanted now with her sing-song prayers petitioning their powers of prosperity in the form of divine providence. The Magical Moon Maiden calls them in to then call them down to where she is there in the Milpa of Magical Maize where the One Head of Maize-Jun Wi Aj is waiting for her command to fill the One Big Net of Sustenance-Jun Nimaʼ Kʼat Echaʼ with the harvest that is soon at hand.

This then is when she knew just what she had to do; which she could see as clearly as clearly seen solution are seen; for like the other four providers and sustainers of the milpa, IxKikʼ was borne into the World of the Sky-Earth to embody the Mother Goddess of the Full Moon whose now completely ʼfull wombʼ was ripe with abundance in the form of her Two Boys, Two Sons who were themselves were of the essence and nature; condition and quality of the Sun and Moon that took the form and shape of a Sacred Bundle of Sustenance-Water known as Wa-Ja or Way-Ya this is the ʼCarrying Net-Kʼat-Harvest Net of the One Big Net of Maize IxKikʼ must bring home to feed those who must be fed.

This then was when IxKikʼ took the corn silk-tzamiy that flowed as the long silky locks of the single head of maize-uwiʼ jal growing in the milpa of Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen; she pulled ever so gently on ʼjust one-xa junʼ of those fine golden hairs; one by one she drew forth the long yellow tresses of that one head of maize; one silken strand at a time she pulled on so that up and out they came: the corn silk transformed into perfect ears of maize that were heads of maize brought forth before her with which she began arranging the harvest of  her one big harvest net: jun nima kʼat.
