body:
She didnʼt harvest the ear of maize growing on the one cane, but instead she just drew out the corn silk, one by one she pulled out the hairs and one by one out came heads of maize: the mazorca of maize came forth from IxKikʼ pulling up on the fine silky hairs of the corn silk on this one head of maize-utzamiyal uwiʼ jal.

In this way the maiden was able to harvest ʼone big net-full of maizeʼ from just one head of maize-xa ju wiʼ jal. Each one the fine hairs transformed into one perfect ʼheadʼ of sacred sustenance, perfect ears of corn-ju yakaj jal came forth as perfectly formed heads of maize-jal, that were perfectly formed mazorca-qʼanil. And so it was IxKikʼ brought forth great abundance from where there was just one head of Maize; Jun Qʼanil as it is said today.

Qʼanil Jun Kabʼawil:  Jun Nimaʼ Kʼat qechaʼ Qabʼix

Qʼanil is the name of the ʼmazorca of maize or heads of maizeʼ that are invoked to this day by Day-Keepers and Diviners in the Kʼicheʼ. Qʼanil refers to a mazorca of maize that is a fully filled out head of maize with each seed seen as a perfectly rounded, filled out golden yellow skulls of abundance; this is the shiny golden abundance of the Ixim Winaq; this is the fully filled out sense of precious perfect perfection of golden star-like; white skull-like; tooth-like seeds of resplendence this is the sense of Kabʼawil; the Mayaʼs full-kabʼal sense of completion-kabʼal that is Divinity.

The Kʼicheʼ lived to experience this divine kind of complete sort of fully filled out sense of  wholeness that is the perfection of completeness that is kabʼal; where the full sense of kabʼal provides one with a complete sense of fullness. This sense of fullness fills one with a whole, full, filled out sense of Divinity that is the complete bountiful sense of the Kabʼawil that one feels here as this One Big Net of Maize fills out to become a perfectly round sphere of a natural gift of bounty.

body:
A natural gift of bounty that creates a perfectly whole, perfectly full sense of the divine-will come to fruition that is a divine kind of fulfillment that forms to fill the world with a complete sense of abundance; a sense of abundance that comes forth up and out of the Earth  by calling upon the nawal powers of the Sky where  the Kabʼawil wait upon the Formed Beings; the Shaped Beings to call them down to the ground there in the milpa as IxKikʼ does when she ʼnames the namesʼ of those who she calls into play to bring about the fulfillment of Divinity as they take the form and shape of ʼnames namedʼ as the Kabʼawil who are called down to create abundance there in the Milpa before the One Head of Maize; Ju Wi Abʼix.

So let us call down these Mother Goddess one last time:

IxKikʼ: She of the Blood, She of the Moon, She of Rubber; She of the Copal and Pine Trees

IxToj:  She of Sacrifice, She of Rain-drop, She of Blood-drop

IxQʼanil:  She of Maize, She of the Mazorca, She of Golden Resplendence; of Abundance

IxKakaw:  She of Sacred Sustenance, She of Wealth, She of Prosperity

IxPuTziYa:  She of the White Lime Sustenance, She of the Active Essence of the Maya Civilization, She of the Ancestral Place of Profuse Plenty, Bountiful Abundance

Let us remember these Mother Goddesses of the Ixim Winaq

IxKikʼ: Moon, Blood, Rubber, Rubber Ball, Sap, Copal Incense, Pine-Resin, Chicle

IxToj: Water-Moon-Blood-Sacrifice-Debt-Payment-Mother Goddess of Ixim Winaq

IxQʼanil: Maize-Milpa-Mazorca-Mother Goddess of Ixim Winaq

IxKakaw: Cacao-Chocolate-Hard-Hard Sustenance-Mother Goddess of Ixim Winaq

IxPuTziYa: White Lime-Nixtamal-Mother Goddess of Ixim Winaq

As IxKikʼ pulled up the fine threads of corn silk that came out as perfect heads of maize; heads of maize that  she ordered perfectly in her one big harvest net where she perfectly arranged her perfect heads of maize; maize she ordered so she could perfectly fill up in order to fill out her one big net-jun nima kʼat.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
She did it all ʼjust soʼ so that she could fill her One Net perfectly full by ʼarranging itʼ with full heads of maize; maize that was gathered up by IxKikʼ as the sacred sustenance to feed those who needed to be fed.

IxKikʼ only felt herself ready to return when she had finished gathering up the perfect heads of maize that came from her pulling up and out on the thin threads of corn silk; and she wasnʼt finished pulling out perfect heads of maize until her one harvest net was completely full of perfectly arranged heads of maize.

It was then that the Animals arrived there with the Maiden, and it was they, the Animals, that carried the net for her. It was they, the Animals of the forest who went along bearing up this great big load of this one big net-full of maize.

When they arrived back home, the animals left the big round net there alongside the house so that it seemed as if this great big load had been carried by the Maiden herself, or so it was seen that way by Grandmother.

When the Old Woman saw all the sustenance perfectly ordered in the carrying-net she demanded to know from just exactly where it had been gathered:

“From where did all this food of yours come? ¿Apa mixpe wi ri echa awumal? I hope you didnʼt just level the place? Where did you get all of this from; I hope you didnʼt just finish-off all the maize there was to be harvested? I have to go see for myself!” said Grandmother-xchaʼ ri Atiʼt.

And so it was that she went to see the milpa; but there was just One Head of Maize; there was just the same One Head of Maize that there had always been there in their milpa-Xawi xere kʼo wi ri ju wi abʼix.

But then the Old Woman saw the print made by the net in the place-ukʼolibʼal below the One Cane, the One Cane of Maize.

Nahua speakers in the North; Maya speakers in the South

One Cane of Maize; Jun Aj rech ri Abʼix; Ce Acatl-Jun Aj-One Cane of Maize

body:
For the Old Woman  could clearly see the place where the heavy load had sat below the single cane of maize, the printed place where the Maiden had filled out her net-full of perfectly formed heads of maize; perfectly shaped heads of maize she had arranged ʼjust soʼ that they filled-up as they filled-out the One Big Carrying Net that left a perfect imprint in the earth there beneath the One Cane of Maize; the One Cane of Maize that stood there growing with just one head of maize-xa ju wi abʼix there in their Milpa; la Milpa de Jun Bʼatz, Jun Chopin.

Quickly then did the Old Woman return, arriving there before her house that was her home. Now it was her turn to speak before the One Maiden; Jun Qʼapoj; IxKikʼ by name:

“This is just a sign of theirs. Truly you are my Daughter-in-law-at Walibʼ! Now I will have to watch all that you do! Those grandchildren of mine are already showing their magical powers of transformation-Nawinaq; they are already demonstrating their essence as Nawal Winaq through their nawal ways of transformation, for they are already showing knowledge of the ancestral ways of their Father; like their Grandfather before him: xa Nawal Winaq all of them,” said then the Old Woman to the Maiden, Qʼapoj.

Mythic Genius; Nawal Transformation

Let us say this all again in a slightly different way in order that we understand how this ʼsign-retalʼ embodies the knot that binds the Nahua Tradition to the Maya Tradition through this One Cane; Jun Aj; Ce Acatl that is a ʼsaqetalʼ a sacred sign that speaks to us in truly sacred sorts of ways. We must bring perfect order to our mythic imagination before the Boys; the Sons of the Maize Father are born on the mountainside.

body:
By doing this now we will be able to follow the beauty in this masterful use of mythic metaphor by the Maya Scribes who formed and shaped this story over millennia so that today we might take some time to appreciate the genius of their mythical thought and imagination. So please, take your time to enjoy the mythic genius of the nawal transformation that is taking place here in this text. Let us do so now so we can appreciation the mythic metaphorical genius we are about to be borne into here on the Kʼiche Mountainside where the Sons, the Boys, the Twins are about to sprout up and out of their Motherʼs Womb of Emergence.

Jun Aj; Ce Acatl Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl; Jun Ajaw; Jun Ixim; Lord One Maize

This One Cane-Jun Aj is the calendar name of the Lord of Maize. Jun Aj and Ce Acatl are the calendar names of Quetzalcoatl-Qʼuqʼkumatz-Kukulkan who is also the Maize Deity of the Nahua World that is spoken of here in Maya ways. This image of the ʼone net markʼ under the ʼone cane of maizeʼ is like looking at a glyph of the Maize Deity and this is why Popol Wuj as Sacred Secret Text is of such immense importance for it is a treasure trove of Mesoamerican imagery known as iconography through which we come to understand the Maya through image, word, and metaphor.

These images come in succession one right after the next. These iconic revelations do not end and now we are presented with the One Mark signed as the One Point, One Dot, One Round Sphere of the Maize Lord Jun Junajpu known as Jun Ixim One Maize of the Classic Period. This then is that One Circle of crosshatching that says Jun Ixim or Jun Junajpu is present. This is his sign left in the dust beneath the One Cane of Maize. What genius, what beauty, what a masterful way to combine illustrated imagery and writing together in one image of maize and the Maize Lord making his mark through spherical imagery left by the Moon Maiden and her iconic ʼnetʼ printed out there on the Face of the Earth in the Sacred Milpa of the Divine Ancestors of the Maize People.

body:
And so it was that Jun Junajpu left his sign there with IxKikʼ below the One Cane of Maize, Jun Aj, so everyone could see the sign of abundance in the sign of the One Net-Jun Kʼat beneath the One Head growing on the  One Cane which says this is the sign of the Father of Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej. And so it is that we find the ʼsignʼ to be speaking another language that tells us of the Maize People whose Nim Ajaw or Great Lord is Quetzalcoatl who is the Maize Deity in the Nahuatl Culture and its Myth Cycle that tells of Quetzalcoatl descending down into Mictlan, the Land of the Dead. This story is similar to Jun Junajpu who descends down into Xibʼalbʼa.  And so it is that this One Big Net of Maize creates a ʼbig Oneʼ mark on the Earth that says: ʼhere is the sign of One Junajpu or Jun, Jun AjPu.

This One Cane or Jun Aj is Ce Acatl that is something I simply ʼcame upʼ with by translating the name of the place where the sign of the net was found in the milpa beneath the One Cane of Maize or Ce Acatl which is the day name of Quetzalcoatl just as Ce Miquiztli is the same as Jun Kame which is the day name of Tezcatlipoca.

This One Cane of Maize as the Day Sign Jun Aj; Ce Acatl; One Cane; One Mazorca tells us so much about these Boys, these Twins who wait to be born there in la Milpa.

This ʼsignʼ left by the One Big Net says in mayúsculo: JUN JUNAJPU is the JUN AJAW known as JUN IXIM known as CE ACATL TOPILTZIN QUETZALCOATL; the Maize Lord; the Maize Deity; the Mesoamerican Lord of Maize. Tollan Tzuy-Wa and its Supreme Ruler: Tepew Qʼuqʼkumatz; Lord Quetzalcoatl the Conqueror: Nakxitl Tepew Quetzalcoatl.

Here then next we shall tell of the birth of Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej. This then is where we will tell of their being born-kalaxik. We will tell of their sprouting forth on the mountainside: when the day was found for their birth, for their sprouting forth-xuriq uqʼij kalaxik; when their destiny was divined as to what would be the day that they were to be borne into the world as sons birthed-xeʼalaxik by their mother here on the Face of the Earth.

body:
This was the day when they were made to sprout forth on the mountainside; when the day arrived that she, the Maiden-Qʼapoj, IxKikʼ gave birth to her sons on the mountain-pa juyubʼ. This was when the One Maiden- Jun Qʼapoj IxKikʼ gave birth to her sons in the wilderness-pa juyubʼ for they were just born on the mountainside-pa juyubʼ.

Grandmother wasnʼt there to watch over her when she gave birth, the Old Woman was not present when they were born;  in an instant they shot up; directly, immediately they rose-up-xeyakeʼik-they just stood-up, the two of them were born standing up straight in the mountains: Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej as they are named.

In the wilderness they rose-up; on the mountain they rose-up-pa juyubʼ xeyake wi; in the wild they sprouted out; emerging on the mountainside they stood-up like heads of maize;  it was on the mountain that they were born erect, upright;  strong and straight-pa juyubʼ xeyake wi. This is how these Boys emerged into life.

They Stood-up on the Mountain; Pa juyubʼ xeyake wi

Pa juyubʼ xeyake wi: In the wilderness like Yaki-xeyake wi warriors they were born standing up ready for battle these Maize Boys; these Warrior Boys stood up straight at birth in the wild prepared to meet their future; their fortune; their fate on their birth day with its divine destiny, defined day, and its divine-deified date.

It helps sound out the original Kʼicheʼ to hear the ʼsub-textʼ of this ʼWarlordʼ culture of the Kʼicheʼ Maya Lords.

Jun yakaj jal is an ʼearʼ of corn which is a head of maize…yake is when the wind rises up…yakoj is to rise-up…It is astounding how all past translation simply want to see the Boys ʼborn on the mountainʼ without ʼentering intoʼ the divine enchantment of the original text with its ʼdouble entendreʼ and those double-meaningsʼ rising up to create deeper understanding.

body:
This sentence: Pa juyubʼ xeyake wi; ʼon the Mountain they rose-up as Yaki Chiefs; Yaki Warlords: Yake Wiʼ is masterful to ʼsayʼ the least! And, what is kind of funny is how much more conservative I am as a Kaxlan-Foreigner instead of the Maya Day-Keepers, Maya Prayer-Makers who ʼseeʼ much more in these mythopoetic plays that reveal much more than what is brought forth here in this interpretation of the Ancient Word of the Ancestral Account! What is interesting is how my left arm began vibrating while writing this a ʼsignʼ of ʼlighteningʼ in the blood to confirm what is written here is indeed what is meant to be revealed…oh, there it is again in my left thigh; of which I have not felt all along the way of this revelation of the Ojer Tzij; Ojer Natbʼal. ʼInterestingʼ; as young people tend to say these days.

So when they-the Infant Boys-were made to enter the House-the House of IxMuqane-then they would not sleep.

“Just throw them out! Truly, they just seem to scream their mouths off-qitzij chach kichiʼ,” cried Grandmother.

So then Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen placed them on an ant pile, and it was upon that pile of ants they slept sweetly.

This was when their Older Brothers took them away from the ant pile and placed them on top of the wild blackberry bushes with their nasty thorns.

This then was when Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen wanted them to die; they wanted them to be killed by the ants; they just wished that they would die there atop the poisonous spines, infectious spines of the wild blackberry brambles.

They yearned for their death, they longed for their demise because of the hatred and jealousy that Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen had for them; the anger and envy they held within them for their Younger Brothers-Kichaqʼ.

For the Boys, the Sons, Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej were not well received in the house of their Father, the home of their Grandmother by their ʼyounger brothers-kichaqʼ; in fact, Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen didnʼt acknowledge the presence of Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej at all in their home and because of this the Boys just grew-up wild in the mountains-xawi kʼu pa juyubʼ xekʼiy wi.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
These then were great flautists, Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen; these two play flute; truly, they were great pipers, great flute-players were they, these two Boys; these two Sons were great singers of song; tellers of tales sung in song; these Boys were born with prodigious talent: great flautists; great singers were they; these two musicians and singers who played and sang the Ancient Songs in the Ancient Traditional Way.

Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen were those who quickly became exceptional in all that they that did; they brought everything they came to do to the greatest fruition; for truly exceptional were they in all they came to do.

They grew, they excelled only through great suffering, for it was difficult to become the great artists and artisans they came to be; these two; the two of them there.

Indeed, it was only by overcoming suffering and affliction that they became the talented artists that they came to be.

For Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen came to be great masters like other sons of great lords; sons who distinguish themselves through the constant struggle and endless effort it took to be as great as they came to be; it was only by their proving themselves before others that they overcame the constant suffering and anguish they faced.

In time they came to be wise, sagacious seers and genius, knowers of knowledge because of all they came to see and all they came to know through their ability to endure hardship and suffer affliction.

For truly, they were talented at all they did: thus they grew-up to be great flautists, singers, and scribes who became great wood-workers and carpenters; who came to be sculptors, too.

Everything they did was certain to come out exceptional; all they started they brought to perfection; creating great beauty and splendor as flautists and singers; scribes and painters.

They had talent, they were born with it; it was just through their nawal powers that they did all they came to do. It was just their ancestral powers of transformation-xa xenawinaq that made it so.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
For it was just their nawal way of thinking that gave them their nawal thought which was their  ancestral way of thinking their ancestral thoughts that made them who they were. In this way Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen were Nawal Winaq.

For it was just their ingenious imagination that made them who they came to be; and, who they came to be, was who they were born to be; and who they were born to be; and who they were born to be was who they were known to be; and who they were known to be were those who were Nawal Winaq. In this way Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen were Nawal Winaq.

These Boys, these Sons, these Twins were born with their Fathersʼ nawal genius; they came into the world with this nawal gift of being born into the world as Nawinaq.

Yet is was only because of their endless practice playing music and constant work creating beauty that they came to be those who they came to be; which, was the nawal artists and nawal artisans who they now were; nawal artists and artisans that became the nawal musicians and nawal singers that they now were and always would be. In this way Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen were Nawal Winaq; which, was who they were born to be.

It just showed in their face; the face of their Fathers. Thus they knew it was they who were their Fathersʼ replacements-kʼexel, the remembrance of their Fathersʼ ways of being; their Fathersʼ ways of speaking and acting-ukʼexel kiqajaw; their Fathers who were those who had gone to Xibʼalbʼa and not return as they promised their Mother and Sons they would.

Their Fathers were defeated there in Xibʼalbʼa by Xibʼalbʼa through humiliation. Their Fathersʼ were destroyed through deception which brought about their disgrace and demise which ended in their death and disappearance.

Their Fathersʼ being deceived by Xibʼalbʼa to then be disgraced by Xibʼalbʼa caused them to be humiliated by Xibʼalbʼa which led to their defeat by Xibʼalbʼa that ended in their being sacrificed by the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
It was they-the Lords of Death-who had the Fathersʼ of Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen beheaded there in Xibʼalbʼa on the Altar of Sacrifice at the Sacrificial Ballcourt of Ballcourt Sacrifice known to all as:  Pusbʼal Chaaj.

Everything the Sons of Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu did came out well since they were born with the knowledge to do all they came to do for they were just Nawinaq as it is said of those Winaq who were born to be Nawales and so it was that they were the kʼexel of their Fathersʼ; Fathersʼ whose Sons were their replacements; Fathers who went walking down into Xibʼalbʼa; dead Fatherʼs who were sacrificed in Xibʼalbʼa.

And so it was that Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen were great knowers-nimaʼq etaʼmanel-great seers; knowing everything clearly, seeing everything clearly. And what they knew clearly and what they saw clearly was everything there was to be seen and known as the replacements-kʼexel of Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu-their Fathers so that they-Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen-came to know all and see all as great knowers and great seers: nimaʼq etaʼmanel.

And this they held within them as their way of knowing and seeing; they knew and saw this from the very beginning; from the time they were born and came into the world for they were their Fathersʼ replacements; successors; kʼexel.

Yet when their Younger Brothers were born the all knowing, all seeing ways of Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen came to an end; their knowledge, their wisdom no longer came forth as it always had come forth in the past.

This was just because of their envy; it was just because of their red-faced anger that they lost what was given to them at birth as a gift.

It was only upon them that fell their envy and anger; it was their own ill-will and resentment that fell back on them; it was just jealousy that turned their hearts against their Younger Brothers and this is what would cause their defeat; the defeat of  Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen, their Older Brothers by their Younger Brothers, Junajpu, IxBʼalamkej.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
There Younger Brothers brought home the birds they hunted with their blowguns to give them to their Grandmother for the Older Brothers. This is what they did; they just brought home what they hunted on the mountain every day.

But the Older Brothers showed them no thanks they just treated their Younger Brothers like servants, as if they were their ʼboysʼ.  That is how they treated Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej never practiced ʼwitchcraftʼ on them, never did they try to take their Older Brothers down; for certainly they could have; they could have done them harm; but they didnʼt do them any harm through twisting-up ʼgrass dollsʼ to bring about the downfall of their adversary; to cause the demise of their enemy. Mawi bʼanoj xepoysaxik kumal ri Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

They didnʼt get mad; they didnʼt get angry because they knew what that was no way to live life.

It was just getting up at dawn to go hunting with their blowguns that the two Younger Brothers did; it was just wandering about on the mountain-pa juyubʼ taking birds down out of the trees that the Two Boys, Two Sons did; this is how they spent their every day-juta qʼij.

This was what they did because this is what they loved to do. They brought home the food to feed their Older Brothers, their Grandmother, and their Mother.

Feeding those who had to be fed is what fell on the Younger Brothers, Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej who shouldered their blowguns as they took up their path up into the mountain or down into the canyon there before the first rays of Sun illumined the Dawn on each and every day that broke over the horizon; over there at the Coming Out Place of the Sun.

Nourishing and nurturing others was just their burden to bear; the burden that was theirs was their burden to bear; the burden they took up every day; the burden they enjoyed as they took it up and bore across the sky, across the face of the earth like the sun that Day-Keepers bear as Cargadores del Sol; Cargadores del Tiempo.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
They knew what was theirs in life and had always been content to be those who brought home the birds that their Grandmother stewed up for their Older Brothers who made their Grandmother content with all that they did to warm her heart. Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej did what they did because they knew what to do through the nawal way of living that came so naturally to them who were born into the world to bring back the food of those who must be fed.

Yet they were not well loved by their Grandmother, Ixmuqane nor by Jun Bʼatzʼ nor Jun Chowen. They were not given any of the sustenance that was brought home by them.

It was only after Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen had eaten that the Younger Brothers were allowed to enter in there beside their Grandmotherʼs three-stone-hearth when there was nothing left for them-the Blowgun Boys-to eat.

But the Boys, the Sons didnʼt get all burnt up about it; they didnʼt get all red-faced and angry, no. No, they didnʼt do that at all; instead they just took it like they had always done.

They knew the nature of their situation; they understood the condition of their existence: kikʼojeʼik. They saw everything just as it was; they saw everything crystal clear.

They brought back the birds they hunted everyday when they came down from the mountain. All of which were finished off by Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen who ate all that they were given. And so it was that there was never anything left for the two of them, Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej to chew-up.

Just playing their flutes, just singing their songs was what they did, the two of them, Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen warming the heart of their Grandmother as their Fathers asked when they took leave of them there on the Face of the Earth before they dropped down the kumuk-the stairs to Xibʼalbʼa; so what else could they, the Younger Brothers do but bide their time knowing that someday the chance would come to do what they had to do; what...else…could…they…do…?

body:
Just playing their flutes; just singing their songs is what they did; this was what they were doing; those named Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen. They were there making their music; they were there just singing as they sang their song; they just played their flutes as they piped away on their tunes, this is what they did: Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen.

This was when Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej came down off the mountain like they always did, only this time they didnʼt bring anything home with them.

This then was when they came in without a single bird; not one bird did they bring with them when they came down from up on the mountain; not  one bird was hanging off of those Boys when they came in to the house; when they came home with nothing; nothing at all; when they brought home nothing this time when they came home with nothing to cook, with nothing to eat; nothing, nothing at all.

This just burned up the Old Woman; furious is what she was as she erupted red-faced with anger that only she knew:  “Why havenʼt you brought back any birds?” she demanded of Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

This then was when they ʼmade their wordsʼ for her, as agreed upon by the two of them after talking council with one another to talk it all over.

And so they said: “Well it is like this, you esteemed Grandmother of ours-Ix Qatiʼt our birds just got hung-up-xa mixetanatobʼ in the treetop; our birds just got snagged in the branches. There is just no way that we can climb-up there to bring them down; oh you, our Grandmother; Ix Qatiʼt.”

“So, we wish to ask our ʼOlder Brothers-Qatzʼ that they might go with us, to perhaps climb-up in the tree to bring the birds down;  the birds caught in the branches; the birds snagged up in the tree,” they said then to their Grandmother there in the patio of her house.

They said what they said to their Grandmother where their Older Brothers could hear what they said.

And, they did, their Older Brothers did hear what was said for them to hear of the words the Boys prepared so well for their Grandmother to hear there where they could be heard by their Older Brothers because they answered right away.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
“Utz bʼa la, very well, we will go with you at dawn!” Answered their Older Brothers-Katz without even speaking to their Grandmother before speaking to their Younger Brothers-Kichaqʼ who were happy as could be that their Older Brothers were going to accompany up on the mountain at dawn.

And that was that for them, the Artisan Twins; the Monkey Twins; those Artists; those Artists who may well have tasted their downfall that was their defeat that was their demise like others who had hungered; others who had hankered for just a taste of a brazed piece of meat to eat as a tasty, tasty treat…

They, Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej, brought forth then their imaginative thinking as companions who acted as one by gathering  together their thoughts about to bring about the defeat and disappearance of their Older Brothers; Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen.

This was when Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej spoke between one another to say what called to be said as they spoke together about their defeat of Jun Bʼatz, Jun Chowen.

“We will just transform their nature, their essence; their way of being-kikʼojeʼik! This is our word, our truth; for this is all we have to say; may it reveal the longing within us; may it speak of our appetite; may it tell of our truth, of our hunger-E upam qatzij.”

“So be it! Ta chuxoq! May it come to be because of the great suffering they have caused us! They wanted us to die; they just wanted that we should disappear, us, their Younger Brothers.”

“They treated us just like vassals; we were seen as servants in their eyes, servants who did as they ordered; we were expected to provide for their every need so that ʼpoco a pocoʼ we came to be seen by them as their boys-kʼeje ri ala-we, their servants; and, they, our masters!”

“This is how they treated us so that in their eyes we were seen as dutiful subjects; born to be obedient; born to be punished; born to serve them here in their Fathersʼ house; here in  their Grandmothersʼ home.”

And so it shall be that in this same way we shall defeat them; we shall make a fine example of them!” This then is what they said when they took council with one-an-other there as true companion, as complements of one-the-other as it is said; as complementary-cooperative-collaborative twin brothers-kibʼil kibʼ kikabʼichal.

Under the Yellow Tree; Chuxeʼ Qʼan Cheʼ; Beneath the Big Yellow Tree

This then was when they went walking over there to where they would eventually come to the Yellow Tree; Qʼan Teʼ ubʼiʼ; Qʼanteʼ ubʼi: Yellow Tree                                       is its name the Dye Tree as it was once known.

Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej; the Younger Brothers-Kichaqʼ went walking towards the Yellow Tree accompanied by their Older Brothers-Katz.

They came along testing their skills as they made their way walking just trying their luck with the blowguns on the innumerable birds there in the forest kechʼititik-chittering away in the treetops especially there beneath the Yellow Tree where they now stood looking up at all the birds they heard chattering in its limbs.

Yet despite the countless birds they came upon there not ʼa one of themʼ fell from where they were caught snared in the branches; just snagged in the limbs of the Yellow Tree below which the Older Brothers had arrived after accompanying their Younger Brothers as they made their way afoot in the forest with its many trees.

Infinite quantities of birds were there in the forest just chittering; just chattering up in the treetops but none more than the Qʼan Teʼ the Yellow Tree.

Their Older Brothers were awestruck by the great multitude of birds they saw there. But of all the great many birds they saw, and of all the great many birds that now lay motionless not one of them fell from where they were apparently left stunned in the branches of the Yellow Tree; the Yellow Tree below which the Younger Brothers now stood with their Older Brothers.

“Our birds just wonʼt fall! Why donʼt the two of you just climb up into its branches to bring them down from where they are snared in the limbs,” they said to their Older Brothers-Katz.

body:
“Utz bʼa la, very well then,” said the Older Brothers-ri Katz-to the Younger Brothers-ki Chaqʼ.

As soon as Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen climbed up into the tree it instantly began growing; and, as soon as it began to grow so did it begin to swell; and, as soon as it began to swell so did its great girth begin to bulge-sipoj upam.

It was then that the two Older Brothers wished to come down; but they couldnʼt come right back down, because the two of them, Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen, were now high up in the branches of this now Giant Yellow Tree-Qʼan Teʼ.

That was when they called down from where they were doing their best to hang on to the giant branches of this now enormous tree.

“How can we hold on, You, Our Little Brothers-Ix Qachaq? How can we hold on to this tree? Please, Little Brothers; help us Boys-toqʼobʼ qawach-pity us Little Brothers! Please, forgive us Boys-toqʼobʼ qawach-por fa, do something to save us because this tree is so very, very scary, as you can see, you, our Little Brother-Ix Qachaqʼ it is such a big, big tree that is just getting bigger and bigger all the time!” They called out as they screamed down from high in the branches of that Big Yellow Tree.

This then was when Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej yelled up to them: “Donʼt worry; Itʼs alright, just untie the long sash of your pants-chikiraʼ iwex, chixima xe ipam-just tie the sash of your pants around your waist and then let the ends of your sash hang down long; just let them hand down your backside, like a tail, then you will be able to move about with ease in the branches of the tree.”

This then is what they were told to do by their Younger Brothers-Kichaqʼ when the Older Brothers-Katz called down from way up high in the branches of the Qʼan Teʼ.

“We!  Fine!” called down the Older Brothers high up in the towering tree.

body:
They answered back as they pulled on the free ends of their long sashes and then wrapped the sash around their waist so that instead of having two ends of the sash hanging down the front their wrapping and binding of their sash was left with only one long end that they tied off ʼjust soʼ that it hung down their backside nice and long. Once they finished working wrapping, binding, knotting and hanging then…puuj…puuj…all of a sudden, just like that, those long sashes of theirs turned into tails-kijeʼ; and in an instant-xa pu jusu; ʼin just a flicker…pu…in just a flashʼ their sash became a tail that hung down their back like the monkey tail it had suddenly become; those who had been their Older Brothers had transformed into Spider Monkeys-Kʼoy.

This then was when they went through the trees of Small Mountains; Big Mountains making their way through the forest now howling out as they swung through the limbs of the trees with the greatest of ease. This is how Jun Bʼatz, Jun Chowen were defeated by Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej. It was just because of the nawal powers of transformation that they were able to make it so Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen looked just like Spider Monkeys: Kʼoy.

Spider Monkeys: Kʼoy

It was these Spider Monkeys who now playfully hung in the Qʼan Teʼ by their long arms and long legs with four hands  and long, long tail that they used most gracefully to hang from the limbs and branches of this enormous tree that they now moved through with the greatest of ease.

Their being saved was no longer in question. They werenʼt worried a bit anymore because they could grab hold and hang on with four hands now and all as if they had somehow done this before!

Now, with their nature transformed and their condition changed the appearance of the two Older Brothers had become that of another more mischievous essence; which was that of the Spider Monkey or Kʼoy as these badly-behaved tricksters are known to this day; bothersome greedy creatures, real nuisance in the jungle forest especially for those who grew milpas of cacao and maize or groves of fruit trees.

body:
But what could be done now? It was too late to go back to who and how and what they once were just a short time ago; the Elder Brothers were now Kʼoy just as their Younger Brothers had conceived and imagined with their Naʼoj: their Nawal Knowing.

And so it was that those Two Spider Monkeys went swinging off through the trees as the animals they had become. For it was they who now looked just exactly like they had always acted with their Younger Brothers which was just exactly how these irritated looking furry-faced fuzzy-headed Boys appeared to be; monkeys of the forest, creatures of the trees-xa kʼoy xkiwachibʼey chik!

They took on the look as they matched the exact appearance of Spider Monkeys who went swinging through the canopy; just flying through the trees of the Small Mountains, Big Mountains.

They moved with ease through the branches of the trees howling out as they hurled themselves about the forest up through the limbs of the treetops swinging with both hands and feet as they moved through the forest like the breeze in the trees.

And so it was Jun Bʼatzʼ Jun Chowen looked like the Spider Monkeys they became; like the Spider Monkeys they now were; like the Spider Monkeys they were meant to be; those wild animals who made their home in the trees. Just like that Jun Bʼatz, Jun Chowen were defeated by JunAjPu, IxBʼalamKiej.

It was just their magical powers of transformation-kinawal that made it so; it was their superior genius and inspired imagination that gave them their ancestral powers of transformation which bestowed upon them the ability to change themselves into anything they need to be to ʼget the job doʼ and so it was they could transform other into whatever it was those being truly were in their heart, in their soul so that they transformed into who or what they truly were; and it was all done in an instant; for truly they were Nawal Winaq known also as Nawinaq.

So then they returned home. And as soon as they returned home they spoke to the Old Woman who was there to speaking with them as soon as they arrived back home; and so it was that they spoke with their Grandmother and their Mother.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
When they arrived then at their home, they immediately went to speak then with their Grandmother and their Mother. This is what they did when they returned home; they went to their Grandmother and Mother to talk to them about their Older Brothers and how they had ʼjustʼ changed face and how that ʼfaceʼ was now a Spider Monkey face-xa Kʼoy xkiwachibʼej chik-they said.

“You, our Grandmother, whatever could have happened to our Older Brothers-qatz-for they ʼinstantly took on a new lookʼ as it is said ʼthey took on a new image; a new face; a new way of beingʼ when they took off into the mountains looking like animals-chikop; they looked just like animals when we last saw them,” they said.

“If you did something to your Older Brothers; if you caused them to be lost to me so that I might no longer see them; if you somehow caused me ruin or for some reason caused me disgrace! I hope you havenʼt done something like that to your Older Brothers, you my precious Grandsons of mine; you, my beloved Descendants of mine-Ix Wi. I hope it is not something like that you have done to me, your Grandmother,” said the Grandmother-ri Atiʼt-the Old Woman to Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

“Donʼt be sad, you Our Grandmother-Mixbʼisonik, Ix Qatiʼt, donʼt be worried, you Our Grandmother, for you will see their faces again, the faces of our Older Brothers, you will see them again because they will return here, again.”

“They will most certainly return and when they return their return will ʼjustʼ be a test for you, ʼjustʼ a trial for you, an ordeal for you; you, our Grandmother; Ix Qatiʼt.”

“It is a simple matter; it is just a simple matter of you not laughing at them when they come in; when they come in dancing.”

“This is just a trial of sorts, a kind of travail; for its is just a test; just a question of their destiny; a question of their future that is a question of their fate; so whatever you do, donʼt laugh when they come back in, because when they come back in they will come back in dancing,” they said then when they spoke to their Grandmother there in the ʼpatio or sitioʼ of her home; the ʼsitio or patioʼ of her Sons who died in Xibʼalbʼa.

body:
And so it was Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej who began the articulation of the song that they began playing on their flute; the song that they began playing was the melody known a Junajpu Kʼoy, the Original Ancestral Spider Monkey Song as it is known, Junajpu Kʼoy; they played it on their flutes first; then they sung as song; then they drummed it out as the beat of this ancient ancestral ʼsonʼ.

Then the two of them, Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej, just sang it as they sung it out in song; they just played it on their cane flute as they piped it for the ancient, ancient tune it was; they just drummed it out on their drum; xebʼixanik; xesuʼanik; xeqʼojomanik; they sung it, they sang it; they piped it, they played it; they drummed it, they hummed it so that it rang out in the mountains and hills calling their Monkey Twin Brothers back home.

This was when they took up their flute and drum to play their enchanting tune in order to sing their captivating song along with the Old Woman who came in to sit with them there in the patio; and so they played on their flute-xul, they just piped on their cane-aaj su, aaj-xu; they just drummed on their double-headed drum-qʼojom as they sang, as they sung out their sweet sonorous song-bʼix.

And so it was that they just played their tune to call them in, the Boys who were know Kʼoy who came swinging in from afar as they felt the call of this ancient, ancestral incantation that was played just for them to come in from the wild; the musicians just called them in with their melodious melody; calling them back home with their enchanting flute upon which they played their enchanting song: Junajpu Kʼoy.

Junajpu Kʼoy was the Ancient Ancestral Spider Monkey Song that was the name of the tune they played up into the forest crying out, calling out for the Older Brothers to return.

Junajpu Kʼoy

They just sang and played this ancient, ancestral song of the animal ancestors calling them forth so that they might come dancing in so Grandmother could prove she was able to hold back her laughter and win the victory that was certainly hers to win.

body:
It was just a test to see if she could keep from laughing at these entertaining Young Men, her Grandsons, who had made her laugh so very easily her whole life long with their funny ways they acted and the silly thing they said that always warmed their Grandmotherʼs heart lifting the weight of loss she felt for the grief she knew so well because of the defeat and demise; death and disappearance of her Sons in Xibʼalbʼa.

When they took up their flute and drum Grandmother sat down beside them in the patio there in front of her home anticipating the arrival of those who were sure to return as Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej played away on their flute calling their Older Brothers back with their tune; coaxing them back home with their song.

Junajpu Kʼoy; a Song of Enchantment; an Ancient Ancestral Song

They sang them down from the trees; they called them out of the forest with their ancestorsʼ ancient ancestral tune; they beckoned them in from the mountainside with the mesmerizing melody known to all as Junajpu Kʼoy; an enchanting song if ever there was an incantation with the strength to call the Boys back home and into their house, out of the forest, down from the trees and into their Grandmotherʼs home.

This spellbinding song was now played and sung to call them in dancing to this ancestral incantation of the Ancient Ancestral Spider Monkey Song: Junajpu Kʼoy was its name; the name of the invocation played as enchantment to invoke the Ancestral Soul of the Ancient Ones.

Junajpu Kʼoy was the name of the tune that they piped away on their flute; it was the rhythm they drummed away at on their drum; it was the song they sang away at their Ancient Ancestral Spider Monkey Song: Junajpu Kʼoy is its name. Their effort of ancestral enchantment began to work for their incantation was heard near and far.

body:
Before long the Monkey Twins came in dancing as they danced into the patio of Grandmotherʼs home.  It was then when the two of them returned; when the two of them arrived there where the Boys played and Grandmother watched the Monkey Boys as they danced now completely captivated by their song; it was then that the Kʼoy-Spider Monkeys entered their song and dance known as Junajpu Kʼoy with its tempting tempo; its beguiling beat; its mesmerizing melody that got the dancers dancing with its enchanting sound.

This then was when Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen came in dancing as they came dancing along to the singing of their song that grabbed hold of them and would not let then go; a melody, a song, a tune that wouldnʼt leave them alone.

They just danced round and round spellbound by this song that was played just for them; a song sung just for them; an ancestral song played and sung for a long, long time as a song that was a ʼsonʼ that was played just for them; Jun Bʼatz, Jun Chowen who now danced about with pure joy to the song that was theirs and theirs alone to sing and dance: Junajpu Kʼoy.

And so then their Grandmother saw them; and when the Old Woman saw their faces that looked so dirty and scruffy; so unclean, so unkempt she could help but smile a bit; they looked so funny.

The faces they made and the way they danced was more than enough to make her break into big broad bright smile and when she smiled she couldnʼt help but chuckle, just a bit. But then as she watched she could help herself she just had to laugh and once she started laughing there was no stopping her laughter.

And so it was that the Old Woman laughed and laughed the kind of laughter that came so easy to her; for this was the Grandmother whoʼs Boys lived to make their Grandmother laugh.

The Old Woman laughed as she always laughed because that is what she did when her Boys danced their dances and sang their songs and played around in the patio to warm her heart.

body:
Grandmother simply ʼcouldʼ not control that which she thought she ʼshouldʼ not control because of the funny things those dancers did to tempt her laughter; laughter that came so natural to her; as natural as it was for her Grandsonsʼ piping hot tunes on their flutes, drumming blazing rhythms on their drums, and singing soulful songs with their cheerful voices all of which were performed to warm their Grandmotherʼs heart.

No doubt this was going to be much more of an ordeal than the Old Woman could have imagined or thought possible. Surely she could control her laughter.

Immediately they-the Monkey Boys-Kʼoy-took off, in an instant they were gone; climbing up through the branches of the trees they flew right back up into the forest to then shoot straight up into the canopy.

Once they were out and away in the wilderness-pa juyubʼ no longer could their faces be seen by anyone who could be made to laugh uncontrollably but that didnʼt stop them from goofing around anyway because that was their nature; that is the way they were by nature; that was the very essence of who and how they were formed and shaped to be in the world of the Sky-Earth.

Up and away they went swinging as they swung along until they returned to the Forest-Kʼechelaj from where they had come before they had been summoned by the enchanting enchantment; the beguiling beckoning; alluring allure of their ancient, ancestral song, Junajpu Kʼoy.

In no time they were back to where they had come before they had been humiliated by the laughter of their Grandmother; before they had been called into the patio of the house that had been their home where they were laughed at hysterically by their Grandmother. Those Monkey Boys had come and gone quicker and faster than any of them could have or would have ever thought or imagined being possible.

body:
Surely their beloved Grandmother ʼcouldʼ do better than that; or, perhaps ʼshouldʼ do better than that if only she ʼwouldʼ do better than that ʼif onlyʼ she ʼcouldʼ make up her mind to really do better than that as her precious privileged prized Boys now wished she ʼwouldʼ as they thought she ʼshouldʼ at least for them like they now hoped she ʼwouldʼ if only she ʼcouldʼ do better than that but she was an Old Women who fell easily into laughter as all Old Woman ʼshouldʼ. What ʼcouldʼ one do?

“What have you done, you our beloved Grandmother? Just four times will we test you; just three more times will we call them in and out of the forest with our flute, with our song; so just do what you have to do to pardon your laughter. We are going to try again!” said Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

So then they called them by piping them in; it didnʼt take long at all for them to return dancing.

They danced right on into the patio, onto the terraza they came dancing; just dancing all about they did come prancing when they came in dancing to the song that was the ʼsonʼ that was dance known as Junajpu Kʼoy; their song that was their dance; with its tempo; its timing; its pace; its rhyme, its rhythm; its running; its racing; its climbing; its chasing; the dance that was a hunt thus the name Jun Ajpu Kʼoy or One Hunter of Spider Monkey: Jun Ajpu Kʼoy.

This is the dance that is the song that the Boys came to sing as the song that sung within them as the dance that they danced as a hunting chase of their hunter chasing the Spider Monkeys all about.

They just danced their Spider Monkey dance by dancing their ancestral dance with elegance and grace; this dance they danced by dancing all-around their Grandmotherʼs place.

They came in dancing right there as they danced onto the terraza that was the open space there at the center of the sitio. This is when they danced their dance when they came in dancing, to dance entranced by the flute; enthralled by the drum they just pranced about dancing as they danced about prancing; as they pranced about dancing about enchanted by their song:  Junajpu Kʼoy.

body:
There in the patio of Grandmotherʼs house is where Grandmother now sat where the Monkey Boys now danced up and down while climbing all around as the they scurried and chased one another all about.

Those named Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej are also known One Hunter and Little Jaguar-Deer; spoken of as the Hunter; One Blowgun Boy and the Hunted; Jaguar-Deer.

It was these who were those who played out this Ancient Ancestral Hunting Song of Jun-Ajpu, Ix-Bʼalam-Kej and it was they who sang and piped and drummed and played the song that called down the Spider Monkey Boys to dance all around; all around the patio, up along the adornment of the crown high on the walls, there was nowhere these dancers didnʼt go for it was just in their nature to go where the chase carried them forth as they swung from the beams on terraced porch from where they climbed up on top of Grandmotherʼs House to then start over again.

They just danced dancing up and down as they pranced in and out of the patio where they whirled all-around and twirled all about to the uproarious tune named and known as Junajpu Kʼoy the song that was the son that echoed all around as it bounced up and down to resound all about.

This was when the Boys drummed and piped and sang the song that was the dance that the Monkey Boys danced when they danced their song in the sitio of Grandmotherʼs home that was of Grandmotherʼs house where the song Junajpu Kʼoy was heard as the song of the chase of Jun Ajpu Kʼoy.

Entranced by the spellbinding sound they just danced and danced, when they came in dancing as they danced spinning round and round while climbing all about; those Monkey Twins really knew how to dance their dance that their Younger Brothers now began to play in the most delightful way to enchant and enthrall; beguile and bewitch; invoke and provoke those to dance who were summoned to dance to the song known as Jun AjPu Kʼoy.

body:
Those Older Brothers really knew how to dance their dance of this song that was theirs; the song and dance that was their Ancient Ancestral Monkey Boy song; the dance that was theirs that no one ever knew why it was danced and played as a song that was a hunt that was a dance that was a chase that carried its dancers all over the place. Grandmotherʼs face now wore a smile as she watched all the while as her favorite sons ran about dancing wild.

They just acted funny; making really sweet faces; they couldnʼt help but try to make their Grandmother laugh with all the silly expressions they made and all the goofy things they did, and sure enough the Old Woman couldnʼt keep from breaking open into a sweet smile that soon rang forth as a beautiful broad faced laughter that she had no way of keeping down, a laughter she felt was more like an ecstatic release and rapture of the laughter she was told to hold down as a caged sort of captured kind of captivated laughter.

But Grandmother could not contain her laughter because of the funny ways     her Boys acted and all the goofy things they did to amuse the Old Woman who was prone to laughing and laughter. These two knew just what to do to get her laughing knowing what was just enough to provoke her honey-hearted-kikakʼux laughing; her sweat-hearted-kikakʼux sort of mirth; the Old Womanʼs love of laughter was much too much for her to repress even under serious duress like this.

Those Monkey Boys knew no better than to do all they were called to do to make their Grandmotherʼs heart warm by keeping her laughing with their enduring humor that was always hilarious to those who stuck around to laugh and laugh at these two natural born clowns.

body:
Through and through their kind of humor was funny and fun for those who lived with them at home and knew the ways of their clever acts and gesture that they performed without ever attempting to control their antics in order to create a house filled with song and laughter; laughter and song was the way it was in this house that was a home where there was nothing wrong with laughing or laughter; the flute and drum; the story and song that were always welcome; never taken to be mistaken or wrong.

Before she knew what was going on the Old Woman was doubled over laughing; laughing  with uncontrollable laughter causing tears to well-up in the corner of her eyes from the laughter that came so easily to those who were born and raised on lament and laughter; weeping and sobbing one minute that were jokesterʼs loving laughter; tricksters mocking mirth.

This was just their natural condition, the way they were made to be; the two of them, the Monkey Twins; her Grandsons-Iwiey Mam her constant companions since they were wee little newborn infants who made their Grandmother laugh and smile with their silly ways and the silly things they said.

Truly hilarious were the funny faces they made that came from the fuzzy faces of these Monkey Boys and the laughable way that, that ʼlittle thingʼ that hung down below their bellies swung about; and, their incessantly moving tails that constantly waved up around their head and chest to just swirl up and around their wild eyed, big-eared fuzzy heads. They were a sight to see that would make anyone laugh; so funny were their ways poor Grandma had no chance.

So that then was when they came in dancing again the funny, funny way they did that  instantly made the Old Woman laugh even more than ever knowing she had somehow lost the wager what could she do about these Boys and their hilarious behavior.

So now when she laughed she just kept on laughing and laughing; there was no stopping her laughter; the uproarious laughter of Grandmother; the Old Woman.

body:
And so it was and so it seemed to be that no matter what those Boys did it tempted Grandmother to laugh the kind of laughter that just kept her laughing; which, was something storytellers would come to repeat again and again about the easy way of laughing of Grandmotherʼs easy going laughter; the laughter that drove the Older Brothers back up into the wilderness of the mountainside.

And so they sprang up, and then off and away they went; they rose limb by limb through the trees to quickly climb up ever so briskly straight on up into the canopy of the many trees of the great forest. Keyakatik xebʼe pa kʼechelaj.

“What are we going to do with you, you our beloved Grandmother? Because this time is the third time that we will try; this is the third chance to get it right, three out of four; before it will be four and then no more. That is all you have in store if you want to bring back your Boys who you care for more than any Grandmother has ever cared for her Boys; the Sons of your Sons, each one your Grandson; so this is it, one more chance and it will be three chances; but you have two more chances to come and then we are done,” said Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

And so they piped again, just as they drummed again, so that they could sing again. And so it was that they sang Junajpu Kʼoy again, and again they came in dancing.

The Dance of Junajpu Kʼoy; the Song of Junajpu Kʼoy

Once they came in dancing they began to dance their dance that they had already begun to dance their dance Junajpu Kʼoy as they made their way back home dancing as they danced right into Grandmotherʼs courtyard of Grandmotherʼs Great House; the Great House of the Great Mother, Great Matriarch who her Grandsons and Sons danced; for they danced for her, the Grandmother; the Grandmother of their Ancestral Lineage of the Monkey Ancestors of Painters and Scribes; Musicians and Singers; Flautists and Drummers; Singers and Storytellers.

body:
All of whom were celebrated through their dancing the dance of Junajpu Kʼoy that was danced to entertain her, the Great Matriarch of the Hunters and Gatherers where Grandmother was entertained by her Boys; her Men  by their dancing their dances for her; the Grand Mother; the Great Mother; Matriarch of the Ixim Winaq.

Junajpu Kʼoy was the ancestral song that was the ancestral dance that the first pair of twins danced when they came in dancing to the ancestral tune of the ancestral song that the second pair of twins performed when they sung Junajpu Kʼoy to the ancestral melody that was played on their ancestral flute and ancestral drum.

These were ancestral flute that accompanied the ancestral drum that they played to the ancestral rhythm that the Younger Sons kept on their ancestral drum; the Second Set of Sons; the Second Pair of Boy; the Second Couple of Twins who brought forth Junajpu Kʼoy as the Ancestral Remembrance of their Ancient Ancestors of their Ancient Lineage of the Animal Ancestors-Fallen and Failed Ancestors brought to life through the performance of the song and dance of Junajpu Kʼoy.

All of which the Younger Sons sung, piped, played, and drummed; these were those known; those who were named Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej who invoked the enchanting dance of their Older Brothers with the ancient, ancient ancestral tune they played out with their drum and flute while singing out their ancestorsʼ ancestral song known and named: Junajpu Kʼoy.

The tune they played was the tune they piped; the tune they piped was the rhythm they drummed to give form and shape to their ancestorsʼ ancient song that was the Original Ancient Ancestral Song of Junajpu Kʼoy; a song so enchanting that it captivated all those who heard it; a song so beguiling that it caused those who heard it to stand up to begin dancing along; for this was a deeply moving melody; this was a tune and rhythm that created movement by causing it to sprout forth by the way it was played and piped, sung and drummed with the flute, drum, and voice of the Ancient Ones who played this Ancient Ancestral Song in its Original Way. Just as the Hero Twins, Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej played it out here.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This time their Grandmother controlled her laughter, truly she did. She did not laugh; she just did not do it; she didnʼt smile; she was determined to go through it; she wasnʼt going to laugh that was all there was to it.

The Old Woman just watched the dancers dance their dance without laughing at all for she was determined to excuse her laughter by not laughing out loud as she had done twice before.

The Monkey Boys: the Older Brothers; the Dancers of Junajpu Kʼoy climbed up upon the upper edge of the ledge that crowned the patio walls. That is when she noticed that the rims surrounding their eyes turned bright red, while their mouths frowned, sort of sadly, more or less pathetically; the whiskers stood-up straight on their fuzzy-faced muzzle and furry-faced eyes that looked like saucers; just like thatch grass stood their whiskers standing erect to give them a furry-fuzzy look that made them appear perpetually excited.

They looked as if there was nobody to groom them anymore; as if there was nobody to who cared about the way the came to appear; which made them look like they were panicked more or less full of fear.

When Grandmother looked upon them with their scruffy unkempt faces the Old Woman just burst out laughing, she could not hold back anymore so she just laughed and laughed as the Monkeys danced across the floor.

She was over trying to hold herself together so she just let herself enjoy the laughter provoked by these wild looking Boys who she had always kept so groomed and dapper; so very prim and proper as artists and artisans like to appear.

Well that was certainly not how it was now that they were off on their own out in the forest to make it in the wilds of the mountain forest where they now made their home among the other animals that they now joined.

What else could she do but laugh at these two? And so she laughed at the wild untamed way they appeared; the rustic and unrefined way they now looked; now that they looked like feral beasts without anyone to care for them in their newly assigned habitat of the dense forest with its many, many trees they could climb in search of birds to have a bite of flesh theyʼd become so very accustomed to.

body:
And so it was that they were faces were no longer seen again by them because of their Grandmotherʼs laughter.

Ma chi kʼu xil chi kiwach rumal utzeʼbʼal Atiʼt.

But they tried anyway to call them with their flute, drum, and song because that was the way of the Boys, the Sons; those who were the Twins: Jun-Aj-Pu and Ix-Bʼalam-Kej. One Blowgun Boy and Little Jaguar Deer did what they did to make an example of the Monkey Twins: Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen.

“Just this time, just one more time, you our beloved Grandmother, we cautioned you, we advised you, we counseled you that we would only try four times. And this is the fourth time, the last chance, so do your best to pass this test to prevail over this ordeal to reveal you can overcome this trial.”

They took up their flutes to begin piping on their pipes as they played again on their flutes; but this time they didnʼt come back, the fourth time, straight-away they-their Older Brothers-went off into the forest and never came back again, they never returned home to their Grandmother.

It was there with their Grandmother that they learned so much beside ancestral fire that burned in her three hearth stones; the fire that warmed their hearts; the fire that sustained their souls. But that was all lost to them now as they entered the forest where they would be kept warm by the fur that now covered their bodies; the fur that now protected them from the cold.

This is when Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej spoke to their Grandmother: “Well we just did our best, you our Grandmother, Ix Qatiʼt  at first our Older Brothers returned dancing to our playing and piping, drumming and singing; and then we tried to call them back again a fourth time but they did not return.

Donʼt be sad, we are here-Oj kʼolik, Oj iwiey, we, your grandsons, we your teeth-oj iwiey-we your replacements, we your descendants, we your remembrance who are here to make you happy; to make you content with our ways of warming your heart.”

“We just love and care for our Mother and you, our Grandmother. Our Older Brothers will be remembered for we shall remember them when we name them every time we play their song; Junajpu Kʼoy! So be it! Ta chuxoq!”

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
“Was it not they who became vain and arrogant; was it not they who acted as entitled lords to humble and humiliate their Younger Brothers? And are they not entitled and are they not named Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen because of this, as it is said; as it is spoken; as it is remembered by all,” said Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

They, Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen, were invoked by flute-playing flautists, song-singing singers, by the Ancient Ones, Ojer Winaq; the Ancestral People remembered them by playing and dancing out the ancient ancestral ways of their song: Junajpu Kʼoy.

But they never returned again to where they original came from; they just made their home in the forest on the mountainside as the reversal of their destiny called for. For it was they who just swung-up straight into the mountain as they moved about limb from limb; up and up they went on and on as they climbed as they made their way up and across the mountainside as they kept going higher and higher to be those who came to live at the very top of wilderness where they live today as Lords of the Mountain.

Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen were invoked by scribes and sculptors, painters and carvers, in ancient times. It was they who were transformed into animals; for they were transformed into the Spider Monkey, Kʼoy that is what became of them because they made themselves out to be greater than all the rest.

It was just their endless acts of self-aggrandizement that brought them down like it did to others and always does to those who believe their essence shines as bright as the day in the light of the Sun; as bright as the night in the light of the Moon.

The Older Brothers humiliated their Younger Brothers for a long, long time by holding them in their hearts as their servants-kʼeje wi kalibʼil chi kikʼux as it is said in the Ojer Tzij.

Older Brothers-Younger Brothers; Noble Lords-Engendered Sons

body:
Which is to say the Older Brothers treated their Younger Brothers as if they were their subjects; they treated them as if they were their vassals known as Al, Kʼajol; Daughter, Son as the original invocation of the Popol Wuj speaks of the Saqil Al, Saqil Kʼajol; Precious Daughter, Precious Sons which is a fine refined way of speaking of the descendants; but this is not how these Pairs of Twins that were Couples of Twins treated one another and so those who acted as animals and by doing so caused suffering and pain; affliction and anguish were transformed into animals.

These animals are those that are perceived as they are seen which is as talented yet failed animal ancestors; animal ancestors who are seen as the First Ancestors-Nabʼey Winaq of the Ixim Winaq who will be formed and shaped from maize to become Maize Beings. But these Elder Brothers were formed and shaped from the flesh of animals for they ate the animals brought down from the mountains by the Hero Twins and so the flesh of their bodies did become animal flesh that was always hunted and eaten by the Ancient Ancestors of the Ixim Winaq as it is said here in mythic metaphorical ways.

It was just because of this disgraceful humiliating treatment of the Younger Brothers by the Older Brothers that those Older Brothers disappeared-sachnaq chik; they were just lost to the remembrance of the lineages except as perfectly good examples of perfectly bad examples of acting and speaking that should never be followed except as good example of what becomes of those who practice self-magnification.

And so it was that they, Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen were reduced in rank, just lowered in stature, lessened in status like the Wooden People who were transformed into the Spider Monkey-Kʼoy.

body:
This was when Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen disappeared from being the talented Artist and Artisans they were born to be from birth and through the training they received through their lineage of Artists and Artisans who and what they once were to become the fallen and failed kinds of Wild Animals that were there within them as their animal nature and essence that always lurks within beings who have no control over their appetite with its great power and potential to pull human being down into the lower forms and shapes of existence for humans and their struggle to be and become perfect and precious replacements of their Divine Ancestors; those known as the Nawal Winaq; the First Perfectly Formed and Shaped Beings of Maize. This is the story that tells of those First People of Maize and their first perfect and precious sacred way of being and becoming human on the Face of the Earth.

Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen, the First Sons of Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu were ʼcausedʼ to be lost; they were ʼcausedʼ to disappear in order to become in an instant that which they had called forth into existence as the animals they always acted and spoke before their perceived rivals; their imagined adversaries their Younger Brother. And that is how they became the animals that they always had been and continue to become as this very mischievous and ruinous; injurious and dangerous Kʼoy.

For truly they became ʼanimalsʼ and their descendants can be seen swinging and heard howling through the jungle forest as the Kʼoy who Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen were transformed into being; they just became those known as the Spider Monkey that is who and what they came to be.

These Two Boys molded and modeled themselves into perfectly fine example for those who wanted to become Wild Animals just like them: e chikop xeʼuxik.

New Domestic Life of the Domesticated Twins: Ixim Acha

New Life of Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej as Men of Maize: Hombres de Maíz

body:
It was then that they made themselves at home. As flautists, they just played their flutes; as singers, they just sang their songs as they began to play-out the new ways of their new domestic lives as the kʼexel of Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen entering where they once had been not so long ago.

They-JunAjPu, IxBʼalamKej-accomplished great things in no time that demonstrated as it revealed in order to express their nawal essence-xekʼojeʼik that was the nawal condition-kʼojeʼik of their true nature while living there with their Grandmother and Mother who now showed them the care and concern that manifest as deep respect and regard, even favor, for the Boys, the Sons, ri Kʼajolabʼ.

They eagerly began showing all they could do as they revealed their many capacities and capabilities working while playing flute and singing songs there before their Grandmother and-pu their Mother; chuwach katiʼt, chuwach pu kichuch.

Again this use of ʼpuʼ for the conjunction ʼandʼ is a stupendous play on this ʼnawal puffʼ of magical exaltation-expiration of breathe is the way ʼprayer-makers and day-keepersʼ transforms that which calls to be magically transformed through the shamanic aspiration of ʼpuʼ as an expulsion of undesirable beings or essences or conditions or natures as an ʼacting of blowing awayʼ that which is not wanted to then invoke, in order to petition, in order to receive the that which is desired through this ritual act of ancestral transformation. This is the ancestral exaltation leading to change and transformation that is the work and way of AjPu.

Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej began to know what it felt like to be settled down-e ramaqʼelal into a domestic life of sowing and tending the milpa now that their living as the servant-alabʼil-hunters were over.

The first work that they wished to perform was to walk out to where they would begin working in ʼla milpa-ri abʼixʼ that was their family field of maize-ri abʼix.

“We are just-xa going to go work the maize in the milpa you our Grandmother, and you our Mother,” they said. Xa kojabʼixik, ix QaTiʼt, ix pu QaChuch.

body:
“Donʼt be sad, we are here; we, your Grandsons; we, the replacements of our Older Brothers,” said Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

So then it was that each one of then took up their axe-ki-kaj as they took up their hoe-ki-mixkina to carry them on their shoulder-ki-xokem before heading out to the mountainside, each one of them shouldering their blowgun-kiwubʼ xkitelej.

They left their house after giving instructions to their Grandmother as to when she was to bring them their sustenance: “When the sun is straight overhead come bring us our mid-day meal, you, our Grandmother,” they said.

“Utz bʼa la, you my Grandsons-Ix Weʼy-you my teeth, you my replacements,” she said then, their Grandmother.

When they arrived there at their milpa they took up their hoe and sunk it in the ground where they wanted it to begin doing their work in the earth; the work to hoe the milpa to sow the seed to grow the maize; all of which was theirs to do.

And just like that their hoe knew just what a good hoe must know, which was where to go and what to do.

And so their hoe formed row after row of milpa so the Boys could sow the seed that would sprout out as row upon row of maize that would grow in perfectly formed rows of milpa; milpa that was shaped into perfectly formed rows of sprouts that grew as perfectly shaped rows of maize.

Their hoe worked all by itself because it knew just what to do and just where go as a hoe that knew what a hoe has to know in order to know where to go and what to do. This was the work of their hoe that worked all alone doing all that it was asked to do which was to work the milpa all alone for the Boys who knew this was their work to do by themselves without any help from any others.

It wasnʼt only the hoe that was asked work by itself, to what it had to do entirely alone, on its own but their axe too worked as it was asked to do by itself, entirely alone, utterly on its own to clear the forest for the sowing, sprouting, and growing of their milpa-pa abʼix.

body:
And so the hoe and the axe were asked to work by themselves.  The Boys just sank their axe into the trunk of a tree for the axe to begin chopping the tree down to the ground; once the axe chopped the tree down it turned to the branches to cut them up into pieces; before long, the trees and vines came down one after the other where the forest once stood and where the milpa was soon to be sown by the Boys who worked their milpa with their hoe and axe who did their work alone, left to themselves to do all that was theirs to do on their own.

Perfectly stacked rows of firewood were what had become of the many felled trees that just one hard-working axe had chopped-down and cut-up all by itself as the axe of the Boys had done as it worked totally on its own; perfectly alone; all by itself; that was the way of their axe; the axe of the Boys who were hunters by nature of their names One Hunter and He/She of the Little Jaguar-Deer.

And as for the hoe, it plowed up a great big area of milpa; immense was the area of thorny brush that this one hoe cleared away, all by itself, left alone doing the work of those who were Nawal Winaq; those who were quite capable of animating their tools to perform the work that wasnʼt truly theirs to do unless done in the nawal way that the Boys used their axe and hoe to do their work in this most magical way.

Truly vast was the piece of land that this one hoe of theirs turned over all by itself as it moved over the milpa plowing the ground up and down, row after row. This how their nawal hoe worked as it hoed up the earth as it moved over and across ground; the ground of the earth where they worked their milpa there on the Small Mountain; there on the Big Mountain doing the work that was their work to do; or so they assumed to be true.

Their hoe knew just where to go just it knew just what to do, as it moved about not too fast, not to slow clearing away the weeds, to then cut and clear the thorny brambles and spiny brush of the mountainside where the Boys, the Sons, the Twins were called to prepare the ground to sow the seed to grow their Grandmother and Motherʼs milpa.

body:
Their nawal hoe knew just what to do as it worked the soil without a bit of toil as it turned to working the earth by plowing up the ground, preparing the rich ground of the newly cut and cleared forest.

All alone, all by itself went the hoe doing its work without the least bit of effort; without the least bit of toil as it transformed the mountainside into milpa where they would sow their maize seed in its perfectly prepared soil.

And so it was that these Two Boys gave their instructions to an animal-jun chikop Dove-Xmukur-Paloma was her name.

They placed the Dove-Xmukur-la Paloma on the trunk of a tree and then Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej said: “Just watch for our Grandmother when she comes to give us our food, just cry out when she comes up the trail, so we can grab-hold of our hoe and our axe so it looks like we are working.”

“Utz bʼa la,” said then the Dove, la Paloma-xechaʼ kʼu ri Xmukur.

Meanwhile they were just out hunting with their blowguns-xa wubʼanik. This was what they knew; this was the only thing these two knew how to do that was truly theirs; so it wasnʼt true that they were out working the milpa, as they said they were going to do.

So this then was when Ixmuqur-Dove-Paloma cried out as a sign, as a signal that Grandmother was coming. They ran right back to their milpa where they were working: one grabbed hold of the hoe and one grabbed hold of the axe.

They just bundled up their heads like real workers would; each one bound their head with their headscarf-chipis kiwi.

One of them ʼintentionally-xloqʼ-deliberatelyʼ covered his hands with earth; the other one dirtied his face dust just like a true maize worker would do who worked the milpa-qitzij abʼixom-un milpero de verdad.

The other one ʼintentionally-xloqʼ-deliberatelyʼ threw woodchips all over his head as if he were a true woodchopper would do and this is how he wanted to present himself to his Grandmother who was the ancestral authority when it came to the growing of their milpa.
