body:
And so it was that when Grandmother arrived they were seen as humble workers of the milpa; one a hard working ʼmozoʼ with his hoe and the other a hard working woodchopper with his axe; and, that is how they were seen by their Grandmother who climbed up the mountainside with their mid-day meal.

This was when they sat and ate their mid-day meal with their Grandmother. They ate the food their Grandmother carried-up the mountainside to bringing to them where they worked.

They just sat and rested to eat together alongside their work in the milpa where they worked with their axe and worked with their hoe that they had used to do the work of clearing the forest for the growing of their milpa that they would soon sow to then tend when it sprouted out and began to grow.

For truly, the milpa of theirs that was to be sown to be grown like a true milpa was the milpa that they would be sow like a true milpa but first they had to prepare the milpa with their axe and hoe.

But it wasnʼt true; they werenʼt really working in the forest clearing there where their milpa would be sown and grown by their axe and hoe that worked all by themselves; absolutely alone even though their Grandmother brought them their food as if they were doing their work completely on their own.

They just made it look like they were working with the hoe and axe when they were just doing what they liked most and were born to do with names like Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej; One Blowgun Boy and Little Jaguar Deer; these two were natural born hunters who would come to see the milpa as a lure to entice the animals they came to hunt at night as much as the place from which their sacred sustenance was harvested. The milpa of the Maya is truly an enchanted place where nobody goes unless it is theirs to know and protect.

As soon as they arrived back home they said: “Truly we are just all tired out, you our Grandmother, Ix Qatiʼt!”

Then they ʼintentionallyʼ that is to say ʼdeliberatelyʼ rubbed themselves down while stretching their legs and arms there before their Grandmother feigning the soreness and exhaustion of true workers.

body:
Right there in front of their Grandmother they made a show of all the work they performed in the milpa that day with their hoe and axe; axe and hoe that knew just what to do and just were to go to work not too fast, not to slow preparing the milpa for the seed to be sown where the maize would be grown by the axe and hoe that worked entirely alone; by themselves; on their own.

The following morning the Boys returned where theyʼd worked the day before in their milpa-pa kabʼix-where all the trees; all the vines stood-up straight once again-kʼisyakatajinaq chik.

The trees, the vines of the forest were bound back together, twisted up tighter than before so that the forest was sealed by a knot of thorny bushes; bristling brambles.

“Who has pulled this over on us?” they asked then.

“Apachinaq kojmichʼowik?” Xechaʼ kʼut.

This was the doing of those who are the:

Small Animals; Chʼuti Chikop,

Big Animals; Nima Chikop

Who were known and named:

Puma; Koj

Jaguar; Bʼalam

Deer; Kiej

Rabbit; Umul

Fox; Yak

Coyote; Utiw

Jabali; Aq

Coati; Sis

Small Birds; Chʼuti Tzʼikin

Big Birds; Nima Tzʼikin

These are the ones who did it; in just one night they did it by rising-up together in the darkness to then incite the forest to rise-up again.

In one night under the cover of darkness the Birds and Animals summonsed the Trees and Vines to  stand-up again there the forest where the limbs of its trees and the arms of its vines had always been the dwelling place of the Animal People; the Ancient One, the Ancestral Residence of the Forest; the Abode; the Dwelling Place of the all many Birds and Animals who had been given their Mountain Places and Canyon Country as their Home that had always been their place to multiply and grow.

It was in just one night that they did it; they brought the forest back to life to then raise it up once again in order to leave it standing as it stood before.

So once again the Boys began working their milpa with their hoe that knew just what to do and just where to go in order to perform their work as it had done before to prepare the earth where their milpa would be sown where the maize would be grown.

body:
Once again their axe knew just where to go and just what to do to cut down the trees to then clear-out the branches and clean-up the brush, tear-up the roots, and bury the limbs and leaves before helping the hoe clear away the weeds to prepare for the seeds to be sown so milpa could be grown were the axe had been left to do its work all alone, by itself, on its own.

And this is exactly what they did once again so that the axe and hoe could complete the work of the Boys with their hoe and axe working all by themselves, by knowing what they knew which was where to go and what to do on their own.

And this was to clear the land of trees and vines for the sowing of the seed that soon would be sprouting and growing as the sign of their work that was their cutting and chopping; clearing and hoeing that was a sure way of showing their nawal way of knowing just how to transform the face of the earth for the sowing and dawning of Maize Peopleʼs nawal way of life of axing and hoeing for the seeding, the sowing of the sprouting and growing of the milpa of maize.

These Nawal Boys preferred to accomplish their work in the milpa with their ancestral magic and its way of knowing how to prepare the ground for sowing the seed that was to be sown where the milpa was prepared to be grown by their axe and hoe working alone, by themselves, on their own.

Then the Boys gathered together their thought-kinaʼoj their genius-kinaʼoj their insight-kinaʼoj in order to take council with one another there where the trees had been cut-down by their axe on its own; where the earth had been cleared off and cleaned-up with their hoe working all alone.

Ta xkʼam chi kʼu kinaʼoj chiriʼ pa qʼatoj cheʼ pa qʼupuj puch…

body:
This was when they brought together their thoughts-naʼoj…their genius-naʼoj…their insights-naʼoj where they cut-down the trees and where they cut-open the earth…This is a metaphor that speaks of ʼheart sacrificeʼ as the reciprocal payment of the human debt for cutting-chopping down the trees and cutting-chopping open the earth in very metaphorical, mythic sorts of ways…pure ancestral thought…pure ancestral genius…pure ancestral insight…Ojer Naʼoj…as one might say today in a genius sort of thoughtful kind of insightful type of way…

These genius phrases speak of the Maize Peopleʼs sacrifice Mountain-Plain with its trees and vines of the forest and the soil of the ground of face of the earth.

This sacrifice of the Trees and Vine; Bushes and Grass; Earth and Ground; Land and Soil creates the ʼgreat debtʼ of the ʼmaize peopleʼ that must be paid back to the Ukʼuʼx Kaj; Ukʼuʼx Ulew through human sacrifice where and in which the human head is ʼchopped-offʼ through ritual decapitation and the chest ʼcut-openʼ to then the heart ʼcut-outʼ to be fed to the ʼheart of the fireʼ as the beating rubberball of human heart sacrifice. So realize there is much more going on here than what appears by a superficial reading of this magic metaphorical mythic text.

Kʼate chi kʼut xkitikʼibʼa chik abʼixik. Xawi xubʼan chi ribʼ ulew rukʼ qʼatoj cheʼ. Ta xkʼam chi kʼu kinaʼoj chiriʼ pa qʼatoj cheʼ; pa qʼupuj pu…This is what is spoken of above as the ʼcutting-offʼ and the ʼcutting-throughʼ the head and the chest…the trees and the earth…the trunk of the trees and ribs of the earth…

So then it was there that they began working the milpa where the Boys stood-up where their hoe cut open the ground to prepare the land and its soil for the sowing of the seed; where the forest had been cleared and cleaned by the axe that cut-down the trees and vines to clear the bushes and grass; limbs and leaves to ready the milpa for the planting of its seeds.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This then was when they brought together their thoughts to contemplate their imagination to reveal their genius as the celebrated council with one another as to what was required from them to bring about the sowing of the seed in the planting of their milpa.

“We must just sleep here in our milpa to keep watch; this way we will catch them by surprise doing what they are  doing in our milpa,” said the Boys when they gathered together their thoughts.

“We must remain here vigilant throughout the night to surprise those who did what they are doing, so that we capture them in the act doing what theyʼre doing,” said the Boys as they made plans.

“We really must just stay up through the night out here in our milpa so we can find out who did what they did so we can stop  them from doing whatever they are doing so they canʼt do what they did again,” said Boys as they revealed their brilliance.

This is what they said when they gathered together their thoughts; when they took council with one another; when they came to an accord there in the forest before their Grandmotherʼs milpa.

This then was when they went back home to talk it over with their Grandmother and Mother about what had happened during the night before in the milpa where they had worked so hard to prepare the land for the sowing of their milpa; there where they readied the earth for the planting of their maize.

It was then that they arrived home.

“Who is pulling one over on us, you our beloved Grandmother? The thatch-grass has grown right back and the forest once again stands where the earth had been left so perfectly prepared-clear and clean-for the sowing of our milpa. We found our milpa completely grown back with tall pajón-bunch grass and a great big forest when we arrived there just a short while ago, you our Grandmother, Ix Qatiʼt,” they said then to their Grandmother and Mother.

“So then, we shall just be going. We will sleep there on the mountain because it is just no good what they are doing to us,” they said; the Boys, the Sons, the Twins: Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

body:
Then they readied themselves, they bundled themselves up with protective cotton armor-xebʼatzonik; they covered themselves with a light armor suit of cotton bating not knowing who or what they would be combating.

So then they went to where they had cut down the trees of the forest to clear it for their milpa; it was there that they hid themselves-xematzeje wi; it was there where they buried themselves in the damp earth there-e muqumuxinaq chire.

This is when the animals gathered together; as one they sat on the ground together, all the Small Animals, all the Big Animals came together as Just One: Xa Jun.

And so this then was when the very heart of the night stood straight-up above where the Animals were now gathered; this was when the Animals stood as one to speak out about what mattered most to them: the Animals of the Forest.

And so it was that they spoke straight to the point as one voice when they gathered together in the middle of the night as Just One: Xa Jun.

This then is the language they spoke when they spoke their language at midnight, “Yaklin Cheʼ, Yaklin Kʼaʼm, Rise-up Trees, Rise-up Vines…Yaklin Cheʼ, Yaklin Kʼaʼm, Rise-up Trees, Rise-up Vines.”

This is what they said, this is what they sung, as a beguiling incantation to enchant the trees and vines of the forest by those who had been given this place of the trees and vines; the forest where they were gifted their sleeping places among the canyons and ravines where the sustenance was always there to be found as long as there were no people around to cut the trees and vines to the ground.

The Big Animals and Small Animals entered there together in order to form a line to bring forth the forest that had always been theirs.

They lined up under the trees, under the vines in the forest, in the brush and brambles; this is when they appeared, when they showed their faces; then and there they just called upon the trees as they called upon the vines of the forest with their enchanting incantation spoken together as one invocation there in the middle of the night:  “Yaklin Cheʼ, Yaklin Kʼaʼm, Rise-up Trees, Rise-up Vines…Yaklin Cheʼ, Yaklin Kʼaʼm, Rise-up Trees, Rise-up Vines.”

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
The first ones were the Puma-Koj; the Jaguar-Bʼalam. The Boys tried to catch them but they did not give themselves up easily, they just bound away with their long tails waving up and all about them; there was no way to catch them because they moved so fast the Boys couldnʼt even touch them.

Then came the Deer-Kej; the Rabbit-Umul it was they who would appear next. The Boys almost got them when each one of them caught one by their tail but it was all to no avail because the tail of the Deer just popped off in the grasp of the first brother just like the tail of the Rabbit dropped off in the hand of the other brother who barely caught that bounder in his grasp. And so it was the Deer and Rabbit gave up their tails as a remembrance of useless lopped off things of the past.

The tail that popped of the Deer and the lopped tail of the Rabbit were snatched away by the Boys who pulled too hard on their luckless prey thus leaving their tails bobbed to this very day.

This is the way Deer and Rabbit look today with popped off, lopped off tails so that nobody can catch them eating maize in the milpa in a  fair exchange for their losing their tail in their bounding, bouncing get-away.

The animals didnʼt give themselves up easily; Fox-Yak, Coyote-Utiw, Jabali-Aq, Coati-Sis all these animals passed right there in front of the Boys; Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej never touched them.

And so it was that the animals just ran right passed where the Boys were dug-in the damp earth; and so it was that the Animals crossed right before Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej who never even touched them.

This just burned up their hearts; the truth that they could not catch a single one of them; for the Animals slipped right through the Boys grip to avoid the Boys grasp when they tried to catch the Animals to find out what they were doing there in the forest.

body:
These were the forest Animals who the Boys thought would be so easy to catch by grabbing them by the tail. ʼButʼ the reason for that will reveal itself at the ʼendʼ of this ʼtaleʼ that speaks of the Boys quest to find in the ʼendʼ that which was truly theirs in life which is the story that is told here of the Animals who knew what was theirs in life to bring to completion; what was theirs to bring to fruition in life that one needed to know what was oneʼs to do to then just go out and do it. And this the Boys would find out soon enough to then take up the road to begin doing what was theirs to do in life. So letʼs get on with it to tell that tale of tale that tells of tails and their getting burnt!

So then came one more, he was the last one: uxambʼe chik. Just bouncing, just bounding down the path he came, as he came jumping as he came bumping along the road not seeing where he was going.

This is how Mouse came when they saw him coming hopping and bopping along-xa katzotzotik ta xpetik towards the First and Second Son. It was they who then grabbed him by the throat as they grasped him by the neck there behind his head-kʼate kʼut xkiqʼatej, xkise kʼut pa qul ri chʼo kʼate puch xkichapo, xkiyotej puch chirij uwi xraj kibʼiyo-they just wanted to strangle him to finish him off right then and there.

They tightened their grip around his throat thinking that by strangling him he would talk but then they realized that was no way to go about getting what they wanted so they burnt his tail over the fire and got just what they needed.

Why were the Big Animals, Small Animals there beseeching the Trees and Vines to rise-up; to rise-up again out of the place where they had cleared the Forest to clean it for the Milpa for the sowing of their Maize? But the Mouse said nothing; keeping what he knew within him not wanting to reveal what he knew so well was theirs to have; so he kept quiet not saying a word until he got what was his in life in exchange for that which was theirs in life.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This then was when the Boys brought Mouse over to the fire to then burn his tail over their flames and that is why the Mouse has no hair on his tail. While causing his eyes to bulge out of his head because of the way the Mouse was throttled by the Boys, the Sons Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej. This then was when he began crying out; when he began calling out as best he could!

“I should not die because of you! Ma ta kinkamik iwumal! I should not die because of you!”

“What is yours in life is other than your working in the Milpa! Mawi are ipatan ri abʼixik! Your destiny is not that of a Milpero; not you two; this is not that which is yours; but there is that which is yours; Kʼo iwe; Kʼo iwe-there is yours; there is that which is yours!” Cried the Mouse.

“This working the milpa is not for you; this is not what is yours life; this is not what is your burden to bear; but, there is what is yours! Ma to kinkamik iwumal! Mawi are ipatan ri abʼixik. Kʼo iwe!”

“I can tell you what is yours! Donʼt kill me; I will tell you what is yours in life; and what is yours is what I carry within me; so donʼt finish me off; for I should not die because of you!”

“Tending Maize in the Milpa is not yours do; it is not your calling; it is not your destiny-Mawi are ipatan ri abʼixik.”

“The Milpa is not yours to bring to fruition; the Milpa is not your burden to bear; the Milpa is not yours but there is what is yours; and, that which is yours is what I bear within me,” said Mouse.

“La Milpa: its four precious corners; its four perfect sides; its jade seeds; its ancient roots; its resplendent sprouts; its green leaves; its sweet canes; its golden heads; its shimmering tresses; its flowering tassels; its buzzing bees; its whispering wasps these are  not yours to bring to fruition-mawi are ipatan ri abʼixik; chopping with the axe in the Forest; hacking with the hoe in la Milpa; working its perfectly aligned rows; hoeing row after row of maize that grow in milpa is not the burden you were born to bear in life; but there is what is yours and its is right over there.”

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
“Working the Milpa-Abʼixik is not yours to fulfill; your ʼgeniusʼ is not tending and protecting la Milpa; it is not yours to do, for it is not your calling; it is not your truth! Yet, there is that which is yours; there is yours to come true; it is over there; over there is what is yours; there is your ancestral essence, the ʼgeniusʼ that is you,” said the Mouse-ri Chʼo-el Ratoncito.

“Where is it; this that is ours? What is it; that which is ours? ¿Apa kʼo wi qe? Tell us now!-Chabʼij na kʼut! Speak then; tell us now; what is it; where can we find that which is ours that can be found!” asked the Boys to the Mouse.

There is that which is yours-e kʼo iwumal. What is that which is Oneʼs Destiny?

The question raised here is of the greatest importance to the Kʼicheʼ Maya who like all of Mesoamerica will follow the Divinatory Calendar know as the Sacred Count of Days from which they will be provided guidance and protection in all they do and wherever they go. The question for humanity is how do we human beings know what is ours in life; and, how do we know what to do once we find what is ours?

The Boys, the Twins find out what is theirs by catching ʼa ratʼ that is ʼa mouseʼ who they must give up everything that is of valuable to the Maya which is their  sacred sustenance in exchange for what they want and need in life to survive. Popol Wuj is founded in this primordial exchange between Divinity and Humanity: What do we need to survive and what are we willing to give in exchange to receive what we must have to survive? This is the character and condition of survival just as it is essence and nature of sacrifice: what is our sacred sustenance and what must we sacrifice to attain it in abundance?

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
The Boys who are the Engendered Sons of Jun Junajpu receive a boon; a great gift from the Mouse known as Chʼo for the Knowledge of Destiny that they receive from him that is a ʼlife and deathʼ question of survival. The Mouse provides the Boys Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej with what they want but the cost of this exchange made for this Knowledge of Destiny is outrageously expensive indeed. For they are willing to sacrifice all the sources of human sustenance to receive what they receive from Choʼ the Mouse who tells the Boys not only what it is but where to get while they must use their nawal  genius to deceive their Grandmother and Mother; IxMuqane and IxKikʼ

“Working the Milpa-Abʼixik is not yours to fulfill; your ʼgeniusʼ is not the sowing and growing of your Grandmotherʼs Milpa; it is not yours to do, for it is not your calling; it is not your truth nor is it your true longing! Yet, there is that which is yours; there is your dream to come true; it is over there; over there is what is yours; there is your ancestral essence-kʼojeʼik, the ʼgeniusʼ that is yours; your ancestral presence-kʼojeʼik,” said the Mouse-ri Chʼo-el Ratoncito.

“Where is it; this that is ours? ¿Apa kʼo wi qe? What is it; where is it; this that is ours?” asked the Boys who now begged the Mouse to answer their question.

“Tell us then now!-Chabʼij na kʼut! Speak then; say then what is ours; tell us then where this that is ours can be found!” pleaded the Boys who began to feel a certain sort of obligation to now take care of this Mouse; and so they continued.

“Well let up on me a little bit then because the truth of my word is within me; release me and I will tell you what I have to say; just give me a little bit of that which is mine; give me a little bit of that which is my sustenance!” said Mouse.

“So then, we will give you what is yours when you tell what you have to say,” they said to him. “Kʼate chiqayaʼo awechaʼ, chabʼij na,” xuchaʼxik.

body:
“Utz bʼa la! Very well then! All that is your Fathersʼ, all those things that belong to them, those whose names are Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu; those who died in Xibʼalbʼa; their ball-game equipment, their ball-playing gear; all of those things that what theirs are yours; all that they left behind is yours; this is that which is yours. That which was theirs is that which is yours; their ballgame regalia is what stayed right here, it remains where they left it, hanging down from where they left it tied up in the rafters of their house-pa utum ja:

Their wooden yokes, kibʼate for ʼbeating-bʼaʼ the ball on your hip

Their arm guards, kipachqʼabʼ to protect your arms from the ball

Their rubber ball, kikikʼ from the rubber sap they tapped from their trees

“Just donʼt show them to your Grandmother; it was ʼjust-xaʼ because of them that your Fathers died,” said the Mouse-ri Chʼo-el Ratoncito.

“Can it be true all that you say?” asked the Boys to the Mouse, chi re Chʼo.

They felt such great contentment knowing that there was something that was theirs in life left behind by their Fathers; their hearts-kikʼux where made sweet when they received the news, the word, the truth about the rubberball-utzijel kikʼ.

It was time then that they gave Mouse what was his; the sustenance that would always sustain Mouse-rechaʼ Chʼo the food that was given to him is what it continues to be:

Maize-Ixim

White-seeds of Chilacayote squash-Sakil

Chili-Ik

Bean-Kinaqʼ

Pataxte-Peq

Cacao, Kakaw

“This then is what is yours-Are kʼut awech ri! All of the food that ends up in the trash is yours to find. All of this that is hidden away and poorly stored is yours to enjoy; just eat it up! Chakʼuxu! Chew it up! Grind it up!”

This is what was said to ri Chʼo, the Mouse by Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

“Utz bʼa la, Ix Kʼajolabʼ; Well alright Boys, I just wonder what should be said if your Grandmother sees me? What should I say?” he asked then, ri Chʼo. And so they explained to him what they would do to retrieve what was theirs from where it was now hanging in the rafters of Grandmotherʼs house.

body:
“Donʼt lose heart Ratoncito mio, you donʼt have to worry about that, we will be there, we know how to speak to her; we know just what to say. Straight-away we will leave you there in the corner of the house from where you will make your way to where the ballgame equipment is hanging.”

“There we will see you clearly through the hole that opens up into the rafters of the house, the tabanco-utum ja-as it is known, as it is named; utum ja; en el tabanco de la casa; in the rafters of the house. Only we will be looking down in our soup to see you up above,” they said to the Mouse when they gave him his instructions, when they took council with one-an-other when they brought forth their plan, the plan that was the idea of Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej. And so they went walking down the mountain from where they had once wished to sow the seed of their Grandmother and Motherʼs milpa. Now they were returning home with a different sense of who they were and what was theirs in life.

When the Sun stood straight overhead was when they arrived where they now returned-kʼi kʼu tikʼil qʼiij xeʼoponik.

For it was exactly at ʼMid-Dayʼ when they arrived; the Sun was ʼplantedʼ ʼstandingʼ directly above when they returned.  The Mouse, Ri Chʼo could not be seen when they carried him in to Grandmotherʼs house when they came in.

One Son entered straight into the house-jun ri yakalik xok pa ja;

One Son entered at the corner of the house-jun kʼu xok xikin ja where he quickly set Mouse up under the rafters of Grandmothersʼ house.

This was when they asked Grandmother for their food, their ground chili-water soup-qʼutum ik: “Perhaps you might grind-up a bite for us to eat, we would just like to have a little ground chili-water soup; a nice warm broth of ground roasted red chili-qʼutum ik-you, our Grandmother- Ix Qatiʼt,” they said then there when they spoke to their Grandmother there in her kitchen; there in her house where she slept to tend the embers of her fire that never went out there in her three stone hearth place.

body:
And so then she fixed them their meal, just a bite to eat. One bowl of ground chili broth was ʼplantedʼ before them there as their food that was ʼplacedʼ in a bowl before them to eat.

Only they pulled a fast one on their Grandmother and Mother. They emptied the water-pot; the water-jug; the ʼtinajaʼ by evaporating it away with their nawal powers of evaporation-kitzajisaj kʼu ja pa qʼebʼal.

The Boys Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej use their powers of evaporation to evaporated the water out of Grandmotherʼs big round water jug: qʼebʼal known as a ʼtinajaʼ from here on out in this story of Grandmotherʼs water jug-qʼebʼal that will be spoken of as a ʼtinajaʼ.

“Truly our mouths are dry from our great thirst, Grandmother. Perhaps you might bring us something to drink,” they said to their Grandmother.

“Wee! Fine,” she said then, when she left.

So then they went on eating. But it wasnʼt true that they were hungry. Just deception alone was their doing; just veiling the vision of their Grandmother was their way of making this way of deception of theirs; they just wanted to hide what they were doing there.

It was then that they saw the Mouse in their ground-chili-water soup-qʼutum ik. He was there curled around the rubberball; the rubberball that was hanging down from up above in the house: xekel wi puwi ja.

They saw this in their ground chili water soup that Grandmother ʼplantedʼ before them; they looked up above into the tabanco when they looked down below in their bowl of soup.

This then is when they sent for the strong little black Gnat that was a strong little Fly that bores holes in the side of the earth before the rains came; this is the one known as Xaʼn who they sent on an errand of theirs; just a sign of the rains that were about to fall from above.

Now this Xaʼn is like an Us who is a tiny Black Gnat that leaves a swollen round mark and a little spot of blood where it bites hard to suckle the blood from oneʼs flesh.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
They just sent Xaʼn to where Grandmother was beside the River, by the waterside-chi Jaʼ and there it was that Xaʼn began drilling out the ʼfaceʼ of Grandmotherʼs tinaja-qʼebʼal from which water now sprang forth from all the little holes that Xan bored out from which water now poured out of Grandmotherʼs tinaja-qʼebʼal. This was the drinking water she had scooped up from the river to calm the thirst of her Boys.

The Old Woman tried but she just couldnʼt do it; she couldnʼt close-up all holes that the Xaʼn bored from which water now poured from the earthen face of her clay tinaja: qʼebʼal.

And so then they spoke so all could hear what they had to say:

“Whatever could have happened to our Grandmother? Where is she? What could she be doing?  We are just desperate for a bit of water. We will soon be finished off by our thirst,” they said then now, this time they directed their speech directly towards their Mother.

This was when they sent her out for a little bit of water to quench their burning thirst that came from their chili-water soup; there was nothing else they could do they just had to send her out for their water, so truly parched were they now.

It was then that the Mouse gnawed away at the twisted rope from which hung the rubberball and all that hung bundled together with it.

It wasnʼt long before it all took a fall to where they were waiting to catch it down below; this ancestral bundle of their Fathersʼ ball-game equipment and rubberball that hung down from up in the tabanco-pu tum ja.

This was when the Chʼo cut it so it didnʼt make a sound when he made it fall down to the ground where the Boys were there to receive it;

The wooden waist yoke: ri bʼate.

The jaguar-skin arm guards:  pachqʼabʼ.

The deer skins: ri tzʼum for protection.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Immediately then, they gathered it all up; they just gathered it from where it fell to the floor. Then they went off to where they hid their bundle beside the road; there on the Road to the Ballcourt; there on the road to the Ballcourt-Burial Grounds-Jom; ubʼeal Jom. The Road to the Ballcourt is where they hid what had been their Fathers and was now theirs with which to play the ballgame which was theirs to play with their rubberball which was theirs to play ball for now they had it all: their ballgame equipment and their rubberball.  For truly what was theirs was what was theirs; and what was theirs was what had been their Fathers.

Quickly then did they arrive to where their Grandmother was beside the water-chi yaʼ.

Their Grandmother-Atiʼt and Mother-Chuch were there beside the river where they were doing their best to seal the face of each one-jujun-of their tinajas-qʼebʼal or water jugs specially made for carrying water.

They arrived beside the river, each one-jujun with a blowgun. This is when they addressed their Grandmother and Mother.

“What is going on?  We ran-out of patience; truly, our hearts tired of the wait, so we came to see what may have happened to you here beside the river; here beside the water-chi ya,” they said.

Grandmother said: “Just look at the face of my tinaja, there is no way to seal it; drip, drop; drip, drop; there is no way to make it stop,” said Grandmother.

But the Boys, the Sons, they sealed it up immediately; instantly they closed up all the tiny holes on the face of Grandmotherʼs tinaja. And together they returned home, this time it was they, the Boys, who walked before their Grandmother.

In this way the rubberball ended up with them, for it now ʼremainedʼ with them to ʼstayʼ in their possession; this ball of theirs that was their Fathersʼ rubberball. And so it was that the Boys, the Sons were left with their Fathersʼ ball-playing ball and their ball-playing equipment; their protection and adornment, their headdress, gloves, yoke, and skins.

Utum Jaʼ; Utum Ja: the Dew from Dusk to Dawn;

Horizontal Rain of the Warm Wet Nights of the Dry Season

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
The maize sprouts that come up and out of the ʼapparentlyʼ dry earth at the beginning of the growing season are watered from the night time dew known as utum jaʼ or water gathered inside the ʼtwisted conical coneʼ of corn plants. This is what the Popol Wuj is telling us here through this masterful mythic metaphor of maize. Let us discover how this comes forth as the Boys call out to the Grandmother and Mother for water to quench their thirst because the heat of their chili water soup has left them parched.

This is secret sort of sacred language of mythic metaphor is known to the Maya as the language of Tzuy-Wa or Suywa or Suyua. Tzuy-Wa is known as the language of the Gourd Head People or Tzuy-Gourd and Wa-Head or Gourd-Tzuy Wa-Sustenance which is the Divine Sustenance drank from a gourd vessel or tzuy.  Tzuy-Wa is Divine Knowledge of the Changing-Transforming Way of Life, Death, and Rebirth on the Face of the Earth.

In this magical metaphorical world of Popol Wuj; it is the imaginal realm in which the words that are spoken are heard as a secret sort of sacred language shaped from words that are often homonyms like Jaʼ and Ja in which Water-Jaʼ and House-Ja sound ʼalmostʼ identical to one another.

And this magnificent play on words is a play I would have never known had I not been out walking early one morning to accidentally meet up with an elderly old Maya Man of Maize who was up early on the mountainside tending his milpa. Who mentioned the utum jaʼ the gathered dew water that had collected through a very wet night to leave his milpa completely watered by the ʼhorizontal rainʼ that falls as dew throughout the dry season on the mountainside of the exceedingly wet countryside surrounding Lake Atitlan and the forests that surround it.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
What is most remarkable now is that we have arrived at the time of year from late January to May when heavy dew fall like horizontal rain to provide the water that falls out of the sky all through the night from dusk to dawn. Like sap that drips from the Moon Goddess IxKikʼ, this watery essence once known as ʼitzʼ drops as the heavy dew that drenches the milpa from sunset to sunrise during the first two moons of the lifecycle of maize in the highlands and lowlands of the Kʼicheʼ. As in the word pitz that may come from: pa itz or from its essence or pitzʼ.

The Maya speak of ʼitzʼ or ʼengendering energy of the skyʼ is the ʼspiraling light waves or light particlesʼ kind of energy that comes from the rays of the sun that strike the atmosphere to create this ʼitzʼ energy that is the very same as the ʼprana-energyʼ of spinning and spiraling-spermatic sort of light particles one is able to see by looking up in the daytime sky to then look up into the sky with an open unfocused gaze. This ʼitzʼ or ʼpitzʼ is rather easily observed in the blue sky with oneʼs ʼopen visionʼ where appear these shooting, spinning, spiraling, ʼparticles of light or waves of lightʼ that are ʼseenʼ coming out of the sky. Or is it oneʼs eye that creates the phenomenon as an ophthalmologist one suggests was more likely the case.

Whatever is the case these ʼstreaks of lightʼ where known as pitz to the Maya who saw the Sun inseminating the growth of plants with this ʼcosmic energyʼ that engendered the world with the energy of prosperity and abundance. Yet ʼpitzʼ is the name of the Maya Ballcourt during the Classic Period with its epigraphy or hieroglyphic writing of logographic signs and pictographic symbols. I will leave it to the reader to imagine how these two ideas are brought together in the magic bounce of the rubber ball that was so much of the mystical destiny of Maya ball playing.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
The rubber ball of Mesoamerica was experienced as an animate being whose bounce was controlled by forces beyond ʼjustʼ the physics of the rubberball in a world where all being were animated by an ancestral soul that was influenced by divine spirit.  The spirit essence of the Heart of the Sky; Heart of the Earth; Heart of the Lake-Sea was experienced in the water that ʼevaporatedʼ into the sky during the day that was seen as ʼitzʼ and the ʼutum jaʼʼ or water that came from the vault of the sky or rafters of the ʼgreat houseʼ as the sky-earth was once conceived by the Maya.

So there is the evaporating powers of the Hero Twins that cause their Mother and Grandmotherʼs water jars to empty and there is the evaporating powers of the Sun that pull the water up into the Diurnal Sky while there is the Nocturnal forces of the Moon that cause that evaporated water to be pulled back down to earth. The Maya Highlands is a very wet place to spend the night especially after a hot day in the Dry Season with a warm Full Moon night. Then the Face of the Earth is literally drenched with water. Our text is telling us this as it tells of the horizontal dew watering the newly sprouted maize in la Milpa.

Utum ja is named here as the ʼtabancoʼ or ʼraftersʼ of the house of Jun Junajpu, the home of Grandmother who has not been called IxMuqane since IxKikʼ gathered up the One Big Net of Maize. That is interesting in and of its self. Grandmother becomes a Mythic Archetype who loses all of her individual personality. But we are in her Sons House or Ja that is not called a House or Ochoch which is a structure where a Ja is a Home.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
But utum jaʼ is also the leafy ʼcupʼ that the maize plant forms with its long broad leaves that come ʼtwistingʼ up and out of the center of this highly ʼintelligentʼ and rather ʼingeniousʼ maize plant. This spiraling cup shaped by the leaves of maize gathers the dew that falls on the rough feeling leaves that have tiny hair-follicles or ismal or ʼpeach fuzzʼ that catch the dew collects upon the furry, hairy surface of the maize leaves to then have that water begin to drip and then drop down inside the maize plant that creates a true ʼflowʼ of water into ʼutum jaʼ or ʼgathering cup of dew waterʼ of the maize plant.

My wish for this translation is that the coming generations may experience the perfection of their ancestorʼs noble ancestry experienced in every single word that are all metaphors for those objects, acts, beings, and events spoken of here in the sacred secret language of Popol Wuj. Words just like utum ja that are always translated away into ʼthe hole that opens up into the rafters of the houseʼ or the ʼlashings of the houseʼ and there the word play and deep understanding evaporate like the power of the sun at mid-day.

This word-play will continue with the food the Boys ask of their Mother, Grandmother that is known as ʼqʼutum ikʼ which is ʼground-up chili water soup, but that is another matter completely or is it. Because it is down into their chili water soup that they will look up into the utum ja or opening into the rafters of the house, the opening into the sky; this reflection of the above and below of the evaporating water and the falling dew create the movement through this passage of the Popol Wuj throughout with one feels the water flowing forth from the tinaja or qʼebʼal of Grandmother and Mother. And so one must follow those images to find out what they are saying to us who have entered the Ancient Word of the Popol Wuj.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Utum Ja or Utum Jaʼ, the opening up into the conical roof of thatched covered houses of the Highland Maya mirrors the conical cup of the maize plants as inverse images of one another as the Sky reflects the Earth; as the Earth reflects the Sky to form and shape the Sky-Earth where water flows from the outer darkness to fill the inner spaces of these little leaf cups of gathered water, utum ja. IxKikʼ comes from a family of gatherers and so it is here sons will gatherer water within themselves as maize plants who survive to thrive from gathered water from the Night Sky that is planted straight up above ʼas ifʼ a star that was planted like the Red-Giant Arcturus that is there at the very center of the Night-Sky..

And here is the twist you have been waiting for: tumaj is the verb that signifies the action of twisting, tumin is to twist chord and tumaj is to ʼtwistʼ and that is exactly how the maize leaves twist themselves into a cup, ʼutum jaʼ translated as ʼits twist of waterʼ and that my friends is how a translation of ancient ancestral mythic language becomes a mystical journey that simply leaves one not only mystified by the beauty of the Mayaʼs Ancient Word but misty eyed because of the deep hope one has for the Maya to renovate their world and culture by forming something new out of something that is very, very old.

Utum ja, a twist indeed. Utum ja, the place in the Sky-Rafters of Grandmotherʼs house. Utum ja from where Jun Junajpuʼs noble ball-playing gear will enable them to go to war with the Lords of Death, Lords of the Underworld, Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

This is where the Boys will dance their rivals towards defeat and fiery sacrifice by dancing them into the sacrificial stone oven of sacrifice seen as the very Heart of the Sun there in the very Heart of the Sky: Ukʼuʼx Kaj. Pu tum ja is the opening through which the ball playing equipment of the rubber-ball-players falls to the Boys, the Sons who will take it up to give form and shape to those who will defeat and destroy the Lords of Death.

body:
This is the ball playing gear that will Boys to defeat the Lords of Death; Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame who will be defeated by the Boys, the Sons, who will be ʼdressed in precious jade and turquoise adornment of their Fathersʼ so that these Twin Maize Beings will take up the eternal return on the path of the Sun, on the road of the Dawn; at the time of the Sowing and Dawning.

The jade jewelry, the turquoise embellishment accentuated by the translucent green emeralds are the finery that will be worn by the Maize Deity; those who are Dancers known here as Jun Ajpu Ixbʼalamkej once known as Jun Ajaw, Yax Bʼalam the sons of Jun Ixim the Maize Lord who as you know is spoken here as Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu.

Out of the utum ja the Boys, the Sons must bring down their fathersʼ ball playing regalia as the insignia that will provide them with magical ancestral protection  just as the maize plants growing in the milpa will gain more and more protection against the dryness by growing more and more leaf with more and more follicles that gather more and more water to fill their utum ja, their spiral twisted cups of water to drink in the night sky through gathering power of the Moon Maiden, Moon Mother IxKikʼ.

This dressing the Sons with their Fathersʼ cotton armor is much, much more than our limited understanding of the Maya Civilization enables us to comprehend. But what we do know we are on the path that will led us deeper and deeper into the twisting motion that this art of translation and interpretation we are participating through our forming, shaping of this translation.

That is very much like the dressing of the Maize Deity by twisting its leaves over one another in Twin leaves that shadow one another as they complement one another as the maize plant, maize being comes up and out of the Earth to reach into the Sky spiraling up oh so invisibly to then flower with a tassel, to then fruit with two heads of two Boys, two Sun, the Twins of the Mother Moon IxKikʼ whose breast are suckled by them throughout the outer dark of night.

body:
This is the water gathered by the maize plant in its little twisted cup of twinning leaves; water that becomes the flesh of the body of the maize plant that becomes the flesh of the mazorca filled with fleshy kernels, with fatty grains, with oily seeds; rich seeds that become the sacred sustenance that feeds the fleshy bodies of the Ixim Winaq; Ixim Winaq who drink their rich thick fleshy sustenance from skull-headed gourds known Tzuy Wa: Gourd Head, Gourd Sustenance.

Wa is word that speaks of the food, the sustenance made of ground white maize or saq ixim or saqijal; and ixim is always translated as maize, sometimes as sustenance but now we know it means that which feeds us through our suckling of our mothersʼ breast. Ixim, that word formed from ʼIxʼ-that which comes from or they who come from; and, ʼImʼ-the teat on the breast that is suckle by the hungry infant, Ix and Im to create the word and the world of Ixim, that which is suckled from the breast, that which is suckled to create the Ixim Winaq, where Ixim is the sacred sustenance suckled from oneʼs motherʼs breast where Mother Earth is the place we must all search for our sustenance.

Feed to be fed; feed and be fed; feed to feed others who canʼt feed themselves and so goes the profound struggle to provide a meaningful translation that will fed its reader so they may be fed to then feed others. This is the way of the Maya, this is the way of this mythic metaphor of maize found in the words and idea of utum ja, the little cup of doubling, twinning, pairing, kenning, maize leave that twist their way up the cane to assure they feed the plant who they are in a cycle of fed and be fed without end. The Ixim Winaq, those grateful people who know the origin of their essence, maize, as well as the sacred story that tells of the essence of the Mayaʼs origins: Popol Wuj.

body:
Popol Wuj, sacred sustenance of the soul no matter who you are, and so here it is to be suckled as the very motherʼs milk to fed oneʼs forming and shaping in creative process of feeding the Nawal Winaq coming into being through being fed through the images and archetypes, myth and metaphor that come to life in the miracle known as the imagination of matter.

Come, it is time to get a move on, down the road to the ballcourt that leads to another invitation to play ball in Xibʼalbʼa on the Ballcourt of Sacrifice.

Fathersʼ Ball-playing Regalia;

Fathersʼ Rubber-ball;

Fathersʼ Ball-court

Truly content were they when they took their Fathersʼ ball everyday to their Fathersʼ ballcourt where they went to play; and, for a long time they just played with their Fathersʼ ball on their Fathersʼ ball-court.

They swept their Fathersʼ ballcourt making certain that their Fathersʼ ballcourt was kept swept; everyday.

But then the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa heard they had returned:

“Who is that who is playing ball over and above our heads; who has begun to play over and above us again; who is that?”

“Just who could that be? Have they no shame to be jumping around up there the way they do?”

“Where is their sense of deference, regard, and respect? They just bounce that ball up and down on those thin plaster walls and thin plaster floors completely ignorant of ancestral tradition and the decorum of the dead; those who are up there have no sense of propriety; for truly they play without any consideration or concern for the proper ball-playing behavior and etiquette. They are just ill-bred, ill-mannered players who continue to play with their rubberball without the least sense of propriety and protocol at all? They are as arrogant and inconsiderate as proud ignorant bigheaded ballplayers can get?”

“Didnʼt Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu die because of their self-aggrandizement before our noble presence?”

“Didnʼt they die trying to show off in front of us the way they did without knowing a thing about what they were doing or what they were getting into before they descended here to liven up our lives; the lives of us who are those of Xibʼalbʼa?”

body:
“Go then at once to summons them here,” roared the Lords. Those who spoke were Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame known as One Death, Seven Death; the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

One Death and Seven Death sent for their messengers; the called upon them to come to where they were; and so it was that their Messengers came; and when their Messengers came the Lords said this to them: “Say this to them; say this when you arrive with them there up above: ʼCome then-Kepetoq,ʼ say the Lords. ʼHere is where we want you to play, come play with us, in Seven Days we want to play with you here, say the Lords,ʼ this you will say when you arrive with them there,” so then, that was what the Messengers were told to say when the Messengers were sent by the Lords to summons the Boys to come play them in Seven Days.

And so the Messengers went with their message along the One Great Wide Road-Jun Nima Jok; it was one wide open road; it was one flat open road.

And so it was that they arrived directly at the House of the Boys-chi Kochoch ri Kʼajolabʼ. And so it was that the Messengers-ri Samajel-the Workers of Xibʼalbʼa went straight to their House of the Boys: chi Kochoch ri Kʼajolabʼ.

It was just straightaway that the Messengers of Xibʼalbʼa arrived there with their Grandmother, the Old Woman-Katiʼt.

The Boys were out playing ball on their ballcourt when the Messengers of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa-AjAwabʼ Xibʼalbʼa arrived for them with an invitation that they left with their Grandmother saying: “The Lords say that they must come here with us. ʼTruly come-Qitzij kepetik-Truly come!ʼ  Truly, come play with us say the Lords,” said the Messengers when they left their Lordsʼ message with IxMuqane.

Then the Messengers indicated the day they were to arrive; and so it was that the day of the Boys arrival was left well indicated by the Messengers of Xibʼalbʼa: “In Seven Days they, the Boys, are expected to be seen playing ball in Xibʼalbʼa,” this is what they left said to IxMuqane!

IxMuqane: the Matriarch of the Ixim Winaq; the Old Women-QaTiʼt-Grandmother

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
For the first time in a long time the Old Women-QaTiʼt-Grandmother is named by her proper name: IxMuqane. A subtle change is felt for we are made to feel a general sense of unity formed and shaped around the ʼMaize People-Ixim Winaqʼ who are formed and shaped into a family that consists of the a dead Grandfather and dead Wives and dead Father and Uncle as well as those who make-up the living family that consists of Grandmother, Mother, and Grandsons-Sons.

The separation between family members is now replaced by a deep sense of familial unity and familiarity between them as a family. We are going to be getting ʼclose and personalʼ with the nasty Lords of Xibʼalbʼa again, those cheaters, liars, and deceivers where ʼbait and switchʼ is the name of the game with the not so Noble Lords of Xibʼalbʼa: Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame and their Messengers who are vitally important to this Ancient Ancestral Account of the Ixim Winaq and their Ache nemesis: those of Xibʼalbʼa.

They who have much in common with the ʼnimarisaj ribʼ likes of  Wuqubʼ Kaqix, Sipakna, Kʼabʼraqan, Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen in that they are all excellent examples of how not to act in life. We feel the aggression just like we felt it with Wuqubʼ Kaqix, Sipakna, Kabʼraqan, and Omuch Kʼajolabʼ the Four Hundred Boys.

We canʼt help but take this family feud personal; we feel like we are getting summonsed when the Messengers arrive before IxMuqane: “Not again, and so soon, heck, they just started to play, those Lords of Xibʼalbʼa are rather sensitive for being formed and shaped from skull and bone.”

And that is it; this is the point to be made about the Dead and Deceased. The dead and deceased are very delicate types and the living had to make sure that didnʼt upset them in any way! Because they were very touchy about what went on where they once lived with bodies as fleshed out as any other but now they are Dead who live amongst the Dead and that is why they are so wild about inviting those with life to liven up their lives in the Land of the Dead: Xibʼalbʼa.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
IxMuqane as Matriarch of the Ixim Winaq Tribe speaks to the Emissaries, the Messengers of Xibʼalbʼa and with their arrival one can hear the difference and feel the deference for the Mother of Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu who will always grieve the loss of her beloved sons who died meaningless, unnecessary deaths by decapitation in the Underworld of Xibʼalbʼa: Place of Fear, Place of Intimidation, Place of Trials, Tests, and Ordeal.

IxMuqane is the Head-Woman who rules her household sitting upon her reed mats by her three stone hearth place and its fire, where fire equals power and authority.

IxMuqane is the Mother who provides her people with guidance; she is the Grandmother who sustains her people with her prevailing order and traditional way of spiritual and soulful protection.

IxMuqane is a Kʼamol Bʼey she is a Spiritual Guide who helps her people find their way. We care for her because she cares for her people who we identify with since the reader of sacred narrative naturally identifies with the protagonist.

All the Messengers that will become part of this long chain of Messengers of Grandmother are in fact Messengers of Death. They are the animal emissaries that are particular to Death. Each in their own way is a Messenger with the message that says: ʼDeath is announced; Death is coming and its coming your way.”

So realize this because all the ʼanimals or chikopʼ are Messengers of death beginning with the Louse that is about to fall down from the rafters of the house where the ballgame gear and ball fell from above. These Messengers are the Messengers of Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu who are buried by the ballcourt but have not been buried by their sons Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej who want to ʼknow the face of their Fathersʼ the Ancestral Dead who are in many ways calling their sons to them.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
There is a profound moment of ʼatonementʼ experience between Father and Son which is the direction this mythic narrative is moving. This knowing the ʼFace of the Fathersʼ is the goal of the narrative and the obstacles that lay between that transformative experience are the obstacles that will bring about the transformation of the soul and character of XJunajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

These Boys must die like their Fathers but they are vastly different from their Fathers because their Mother is from Xibʼalbʼa their Grandfather is a Lord of Sacrifice being a Blood-Gatherer. The Boys are Nawal Winaq thus they dream and imagine all the Ancestral Knowledge they need to bring about the transformation of their world but most importantly their own souls.

So to recap slightly: IxMuqane is best understood as the Matriarch of the Maize People. In this sense she might best be thought of as IxMuqQʼanil: She of the Buried Mazorca of Maize. As Mother Earth IxMuqQʼanil takes in the maize seed as the buried skull of the ancestors that sprouts out as the return of the descendant as kʼexel or replacement that comes forth from the body of IxMuqQʼanil.

Thus she embodies their resilience and resistance as Maize Beings who must face drought, flood, heat, sun, predators, hail, wind, fruit bats, thieves who decapitate them in the field, in short the Houses of Xibʼalbʼa.

IxMuqane is the ensoulment of their strength and endurance innate and inherent to her People, her Pueblo.

IxMuqane is quite quiet but there is tremendous power in her silences for she is always present in every page of this sacred history of hers from the very sowing and rooting of the First Words of the Ancient Word all the way through.

This is her Sky-Earth to Form and Shape as best as she is able; and she is extraordinarily able and capable to Form and Shape the World of the Sky-Earth as Former and Shaper; Bearer, Begetter; Mother, Father.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
IxMuqane always make sure her ʼwordʼ is brought to fruition for she is the embodiment of the completion of Creation through her Forming, Shaping but also Destruction through her elimination and  eradication; annihilation and obliteration of her own formation and creation. Her powers are balanced between the two realms of Creation and Destruction.

Now she has a message to send to her Grandsons playing ball on the ballcourt of her Sons and she will get that sending of the ʼwordʼ done with her  Earth-Sky messengers, all of them significant in profoundly meaningful ways for they embody the different ʼlevelsʼ of death from up in the Sky down to Earth. Let us take up the road so we can begin our journey with the Twins and their transformative odyssey through the Maya Underworld of Xibʼalbʼa.

Ixmuqane spoke to the Messengers of Xibʼalbʼa: “Utz bʼa la; Fine then; very well, they shall go as they are summoned, you, oh Messengers; you, oh, Workers; Envoys and Emissaries of the Noble Lords. Let it be known that they-the Boys-shall be summoned by me as they have been summoned by you; you oh Messengers of Xibʼalbʼa,” said Grandmother. Then the Messengers left, they returned from where they had come.

Grandmotherʼs heart was just finished off, “Who shall I entrust to summons my Grandsons-ri Wiy? Is this not a message for them from Xibʼalbʼa? Is this not the same as when the Messengers came before their Fathersʼ went off to die there in Xibʼalbʼa?” said the Old Woman-ri Atiʼt-Grandmother.

Sweetly she wept sadly when she wept soft and sweet there in her house; in her home all alone-kus choqʼ pa ja utukel.

It was then that a Louse-Ukʼ fell down from above that IxMuqane caught and picked-up. Immediately she placed it in the palm of her hand. There the Louse wiggled quickly across the open palm of her hand that she opened up wide for the little louse to run across: chimalmatibʼ.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
“You my grandson, you my tooth, you my replacement, wouldnʼt you like it if I sent you on an errand? Wouldnʼt it be good if I were to send you with this message that must be sent to my Grandsons there upon their ballcourt where they now play every day?” This is all she had to say to the Louse there in the palm of her hand when she said:

“ʼJust now Messengers have arrived with your Grandmotherʼ you will say. ʼYou are to come in Seven Daysʼ say the Messengers of Xibʼalbʼaʼ says your Grandmother, you are to say, when you leave your message with them this way,” she said to the little Louse that dropped down from up above there in the House.

This then was when he went running off wiggling his way down the road. Sitting there by the side of the Road was a Boy; his name was Tamasul, the Toad-ri Xpeq: “Where are you going?” asked then the Toad who sat beside the Road to the Louse from the House.

“My word is in my belly, I am going to leave a message with the Boys,” said the Louse to the Boy; Tamasul; the Toad that sat there beside the Road.

“Utz bʼa la, but it looks like you canʼt really run very fast,” said the Toad, on the Road to the Louse from the House.

“Would you like it if I swallowed you? Then you would see just how fast we would go as we make our way hopping down the road,” said the Toad.

“Utz bʼa laʼ,” said the Louse-Ukʼ to the Toad-Xpeq in the Road-pa ri Bʼey. This then was when the Louse from the House was licked-up by the Toad in the Road.

They went far with the Toad but they still didnʼt get anywhere fast. That was when One Big Snake-Jun Nima Kumatz came along there where Tamazul was in the Road: Saqikʼas was the name of the One Big Snake-Jun Nima Kumatz who came upon the Toad in the Road with Louse from the House who he had licked-up with the message in his Mouth.

“Where are you going; you, oh Tamasul, my Boy?” was asked Tamazul, the Boy Toad by Saqikʼas, the One Big Snake Jun Nima Kumatz.

“Apa katbʼe wi, at Tamasul, kʼajol?” Xuchax chik ri Xpeq rumal Saqikʼas ri Jun Nima Kumatz.

body:
“I am a Messenger, my word is in my belly-In samajel, kʼo nutzij chi nupam,” said then the Toad, Tamazul to the One Big Snake, Saqikʼas, known as the White Sparker; Sacred Spark.

“You are not moving very fast, that is all I can see, while I would arrive there much, much more quickly,” said then the One Big Snake-ri Jun Nima Kumatz-then to the Boy Toad Tamazul-ri Xpeq.

“Letʼs go-Katojo; Katojoq-swallow me,” said the Serpent.

The Sacred Order; the Divine Hierarchy of Sustenance

The Snake was instructed by the Toad in the Road asking to be swallowed-up by the One Big Snake ready to carry the Toad down the Road as his Load with the Louse in his Mouth; the Louse from Grandmotherʼs House who the Boy Toad Tamazul licked-up as his Load from the Road so they could go real fast to deliver the Message to the Boys at Court that they swept out every day where they play the Rubberball game with the Rubberball in their very own way.

And so would begin this Maya-Mesoamerican revelation of the sacred order of the Natural World that was and is an Animated Natural World that has its Natural Order that is a Natural Hierarchy of it ʼswallowingʼ itself as Sacred Sustenance as Insects are swallowed by Amphibians; Amphibians that are swallowed by Reptiles; Reptiles that are swallowed by Birds; Birds that are swallowed by Mammals; Mammals that swallow them All…This is the story of the ʼChikop-Animalitosʼ that swallow one another in a fine kind of  Divine Order that is a Sacred Order that is Natural Hierarchy of the Natural World. Louse to Toad to Serpent to Bird to the Boys and their Blow-gun Shot and their healing rubber sheath of rubber skin of this rubber cure known as ʼSangre de Sacrificio-Lotz Kikʼ sliced thin to win the day by regaining the eye-sight of this One Big Bird Wakʼo, Wako it name.

That then was when the One Big Snake, Jun Nima Kumatz known as Saqikʼas-the speedster toad eater swallowed the Boy Toad whole right there in the Road, poor Tamasul.

So now it is that when snakes take their sustenance they do as Saqikʼas did when he gulped down Tamasul  headfirst as is the way for Toads to be swallowed ʼjust soʼ.

body:
Chanim, Chanim-quickly, quickly; fast, fast then did he go, the One Big Snake-ri Jun Nima Kumatz, who sped off down the road.

And then the Snake was come upon by Wak, Wak who was One Big Bird, Jun Nima Tzʼikin.

Laughing Falcon is one of his names: Wako, Wako is his cry. He was mentioned as the Messenger of Jun Raqan Kaqulja Ukʼuʼx Kaj. Wok or Wak is the Ilol or Seer of Heart of the Sky so he was a natural choice to perform this work of Messenger who carried the message to Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej who were those that listened to the voice of Ukʼuʼx Kaj Jun Raqan Kaqulja the Kabʼawil who was the Divine Voice of the Heart of the Sky.

And just like that, this Jun Nima Tzʼikin, this One Big Bird, Wak or Wok, devoured the One Big Snake Saqikʼas, and that is the way Laughing Falcons swallow their prey in the Mountains today, swallowing snakes from head to tail just like snakes always swallow toads without fail by beginning with the head and ending with tail.

Wak swallowed the One Big Snake whole to then fly direct over to where the Boys were ʼseenʼ by Wak on the Ballcourt that Wak could ʼseeʼ was well swept. This is where Wak settled down; Wak settled atop the ornate crest of that finely adorned crown of the Ballcourt.

Wak just perched himself up there on the finely finished crown that ringed around the ornamented crest of the Ballcourt where the Boys were playing down below as content as could be; all alone; completely on their own.

Wak steadied himself easily on the ʼcrownʼ on the ʼcrestʼ of ballcourt known as utzʼutzʼil jom-ʼcorn tassel-utzʼutzʼil-corn flower.ʼ

This headdress crest was an ornate crown; adorned crest of the Ballcourt of the Maize People with their ʼCorn Tassel-Tzʼutuj-Corn Flowerʼ circlet that crowned the Ballcourt just as it encircled the crest of the milpa as a flowering headdress: Tzʼutuj as this tassel is known.

body:
There below were the ballplayers of the Ixim Winaq known as Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej who were happy and content playing ball-kekikot kechaajik not even stopping until they heard his terrifying call-Wako, Wako-and that was when they saw that One Big Bird; Jun Nima Tzʼikin whose call just cried out his name; his name that was his call to fame: Wako; Wako; Food is Here; Food is Here as the One Big Bird calls out letting everyone known someone is going to get eaten alive.

And so it was that as soon as Wakʼ arrived he began crying out his name; he just named his name again and again: Wak kʼo! Wak kʼo! Food is here! Food is here! This is the call of the Laughing Falcon who says: Wak kʼo! Wak kʼo! Here I am! Here I am! Or Wak ko! Wak ko! Here is a Hard Noble One! Here is Hard Noble One!

“Who is crying? Who is calling? Letʼs get our blowguns,” cried the Boys, the Sons who instantly looked up to where Wakʼ called out from the crest that crowned the Ballcourt.

Wakʼ called out from the tippy-top of their Fathersʼ ballcourt where he was able to see all there was to see. But he never could have imagined what he never saw coming.

Those two Blowgun Boys fired their blowguns at Wakʼ who was hit immediately in the eye by their dead-eye shooting of their stone hard blowgun shot.

This One Big Bird-Jun Nima Tzʼikin was shot by one of their blowgun balls; one of their ʼhard-clay-ballsʼ of their blowgun hit Wako smack in the very center of the very pit of his eye-taqal ubʼaq wubʼ.

Which in Kʼicheʼ shapes a sonorous sound of sight and syllabic symmetry to form the sounds that make the statement: ʼtaqal ubʼaq wubʼ chubʼaqʼ uwach-its blowgun bone of the blowgun shot hit bulls-eye on the bone-hard pit of his eye. Just like the shot that hit Wuqubʼ Kaqix; just like the ʼpitzʼ that hit IxKikʼ right smack in the center of the palm of her right hand-taqal ubʼaq wubʼ Ouch!

Wak just whirled around before fluttering down to eventually hit the ground in a puff of dust; Wak was down on the ground where the Boys went running to see what was there to be found.

“Where did you come from?-Jupa apetik?” blasted the Boys wanting to know from whence did this crying bird come.

body:
Wak just respond as he knew he must: “My word is in my belly-Kʼo bʼa nutzij chi nupam-there is just a bit of my truth within me. But first you must heal my eye then I will tell you. If not, then naught; if naught, then no!” he said to the Two Boys who held him down tight like another big bird of his kind.

They did not realizing they shot a Seer-Ilol-Watchman of the Heart of the Sky-Ukʼuʼx Kaj who was this One Big Bird who swallowed the Snake head to tail; a Bird who takes his sustenance like a Snake? Could this be some sort of mythic mistake?  Was the Boys shooting this Crying Bird fake; for wasnʼt Wakʼo a watchman worker of the Heart of the Sky-Jun Raqan Kaqulja who was a ʼnagual-nahual-nawalʼ of the Lords of Death-Ce Miquiztli-Jun Kame  as a bird whose cry is the call of death as it is said?

The Trickster Lord Smoking Mirror; Trickster Deity Tezcatlipoca lurks close by yet this is not made clear which is just fine because asking rational questions of a mythic narrative is a sort of literalist-materialist crime of the settler-colonist mind. This is one reason I ask it; to make the reader aware of this ʼforeign-kaxlanʼ kind of mind that we can bring to the seeing and knowing of Ancient Indigenous Masterpiece of Mythic Narrative formed and shaped from an ancient archaic sort of indigenous type of magical mind that is molded and modeled from a mythical kind of mind and its seriously playful sort of thinking.

“Utz bʼa la! Very well!” they said.

“Very well, we must then heal your eye,” they said with a sigh.

So this then was when they shaved a thin sheath of skin from their rubberball-ri Kikʼ.

Then they placed that thin sheath skin over the eye of Wak. This was known as Lotz Kikʼ or ʼSangre de Sacrificioʼ which they used to heal wounds, just like today when people heal their wounds with thin sheaths of thinly sliced rubber.

Instantly then was this big beautiful eye of this beguiling bird cured. Once again the vision of Wak-Laughing Falcon came out well; so that just like that Wak had his vision back which as a Seer-Ilol was everything and more because now that he was healed by these two magician healers he could see better now than he saw before.

body:
And so it was the Boys who mused that if Wakʼ could see again then he could certainly speak again; which was precisely what they wanted him to do to reveal the message he held within him; the message that was sent for them.

“Say it then,” they said to Wak, the Laughing Falcon; who without any further need for them to plead the One Big Bird agreed to bring-up the One Big Snake who was known for his speed.

Thus this One Big Snake-Saqikʼas was released from the tight squeeze he was in there within; so that he-Saqikʼas was only too pleased to be freed from where heʼd been kept inside the One Big Bird who called out Wak Kʼo, Wak Kʼo: Here he is! Here he is! Food is here! Food is here! Wa Kʼo! Wa Kʼo! To the Two Hunters; to the Two Blow-gun Boys who called out; yes indeed, yes indeed-We-ya, We ya!

“Speak; Speak; Kachʼawoq!” they said to the Snake: Kumatz.

“Fine, We!” said Saqikʼas, the One Big Snake that brought up the Toad head first and looking down the Road relieved to no longer be the Load of the Serpent inside the Bird where he never heard all that was conferred on the Serpent as gift given by the Bird by the Boys who want to known what Tamazul knew which was what was his that he had swallowed when he licked-up the Louse on the Road not so terrible long ago.

“What is your message? Speak out-Kattzijonoq! Say it now!” Toad was told  in a voice that was quite bold as he deserved being scold.

“There is a bit of truth that is the truth within my belly-Kʼo bʼa nutzij chi nupam-There is a little bit of truth within me this is my message!” said the Toad, Xpeq; the Boy; Tamazul.

body:
So then he tried again to spit-up what he swallowed; but he could not through-up the Louse; just spittle came from his mouth. He tried but, alas, there was nothing that came up, no matter how hard he tried we couldnʼt find the little lost Louse there in his mouth . So then the Boys beat it out of him: “You Trickster!-At Kʼaxtokʼ-You Cheat! You think your deceit can deceive us?” they said-xuchaʼxik and so then they kicked him hard right on his big boney buttocks. Poor Boy they busted the bones on his butt from kicking him so hard from behind but nothing sprouted out no matter how hard Tamasul and the Boys to dislodge that Louse from his mouth.

They kicked him hard on his butt making a bad bump on his flat toad rump; they thought they could kick it out of him by booting him on the bones of his buttocks but nothing came from making such a furious fuss except for a big ass bump on that poor Toad Boyʼs rumpus.

He tried even harder to do what they asked of him, but just a drop of dribble drabbled down out of him to then slide down his chin to then drip as it dropped from his mouth like spit that trickled like dribble that hung as a thin thread of  spittle: chuchubʼ uchiʼ.

Maybe he hadnʼt swallowed him after all so Tamasul asked them to look inside of his mouth a little bit more maybe he was somewhere to be found there in the middle somewhere there amongst the tears he swallowed and constant dribble of spittle.

Then the Boys scratched about in the depths of Toad Boyʼs mouth. They scratched around inside his wide open maw; they searched all about his wide open jaw; up and down, in and out, then they saw what they saw; that lazy little Louse was right there in Toadʼs mouth because he was never was swallowed.

It was just ʼas ifʼ he had been swallowed by Toad when he opened that large open maw formed by those wide open jaws of the Toad whoʼs throat looked like a deep dark hollow every time the Boy would swallow; there was no way the Louse was going to follow down into that deep dark hollow.

And so it was that Toad was defeated. It is not clear what they gave him as the food that became his sacred sustenance.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
But since he couldnʼt run fast he quickly became the sustenance of serpents and snakes who swallowed every toad they met on the road.

For the toad is truly the favorite food of serpents, who, as you know, love to swallow the Toad whole; right side up or upside down, it doesnʼt matter as long as it is head-first.

When the Little Louse was ready they both said at once:  “Speak it! Say it! Tell it! Katzijonoq!”

So this was when he spoke; this was when Louse gave his word; this is when he relayed their message; their message that was revealed thus:

“This is what your Grandmother says to say to you, you oh Engendered Sons of a Father-Ix Kʼajolabʼ:  Go summons them for Messengers have come looking for you with a message that came from them, those of Xibʼalbʼa; a summons that came here for you from Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame; a message that arrived for you Kʼajolabʼ, Sons of Fathers; a message sent from Xibʼalbʼa; a message sent to the Boys, the Sons; a message that came from the Messengers who came from Xibʼalbʼa  who were sent by One Death, Seven Death as their Messengers with the message of the Lords, Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame, that says this:

“In seven days they are to descend, so we can play ball with them here in Xibʼalbʼa. Bring all that is theirs; they are to bring all their Playing Equipment-Ketzʼabʼal; their Ball, Kikʼ; their Yoke, Bʼate; their Arm guards, Pachqʼabʼ; their Skins, Tzʼum.”

““Come, come liveʼn things up down here with us; with some enlivening play you will come to life here!”” say the Lords,ʼ said their Messengers,” says your Grandmother,”ʼ the Old Woman who sent me to send for you; I, who was there with her when she cried and called for you,” said the Louse.

“This is why your Grandmother sent me, to send you, this message, sent to you, from the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa,” said the Louse-ri Ukʼ-Messenger of the Lords of Death.

“Could it be true?” wondered the Boys when they heard what they heard; turning it over in their head; thinking it over in their heart.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Immediately they returned, arriving there where their Grandmother was waiting for them; when they went to take council with her; when they went to take leave of the Old Women; when they went to leave instructions with their Grandmother: IxMuqane.

“Joʼ na, Ix QaTiʼt,” xa Oj pixabʼay Iwe. Waʼe kʼute retal qatzij: “Xchiqakanaj jujun xchiqatik chi re wa aj chunikʼajal qochoch xchiqatik wi. Are retal qakamik we chichaqijik: Ma pa xekamik? kixchaʼ ta chichaqijik. We kʼut ta chipe utux e pa kʼaslik?  Kixchaʼ kʼut. Ix Qatiʼt, Ix pu Qachuch mixoqʼik. Kʼo retal qatzij kakanajik iwuk,ʼ xechaʼ ta xebʼek Jun xutik Junajpu, Jun chi kʼu xtikow Ixbʼalamkej. Xa pa ja xutik wi, mana pa juyubʼ taj, ma nay pu pa rax ulew taj; xa pa chaqiʼj ulew chunikʼajal upa kochoch, xkitik wi kanoq.

Sacred Lifecycle of Maize and the Maize People

I feel important to transcribe the original Maya Kʼiche text because within it is found a ʼsecretʼ sacred sort of Ancient Writing that when read syllable by syllable brings out the sound of this message the Boys, the Sons, the Twins Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej leave with their Grandmother and Mother. It is here at this point that we must stop and consider what is going on in this sacred writing of the Kʼicheʼ Maya because it is here that we find ʼmagical writingʼ that tells the entire story of the lifecycle of maize in ʼsecret sacredʼ language that when revealed ʼsyllable by syllableʼ ʼnames the namesʼ of the stages of transformation in the lifecycle of maize that must have been reflected in the lifecycle of the Maize People through their rites of passage; rites of initiation; and pilgrimage to those sacred citadels and temples that rose-up beside the Sea. So you can either read on here or jump over this reflective interpretation to take up the translation of this precious Mesoamerican Myth known and named Popol Wuj.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This passage tells of Lifecycle of Maize in very specific ways that bring out the imagination of maize as ʼsacred matter, sacred materialʼ that are ʼnawal beings, nawal ancestorsʼ who are living beings that are sown to then grow to then flower and fruit before dying back to then disintegrate in order to return to the earth to rise-up again reborn.

This lifecycle of the Maize Lords Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej is planted in our imagination as the ʼsoul of the Popol Wujʼ in order that the idea of the ʼimagination of matterʼ comes alive in our ʼmythic imaginationʼ of this Sacred Scripture of the Kʼicheʼ Maya. For this Book of Council tells us the Myth of Maize of the Maize People as told by their Noble Lords to be lived out by their Venerable Vassals and Sublime Subjects who gather together here in Council to Celebrate Counsel with One-an-Other in order to write down to inscribe in order to implant the Divine Word of the Sacred Story known as: Popol Wuj.

Above then is the Maya Kʼicheʼ incantation of the planting of maize as the embodiment of the Maize Twins; Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej who are saying: ʼWe are Maize; Oj Wa; this is Us as We who are Maize; Oj Wa; We are Here; We are Maize; We who are the Maize that we plant in Grandmotherʼs House; Grandmotherʼs House the Sky-Earth; Kaj-Ulew is who We are as We transform through the life, death, and rebirth of the sacred rites and rituals of initiation in Xibʼalbʼa.
