source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This is it! This…Is…It… this is the Ancient Ancestors become Maize by planting there essence as ʼAjʼ which is cane; which is the head; which is destiny; which is identity; which is being who one is: Aj.  The Boys, the Sons plant their essence as ʼAjʼ in Grandmotherʼs House as Men-Aj who are Maize-Aj each one is a Lord: Aj-Aw or He of Desire; He of Longing; He of Appetite; He of Becoming: Aj Aw. Aw is the verbal root of those that plant maize as related to us by Charles Etienne Brasseur de Bourbourg who speaks of the verbal particle Aw as something sacred; something divine; golden necklace; to sow maize; awas a command. Aj is the ʼbastón or vara or staffʼ of the Noble Office of Noble Lords and their Authority. We speak of Ajaw as Noble Lords which is proper yet their essence is that of those who plant the bastón of the Maize Plant that is the Cane-Aj of Maize-Aj. This is a World of Maize of those who are Maize People who are those who plant Aj to be known as Ajaw!

This is written in order that the reader understand how absolutely essential and immanent the idea that the Lords JunAjPu and IxBʼalamKej are Maize Deities who originate in this sacred act of their ʼplanting maizeʼ in the House of the Grandmother. This word ʼAjʼ is always translated literally as cane of maize or head of maize when in truth the word Aj that is the name Aj is the divine being known as Aj to become the Ajaw who is he who plants maize as the Lord of Maize or ri Ajaw rech ri Aj or the Lord of the Maize.

These are Maize Men who are Men of Maize spoken of in Maya Kʼicheʼ as Ixim Acha-Hombres de Maize-Ixim Achijabʼ or Maize Men who are Maize Warriors as Rain Men Achi Jabʼ which is a fine sort of divine play on words that are names that are grounded in the Ixim Winaq.

This is the Maya Maize Metaphor that says Man is Maize just as Maize is Men! This is the One-Jun Cane-Aj of Maize-Aj that is planted; that is sown by each of the Boys who are the Sons of Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu left with the Grandmother and  Mother to be raised up as the descendants of the First Fathers of Maize known to us well as those named and known as Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
These Boys, these Sons plant their essence in the patio of the House of Grandmother Ixmuqane and Mother IxKikʼ to plant in order to establish the ʼconnection and communicationʼ of the Maize Lineage that forms and shapes the ʼstaff of lineageʼ that is the ʼtree of lineageʼ that stands as the pillar-raqan that holds up the House of the Earth and Sky that is the House of  the Sky-Earth that is the Home that is the Realm that is the Territory that is the Sovereignty of IxMuqane the Earth that ʼweepsʼ and  IxKikʼ the  Moon that ʼcriesʼ as they prey and plead for their Sons and Grandsonsʼ life, death, and rebirth in Xibʼalbʼa.

This is the story that begins here with their descent and passage through Xibʼalbʼa as the Maize Deities; the Maize Twins; the Maize Boys; the Maize Sons: Twin Heads of Maize on One Cane of Maize. This then is beginning of their initiatory journey of transformation that transforms them into the Sun and Moon as their lives as Maize Being is transformed into the divine deified lives of the Sun and Moon; the Sun and the Moon of the Age and Era of the Maize People that you know and understand so well by now. This is the Mesoamerican-Maya mythic image and mythic metaphor of Men as Maize, Ballcourt, Sun; Road and, Women as Home, as Earth, as Moon, as Milpa filled with Canes of Maize with Twin Grandsons, Twin Sons surrounding the ʼCompoundʼ or ʼSitioʼ where the Inner Patio is the Noble Place and Regal Palace of the Sacred Rule and Divine Authority of the Matriarch IxMuqane of the Ixim Winaq.

This is a Sign from Us left for you IxMuqane;

This is a Sign of Our Journey through Xibʼalbʼa

“Joʼ na, Ix QaTiʼt: We are going now, you our Grandmother. We have come to say, good-bye; to say farewell; for we are here to take leave of you. Here then is a sign of Our Word; here then is a sign of Our Truth; here then is a sign of Our Life: QaTzij: We are leaving you with something to remember us by. Each One of Us shall plant here a Cane of Maize-Aj; a Cane of Maize is what we shall plant; we shall plant it in the center of Our House-Qochoch; we shall plant it in-xchiqatik wi-we shall sow it out.”

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
“Here then is the sign of our death when we dry-up you will ask: ʼCould it be that they have died? This is what you will say then when it has dried out; when the Cane dries out and dies. But then when they sprout back you will ask: ʼAre they alive once again?ʼ This perhaps is what you will ask when they sprout back again.

“This is what you will say, perhaps, you, oh Our Grandmother-Ix Qatiʼt and you Our Mother-Ix Qachuch-do not cry-mixoqʼik-you Woman of the Moon-Ixoq-Ikʼ, you IxKikʼ Mother of the Rubberball; Mother of Ball-players.”

“This is a sign of Our Word-QaTzij-Our Truth, Our Way, Our Tradition-QaTzij that we leave with you,” they said-xechaʼ those of the ʼSacred Sustenance-Echaʼ this is what they said when they took leave of their Grandmother and Mother.

Then they went about planting the maize, One-Jun was planted by Jun AjPu; One-Jun was planted by Ix-Bʼalam-Kej.

Just in the house did they plant it, they did not plant it in the mountains, nor did they plant it in the wet earth either; just in the dry ground found in the patio of their house did they leave it planted; the heads of maize, the canes of maize, the heads on the canes of maize that each One-Jun of the Boys, each One-Jun of the Sons left planted there in Grandmotherʼs House.

Let us sow within our imagination this magical, mythical, mystical incantation of the Maize People left to them by their Divine Ancestors; their Divinities; their Kabʼawil who brought their Tradition of the Sowing of Maize Seed to life by ʼplanting maizeʼ in ʼGrandmotherʼs Houseʼ which is to say within the Heart of the Earth where maize is sown to be grow and grow until it is fully grown into the flowering and fruiting heads of the Lords of Maize: Jun-Aj-Pu; Ix-Bʼalam-Kej.

This then is when it gives thousands of replacements seen as the thousands of seeds found within the husk of head of the Maize Lords; seeds that look like the ancestral teeth of Grandmother and the ancestral skull of Grandfather; teeth and skull that appear to be ʼlong goneʼ yet are never really dead.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
They are never really dead because once they are buried within the womb of the Earth they come sprouting back to life to begin their sacred lifecycle once again. This is just as it has always been since ʼtime immemorialʼ when the hand of the Divine Ancestors took up this sacred sustenance to sow it in the ground to then tend it until it came to fruition in its fruiting into perfect heads of maize which is to say into the heads of the Maize Lords; the Hero Twins; as it is said: Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej as they are named.

Let us sound out this incantation that is a taking of leave; that is an invocation upon the Twins; the Boys; the Sons making it clear there is a way for their Grandmother and Mother to know how they are by knowing in which phase of their sacred lifecycle that they find themselves in. This is that magical story of the People of Maize told through the mythical narrative that reveals the essence of the Maya Culture through the expression, revelation, and recitation of the Mesoamerican Civilization.

This is the culture and civilization where Maize climbs up and out of the Underworld of Death to live again on the Face of the Earth to flower and fruit beneath the Sun and Moon of the Sky both Day and Night in the Darkness and in the Light.

This is that story told here; this is that story revealed here; this is the invocation recited here through this short enchantment of the Maize People when their Sacred Sustenance was first  sown in Grandmotherʼs House; Grandmotherʼs Patio known as Grandmotherʼs Sacred Sitio; there at the very center of her House where the life, death, and rebirth of the Hero Twins is revealed in the mirror of existence that is experienced at the very heart of Grandmother House; the House of IxMuqane. Let us sound it out one more time before moving on.

Just in the house did they plant it, they did not plant it in the mountains, nor did they plant it in the wet earth either; just in the dry ground found in the patio of their house did they leave it sown when they left planted; the heads of maize, the canes of maize, the heads on the canes of maize that each One-Jun of the Boys, each One-Jun of the Sons left planted there in Grandmotherʼs House.”

Down, down, down into the Depths of Xibʼalbʼa;

To Defeat Death; To Bring Forth the Alba

Then they left, each one shouldering a blowgun-jujun chiwubʼ chike. This is the way they made their descent down to Xibʼalbʼa; quickly did they descend down the face of steep stone stairs-kumuk that were there.

And so it was that they dropped and dropped as they made their way down, down, down the steps of the stairs that fell through the warm humid air  into Xibʼalbʼa.

They crossed over Jal-Jaʼ Siwan-Turbulent Water Canyon; then they passed through a great mass of moving, migrating birds; those ones known as Molay Tzʼikin- whirling, swirling Birds; a Great Gathering of Migrating Vultures, a Massive Movement of swirling, spiraling Hawks.

These migrating Vultures known as los Azacuanes and Swainson Hawks signal the coming of the rains in late April and early May and their departure October and November.

The Ancient Word is telling us here exactly when and at what time of year the Hero Twins begin their ʼpilgrimage of initiationʼ through the underworld of Xibʼalbʼa which must be the zenith passage of the Sun on May 3 to 10th when Arcturus is ʼplantedʼ in the center of the Night Sky as the bright Red Giant that is both the tip of the red tail feather of Wuqubʼ Kaqix and the torch of Tojil as well as the tip of the cigar of the Old Man or Mam, the Year-Bearer.

April and May are the perfect time of year for the ritual performance of the Sowing and Dawning of the New Year since the work of preparing the Milpa is finished, firewood is split and dried to be stored, and work of building is brought to completion before the arrival of the Rainy Season.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
The Boys pushed past Pus Rivers-Puj Yaʼ of pus waters to then quickly crossover the bloody waters of Blood River-Kikʼ Yaʼ; both of them places of defeat; both of them places of death; both of them places of traps and snares of those of Xibʼalbʼa.

But the Boys were not left defeated by those rivers; they were not intimidated; they were not taken-under by the water of those rivers. No, no they just crossed right over; they just passed over on their Blowguns.

When they came up and out of where the river canyons ended they arrived at the Crossroads; they arrived where Four Roads Crossed-pa Kajibʼ Xalqʼat Bʼe as it is named; as the Crossroads are known:

Black road; Qʼeqʼa Bʼe

White road; Saqi Bʼe

Red road; Kaqa Bʼe

Green Road; Raxa Bʼe

The Yellow Road is not named here which is fascinating because it is the Qʼan Bʼey the Yellow Road of the South; Road of Abundance; Road of Maize; Road of Flowers and Road of the Sacred Count of Days of Kʼat; Qʼanil, Eey, AjMaq, and Ajpu or Ajaw, known as the Road of Junajpu is not named here; yet, Raxa Bʼe is named, for the Raxa Bʼe will be the road that Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej will take. They will take Raxa Bʼey the Jade Road of Eternal Life, the Emerald Green Road of the Eternal Return, the Road of Renewal and Regeneration, the Road of Rebirth, the Road of Life and the Lifecycle of Maize that has no end; the Eternal Lifecycle of Maize is found by following Raxa Beʼ the Resplendent Jade Road of Rebirth and Eternal Life of the Ancestors through their Descendants known as the Emerald Green Road of Resplendence: Raxa Bʼe.

Thus Raxa Bʼe  is named in the naming of the names of the Roads of Xibʼalbʼa while Qʼana Bʼe the Yellow Road; the Golden Road of wealth and abundance of Qʼanajal, Saqijal Yellow Mazorca; White Mazorca of the Golden Sun; of the Silver Moon is not named yet.

body:
But the Yellow Road spoken of as Qʼana Bʼe will be named as the Golden Road when the time comes for Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej to rise-up and become the Sun and Moon of the Maize People; Maize Pueblo of the Ixim Winaq: the Great Nation of the People of Maize: Maya Mesoamericans. This then will be when the Qʼana Bʼe will be the road taken-up to be walked down to come upon wealth and abundance; plenty and prosperity.

It was there at the Crossroads that the Boys sent off Un Animalito; Jun Chikop; a Little Bug: Xaʼn was its name; the name of the One who listened in on all that was said to be heard to then be passed on to those who needed to know all that this Jun Chikop; this One Insect; Xaʼn-Shawn had to say.

He, was the One-Jun named Xaʼn who was the One-Jun that listened in on the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa when it came to time to hear and remember the ʼnaming of the namesʼ of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa. His name was Xaʼn the same sounding name as Sean or Shawn.

This was when the Boys, the Sons were tested by being called upon to ʼName the Namesʼ of the Lords of Death; Lords of Disease of Xibʼalbʼa, those who were known as Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame and AjAwabʼ Xibʼalbʼa.

And so they-Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej gave him-Xaʼn his instructions when they told that One Bug; Jun Chikop what to do: “One by one you must bite them, first bite the First Seated One, then bite the next one seated next to the First Seated One until you finish biting them all in perfect order; in return for this that is ʼyoursʼ that will be the blood of the people out on the road,” this is what was said to Xaʼn; the Mosquito; Xaʼn who was A Bug; Jun Chikop; Un Animalito.

“Utz bʼa la!” said Xaʼn. “Very good then!” said Sean, Shawn.

This is when he entered upon the Black Road-Qʼeqʼa Bʼe-the Road of Xibʼalbʼa arriving directly behind the Wooden Ones, the Puppet People, the Wooden-Woodworks of Wood-ri Poy, Ajam Cheʼ.  These were the first seated ones; the first seated rivals; those that were well adorned ones; the wooden works of wood; the ornamented wood-worked ones who were seated their first as the first seated ones.

Kʼulel-Rival; Kuʼlel-Seated

body:
These are those who are the first seated ones, the adorned one, the first ones there at the entrance of Xibʼalbʼa. They are the ʼgatekeepersʼ who must be distinguished as the real or the replica; the first or the fake.

These are the Boys rivals or kʼulel; nabʼe kʼulel their first rival are the nabʼe kuʼlel-first seated one or nabʼe kubʼulel-first seated, who are the first enemy ones known as nabʼe kʼulel-rival, enemy, adversary.

This section plays with the homonym kʼulel who is the rival, enemy, adversary and kuʼlel that is the ʼseated oneʼ who is also a kubʼulel or ʼseated oneʼ who is the one seated next kubʼul chik on a kulubʼal a place to sit or seated platform or bench; a word formed from the verb kuʼluj to sit down and shaped from the verb kuʼlik to sit.

This tasting the blood of the Lords of the Xibʼalbʼa is a sure-fire-way for the Boys to taste the essence of their rivals, their enemies, their adversaries. What kind of blood runs through the veins and arteries of Xibʼalbʼa? The answer will tell the Boys, the Sons, the Twins who their enemy is in essence as well as who they are up against and what they need to do to defeat them. So they send their ally Jun Chikop to bite the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa to taste the quality of blood that runs through their veins and by doing so cause their names to be named in order to name their names in perfect order.

Xaʼn, the Mosquito was sent out to bite the Lords in perfect succession; and so it was that he soon arrived there directly behind the Adorned Works of Wood ri Poy, the Embellished Wooden Works of Worked-Wood-Ajam Cheʼ; for it was a Wooden Man who sat there as the First Seated One, Nabʼe Kuʼlel who was their First Rival-Nabʼe Kʼulel.

This first seated one was covered with adornment; he was dressed-up as a decorated doll. It was then that Xaʼn, the Mosquito, bit him, he bit him First, but this Wooden One did not speak, not a word;  not a peep did this First One tweet.

So then the Mosquito, Xaʼn bit the Second Seated One, the Second Rival; he did not speak; he did not purr; so when not a word was heard it was on to the third.

body:
Xaʼn bit then the Third, the Third Seated One, the Third Rival that sat there on the bench where the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa were all seated in a row.

There sat Jun Kame-One Death in the third position after the first two Wooden Beings were bit on after then next but they made no sound; nothing; nix.

Ajii-Teocinte; Ajii-Father-in-Law

The highly talented storytelling scribes will have fun here playing on the Spanish ʼAqui-Akiʼ at the beginning of this narrative to say ʼhereʼ they are.

Then they switch to crying out the exclamation Ajii as a traditional twist on a traditional exclamation of pain: ʼAy yi yiʼ.

Well, Ajii means Father-in-law and Son-in-law as well as ʼTeocinteʼ grass which is a precursor to maize which is a kind of Cane-Aj in and of its very own self.

Today Ajii signifies ʼsugar caneʼ that looks like a Carrizo Cane-Aaj or Ajii-teocinte grasses. Every single written word is written in its very own special way for special reasons which are what makes the Colonial Translators who have always come to the Popol Wuj as if they knew better than the original Maya Scribes. They now come off as humorous kinds of joke on themselves because of how arrogant and proud they have always been since they are always certain the original Maya Scribes and Copyist are the ones who make the mistakes. This exclamation of Ajii is like the ʼword-playʼ  Joli, Joli; Juki, Juki…in which and where they are not ʼjustʼ exclamations although they are that as well; but, this exclamations are making significant statements that say something that provides a pivotal clue to what the ʼsub-textʼ is say: Aki...Aqui…Ajii…Ajii…

So there is something going on here with Ajii-Teocinte and Aj-Maize and Aaj-Carrizo Cane in the context of the development of the lineage of Maize as a cane with kernels that are seeds that were constantly experimented with by Mesoamericans through the creation and production of maize as a domesticated grass with ʼhuge headsʼ filled with ʼmany teethʼ of the Ancestors who are like the Fathers-in-Law-Aji and Sons-in-Law also known as Aji which will come into play soon enough.

body:
ʼAjiʼ is then a play on words that plays with the idea that these Lords of Xibʼalbʼa are the Fathers-in-Law of the Twins just as the Twins are Aji or Sons-in-Law of the Xibʼalbʼa which makes them Family; which makes the Twins be those who inherit ancestral knowledge that is the nawal knowledge of how to speak and act; trick and deceive; misdirect and mislead; lie and cheat like Xibʼalbʼa when their Fathers Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu could not.

The Twins are Maize People who are Maize Beings but those of Xibʼalbʼa; the Xibʼalbʼans are likened to a Prior Age of Teocinte People; Teocinte Beings who are the ʼAncestorsʼ of the Maize People. There are stories of Bean People and Gourd People and Chili People in this Horticultural World that existed for Ten Thousand Years at the least. And these were periods of time when the Plants spoke with those Human Beings who tended them with a level of care and concern that we can no longer image.

Yet imagine we must for it is your capacity and capability of the mythic imagination that will enable you to understand the Popol Wuj in ways that come close to how it was once understood. Imagination is a powerful human gift that is a talent that is a mythical capacity that is imaginative capability that is an ancestral ability than must be engaged to develop a true sense of what our mythic imagination might come to be again after losing it for so long!

There is plant lineage being spoken of here and I am very content to have ʼfound it outʼ through my many translations and those translations needs for me to ʼsound it outʼ in order understand the meaning of this exclamation through the process of my slowly coming to ʼground it outʼ in mythic Mayan way that are Mesoamerican sensibilities for horticultural aesthetics and philological sensibilities that led to my getting a ʼfeelʼ for what is going on here. Ajiii!!! It makes me so happy to begin to understand the deeper levels of the Maya Myth of the Maize People!

body:
ʼAjiʼ is the name given to the relationships of marriage alliance where Father-in-law-Aji-Son-in-Law are created from Noble Fathers of a ʼconquered lineageʼ giving their Noble Daughters in marriage to form Marriage Alliances. These conquerors of the land are ʼusurpers of sovereigntyʼ who can never hold the land they conquered without the cooperation of the people they subjugated. So these Maya or Nahua Warlords contentedly and happily received gifts of ʼDaughter of the Lordʼ to form Marriage Alliances.

These ʼDaughters of a Lordʼ were married to ʼSons of a Lordʼ which is the Traditional Maya way of creating cultural unity and strength that will become of greatest importance in the last parts of the Popol Wuj. So realize this is very important here with the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa calling Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej Ajii! Aji! Aki! Aqui! Here we are your Fathers in Law from the conquered land of Xibʼalbʼa as we ʼforeshadowʼ the defeat and death of Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame by Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

One wonders if the Daughters of the Lords brought their own Maize Seed to be sown in the land of their Mother-in-Law and Father-in-Law to improve the selections of Maize and Bean; Chili and Cacao; Vanilla and Gourds of all shapes and sizes. But it was the cross fertilizing and cross-pollinating of Maize Lineages that create Maize Alliances by combining the collaborative and complementary powers of the cross-cultural seeds of maize to bring about cross-lineage kernels of maize.

body:
Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej are rooted in the powerful Nawal lineage of Maize Beings by their being formed by an Over-World lineage of IxMuqane while being shaped by the Under-World lineage of IxKikʼ. In this way the Matriarchal Horticultural Aesthetics and Ethics of IxMuqane are brought together with the Trickster Lineage of ʼhungry upstarts from the Mountainʼ to create something New and Powerful from: the Sun and Moon; Maize and Cacao; Highland and Lowland; Cold and Hot; Dry and Wet; Hard and Soft; Male and Female; Over and Under; Mountain and Plain; Sky and Earth; Lake and Sea; Sharp and Sweet; Red and Blue; Fir and Water...This constant desire to improve oneʼs seed is something the Maize People have been involved for thousands and  thousands of years over hundreds and hundreds of generations of plant reproduction. How can this not be part of this Myth of Maize?

This is the exclamation that the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa make when they are bit and say: ʼXa Aji!ʼ  Which is their way of ʼnaming their namesʼ to ʼgive up the knowledge of who they are and where they come from which for a shamanic cultural is to give-up and take-over the power to control these Lords through the power of ʼnaming their namesʼ by saying Xa Ajii or Just your Father-in-Law which is the Father-in-Law of the Twins Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej whose Mother IxKikʼ comes from Xibʼalbʼa. You get it right, of course, but itʼs a really big deal for them to say who they are to the Boys, the Engendered Sons: Kikʼajolabʼ Junajpu; Ixbʼalamkej who will never ʼname their namesʼ but never ever will they name their names even though the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa will ask them all the time.

And so it is that the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa will never come to know the ʼtruthʼ about their adversaryʼs lineage until the Boys name themselves which they do it quite ʼtellingʼ ways. Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame wonʼt know this secret until the end and itʼs too late. They wonʼt known no matter how hard the Lord of Xibʼalbʼa try to get it out of the Hero Twins. They never say who they are or where they come from.

This creates great tension throughout this masterpiece  play of ʼnaming the namesʼ from the very first page of the Tzʼaqol, Bʼitol; Alom, Kʼajolom ʼnaming their namesʼ to the very last page of Popol Wuj when the Scribal Lords Mother-Fathers of the Ancient Word; Nim Chʼokoj Ajaw Chuch-Qajaw Ojer Tzij of Popol Wuj name their names by saying who they are and where they come from which is just like the Hero Twins will do when they defeat the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa:  Oj Wa! We are Here! We are Sustenance! This is how and when they say where they are and who they are and what they are all at once in order to name themselves with great pride and dignity after defeating their mortal enemy: Jun Kame; Wuqubʼ Kame.

Popol Wuj is a true work of genius and hopefully someday human beings from around the world will be able appreciate it for what it is as an Ancient American Account of Indigenous Antiquity. Popol Wuj is formed and shaped by Nawal Winaq who are Ixim Winaq who are Kʼicheʼ Winaq, Kʼicheʼ Amaqʼ.

Remember the First Seated Ones are the Men-Made of Wood, those who are known and named as Poy or Ajam Cheʼ which is the first way this naming of the names throws one off sense the first one bit is the third to sit in his noble seat there in the Popol Ja where the Noble Lords meet to be named by the Xaʼn who is a kind of mosquito that is not a mosquito which is again there to make sure the myth-teller instills confusion where order must reign. Good luck with this.

Nabʼe-First; Kabʼ-Second Rox-Third; Kaj-Fourth;  Roʼ-Fifth; Waqaq-Sixth;  Wuq-Seventh;  Wajxaq-Eighth; Bʼelej-Ninth; Lajuj-Tenth;  Julaj-Eleventh;  Kabʼlajuj-Twelfth;  Roxlajuj-Thirteenth;  Kajlajuj-Fourteenth…

This is a foreshadowing of the Fourteen Generation of the Kʼicheʼ Maya Rulers that begin with the First Four Fathers of the Kʼicheʼ Maya. So do realize that these Lords of Death; Lords of Disease may very well be the Ancestors of the Kʼicheʼ Maya as seen in their Ancient Ancestral Way of understanding Death and Disease.

Nabʼe; Kabʼ; Rox; Kaj; Roʼ; Waqaq; Wuq; Wajxaq; Bʼelej; Lajuj; Julaj; Kabʼlajuj; Roxlajuj; Kajlajuj…

body:
First, Second, Third, Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, Eighth, Ninth, Tenth, Eleventh, Twelfth, Thirteenth, Fourteenth…

Naming of the Names of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa

This then was the naming of the names of the Noble Lords of Xibʼalbʼa when they named all their names by their naming the name of One-an-Other: Kʼeje kʼut ubʼixik kibʼiʼ ri xkibʼij konojel chi kibʼil kibʼ.

So Xaʼn bit him, he bit the Third Seated One Jun Kame the First Seated Lord of Xibʼalbʼa:

“Aki! …Aki!” said then this First Seated One when he was bit, “What was that, that bit me here,” said Jun Kame.

“Naki? What is it, Jun Kame?” asked Wuqubʼ Kame who sat right next to him as the Fourth; the Second Seated Lord of Xibʼalbʼa.

“What could it be?  Something has just bitten me?” said Jun Kame.

“Xa Aji! Just Aji!” said the Third on the Bench, the First One to be bitten in a long line of Noble Lords who Xaʼn would bite, leaving Eleven Lords to bite since every single one would be bitten!

“Aji! What has bitten me?” said the Fourth Seated One in the line of lords seated on the bench of the Popol Ja, Council House of Xibʼalbʼa.

“What is it Wuqubʼ Kame?” asked the Fifth Seated One.

“Something has just bitten me,” Wuqubʼ Kame said to the Fifth Seated One.

“Aji!” shouted the next, “What-Naki was that? What has bitten me?” wondered the fifth seated one, fifth one sitting on the bench.

“What-Naki is it Xikʼiri Pat?” asked Wuqubʼ Kame-Seven Death.

“What is it that has just bitten me?” asked then Xikʼiri Pat-Blood-Sacrifice, Blood-Letter!

Then the sixth was bitten; the sixth rival-kʼulel; the sixth seated one-kubʼulel: the sixth seated one-kuʼlel on the bench to be bitten.

“Aji!” said the sixth seated one, Kuchuma Kikʼ-Blood-Gatherer who was seated there right next to Xikʼiri Pat.

“What is it Kuchuma Kikʼ?” asked Xikʼiri Pat-Blood-Letter. “What could it be that just bit me?” asked Kuchuma Kikʼ-Blood Gatherer.

Then the seventh was bit, the seventh seated one: “Aji!” exclaimed then the seventh seated one that cried out in pain.

“What is it Ajal Puj-Lord Pus?” asked Kuchuma Kikʼ-Blood Gatherer who was seated there right next to him. “Who knows what has bitten me; Alay?” remarked Ajal Puj-Lord Pus.

body:
Then the eighth seated one was bitten. “Aji! Ay!” screamed out the eighth one sitting there on the bench. “What is it? Lord Jaundice?  Naki, Ajal Qʼana?” asked Ajal Puj-Lord Pus.

“Who knows what it was, but something bit me,” said Ajal Qʼana-Lord Jaundice. So then it was the ninth seated one of Xibʼalbʼa who was bit.

“Aji!” said the ninth seated one sitting there on the bench found at the Entrance Hall of Xibʼalbʼa of the Popobʼal Ja Xibʼalbʼa.

“What is it Chʼamiya Bʼaq-Bone Staff?” asked Ajal Qʼana-Lord Jaundice.

“What-naki-who has just bitten me?” asked Chʼamiya Bʼaq-Bone Staff.

Then the next in line was bitten, he was the tenth to be bitten. This was the tenth seated one there on the bench of the Lords who was bitten.

“Aji!” called out the tenth seated one there on the bench. “What is it Chʼamiya Jolom-Skull Staff?” asked Chʼamiya Bʼaq-Bone Staff. “Who knows what or who has bitten me?” said Chʼamiya Jolom-Skull Staff.

When the eleventh seated one was bitten he screamed out saying, “Ajii! Aji!” said the eleventh seated one on the bench of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

“What is it Xik?” asked then Chʼamiya Jolom.

“What-Naki knows what has bitten me,” said Xik-Hawk-Wing. Then the twelfth seated Lord of Xibʼalbʼa was bitten; he was the twelfth Lord of Xibʼalbʼa to be bitten when he called out a cry of pain and surprise.

“Aji!” called out the twelfth seated one, sitting seated on the bench of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

“What-Naki is it, Patan?” asked then Xik.

“What-Naki is that who bit me; or what was that, that has bitten me there below the bench here?” asked Patan, Lord Merchant Tump-line; Lord of the Merchant Pack-Strap as he is known: Ajaw Patan.

Then the Thirteenth Lord was bitten, the Thirteenth seated one-Roxlajuj kubʼulel- was bitten there on the long bench of adversary, of rival: kʼulel, kʼulelej but also companions as these pairs are known.

“Aji!” cried the thirteenth. “What is it Bloody Teeth-Naki, Kikʼ Re?” asked Patan, Bloody Fangs, Kikʼ Reʼ. “Naki la mixitiyowik? What is it that, that has bitten me?” roared Kikʼ Re, Bloody Teeth, Bloody Fangs ready to bite back if he found the one who bit him.

Then it was the fourteenth there in a row that was bitten and bitten hard as the last one always is. “Aji!” cried out the fourteenth seated one. “Who was that who bit me?” asked the last in line.

“What is it Bloody Claws; Blood Talons; Kikʼ Rixkʼaq-?” asked Kikʼ Reʼ-Bloody Teeth, Bloody Fangs who was asked the last in the line of those known as Bloody Claws, Bloody Talons-Kikʼ Rixkʼaq.

“Something bit me,” said Rixkʼaq; Bloody Claws; Bloody Talons who began scratching the nasty bite immediately.

With the names named in the order that the names came by the Lords naming each otherʼs name by name.

Xaʼn flew right back down the line so they could see who had bitten them but they could not see him since they were looking down at the ʼOneʼ bite-mark-sign given to them by that ʼOneʼ hard biting insect that left them with a remembrance of the ʼOneʼ sign made by the ʼJun Chikopʼ who had bitten them ʼOneʼ and ʼAllʼ.

Xaʼn Jun Chikop-ʼOneʼ mark; ʼOneʼ sign

Xaʼn then returned to Jun Ajpu, Ixbʼalamkej; One Blow-gun Boy; Little Jaguar Deer who were those that had sent Xaʼn to bite all those he was sent to bite that he bit making sure all the Lords were bitten with a bite that left them both bit and bitten; which left them to ask the question as to who or what had just bit them with a bite that had left them so very markedly bitten?

This question of biting and being bitten with a stinging bite is how the names of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa were named in perfect order because these Xaʼn are a type of Mosquito with a very painful bite that leaves a perfectly circular mark with a pin-point of blood in the center that leaves no doubt this is where Jun Ajpu received his inspiration for the ʼOneʼ mark; ʼOneʼ sign he wore on his skin.

When this One Chikop bites he leaves his mark on those he bits and  no question in oneʼs mind and body that one has been bitten; but by what or who because no one ever sees or saw him this One Little Animal: Xaʼn.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
The Lords were left bit and bitten: but who or what that was that bit them to leave them bitten would never be known. This was because not one of them knew who had done the biting that left them bitten leaving them with a ʼJun-Oneʼ mark of swollen mark with a point of blood left in the middle just like the ʼOne-Junʼ mark of Jun Ajpu!

And just because nobody would say who that was who left each and every one bitten nobody could name the name of the ʼOneʼ who bit them with a bite that left each one bitten.

This one bite each left each one to ask the one question as to who it was who had bit them and by asking this one question was the question that when answered, answered the question of what was the name of each and every Lord in perfect order: which makes one wonder if the name lord comes from sacred ʼorderʼ better known as hierarchy.

And so it was that each and every Lord of Xibʼalbʼa came to name each and every name of each and every Lord as each and every Lord came to name the name of one-an-other.

And so the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa named one-an-otherʼs name in perfect order which was a perfect way for to hear the Lords naming the names of one-an-other as if they were Older and Younger Brothers.

Just like this then, were their names named; they just named one another in perfect order. That is how their names were named. It was just because of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa naming one anotherʼs names that each one of the Lordsʼ names were named when they were named in perfect order.

ʼNaming their Namesʼ

This then is how the Boys brought about the naming of the names; the naming of the names of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa. These were those Lords of Death that Xaʼn bit to bite them so they would be bitten in a perfectly orderly organized fashion; so that in this perfectly hierarchical way the one who was bitten first, and who was the immediate Superior Lord, would ask what was the matter to the one who had just been bitten as the Inferior Lord who had just been bitten, when he was bit next. So that the Superior Lord would name the Inferior Lords name in a most sacred sort of order known as the ʼhierarchyʼ of naming of the Lords.

body:
So that the first bitten Superior Lord would respond to the Inferior Lord who had just been bitten ʼwhat-nakiʼ was wrong; what had just happened; to which the Inferior Lord who had just been bitten would exclaim to the Superior Lord who had just been bitten: Aji! Who is that that who has just bit me? And which point he names the Lord as a rejoinder to this perfectly repetitive question as in: “Who or what was just bit me Ajaw Wuqubʼ Kame? asks Ajaw Jun Kame.

To which the one who had been bitten first-the Superior Lord-names the name of the one who had just been bit-the Inferior Lord; who was the one who had just asked the previous Lord, the one who was bitten first; the one who was bit before-Jun Kame-the one who had just been bitten-Wuqubʼ Kame-is the one who asks: what or who has just bit me?

This way the freshly bitten and the previously bit would end up asking one another who had just bit them while ʼNaming their Namesʼ in perfect order so that they were bit with a bite that hurt so much that they exclaim: “Aji! What has just bit me with a bite that has left me so very, very bitten? Aji! Aji! Aji!”

The Lords of Xibʼalbʼa were named by the Lord who was oneʼs immediate Superior. Each Lord was named by the Lord seated by their side, as they sat there beside one another on the council bench in the Council House of Xibʼalbʼa.

The Lords of Xibʼalbʼa were named by the Lord superior them in hierarchy so that the Superior Lord named the next Inferior Lord in rank; so that the more Superior Lord was bitten first to demonstrate the noble hierarchy of the Popobʼal Ja Xibʼalbʼa with its status and station with its position and power in which the Inferior Lord was named by the Superior Lord until all of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa were named through their being named in the perfect order of Noble Lords naming the names with their precise rank and particular  order.

Nabʼe-First; Kabʼ-Second; Rox-Third; Kaj-Fourth;  Ro- Fifth; Waqaq-Sixth;  Wuq-Seventh;  Wajxaq-Eighth; Bʼelej-Ninth; Lajuj-Tenth;  Julaj-Eleventh;  Kabʼlajuj-Twelfth;  Roxlajuj-Thirteenth;  Kajlajuj-Fourteenth…

body:
This is a foreshadowing of the Fourteen Generation of the Kʼicheʼ Maya Rulers that begin with the First Four Fathers of the Kʼicheʼ Maya. So do realize that these Lords of Death; Lords of Disease may very well be the Ancestors of the Kʼicheʼ Maya as seen in their Ancient Ancestral Way of understanding Death and Disease.

Nabʼe; Kabʼ; Rox; Kaj; Roʼ; Waqaq; Wuq; Wajxaq; Bʼelej; Lajuj; Julaj; Kabʼlajuj; Roxlajuj; Kajlajuj…

First, Second, Third, Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, Eighth, Ninth, Tenth, Eleventh, Twelfth, Thirteenth, Fourteenth…

This naming of all the names of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa was revealed to Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej by the One they sent to do their bidding.

Not one of the Lords escaped being named; each one of them named the name of the Lord seated next until the Boys finished naming the names of all of them there; leaving all of the names of Xibʼalbʼa named; that is how their names were named in perfect order; not one name of the names of the Lords was left out; not one name was left to be lost in his naming of the names of those known as the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

This was when they were bitten by the hair plucked from the skin of Junajpuʼs shin.

But it is not a true Mosquito; not a real Mosquito-mana qitzij Xaʼn that bit them when he was sent to listen to their names that would be named by Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej when they were requested, when they were required; when it was demanded, when it was commanded that they name the names of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

This then was when those named Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej took up their road upon which they went walking; this road they walked until arriving to where those of Xibʼalbʼa were waiting:

“Greet the Noble Lords,” said One of them.

“The Seated Ones!” ordered the One who sent for them to come.

“Ri kubʼulik!” Xchaʼ ri Jun taqchiʼnel.

“The Ones who are Seated!” repeated the One who sent their summons.

“That One there is not a Noble Lord; that one there is just a Wooden Dummy; that One there is just a Wooden Double-xa Poy-just a Carved Creation; a Crafted Deception,” said the Boys who continued.

body:
“That one seated there is just a Deceptive Decoy; just a fake; just a fraud; just a primitive ploy known as a Poy,” said the Boy.

“That one there that sits by the door is nothing more than a Wood-Worked Work of Worked-Wood; xa Ajam Cheʼ just Worked Wood is what that One is because that One there is just a Wooden Figure, a Wooden Formation akin to Man; a Wooden Manikin nothing more.” Said the Boys; said the Sons who stood at the Entrance where sat those devious deceptions; those deceptive distractions known as Poy; named Ajam Cheʼ.

This is what they said, the Boys, Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej when they arrived there in the entrance hall of Xibʼalbʼa before the Seated Lords-Kubʼulik Ajawabʼ who sat all in a row; who sat in perfect order on the bench in the Popol Ja; the Council House of Xibʼalbʼa. This then was when they greeted the Noble Lords; this then was when they named their names:

“Qʼala Tat, Greetings Father; Jun Kame: One Death!”

“Qʼala Ta, Greetings Father; Wuqubʼ Kame: Seven Death!”

“Qʼala Ta, Greetings Father; Xikiripat: Bleeder of Blood; Bloodletter

“Qʼala Ta, Greetings Father; Kuchuma Kikʼ: Blood Gatherer

“Qʼala Ta, Greetings Father; Ajal Puj; Noble Lord Pus

“Qʼala Ta, Greetings Father; Ajal Qʼana: Noble Lord of Yellow Jaundice

“Qʼala Ta, Greetings Father; Chʼamiya Bʼaq: Bone Staff Bearer

“Qʼala Ta, Greetings Father; Chʼamiya Jolom: Skull Staff Bearer

“Qʼala Ta, Greetings Father; Xikʼ: Wing Hawk; Sudden Death on the Road

“Qʼala Ta, Greetings Father; Patan: Merchant-Strap; Crossroads Death

“Qʼala Ta, Greetings Father; Kikʼ Reʼ: Bloody Teeth, Bloody Fangs

“Qʼala Ta, Greetings Father; Kikʼ Rixkʼaq: Bloody Claws, Bloody Talons

This is what they said when they arrived there with the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

The faces of the Lords were just finished off; the Boys named the names of all of their names when they named their names in perfect order.

Not one name was forgotten, not one name was left out; none; not a one; the Boys named them when they named them One and All.

body:
What was desired by those of Xibʼalbʼa was that their names should not be known by the Boys, the Sons.  But that is not what happened because the Boys knew them by name so that when the Boys came they named the Lords by name by naming them One after the Other; from First to Last, the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa were named by the Boys; by the Sons; by the Twins who named their names by naming the names of each and every one of them just as the Lords were ordered when Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej were ordered to do when it came to their naming the names of those who were the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

“Come, sit here!” they were told, knowing the Boys would want to take a seat on their bench. But they didnʼt sit down; they didnʼt sit down because they didnʼt want to sit down.

“That is not our bench there, it is just a cooking stone-xa chojim abʼaj-that bench there-ri tem ri-is just a hot stone bench, a blistering burning bench, nothing more!” said Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

The Boys, the Sons; they were not defeated there by Xibʼalbʼa as the Lords had thought was their destiny; the destiny of theirs; the destiny of their Fathers.

“Utz bʼa la! Well then! Just go on then; the two of you just get going; just get yourselves in that House there!” they were told.

This is when they entered Dark House-Qʼequma Ja but they were not defeated there either.

This was the First House of Ordeal in Xibʼalbʼa, it was the first place of tests; the first place of trials that the Two Sons, Two Boys entered when they entered there in Dark House: Qʼequma Ja.

It was there that those of Xibʼalbʼa began feeling the seeds of defeat for them there in Dark House. They felt like maybe they were going to defeat them; that is what they felt in their heart, they felt they would defeat them, the Boys, in Dark House: Qʼequma Ja.

First, they would have to enter Dark House-Nabʼe, xeʼok pa Qʼequma Ja. That is when they went in to deliver their pine-torches-xbʼeyaʼoq ri chäj.

body:
Those pine torches-ri chäj of torch-pine-chaj were already burning when the Worker-Samajel went in to leave them with the Boys there in Dark House. Each one was given a cigar of rolled tobacco by the Messenger-Samajel of Jun Kame who was the Servant-Samajel of One Death; Jun Kame.

“ʼHere are your torches! Waʼe kichäje!ʼ” says the Lord. ʼAt Dawn come out to give them back, the two of them, the torches along with the cigars. The Messengers will come to collect them from you,ʼ says the Lord,” said the Messenger of Xibʼalbʼa when he arrived there with the Boys in Dark House-Qʼeqʼuma Jaʼ.

“Utz bʼa la!” they said then.

But the torches they carried with them were not burning; for they were not real torches that burned red hot. What they carried inside with them were just replicas that were replacements to replace the burning embers of true pine-torches.

The replacement torches and replica cigars that they carried with them into Dark House were the bright red tail feathers-ujeʼxiʼk of the Scarlet Macaw-KaqKʼix or just: Kaqix.

Truly, the replacements-ukexwach of their torches looked just like those they were given and made to appear to the Sentinels who watch all that went on there in the Dark House-Qʼeqʼuma Ja. For those brilliant red feathers of the Scarlet Macaw burned bright through the night like the very torches they were given in the dark of Dark House.

Red Giant Arcturus

Remember the Red Giant Arcturus planted directly overhead in the Dark House of the Night Sky on the zenith passage of the Sun around the pivotal period time falling between the days and nights of May 3-10 when the Sun stand straight overhead at mid-day: Tikil Qʼij.

body:
Well now we are being reminded of this time of initiation by the long red tail feather of Wuqubʼ Kaqix that ends in the Red Giant Arcturus in the very Heart of the Sky: Ukʼuʼx Kaj. The time has come to begin the New Era; New Epoca of the New Formation; New Creation of these Young Men as they make their rite of passage to become the Ancestral Replacements or Kʼexelʼ as the Engendered Sons of their Dead and Deceased Fathers whose bodies are buried beside the Ballcourt there in Xibʼalbʼa; their Ancestral Souls and Nawal Spirits awaiting their Sons arrival beside the Ballcourt of Sacrifice: Pusbʼal Chaaj.  The Archaic Era of the Cave World is enveloped by the Magical Era of the Gourd-Headed-Tzuy-Wa Memory of their Fathers to call upon the Mythical Soul of the Hero Twins who are well on their way of ordering the Mental Rational Lineal Analytical World of Counting and Naming the Ways of the World.

The Ever-Present Origins of the Mythic Imagination is lighting our way as we enter Dark House illuminated by the magic of myth that renew and revitalizes the Ancient Archaic Cave of Xibʼalbʼa with the newly shaped mental formation of the analytical creations of the Boys who can do what their Fathers could not; which, is Name the Names in perfectly ordered lineal rational ways of these Cultural Heroes who are Twins live, die, and reborn through the powers of Twinship.

The Boys can collaborate with one another in order to cooperative with one another in order to complement one another as Integral Beings who will begin the transcendent work of integrating their Ever-Present Origins into the Empire of the Sovereign Lord Quetzalcoatl the Great Lord and Precious Twin of the Sky-Earth; Day-Night; Sun-Moon; Quetzal-Rattlesnake of the Forest Day and Desert Night; Nim Ajaw Tepew Qʼuqʼkumatz who is the Sovereign Conqueror Sage Wiseman Protector and Guide; Ruler and Leader of ʼAll of the Peopleʼ not just ʼOne Nation of One City-Stateʼ but the Nim Ajawarem the Great Kingdom of the Great Empire of the Tolteca-Chichimeca; Olmeca, Xicalanca; Mixteca-Zapoteca; Popoloca-Nonohualca.

body:
This is the Mesoamerican Empire the Boys are being and becoming initiated into here; an Integral Mesoamerican World we have not been able to see until now; now that we can bring forth that world through very detailed studies of Mesoamerica that exist now. Letʼs go, let us enter Dark House to begin this process of initiation through transformation of the Hero Twins: JunAjPu; IxBʼalamKej.

And as for the burning embers of their cigars; what happened to them? Well they just placed lightning bugs on each tip of their cigars-xa qʼaqʼa chikop xkikojo chuwi sikʼ-so it looked like the Boys just smoked and smoked through the night!

“Have we not just defeated them here then?” cheered the sentries who watched them there in Dark House.

“Have we not just beat them here?” jeered the sentinels that stood watching outside of that House of Darkness where they could see the burning tip of their cigars as they lit-up and dim-down; as they lit-up, they dim-down because of the natural way of their nawal lightning bug animal companions who gave their all to deceive those who kept watch over them throughout the long dark night of Dark House: Qʼeqʼuma Ja as this house filled with darkness is known.

And so it was for their torches and cigars and what was expected to happen to them? Well since the torches just burned with a resplendent bright light and the cigars simmered as embers they both lit up the night with the shimmering shine of their luminous light.

There would be nothing left of them by daybreak from the way they burned there before the gaze of those who kept watch over the torches and cigars that most certainly would be finished off before morning came.

But the torches were not finished off; they were the same as when they had been given to them at dusk the night before. As for their cigars, they didnʼt even light them up, they were just the same as the cigars they were given when they entered Dark House and this is how they, the Boys, returned them when the sentinels came to collect them at Dawn.

Their torches, their cigars; the sentries, the sentinels just went right over and to return them to the Rulers-Ajawabʼ-the Nobles, the Lords of Xibʼalbʼaʼ who asked:

body:
“And these ones, who are they?”

“Of what then are they made?”

“Where do they come from?”

“Who fathered them; who mothered them?”

“Who engendered them; who conceived them?”

“Who then is their Father; who then their Mother?”

“Truly our hearts are going to be burnt up by them; surely our souls are going to be finished off by them! It is just no good what they are doing; doing to us los meros jefes de Xibʼalbʼa. There is something about them; something about them is different; different too is their nature-kikʼojeʼik-their essence!” They said when they spoke to one another; those who were they of Xibʼalbʼa.

It was then that all the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa were summonsed; they were sent for to hear what the Lords wanted to do next; and what they wanted to do next is why they gathered together to celebrate council with one another.

This was when Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame called the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa together to summons the Boys; to speak with the Sons: Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej their names. It was then that they said this:

“Letʼs just play ball Boys; come letʼs take up the rubberball in the ballcourt together to play ball, you, oh Sons,” said the Lords, when the said what they said when they spoke with the Boys.

“Oj ochaajoq, ix kʼajolabʼ” Xeʼuchaʼxik.

And so then they were questioned there by Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame; One Death, Seven Death:

“Where did you come from? We wish you would tell us, you, oh Boys; you, oh Sons, Ix Kʼajolabʼ,” asked those of Xibʼalbʼa.

“Well, we must have come from some place! But we donʼt know where that could be,” is all that they said without naming from where they came.

“Apa kixixpe wi? Chibʼij taj, Ix Kʼajolabʼ,” xchaʼ kʼut Xibʼalbʼa chike

“A la bʼa xojpe wi lo! Mawi  qetaʼm,” xa xechaʼ, mawi xkibʼij.

“Utz bʼa la, letʼs just go play ball then, you Boys,” said-xechaʼ those of Xibʼalbʼa.

“Utz! Fine!” they said-xechaʼ.

“So let us put our ball into play; let us just use our ball-qakikʼ, our blood-qakikʼ” said-xechaʼ Xibʼalbʼa.

“No way! Ma taj! We donʼt want that! We will put ours into play here,” said the Boys-xechaʼ Kʼajolabʼ.

“Not to be!-Maja bʼi! Here, here is where we shall just use ours,” -said Xibʼalbʼa-xechaʼ Xibʼalbʼa.

body:
“Very well then,” said the Sons.

“Utz bʼa la,” xechaʼ Kʼajolabʼ.

“Letʼs go; letʼs play. It is just a striped one-juchʼil-itʼs just a decorated ball, a ball that hides a white flint knife inside as they say,” said Xibʼalbʼa-xechaʼ Xibʼalbʼa.

“That just isnʼt so! It is just a disguised decorated skull with an obsidian blade inside; thatʼs all it is!” said the Boys- xechaʼ Kʼajolabʼ.

“No itʼs not like that!” said Xibʼalbʼa- xechaʼ Xibʼalbʼa.

“Utz bʼa la! Very Well then,” said One Blowgun Boy-xchaʼ Junajpu.

So this then was when they threw the ball of Xibʼalbʼa down into play, landing on the hip-yoke-ubʼateʼ of Junajpu sending the ball flying and the white flint knife sliding across the ballcourt floor; Saqi Toq shimmied as it sailed singing silence-chitzʼininik; chitzʼininik as silence went singing across the fine face of the hard surface of Pusbʼal Chaaj as the sound of silence went sounding as it went resounding across the ballcourt floor: chi-tzin-tzin-tzin; chi-tzin-tzin-tzinʼ nothing more could be heard other than the white flint blade that lay silent on the floor on their now deadly quiet court.

Juchʼil: A Stripped One of Sacrifice

Juchʼil will transform the Castilian word knife or dagger that is cuchillo to kuchʼil the word for knife heard today amongst the Maya  that began with the word that sounds like it sounds here: juchʼil from juchʼ or ʼstripped onesʼ; that is to say ʼstripped one of sacrificeʼ and jun chay or one obsidian blade.

We have already come to see Xibʼalbʼa likes to hide their ʼSaqi Toq-White Flint Knife of Sacrificeʼ inside their ʼdecorated, stripped ball of sacrificeʼ and this is why they are ʼfightingʼ over whose ball they will throw down  into play and what kind of game of sacrifice of sacrifice will they play anyway.

Itʼs hard to say in this Mesoamerican Empire where there are so many ways to play out rituals of sacrifice and rituals of the rubberball game. How shall we Play-Chaaj? With whose Ball-Kikʼ: Ballcourt-Chaaj-Ballgame; Ball-Chaaj-Play all spoken with One single, solitary word: CHAAJ?

body:
Itʼs difficult to say just how this game will be played since the languages that they of speak come from the Highlands and Lowland; North and South; East and West so the language that the  Ball-Players speak arenʼt the same language-tzij; truth-tzij; tradition-tzij with which to play the game.

Juchʼil was a ʼstripped oneʼ and as ʼa stripped oneʼ the person who was painted with red and white strips were those who were distinguished as decorated beings who were sacrificial beings who had become sacrificial gifts of ritual sacrifice; the ʼstriped oneʼ or  juchʼil was headed for the sacrificial stone to be beheaded ritual sacrifice.

The game of Xibʼalbʼa is ʼsacrificeʼ this is what they want for the Boys; they just want to sacrifice them like they sacrifice everyone who comes down to Xibʼalbʼa through the oldest most deceptive trick in the book known as ʼbait and switchʼ which is what this word-play on  juchʼil is about.

The juchʼil or decorated stripped ball of Xibʼalbʼa is all about sacrifice even thought they say otherwise. Those of Xibʼalbʼa are great liars; bold-faced liars who are shameless and faceless sorts of graceless liars as in ʼdescaradamente mentirososʼ kinds of false-face lying deceivers.

Xibʼalbʼa are those who are unashamed to use what seems to be this ancient tactic of ʼbait and switchʼ. Because this is most certainly an ancient ancestral case of ʼbait and switchʼ for these young ballplayers who if they are not careful will become victims of sacrifice; like their Fathers: Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu.

White Flint Knife-Saqi Toqʼ

This is when those of Xibʼalbʼa saw the White Flint Knife-Saqi Toqʼ fly out of the ball to then go zigzagging its way across the finely finished surface of the ballcourt floor making its way sounding out with its ʼchi-tzin-tzin-tzin; chi-tzin-tzin-tzinʼ sound as the White Flint Blade of Xibʼalbʼa echoed the cry and call of their great desire to summons sacrifice.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Their White Flint Blade heard as Saqi Toq  could be heard ringing as it was sent singing as a sacrificial sound that resound as a ricochet obsidian blade sent sailing through the air just like they had wished for their razor sharp shining white flint knife that seemed to shimmy as it shook and shivered as it  slid sliding siding on it side sounding out like shriek, like a sigh sailing over the sleek shiny surface of the stone hard ceramic floor of their sacrificial ballcourt spoken of as ballcourt sacrifice of the White Flint Knife; Saqi Toq.

“What could that be?” shouted Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

“Naki pa la?” xchaʼ Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej

This shows how the Two Boys spoke as One in the singular ʼhe said-xchaʼ instead of the plural ʼthey said-xechaʼ for when they spoke-xechaʼ as one the Scribe write xchaʼ as he said which is a perfect example of how the Two Boys; Two Sons who are  Twins act as One Son who ʼsaidʼ what he said: xchaʼ. You know what I saying? There is no end in finding nawal genius in Popol Wuj; where the Scribes say what they say so that what must be said is left said even when the spoken word is said by the dead.

“If death is all you wanted then why send for us? And why then send your messengers? Why send them up to summon us to down here to play with you? Thank you very much,” said the Boys who quickly got up to go; enough was enough; it was all much too much.

“You will have to excuse us; we will just be on our way!” said the Boys to those of Xibʼalbʼa-Xechaʼ Kʼajolabʼ che ke Xibʼalbʼa.

What the Lords wanted for the Boys, what they wished for them, was that they should die right there on the ʼedge of the obsidian bladeʼ or ʼchi chaʼ as they say-xechaʼ.

ʼChi chaʼ which is to say ʼto die in an instant on the edge of the obsidian blade; on the obsidian blade of the obsidian knifeʼ which is to say ʼjusu ta xkam ri chiriʼ, chi chaʼ which was their way to say to be sacrificed on the obsidian blade of their obsidian knife; to die on the edge of the obsidian blade.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This was the sacrificial blade that was hid inside their blade-bearing ball; the blade-bearing ball of sacrifice that was the sacrificial ball of Xibʼalbʼa known as Saqi Toqʼ the White Flint Knife of Sacrifice.

Yet the Boys did not die as Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame wished for them. It didnʼt happen that way; it didnʼt happen like that because it didnʼt go that way. It was just those of Xibʼalbʼa who were defeated by the Boys, ri Kʼajolabʼ; the Engendered Sons: Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

Now they were going; now they were leaving the ballcourt of the Lords; the Sacrificial Ballcourt of Sacrifice: Pusbʼal Chaaj Xibʼalbʼa.

“Donʼt go Boys-Ix Kʼajolabʼ, we want to play ball, letʼs use your ball; letʼs just throw your ball into play,” said those who spoke to the Engendered Sons; xuchax kʼut Kʼajolabʼ.

“Utz bʼa la!” xechaʼ kʼut- they said then to them.

So then it was with their ball that they began play; their ball was thrown into play; the ball of the Boys was put into play so that it was with their ball that they began to play. And this was the way they continued to play with many good plays made by both sides as it is said; both side making equal plays as they played with equal strength when they played with their ball; when they played that first day.

And so it was that after playing for a while with equal strength and equal vigor they chose to stop for a moment to choose the winnings-kichʼakon of the wager of those whose score was bigger and better; and this is how they decided upon what would be the winnings of their wager:

“What should it be that we wager-chiqachʼako; what could it be that we win-qachʼakon?” asked those of the Xibʼalbʼa known as the Place of Fear, Place of Initiation, Place of Intimidation.

“Well now, why donʼt you choose,” was all that the Boys said-xechaʼ knowing what they knew about the ways of Xibʼalbʼa.

“We would just like to win four bowls each-kajkaj tzel-four gourds a piece of Flower Petals,” said-xechaʼ those of Xibʼalbʼa.

“Utz bʼa la! Very well! What kind of Flower Petals-Kotzʼijal would you like?” asked-xechaʼ the Boys of Xibʼalbʼa. To which the Lords responded in kind and considerate words:

body:
“One big handful of Red Petals; Ju tiqʼabʼ Kaqa muchit

One big handful of White Petals; Ju tiqʼabʼ Saqi muchit

One big handful of Yellow Petals, Ju tiqʼabʼ Qʼana muchit,

One big handful of Big Ones, Ju tiqʼabʼ kʼa ri Nimaʼq,” xechaʼ Xibʼalbʼa.

“Utz bʼa la!” said the Boys, said the Sons-xechaʼ Kʼajolabʼ.

So once again they threw their ball down to begin another round of play; they played one another with equal strength, with the Boys making many good plays. With their hearts made sweet with their ball-playing feats-and with every good intention-the Boys gave themselves up in defeat on this first day of ballcourt play.

Truly content were those of Xibʼalbʼa with their winning a sweet victory and the Boysʼ losing a bitter defeat.

“Havenʼt we done well; arenʼt we then the first to win?” said-xechaʼ Xibʼalbʼa when they said-xechaʼ what they had to say: xechaʼ.

This is when the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa asked themselves: “Where are they going to go to bring back our flowers; flowers that we have won from them?” xechaʼ chi kikʼux, asked Xibʼalbʼa when they spoke between one another; when they spoke to each other heart to heart.

“Truly, at dawn you will give us our flowers-qakotzʼiʼj that are our winnings of our wager-qachʼakom,” they demanded of the Sons-Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej- when they reiterated what the Boys were responsible for with regard to their ballcourt wager and the winnings of Xibʼalbʼa.

“Utz bʼa la! At dawn then we will play again,” is what they said when they took leave of one-an-other; when they gave each other instructions for the next day and its ballgame play.

It was then when the Sons-ri Kʼajolabʼ-the Boys, entered the House of Obsidian-Blades, pa Chayim Ja, the Second House of Tests-ukabʼ Tijobʼal Xibʼalbʼa-the Second House of Trials:  the Second House of Ordeal there in Xibʼalbʼa.

And that is when it was wished for them to be dismembered by the Obsidian-Blades; this was where the Lords just wanted the Boys to be cut to pieces by the Obsidian-Blades-xeqʼatakʼox taj rumal Cha.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Those of Xibʼalbʼa wished with all their heart that the Boys, the engendered Sons would be killed quickly; but they were not killed quickly for they did not lose heart; they did not die there in the House of Obsidian-Blades; pa Chayim Ja.

This was when the Boys spoke to the Obsidian-Blades giving them their instructions: ʼThat which is yours is all the flesh of the Animals,ʼ they said to the Obsidian-Blades.

This was when they instructed the Obsidian-Blades as to ʼwhat was theirs in lifeʼ when they celebrated council with them-the Obsidian Blade-in order to give their advice, their instruction, the understanding of what ʼwas theirsʼ on the Face of the Earth. Ta xechaʼ chi re Cha ta xkipixabʼaj.

No longer did they move. All at once they dropped down from above, the Obsidian-Blades, all of them just dropped to the ground to lay at rest on the floor of the House of Obsidian Blades.

For truly, these were just Leaf-cutter Ants and Warrior Ants who were the Conquering Ants and Cutting Ants that the Boys summoned there into the House of Obsidian-Blades-pa Chayim Ja by calling them in through incantation; by luring them in through invocation that led to their complete captivation; their enthralling enchantment.

It was just by calling them in and calling them up through their singing them in and their singing them up that the Ants arrived there to enter the House of Obsidian-Blades-pa Chayim Ja.

This was the place of tests and house of trials that was right there beside the flower gardens and fruit trees known as the plantings-utikom of Xibʼalbʼa.

And so the Boys sang their song of enchantment as they made their incantation to invoke, to enchant the Ants so that they might file into the Lordsʼ precious plantings of flower gardens and prized plantations of fruit trees.

This then is when and what they sang to summons the Ants; for this was the magic spell the Boys sung as an enchanting appeal to call upon the Ants to steal away the flower petals through their charming invocation that went like this:

“Cutter Ants, Conquering Ants; Come-in, come-in, come in Dancing; come-in, come in Dancing; all of you…Come! Come! Come in! Come in! Come in Dancing!”

body:
“Come carry the fine floral faces; Come carry the fine flower faces; come bear away the flowery façades of their winnings; their precious petal earnings!”

“Come, come carry away the blooming blossoms won by the Noble Lords who believe they are awesome! Come, come carry away the flourish flowers of the Noble Lords who believe they have magical powers!”

This was the Boys way of enchantment as they invoked; as they enchanted the Ants to bring forth their flourishing floral winnings of their blooming blossoming ballcourt wager made to be paid to the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

“Chay Sanik, Chʼeken Sanik: Kixpetoq, Kixojoq iwonojel. Oj ikʼamaʼ ronojel uwach kotzʼiʼj, kichʼakon AjAwabʼ...”

“Cutter Ants, Conquering Ants; Come-in, come-in, come in Dancing; come-in, come in Dancing; all of you: Come! Come! Come in! Come in! Come in dancing! Come in carrying your great shower of their flowers; all the many blossoms of their blooming flowers; the Tribute, the Treasure beyond measure all that was won by the victorious Lords, “Chay Sanik, Chʼeken Sanik: Kixpetoq, Kixojoq iwonojel. Oj ikʼamaʼ ronojel uwach kotzʼiʼj, kichʼakon AjAwab”

The Cutter Ants; the Conquering Ants were instantly enchanted by the Boys who called them into the precious plantings of the Lords to come in dancing carrying the cutting of their prized flower petals won in their wager with those of Xibʼalbʼa yet cut and carried away by the Ants for the Boys to fulfill the debt made with the wager they intentionally created to be paid to those whose plantations flourished with flowers filled with magical powers embodied in the blooms and blossoms of the red, white, yellow, and big flowers that now filled the four gourd bowls with the precious prized petals of the Noble Lords.

“Utz bʼa laʼ!” said the Ants as they marched off to bring back the flower petals from the plantings of Xibʼalbʼa; their plantation of fruit trees and flower gardens spoken of as utikom Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame: the precious plantings of the prized plantations of Xibʼalbʼa.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
The Cutter-Ants, the Conquering Ants were sent off to bring back the blossoms and blooms from the gardens and groves of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa known and named as One Death, Seven Death.

For already-the day before-it was they-the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa-who gave their instructions to the guardians and caretakers of the Flowers of Xibʼalbʼa-chajal kikotzʼiʼj Xibʼalbʼa.

This is what they said: “You, you must watch closely; watch our flowers in our plantings! Donʼt let them be stolen now that we have defeated the Boys-ri Kʼajolabʼ-the Sons.

“Where can they go to find our prize-winnings-qachʼakon?”Asked the Lords as they spoke directly to their Guardians; Chajal Tikoʼn.

Well, we will tell you said the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa: ʼThis is the place to find and take the winnings we wagered; so sleep not tonight so that you remain vigilant; lookout; keep watch; stay awake for our sake; take care of what is really, truly at stake; our fire in the flowers is the heart, the soul of our ancestral powers that bloom and blossom in our flower gardens, our fruit orchards, our flourishing groves and their divine essence of our sacred sustenance where the flowers bloom; where the blooms blossom; where the fruit flowers; grows; sweetens!”

“Utz bʼa la!” they said then-xecha kʼut-the Night Jars; Pu-Juyubʼ; Xpur-Pu-Weq.

The guardians of the blooming rows of flowers and blossoming groves of fruit didnʼt feel a thing when it happened; when it happened to them in the garden; in the night; in the garden in the night when it happened to them: the Guardians of the Plantings; Chajal Tikoʼn.

Known as the Night-Jars: Xpurpuweq; Pujuyu; Xpurpuweq; Pu Juyubʼ; Ix-Pur-Pu-Weq; Pu-Juyubʼ who sing through the warm wet luxuriant moon-lit  nights of the late Dry-Season  when they begin singing at dusk to call the rain when it is warm enough to stay-up through the Night to watch-over the maize sprouts-iwal abʼix shooting up in la Milpa. This is the time of the year that one says: tzuq pa abʼix; the milpa has sprouted.

They just sang from the limbs of the trees while the thieves entered and exited unseen.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
The Sentries just spent the night jumping from branch to branch keeping watch over the blooming flowers blossoming in the fruiting gardens without noticing a thing.

For they did not see or hear or smell a thing; nor did they taste nor sense nor feel nor think a thing about those who came and went with what they came to collect.

For it was just a silent, imperceptible force that moved through the night as they arrived and departed with what they clipped and snipped to then gather-up to then take-away; which, was what they were sent-out to cut and collect: precious petals; prized blooms; beloved blossoms.

The watchmen remained wide awake as they perched themselves on the arms of the blossoming trees that were in full flower; trees that were budding with limbs in full bloom.

There the sentinels kept vigilant as they kept watch over everything that was left under their protective gaze; and so it was that they sang out through the night to stay wide awake so they could watch over all the blooms and blossoms they were given to protect.

The guardian were right where they were told to be; right there amongst the Lords flowering groves of blooming trees with their flourishing flowers with their precious petals and colorful blossoms falling all about as they floated down to the ground in the quiet calm sound with nobody around; in the perfect silence of the bright balmy night where row upon row of blossoming buds were being carried away; nothing seen; nothing to say; everything in order as night stepped ever so lightly out of the dark and into the day…

The care-takers were the birds who sang their songs at night; these sentries who were sentinels; these sentinels who were sentries of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa known as Night-jars to this very day and it was they who just cracked their mouths wide-open to sing their songs into the starry, starry night while they kept watch over the pristine plantings of Xibʼalbʼa.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
They never felt a thing when the Ants came and went throughout the long calm night gathering the Lords winnings that were so easily collected while the guardians and caretakers sang their sweet songs of solitude; their melancholic songs of longing sung through the quiet melancholy of the lonely, enchanted night.

The ants just swarmed about there while the night birds sang out their song of loss; of what they had no idea, no notion, no inkling of the commotion to come as they sang out in the dark warm mist, their somber tenor, sad tone filling the moist night air with solemn enchantment; they sang as the dew covered all that it touched.

They sang as an evocative invocation; a crying, a calling, a kind of clamoring incantation of their very own name: “Xpurpuweq! Xpurpuweq!” sang the night-criers whose night song called as it clamored to be known by its own naming the name of those who named their name only they sang it which was pretty much the same.

Xpurpuweq! Xpurpuweq” sang out the sentinels putting a spell on the haunted humid air ʼas ifʼ the ʼnight windʼ were there calling and crying for the thunder and lightning that now hummed as it hung in the clouds; that holy haven that harbored the divine voice of the sacred, sacred rain.

“Pujuyu! Pujuyu!” called out the other cry, “Pujuyu, Pujuyu” heard as “Blowgun of the Mountain; Blowgun of the Mountain-Pujuyu, Pujuyu-Breath of the Wild; Breath of the Wild.”

Sing the Song; Naming the Name; Calling the Rain by Singing the Song Sung as the Voice of the Mountain

This is the ʼSong of Pujuyuʼ as it is called, “Pujuyu, Pujuyu; Those of the Mountain, Those of the Mountain” as they sing the song of the People of the Mountain-Pujuyu; Pujuyu.

These are those who are remembered by the song they sing that is sung to name the names of the Caretakers of the Mountain whose divine voice sings the song that is sung in the warm nights before the first fallen rain. This is the song sung to call down the waters by naming the names of those who watch-over the magical ways of the transforming Mountain.

body:
The song that is sung as the song of the mountain that they sing is the song that calls for the falling of the mountain rain; the rain that comes as it is called to fall upon the mountain by those who sing their song that is the naming of their names; Pujuyu, Pujuyu.

This is a kind of singing that is sung as a song that is sang as the sacred singing of the call of the mountain that sings the song: Pujuyu, Pujuyu, the song that is heard as a call and a cry on the warm and windy,  balmy and breezy nights by the feathery winged ones who are the singing ones who sing their soft song that is a cry and call for the coming rain that when it comes will fall as the sweet soft song of the voice of the mountain; breath of the mountain of the people of the mountain that sing the song that calls the rain that names the name: Xpurpuweq, Xpurpuweq…Pujuyubʼ, Pujuyub!

Xpurpuweq, Xpurpuweq…Pujuyubʼ, Pujuyub!

Xpurpuweq, Xpurpuweq…Pujuyubʼ, Pujuyub!

This is their song sung all night long to call on the rain to fall as the sacred sustenance that is that which is theirs of those who are the sprouts shooting up in the milpa; that which is theirs is that which reveals what is their sacred sustenance that tells their ancient, ancestral truth; the truth of their ancient word that is the water and rain of the milpa and the maize that sprouts from the Face of the Earth. This is the song that one hears at night when the sprouts in the milpa are calling out for rain by crying out their name of those who are the ʼbreath of the mountainʼ Pujuyubʼ, Pujuyubʼ.

This is that which is their truth and that which is their truth is the water and rain that will quench their thirst; the thirst of the dusty dry parched mountain-plain where maize sprouts shoot up and out of the ground on the now scorching day-time mountainside.

But dusk has come as night has fallen when and where wet dew descends to begin falling and filling the little cups formed by the maize leaves that shape the little cups of ʼtwistedʼ leaves of maize known as: utum ja.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
These cups formed by these ʼhardʼ enduring maize sprouts withstand the strong mid-day heat of the Milpa; the Milpa with its mythical Four Hundred Boys who stand straight-up at attention like ʼlittle warriorsʼ with their heads upright in the direction of the Old Man, the Sun who rises up and over their heads while beating down on the ʼyoung initiatesʼ standing right side up with their heads facing their Father, the Sun, with his scorching mid-day heat.

These sprouts surviving in the Milpa are the ancestral descendants of the First Fathers of the Maize People.

These descendants are the embodied replacements-kʼexel that sprouts forth and grow through this initiatory period of the lifecycle of maize surviving in the Milpa as the return of the ʼyoung menʼ of the Ancestral Maize Lineage.

These are those with their ancestral faces and enduring, hard  traits who come back to life after being buried at death to be born again and survive as the eternal return of the jade green seed that will never die because its essence, its nature, and its condition-kʼojeʼik.

This is the internal essence; the inherited genius borne within that skull-like kernel of maize that will live on no matter how difficult, defeating, and deadly the tests, trials, and ordeals the maize descendants must face in its young life in the Milpa.

The Young Life of the Milpa experienced in the initiatory life as Young Noble Lords who want to be and become the noble replacement of their noble Fathers and Grandfathers who lived and died before them to be born again in lives of the young noble lords who are the replacements of their ancestors and renewal of the life of the lineage that lives again through them and their beautifully enduring ways.

Their Father the Sun is ʼhardʼ on them in the ʼheatʼ of the ʼbattleʼ to survive by Day; but by Night their Grandmother and Mother water them with their qʼebʼal-tinajas in the dewy light of the Moon. The Moon and the dewy light of Mid-night will draw down the evaporated waters of the day will fill-up the maize sprouts water cups-utum ja so they can drink-in the cool fresh water of dew that drenches the Face of the Earth all-night long.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
These resplendent green sprouts of maize are the descendants who now collect the water from the Moon Mother and Earth Grandmother who call out to their Father and Grandfather there in the mid-most point in the Heart of Sky; Ukʼuʼx Kaj the bright burning fire of the Kabʼawil fire will guide and protect them through his guidance and protection all along their arduous path of initiation.

The Mother-Father; the Grandmother-Grandfather  will help guide and protect all of those many formed beings, shaped beings who have been formed and shaped by the Former, Shaper; the Bearer, Begetter; the Mother, Father; Grandmother, Grandfather; the Mid-wife, Match-maker; the Shelterer, Protector there on the Face of the Earth.

This is what is happening in the nighttime in the plantings of those who live to bring their seeds to fruiting fruition.

This is the song that is sung to name the names of those who call the rain to water the milpa to ensure its survival right here on the Mountain-Plain.

Xpurpuweq and Pujuyubʼ were the two guardians, the two sentinels who watched-over the garden plantings of Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame. Yet they never felt a thing when the Ants entered there to steal away what they were given to protect.

No, no they never knew the Ants were there carrying away all that was theirs to keep from being borne away in the long silent lines of Chʼeken Sanik-Zompopo Ants who cut and carried away their burden of flower petals in a magnificent nighttime movement of Ants who marched through the plantings of Xibʼalbʼa without ever being heard or seen.

All the Ants just tumbled over one another as they swarmed all about harvesting the winnings of the Lords. They moved all about gathering their colorful cargos of petals, enchanted by the song they heard being sung through the night; these Ants became bearers of blooms and blossoms; these Ants became pilferers of bright colored petals who ran about gathering up the tribute to be paid that was the winnings that were wagered to become the debt to be settled.
