source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
They climbed up into the flowers on the tree branches to cut them away. Then they gathered up the petals that fell fluttering to earth from above; down below the flowering trees blooms and blossoms were trimmed so the petals floated down without making a sound to then be gathered up and carried away by the Ants ready and waiting below on the ground.

All of it was done in one night by the Cutter-Ants; by the Conquering Ants; Chay Sanik, Chʼeken Sanik who were the Obsidian-Blade Ants; these,  the ancestral allies of the Sons, the Boys since birth; and it was they, the Ants, who gave the Boys victory by carrying out the Lords defeat.

Meanwhile the guardians sang out at the top of their lungs, splitting open their mouths doing so. They didnʼt feel a thing when their tails where trimmed and their wings were clipped.

It was a great collection of flowers: of those that were cut, of those that fell, of those that were gathered to be carried away in the jaws of the Ants, in the middle of the night; work that was finished, work that was complete before the coming of day-break.

They filled the four bowls full of flower petals, the four gourds known as raxa tzel; precious bowl, precious gourd bowls of sacrifice are what the Boys carried to the Lords at Dawn filled with flower petals; blossoms, blooms of their chosen colors.

So it was then that the Messengers-Samajel arrived, as those who were they that summons-taqonel others; as Messengers they arrived to summons the Boys, the Sons, who were summoned by the Messengers:

“ʼCome along thenʼ say the Lords, ʼRight-away, we want that they should bring our winnings-qachʼakon,ʼ say the Lords,” they told the Boys, the Sons, ri Kʼajolabʼ.

“Utz bʼa la! Very well then!” they said then-xechaʼ kʼut.

They arrived bearing four bowls of flowers cradled in their arms;  with four bowls of petals  they entered; with four bowls of flower petals they presented themselves there before those of Xibʼalbʼa.

The Boys brought flowers to pay the wager the Lords had won playing ball. Sweet smelling flowers and flower petals are what they brought to the Lords; the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This is how they, the Boys, defeated Xibʼalbʼa; they just let them win to watch them lose. It was just the Ants that the Boys sent; in just one night the Ants gathered together all the tribute that was won in the wager bet in the ballgame they played; these were the winnings of the Lords; the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

And so they delivered the four sacred gourds-tzel-four sacrificial bowls filled with the blooming blossoms and collected flower petals. That is how those of Xibʼalbʼa were defeated; they were cut down like their flowers.

The Lords just turned white, all of those of Xibʼalbʼa, deathly pale did their faces become because of the Flower Petals: Red, White, Yellow and the Big Ones.

So then they sent for the guardians of the flowers:

“Why did you give them our flowers to be stolen away? Canʼt you see that these are our flowers that are here, just look?” they demanded from the caretakers, the guardians-chajal kotzʼiʼj-the protectors of their flowers.

“We didnʼt feel a thing, you oh Lord, not even did we notice them trimming our tails,” they said. And just like that Xibʼalbʼa split their beaks as punishment for what had been collected under their watch; this was the price they paid for not protecting what was harvested by others under their care: the Flowers of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

This is the origin of why these birdsʼ beaks are split. The beak, the mouth-kichiʼ of the Purpuweq, the Whip-poor-will, is this way today; a split-beaked bird is the Purpuweq.

ʼOn the Edge or Chi Cha of the Obsidian Bladeʼ

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
We are about to leave the House Obsidian Blades where the Obsidian Blades were given a great abundance of flayed flesh to be given out to the Kabʼawil as sacred sustenance. The image of the flowers being harvested by the Cutting Ants and Conquering Ants is an image imagined to be the taking of ʼflowersʼ in the ʼFlowery Warsʼ where flowery festooned warriors and finely feathered ballplayers entered the ʼflowery field of combatʼ to take captives for sacrifice. Both sides of the battle did their all to take home ʼflowersʼ to be sacrificed on the altars of their Divine Ancestors temple tops with their blazing sacrificial altars known as ʼkotzʼiʼjʼ or ʼflowersʼ in a world were flowers burn and blaze like fire just as fire buds and blossoms as flowers. This is a scene of ʼgreat abundanceʼ in the mythic imagination of the Obsidian House that becomes the Flower Gardens and Fruit Groves of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

This mythic place reminds us of Flower Mountain that will become Sustenance Mountain from which the entire world will be fed from the sacred sustenance found flourishing here in great abundance. All of this abundance that was given to the Obsidian Blades by the Boys, the Sons Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej who manifest their power by reapportioning who received sacred sustenance. In this sense the Obsidian Blades are the very embodiment of the Noble Lords, Warlords, and Warriors who enter the Flowery Wars to take ʼwhat was theirs in lifeʼ which was what the Boys, the Sons gave them in exchange for their own lives; lives that are not sacrificed to then be dismembered in the House of Obsidian Blades. It is in this House that the Noble Lords, Warlords, and Warriors received that which was theirs in life as those known a ʼChi Chaʼ or those of the ʼObsidian Edge of the Obsidian Blade.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This is where the Young Noble Lords as Ballplayers and Initiates find our ʼwhat is theirs in lifeʼ and ʼwhat is theirs in lifeʼ is the sacrificial flesh given to the Obsidian Blades by the Boys, the Sons to provide and sustain their Kabʼawil with the sacred sustenance that is the rich red flesh, flayed skins, skulls, jaws, and dismembered members of each and every one of the sacrificial bodies that were given to the Obsidian Blades: this is what was theirs gifted to them in the House of Obsidian Blades.

The text is speaking of Jaguar and Eagle Warriors; Puma and Hawk Warriors and Priests who impersonated the Obsidian Blade Deity or Kabʼawil who dismembered and flayed and cut to pieces the flesh of sacrificial victims. This is what this section is talking about in very opaque sort of dark obsidian glass sorts of ways. It is very hard to see unless you know Mesoamerican Religion and the pivotal role human sacrifice took in the practice of Mesoamerican Religion in which human beings were placed in a variety of categories that the modern mind no longer understands.

Obsidian Blades were the ʼteethʼ of deities that sacrificed human beings to provide and sustain themselves through priests who became the deity impersonation. Priest those became divinity when divinity was an Obsidian Blade that fell from the Sky and came up and out of the Earth. At this point the deity known as the Smoking Obsidian Mirror known as Tezcatlipoca must be seen here smiling in as he grins in on this very bloody, fleshy, and hearty sacrificial banquet to feed those who must be fed through the ritual of human sacrifice.

The image given is that of the Obsidian Blades moving all about like warrior blades with lives of their own in Obsidian Blade House; Obsidian Blades moving all about ready to fall on their victims in order to quickly dispatch them and then flay their skin from their flesh to then begin cutting of that red flesh and yellow fat into strips and pieces to be given as sacrifice to the deities and then passed on to humanity to consume as the flesh of the gods. This was transubstantiation on another level.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This is what the Boys promise to the Obsidian Blades who are the material aspect divinity who are promised the fresh fleshy meat that has become divine flesh through transubstantiation of sacrificial flesh taken by the Obsidian Blades. At which point the Obsidian Blades just lay down like weapons and donʼt move until some other powerful Nawal Deity gets them moving about again to take what is theirs in life to take: animal flesh that is human flesh that is divine flesh.

The image that is given in the text is that of Obsidian Blades that drop down from where they were shimmying and sliding over one another creating a grating, grinding noise that was meant to terrify those who entered the House of Obsidian Blades. Obsidian House is where those who entered there would be cut to pieces by dismemberment; limb from limb; piece by piece. But the Boys stopped this terrifying grating, grinding noise by telling the Obsidian Blades just exactly what they were to do once the Boys gave them what was theirs: the red meat of the flesh of all living red blooded beings who were given up in sacrifice to be cut to pieces ʼOn the Edge or Chi Cha of the Obsidian Blade.ʼ

This will become extraordinarily important when it comes to the taking of captives to be offered as sacrificial victims to the Divinities or Kabʼawil in the last sections of the Popol Wuj. This is when human beings will live off of the flesh of other human beings who are said to be Animal People because they are not Maize People-Ixim Winaq from Sustenance Mountain of Tollan Tzuy-Wa. This most important distinction between humans and animals will become very obscure when the time comes for taking other human beings captive to then be sacrificed. This momentous action takes place in very ʼhidden languageʼ that is hard to make sense of unless one begins here to bring its being understood forth as the scribes do here in genius ways.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Human beings eaten by other human beings will be seen as animal beings from the mountains and canyons in one sense. But in another sense human beings will be seen as maize beings whose flesh is formed and shaped from ground maize. Let me repeat this so you understand this because this is vital for us to understand if we are going to write about human beings consuming human flesh. Because the Maya as Mesoamerican People never consumed human flesh; they either consumed transubstantiated flesh that was seen as animal flesh of those human beings who lived like ʼwild animalsʼ in the mountains and canyons or they ate human flesh that was actually the flesh of maize people which means they consumed maize in the form and shape of transubstantiated human flesh.

It is a very subtle argument and discussion indeed but if we do not allow ourselves to understand this move to understand the ʼessence of fleshʼ in Mesoamerica we will never understand human sacrifice as the sacrifice of ʼbeingsʼ that are not ʼhumanʼ beings but maize beings. The category of ʼhumanʼ being does not exist because there is nothing in the cosmos understood as ʼhumanʼ flesh but there is ʼanimalʼ flesh; just as there is ʼclayʼ flesh; just as there is ʼwoodenʼ flesh and ʼreedʼ flesh; just as there is the flesh of ʼmaizeʼ but ʼhumanʼ flesh is not a kind of ʼfleshʼ that exists in the Maya-Mesoamerican World; which is a massive difference in our understanding of the essence, kʼojeʼik condition, kʼojeʼik, and nature , kʼojeʼik of flesh and sense of its existence, kʼojeʼik; its sense of being, kʼojeʼik.

For all being is formed and shaped from an essence that sustains that being with its sense of being; and, this is how everything that exists is understood so that everything can feed another with the essence that sustains it and its sense of being. These categories are vital to the understanding of giving of sacrifice that provides for every beingʼs specific needs.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This understanding of the essence of the flesh of the Maize People or Ixim Winaq is indeed what the Popol Wuj is all about. In fact, it is the only thing that the Popol Wuj is about since the question asked in Popol Wuj is: what is the essence of the flesh from which ʼpeopleʼ will be formed and shaped. The Popol Wuj is the Maya Cultureʼs attempt to understand what the essence of the flesh ʼpeopleʼ is here on the Face of the Earth.

The Popol Wuj is Mayaʼs sacred narrative that asks its reader to contemplate the essence, nature, character, and condition of the flesh of formed beings and shaped beings who were first formed and shaped from the essence of the trees and vines. Then the formed beings and shaped beings are formed and shaped from the flesh of animals to form and shape animals from animal flesh. Then come the formed and shaped being of earth, mud, and clay; then the essence of flesh of the formed beings, shaped beings were formed and shaped from Tzʼite Tree for Men of Wood and Reeds for Women of Reeds. And now we are headed towards the forming and shaping of formed and shaped beings of maize.

There is not one place in the Popol Wuj that talks of ʼhuman beingsʼ because ʼhuman beingsʼ do not exist as a category in the Maya-Mesoamerican Cosmos of formed beings and shaped beings who are known as ʼpeople or winaqʼ but never should we use the word ʼhumanʼ when translating the Popol Wuj.

So then they threw their ball down into play where they had gone down to play ball on their ballcourt; their ballcourt where they threw their ball down into play; there down below on their ballcourt.

They played one another to a draw; no one won; and, no one lost; they just played each other to a tie.

They just played each other even so they played to a tie; no two winners; no two losers; neither one felt the agony of defeat; neither one felt the thrill of victory.

When they finished their game they hung up their ball before gathering together in council to take leave of one another until the next day at Dawn: “Saqarik chik,” xechaʼ Xibʼalbʼa-“Again then at Dawn,” said those of Xibʼalbʼa.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
“Utz bʼa la! Then again at Dawn” repeated the Boys, when they left them and hung up their ball to take their rest before taking up their ball again at dawn to be thrown back down into play on the Sacrificial Ballcourt of Sacrifice; Pusbʼal Chaaj of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

This is when they were finished-ta xkelej which is a fine pun on their ball was hung up and the Killer Bat-Kama Sotz that will hang there at the end of Junajpuʼs blowgun waiting to take his ʼhead-offʼ with his Obsidian Blade fangs just before dawn comes. Now be careful as we will move through the Houses of Xibʼalbʼa one after the next until we come to the sacrificial death of Junajpu in the House of Bats: Sotzʼi Ja.

Xibʼalbʼa: Houses of Ordeal; Houses of Trials; Houses of Tests

Many Houses of Xibʼalbʼa: Ki Ja Xibʼalbʼa

Dark House: Qʼeqʼuma Ja with its endless deep dark nights eased only by the warmth and light of the burning torch and lit cigar.

Obsidian House: Chayim Ja with its razor-sharp Obsidian Blades resting on the floor but still ʼon edgeʼ ready to jump up in order to take what is theirs.

Ice House: Tew Ja with its shivering cold freezing drafts of icy sheets of hail and sleet driven by gale force winds this is the Cold House where one gets no rest.

Jaguar House: Bʼalami Ja home of many Jaguar with their crushing teeth and thrashing claws who dismember their prey by tearing them limb from limb.

Fire House: Qʼaqʼa Ja with its furious flames and scorching heat where one must overcome this blistering blaze where the Sun is felt as a burning bonfire on fire.

Bat House: Sotzʼi Ja with its decapitating Killer Bats-Kama Sotzʼ whose terrifying cries sound more like Xibʼalbʼaʼs screams that squeal as only Bats in Xibʼalbʼa can create freight-xibʼal as they screech and shriek as they cry out causing fear-xibʼibʼal as only Killer Bats in Xibʼalbʼa can do with their intimidating shrieking and threatening screeching throughout the long nights of terrorizing freight of those who find themselves wide-awake in the House of Bats-Sotzʼin Ja in Xibʼalbʼa...

Cold House, Ice House: Tew Ja

body:
Then they entered Ice House: Tew Ja. Unimaginable cold was encountered there where freezing hail fell thick in this frosty frozen frigid place: House of Shivering Cold.

Immediately the Boys finished off the Icy Cold with their heat and nawal way of dissipating frost, evaporating water, creating vapor on freezing cold morning dawns; gone was the cold and up came the mist that rose in the crystal clear sky with its warm moist Sun. The cold was vanquished; finished off as they say because of the Kʼajolab, the Engendered Sons; the Twin Boys they just vanished it away by evaporating it all back up into the Sky.

They did not die; morning came with them sparked full of life-kʼaslik; just shining bright were these two boys when the Sun rose into the icy morning Sky; the morning Sky with its rosy red dawn; the morning Sky with the frozen earth covered with white frost: saq tew.

All that Xibʼalbʼa wished for was that those Boys should be killed by the freezing cold; that they should be left dead once and for all is what those of Xibʼalbʼa wanted most for these Boys.

For what those of Xibʼalbʼa desired for those Boys was that they should die there from the freezing cold in that frigid place called Ice House, also known as Xuxulim Ja-Shivering House that was a very, very Cold House: Tew Ja.

But it was not like that; it did not come about like the way the Lords wished it for them; for it was they-the Boys, the Sons-who did not die there in Cold House.

They were just as alive as could be there when the Sun rose at Dawn; when the Dawn came up at the Coming Out Place of the Sun-Relebʼal Qʼij they were very much alive; they were not dead; they were not defeated; they were there to be greeted by the Sun; by the Day; by their Destiny that said they were very much alive: xawi e kʼaslik ta xsaqrik; e kʼaslik chik ta xsaqrik; for they were alive when the Day Dawned; they were alive there come Day-Break; they were with life there at the Break-of-Day.

So then hanging bats-xekel were ordered to watch over them there as sentinels; but once again these sentinels, their guardians, were given cause to leave, they went somewhere for they did not stay there hanging around to watch-over the Boys in Cold House.

“Why arenʼt they dead?” said the Lords-Ajawabʼ Rulers of Xibʼalbʼa.

Those of Xibʼalbʼa were awed by all they did, the Boys: Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej; Ancient Ancestral Blowgun Boy, Little Jaguar-Deer; they were those that left the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa awed by their power over the freezing cold in Cold House.

Jaguar House, Bʼalami Ja

Then they entered Jaguar House-pa Bʼalami Ja, thick with Jaguars was the House of Jaguar; Jaguar House: Bʼalam Rochoch.

“Donʼt eat us! There is what is yours that shall come to be that which is yours,” they told the Jaguar. So then the Boys poured a great bundle of bones before the animals. This then was when the Jaguar there in the House began to brawl over the bones that the Boys threw down to the Jaguar there to fight over when they were there in Jaguar House; furious were the Jaguar there as they fought over the bag of bones the Boy gave to the Jaguar-Bʼalam in Jaguar House-Bʼalami Ja.

“They are finished off now! Arenʼt they just being torn to pieces; their heart-kikʼux-their soul devoured now by the ferocious Jaguar there all closed up in the House of Jaguar: “that is there body and bones being chewed up,” said the Sentinels but it wasnʼt so; it wasnʼt like that because the Boys were not devoured there in that House of Jaguar.

Those of Xibʼalbʼa were made content for truly happy were they when they heard the Jaguar balling and brawling over the Boys; they were made sweet of heart-kiʼ kikʼux-listening to the Jaguar fight over the body and bones of the Boys being torn apart by their bloody claws; bloody fangs of the Jaguarsʼ bloody teeth.

But they did not die; for they were not defeated! They were as strong as ever when they came out of Bʼalami Ja, Jaguar House without a scratch on them; not once did those Jaguars take a bite out of one of those two Boys who lived to survive Jaguar House from where they came out very, very much alive.

body:
“What kind of people are these? Where did they come from?” asked those of Xibʼalbʼa.

“Naki pa kʼi chiʼ e Winaqil? Apa kʼi xepe wi? Xechaʼ ri Xibʼalbʼa konojel.

Fire House, Qʼaqʼ Ja

Next they entered Fire House, House of Fire-Qʼaqʼ Ja where fire alone was there inside this House of Fire. But they did not burn up in the fire. It was just trunks, just great logs, just big chunks of firewood burned as they blazed the House of Fire; in Fire House: Qʼaqʼ Ja.

They were just fine in the morning; they were perfectly well when the dawn came. What they, the Lords, wanted for them was that they should die there inside of where they were made to enter; for the Boys were made to enter the House of Fire to be killed by the flames that were lit to burn to blaze in ways that turned those Two into ashes.

The Lords wished that they should die in the many different Houses they were made to enter. But they did not die there for the Boys were not overwhelmed by the ordeal they met there; the Sons were not overcome by the tests and trials of the Houses of Xibʼalbʼa.

The Lords of Death only wanted Death for the Boys when they were made to enter the Houses of Xibʼalbʼa where Death awaited them.

But it was not like that; it was those of Xibʼalbʼa who were made to lose heart; they were the ones left defeated by the Boys who were ordered to enter each and every House so that they, the Lords, would kill them dead there in those deadly, deadly Houses of Death where Death and Sacrifice alone were the essence, nature, and condition of the Noble Lords who wanted those Two Boys; Two Sons deader than death.

But it was not like that because Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej survived each and every ordeal of each and every House that they entered and exited one after the next where they were expected to be killed but each and every Dawn they came out alive to welcome the day and their destiny that was to live to face another ordeal in some other unforeseen test; unknowable trial.

body:
But there was one more House; there was still one more House of Ordeal; House of Tests and Trials: Bat House-Sotzʼin Ja was its name; the House of the Killer Bats-Kamasotzʼ was their name; the same name as that of the Death Bats: Kama Sotzʼ.

Bat House-Sotzʼin Ja

So this then was when they next placed the Boys, the Sons in Sotzʼin Ja, Bat House. Just Bats alone existed in this House of Bats, this One House was the home of Killer Bats known as Kamasotzʼ making it a House of Killer Bats-Jun Ja chi Kamasotzʼ.

This was the House of Kamasotzʼ who was known as One Great Big Beast; Jun Nimaʼq Chikop; who was One Great Big Fiend that the Boys now had to face in its very own place: House of Bats.

For truly Kamasotzʼ was a massive malicious kind of mean sort of malevolent monster with fierce ferocious fangs set beside a long sort of blood-lapping tongue and wicked sharp obsidian bladed teeth. Kamaʼ Sotzʼ was one nasty, nasty winged rodent that nobody wished to face in its very own House of Bats much less night after night of being deprived of sleep.

These giant blood-thirsty beasts were highly mobile, exceedingly agile creatures that  had Obsidian-Blades on their snouts, razor-sharp knives were they; whoever came upon one of them in the open was instantly finished off in the most brutal way; for their victims were decapitated in an instant without having a word to say.

Killer Bats; Death Bats were there inside; there they were inside the House of Bats with the Boys, so the Boys slipped inside of their blowguns where they slept through the night till the break-a-day. They never looked out when they were there inside their blowguns inside Sotzʼin Ja they had a plan; they knew their way.

Nevertheless it was there in Sotzʼin Ja that they gave themselves up for dead; just the ʼOneʼ of them lost his head. Just the ʼOneʼ of them was decapitated as it is said by the Kamasotzʼ; those known as Death Bats thatʼs to say Killer Bats. And as it is said:  It came down from above; it came down out of the Sky-chi Kaj xpe wi.

body:
Yet it was ʼjustʼ their way of showing ʼjustʼ who they were; the Boys, it was their way of showing ʼjustʼ what they were made of; and, what they could do to be true to who they knew they were as those who listened to the Heart of the Sky.

After all, there was the ʼOneʼ who they could call upon for their insight, their knowledge, and their genius. Kʼo kakitzʼonoj wi kinaʼoj. There was the ʼOneʼ who guided them to answer the question of what to do next; and what they did next is what was theirs to do next.

All night long the Bats flittered and fluttered all about the House as they flitter-fluttered; flutter-flittered all about their House; the House of Bats where Killer Bats zipped and zagged all around to zig-zag up and down; in and out to then go round and round that House of Bats that was a House of Killer Bats; a House of Death Bats-Rochoch Kamasotzʼ was its name.

Flitter, flutter; flitter, flutter, flitter mean malicious malevolent creatures fluttering and flittering all about while screeching out: ʼKilitz, kilitz-Wicked-bad, wicked-bad!”

All night long they shrieked out screaming aloud: ʼKilitz, kilitz! Kilitz, kilitz! Wicked-bad, wicked-bad! While they flutter-flittered; flitter-fluttered up and down; in and out; zipping and zagging all about as they zipped and zagged up and down; these Killer Bats just spent the night zig-zagging all around in that House-Sotzʼin Ja, that House of Bats that was their House; their House of Bats; House of Killer Bats where Kamasotzʼ zipped round and round and round that House like the Death Bats they were that flittered and fluttered while flitter-fluttering about while doing their all to call out loud: kilitz, kilitz in Sotzʼin Ja-wicked-bad, wicked-bad the call they made in the House of Bats.

But then suddenly it stopped, no longer did the Kamasotzʼ move about. This was when one of them began sneaking up the blowgun of Junajpu and there the creature waited at the tip, at the top; at the tippy-top where the long circular cylinder came to a stop on that one blowgun of that One Blow-gun Son known to all as JunAjPubʼ.

This then was when Ixbʼalamkej called out: “JunAjPu: how much longer till Dawn?”

body:
Junajpu said, “Who knows how much longer until Dawn; let me see!”

Junajpu was waiting already for such a long time to see the Dawn: Saqirik!  So it was he who thought nothing of it when he stuck his head out of the mouth of his blowgun-chuchiʼ wubʼ

In an instant the head of Junajpu was lopped off by Kamasotzʼ leaving the body of Junajpu resting quietly inside his blowgun.

Ixbʼalamkej, Little Jaguar Deer, called out: “What is going on? Juchaʼlik?”

Juchaʼlik?

This is a playful double entendre ʼjuchaʼlikʼ used by Ixbʼalamkej when he asks Junajpu if he had lost his head.  Juchaʼlik? Were you decapitated by an obsidian blade? Juchaʼlik? What do you say? Juchaʼ lik? Whatʼs happening? If this expression is pronounced jachʼalik then it would refer to the harvested head of a mazorca or jachʼ: Jachʼalik chik: Was your head harvested as a mazorca of maize?

What a great display of the Ancient Awe of Myth and its Magical Way of Words with their bedazzling play of sounds and beguiling array of meanings where ʼwordsʼ transform into ʼswordsʼ…that cut through to the deepest most eloquent levels of mythopoetics…

This is the true genius of the mythic eloquence written out as a literary masterpiece that is meant to be heard as a play on words that is a play on sound that is a play on meaning in a literary play of writing that once was a long performance of the articulated word that is first expressed to reveal what calls to be manifest as the secret sacred language of the Divine Ancestors and Kabʼawil. Yet silence is heard as well and this is which causes as it creates a kind of mythic spell over the storytellers ancient tale.

Ixbʼalamkej got no answer; Junajpu remained still, silent; so that a soundless sort of stillness reigned over the atmosphere as fear hung in the air; fear that until now had never felt like it felt here and now when and where they-the Boys-were so near to being freed from feeling the fear of Xibʼalbʼa.  Could it be here where they were made to bear the loss and defeat that suddenly crept up out of the still, quiet air in the form of this Killer Bat from the netherworld?

body:
Was this the end when they were so close to seeing the Dawn of the next Dayʼs Sun and its Destiny?

And then Ixbʼalamkej asked: “What do you say? Has it dawned yet; has dawn come yet? “Juchaʼlik? Ma mixsaqirik chik?”

But again no answer, not a word, there was no reply for no longer did Junajpu move.

“What do you say?” asked Ixbʼalamkej when he said: Jupa chaʼ?

Another masterful double entendre: “What about the obsidian blade? Jupa chaʼ? What do you say?”

“Can it be that Junajpu is already gone? What could he have done?” wondered Ixbʼalamkej.

Junajpu didnʼt move about any more; just a great deal of heavy breathing was all that could be heard. Now it was Ixbʼalamkej who was made to feel the anguish that was the agony of their defeat.

“Aqaroq! Ay! Alas the Dawning! The Sowing! Have we not then given ourselves up to them?” Ixbʼalamkej cried out there in the dark before the dawn.

So then it was that his skull-ujolom-his head was placed up above the ballcourt-chuwi jom. That is the place above the ballcourt where those of Xibʼalbʼa went to place the head of Junajpu.

Placing his skull-ujolom-his head up above the Ballcourt was done upon the word-utzij-upon the command of Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame. This was their doing; the placing of the head, the skull of Junajpu up above the Ballcourt; there where they placed his head; the skull of Junajpu.

Those of Xibʼalbʼa were overjoyed with the skull of Junajpu-ujolom Junajpu; truly the head of Junajpu made the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa more than content.

Finally, they had what they wanted and so they had placed it where they could see it above the ballcourt; which made Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame as happy and content as these Lords of Death could be.

Morning Star Venus

This very well could be an image of Venus rising as the Morning Star above Orion as Orion rises in the East with the coming of the heavy rains to feed the Milpa and its growing heads of maize in June when the ʼfirstʼ elotes are taken after the June Solstice when the ʼfirstʼ heads of maize is ʼcutʼ green; which, is experienced as the decapitation of the Maize Deity.

body:
But this is just the translator and interpreterʼs arrangement of this celestial imagery of the constellations of stars and appearance of planets as they mirror this sacred narrative to create an image of Junajpu as Venus as Morning Star set over the Ballcourt as Orion as so many scholars have interpreted this story and its talking to us about the celestial movements above through its mythic metaphors below in this mirrored reflection of the sky above and the earth below.

These mythic metaphors are seen to be experienced in nature as divine natural phenomenon known as a hierophany; which is the human experience of the sacred in a natural occurrence in nature. Such as the Morning Star Venus rising in the East within the ʼBallcourt Constellationʼ of Orion or in the ʼHouse of Dawnʼ in the ʼTemple House Constellationʼ of Scorpios as Venus is often seen in the East at Dawn as the Morning Star when it becomes Lord of Dawn who rises in the ʼHouse of Dawnʼ.

After all, Venus can also be seen as the Morning Star placed in the ʼHouse of Dawnʼ in the eastern dawning sky at and about the December Solstice; this is when Venus sits inside of the Temple-House formed by Scorpius at the beginning of the Dry Season. This is a hierophany which one experiences as sacred for those who live their lives in the Maya-Mesoamerican latitude of 14˚41ʼʼ as we do here in the Western Highlands of Guatemala.

Ixbʼalamkej called upon the Animals; he summons the Animals: Coati, Jabali known as Coatimundi, Peccary spoken of as Sis, Aq were they who were invoked by Ixbʼalamkej. It was he who called up those known as the Small Animals, the Big Animals; Chʼuti Chikop, Nima Chikop.

In the night, it was just in the dark before the dawn that Ixbʼalamkej asked them to bring their sustenance, their food-kechaʼ: Naqi taq pa iwechaʼ chi jujunal?

“What is the food of each one of you; you, who are the Animals? This is what I ask; I ask you to bring me your sustenance,” he asked them there, the One known as Little Jaguar-Deer.

“Utz bʼa la!” they said then when they went out to bring back their sustenance; the sustenance that was theirs and theirs alone.

body:
It wasnʼt long before they returned with all that was theirs:

There were those who went out to bring back only rotten things;

There were those who went out to bring back only flat leaves of maize;

There were those who went out to bring back only rocks;

There were those who went out only to bring back earth as the food that fed      them; the sustenance that sustained them is what the Animals brought back to Ixbʼalamkej there in the Night; there in the Darkness before the Dawn.

Truly varied was the diverse sort of food that was brought back by the Small Animals, Large Animals-Jalajoj kechaʼ ri Chʼuti Chikop, Nima Chikop.

For it was the Animals that brought back all kinds of different sorts of food to Ixbʼalamkej: Little Jaguar-Deer.

Finally, the last one came in; he was the ʼlast one to come up the roadʼ or xambʼe.  This was the one known as Sis-Coati, the Pizote, the Kinkajou who came up the road rolling a great big watermelon look-a-like squash known as Qʼoqʼ: Chilacayote. Chilacayote-Qʼoqʼ was what the One known as Sis the Coati rolled up the road; it was his sustenance; for the sustenance of the sharp toothed Sis was  the enormous elongated oval squash which Sis just rolled along the road with his long whiskered snout and long tail swirling all about.

Coati or Sis came into where they were gathered. He came in rolling a big oval squash with his long, elongated snout; it was a Chilacayote-Qʼoqʼ that he rolled in to where all the other animals were gathered about.

It looked just exactly like an elongated head of a big headed man, perfect for using as a replacement for Junajpuʼs head; the head he lost to the Lords of the Dead as it is said; Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame.

Qʼoqʼ was the beloved sustenance of Sis the Coati and so it was the Chilacayote that Sis brought to Ixbʼalamkej. This Chilacayote squash was used immediately to carve and craft the replacement head that was the replacement skull of Junajpu-jalwachibʼal ujolom Junajpu.

body:
Quickly then did Ixbʼalamkej carve out his eyes-kʼotox ubʼaq uwach. This then was when XBʼalamkej, XJunajpu felt themselves to be filled with the thick insight of the Knowers-AjNaʼoj; filled were they with the thick knowledge that they felt to be the intuitive genius that was the thought of the knowers.

Thick with the genius of the Sky came the visionary sight of the Seers that saw all there was to be seen; thick with the knowing of the knowers of all that there was to be known came to them as the ingenious insight that filled them from the Heart of the Sky above known as the One-Footed-One Heart of Sky-Ukʼuʼx Kaj Juraqan.

This is when the divine ancestral mind of Ukʼuʼx Kaj Juraqan entered Junajpu with his newly crafted and created replacement Chilacayote head with Junajpuʼs newly carved eyes filled with ancestral vision that was so carefully crafted by Ixbʼalamkej who became the carver and creator of this new look-a-like head of Junajpu. Are kʼut xok jalwachibʼal ujolom Junajpu.

And so it was Ixbʼalamkej took up the carved head of Junajpu to then quickly place that replica of Junajpu on headless, decapitated body of Junajpu.

It was just Ukʼuʼx Kaj Juraqan that entered there with Junajpu; it was just Ukʼuʼx Kaj; Heart of the Sky that descended there to then enter there as the knowing mind and insightful vision that came down to Junajpu through the One known as Jun Raqan; One-Footed One; the One Pillar who was the Knower; who was the Seer that provided Junajpu with his knowing vision that was the insightful knowledge he now possessed there in the House of Bats-Sotzʼi Ja-Bat House.

It was there that Ukʼuʼx Kaj Jun Raqan Kaqulja filled the head and body of Junajpu with ancestral mind of Jun Raqan Kaqulja with its celestial knowing and terrestrial seeing so the Boys could continue on with their ballgame play. It was only in this way that the Sons could continue on playing ball with the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

Ixbʼalamkej was almost finished with his work when he realized the dawn sky was lighting up with the first rays of sun.

And even though it wasnʼt easy to finish his face, it still came out quite well. His skin began to show signs of life as it gave off a lovely, rich warm glow; so his attractive appearance once again began to show; he was able to speak a bit but how much it was difficult to know.

Since he could now breathe, he could now blow and so he was once again able to speak in order to say he knew all he needed to know; so that now everyone knew that presto just like that Junajpuʼs head grew and continued to grow.

Meaning they were just about ready to go; which meant they were almost ready to play a game that would be more of a show since  Junajpu would only be able to move to and fro while Ixbʼalamkej would do all the rest when it came time to throw the ball down into play.

It was only through the knowing thought and insightful vision that came from Jun Raqan Ukʼuʼx Kaj that Junajpu was able to do all he was now able to do in order to put on a good show even though he didnʼt really know where to move in order to know where to go.

It was just about then around the break-of-day that the Sun wanted to come up at Dawn; this was when the horizon began to redden there below the edge of the Sky-chi kaqtarin uxeʼ Kaj.

And so it was that the Dawn was asked to be held back by the Old Man; the Ancient One; Mamaʼ, Grandfather of the Dawn; the Possum: Wuchʼ.

“Darken it back again, Old Boy,” Possum was told.

“Fine,” said the Grandfather-Possum-Wuchʼ, “Burn it back, Blacken it back again.”

And so it was then that the Dawn was turned back again, the day-light made dark once again and then again and again.

Four times the Ancient Animal Ancestor known as Wuchʼ spoken of as the Old Man Possum blackened it back; once again the Old One, the Ancestor known to be named as Mamaʼ the Grandfather blackened it back, he just burned it back as was asked of him there before the coming on of Dawn; there at the arrival of the Rising Sun.

“Blacken it back Possum-kaxaqin Uch-burn it back Old Man,” people say today at Dawn when the Sky darkens ʼjustʼ before the Sky lightens ʼjustʼ before the coming up of the Sun at Dawn: Saqirik.

body:
But then the Sky of Dawn turned red-blue; kaq-rax-as the dawning came to completion; as the Dawn of a New Day rose up with its own nature-ukʼojeʼik-with its own character on the edge of the Sky-Earth; so that the Dawn established its way of being there on the red-blue horizon of the Sky-Earth.

“Isnʼt it good?” was asked of Junajpu.

“Yes, yes it is good,” he said then.

His head really looked good, it even nodded; it just moved from side to side like a real head.  Truly like a real head did his head appear to be; it took on a look that was very good; since the look that Junajpu now took was as good as Junajpu had ever looked which meant he was ready to get back into the game.

This time they would play to win the game whatever it took to them it was no longer the same, win or lose; by now the twins were tired of accepting defeat by allowing the winners to lose by enabling the losers to win. That was all over now that the jolom of Junajpu was placed there above the ballcourt as the trophy that the Boys had to get back by winning it back through their ingenious thoughts and insightful vision.

So once again they made their words-xkibʼan kitzij; xepixabʼan kibʼ when they gathered together in council to give one another advice while they formed their ideas; when they made their plans in order to know exactly what they were going to do next. This is how they made their decision and came together in accord with what they needed to do to defeat the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

They celebrated council together there beside Pusbʼal Chaaj; Sacrificial Ballcourt of Sacrifice, where they came up with an idea that quickly transformed into a plan that prepared them for the way they would play the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

“Perhaps it would be best if you were not to play, just intimidate them as if you were making plays while I do everything else,” said Ixbʼalamkej to Junajpu.

Then Ixbʼalamkej instructed the one known as One Rabbit; Jun Umul. One Rabbit was instructed as to what needed to be done next.

“Just place yourself there above the ballcourt; that it is where you must be; there among the acorns-pixk-amidst the oaks-pixk,” said Ixbʼalamkej to the Rabbit; Umul.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
“When the ball comes to you just do your best to take off with it bouncing like a ball and then I will do the rest,” said Ixbʼalamkej to the Rabbit.

This is what Rabbit was told when he was given his instructions there in the dark before the dawn as it is said as to what needed to be done there beside the ballcourt on the edge of the oaks growing there in the forest amongst the many trees where the acorn-pixkʼ lay beneath the branches; the branches of the oak trees: pixkʼ.

So then Dawn came; the Sun rose with both of them there in good shape; the two of them were back together now and content to get back into the game to play with one another once more with the Lords on their ballcourt but this time ready to defeat the Boys in order to beat them like never before.

There the two stood together as one twosome that was formed from the couple of them as complementary companions that were now standing there together on the ballcourt as two who planned to play as one. They looked good as a duo, as a pair; as a couple of twins who were two companions-dos compañeros-kikabʼichal who were ready for the ball to be thrown down into play there on the ballcourt; there at the break of day.

They began to play again only they started out with the skull-head-jolom of Junajpu being rolled out into play on the ballcourt of Jun Kame and along with the ball that was a skull came the boasts and banter of Xibʼalbʼa whoʼs tough talking play was meant to make the Boys easy prey but this didnʼt intimidate the Boys there on the court and their refined kind of dignified way they played.

It was then that those of Xibʼalbʼa tried o frighten the Two so they would give up themselves up in defeat; to then be sacrificed like their Fathers but this was not how it was; this is not how it came to be for those of Xibʼalbʼa who did their best to threaten the Boys before they even struck the ball.

“Have we not already won; give it up?” screamed out those of Xibʼalbʼa.

“Youʼre done for; youʼre finished!”

“Itʼs over; forget about it!”

“You two are finished!”

“You already lost!”

“Youʼre already beat by your own defeat!” cheered Xibʼalbʼa as they jeered.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
To which Junajpu cried out in a mocking way:

“Hit the skull like a ball; hit the ball thatʼs a skull.

Just chop at the skull like a ball;

Chakʼaqa ri jolom chi kikʼ;

Chop the skull like a bloody ball!” he mocked in order to provoke those of Xibʼalbʼa to begin play with the skull-head-jolom of Junajpu.

Then Junajpu cried out, “It wonʼt hurt any worse than us hitting ourselves; so go ahead, have at it; just knock the skull like a rubberball!”

This then was when the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa picked up the ball that was the head of Junajpu and threw it down into play-xetzaqow kikʼ.

Ixbʼalamkej went right to it so that the ball-skull-head landed directly on his yoke-bʼateʼ with which he ʼbeat itʼ just so that it pop up and off of his hip to knock it up and out of the ballcourt so that it passed up and over the ballcourt wall to fly and then fall far out of play where it began to bounce down the hill.

Just one, just two bounces before it landed in the acorns-pixk there below the oaks-pixk.

Immediately Rabbit-Umul bounded off to then bounce up and bound off from where the skull-head of Junajpu had dropped and now lay in the acorns there beneath the limbs of the oaks.

A tumultuous uproar burst from those of Xibʼalbʼa as they dashed off in pursuit of the bouncing ball that had transformed into a bounding rabbit that now bounced and bound its way down through the forest as if it were the skull that had been a ball that had become a Rabbit that was now seen bouncing and bounding off down through the forest. It was in that direction that the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa now flew in search of the skull-head of Junajpu.

Immediately the Boys brought back the head of Junajpu that they had gathered up when they charged off after it with the Xibʼalbʼans in fast pursuit of the flying skull that bounced like a ball to then bound like a Rabbit.

Once the Lords bounded after the bouncing Rabbit the Boys grabbed the jolom of Junajpu to then spin on their heels as they turned tail on the Rabbit and Xibʼalbʼa who were left to have at it.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
The Chilacayote that was the sculpted head of Junajpu was left ʼplantedʼ on the ballcourt by Ixbʼalamkej; so that once again the real head of Junajpu was once again placed in its proper place as the body of Junajpu, making the companions more than content now that they were put back together again as they had been before Junajpu lost his head; the Two that were One were once again the One that were Two.

This then was when the Boys called down to where those of Xibʼalbʼa were searching for the ball in the acorns-pixk beneath the oak trees-pixk.

Just then the Boys appeared to bring back the lost ball from where it was there among the acorns beneath the limbs of oak trees-pa pixk. They called out to those of Xibʼalbʼa, “Come back, here is our ball. We just found it here!” they said. They had already placed the ball on the ballcourt when the Xibʼalbʼans arrived.

“Where was it that we couldnʼt see it?” asked those of Xibʼalbʼa while wondering what was going on.

And so they began to play once again. They played against one another there in equal, equivalent play so that their play was the same on both sides; they made many beautiful plays while playing one another with equal, equivalent strength.

But then the squash-ball was struck by Ixbʼalamkej. This was when the chilacayote-qʼoqʼ-burst open once it came smashing down hard on the hard cement floor of  the ballcourt, splattering white seeds in the brilliant sunlight; the bright white seeds sparkled as a sign of abundance just as they shined as sacred sustenance!

“What is this that you have brought here with us?” demanded the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

“Where is the one who brought that here?” insisted the Xibʼalbʼa.

“Where is he? Where? Show me the one who brought that here?” cried Xibʼalbʼa.

This then was the defeat of the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa by Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.  Great suffering did they endure, but the Boys did not die there despite everything that was done to them in Xibʼalbʼa.

Ixim Winaq-Maize People; the Divine Ancestors of the Maize People

IxMuqane, Xpiyakok; Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu; Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
The Boys just left maize planted as a sign through which their Grandmother, Ixmuqane could remember them as a sign of their living and dying; sowing and sprouting; dying and drying to be sown again in order to return to life reborn as the replacement of the original of face of the ancestral seed.  Indeed, this is the story of the perpetual lifecycle of maize with its eternal return from death comes rebirth; from death comes life just as life leads to death. Death, the time and space into which the hard dry skull headed seed is sown by being buried; by being hidden beneath the earth in order to sprout forth again in an everlasting lifecycle with neither beginning nor end.

Yet, a lifecycle that necessitate those who will act and speak as the Twins act and speak when they seed their ancestral seed within ground just as their mother received the spittle as the shot of pitz from their father who engendered them ʼas ifʼ he had scored a goal by sending a shot through the ballcourt marker on the right side of the court as in the right hand of IxKikʼ the Moon Maiden who hungered to ʼenter the wordʼ like Young Maidens often hunger for the fruit that they are forbidden. But now her Boys the Engendered Sons of Jun Junajpu are sowing the seed that will produce the maize from which the First Four Lord of Kʼicheʼ will be formed and shaped in the hands of IxMuqane. There is perfection in this Myth of Maize known as Popol Wuj. Now the Hero Twins must do the sacred work of sowing their people maize seed when their Grandmother defied maize by naming it with divine names.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This was when maize was deified to make it divine by naming the name placed upon it by Ixmuqane; Mother of Maize-Grandmother of Maize; Mother of Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu; Grandmother of Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej. IxMuqane “she of the buried maize seed, she of the buried mazorca” as her name states: Ix-muq-qʼanil-She of the burial of the mazorca seeds of maize; Ix-muq-kan-eey-She of the burial maize teeth, maize kernel, maize seeds, maize descendants; Ix-muq-qʼan-eey-She of the buried resplendence of the maize seeds descendants;  the golden teeth of maize kernels; the silver teeth of maize kernels; those who are the ancestral descendants; the ancestral replacements of those who came and went to return again changed and transformed.

Grandmother Ixmuqane embodies the archetypal image horticultural essence found in the seed being buried in the body of the Great Mother Earth; Great Mother; Grandmother of the Maize People. In this image is the buried image of the horticultural ideal of the hidden treasure that will bring joy to those who watch and wait for the Sun at Dawn only now they are watching and waiting for the hidden to come spiking up and out of the earth ʼas ifʼ it were some mythic infant ʼsunʼ rising up and at of the earth only this infant ʼsonʼ are twins who are borne into the world by standing straight-up like maize sprouting up on the mountain side.

This is the mythic image of maize being sown here by those Boys now come of Age who will soon become the Sun and Moon themselves. But before they go they must leave the world well sown with ancestral seed planted in the Middle of the House-Nikʼaj Ja; Middle of the Harvest-Nikʼaj Bʼichoqʼ; as Living Maize-Kʼasam Aj sown on the Flat-bed of Earth-Chʼatam Ulew by its being buried with in the womb of the Earth Mother.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
The Earth Mother who takes in the skull headed seed of the her ancestors and descendants embodied in the seed sown within her body that is the gold and silver treasure hidden below the earth; seeds sown below that the Boys sow as ancestral skulls lined up buried in a row that call out to be twinned from within by the equal and opposite forces of the Sky and the Earth; the Above and Below. The Earth Mother pulls the roots down below while the Sky pulls the sprouts up above and out into the Sky where the Sun by Day and the Moon by Night delight in the nourishing, nurturing of maize with Sun lightʼs warmth and the Moon lightʼs pull.

These forces that are the powers and strengths of IxMuqane are complemented by the equal and opposite complementary forces of Grandfather Xpiyakok whose strengths and powers are named in the naming of his name Xpe-ya-kok which is the name that forms the mythic image that shapes the mythic imagination through this ancestral archetype of the Maize Deity of the Classic Period known as Jun Nal Eey and in the Post-Classic Period as Jun Junajpu. The Classic Period Maize Deity Jun Nal Yeey or Jun Nal Eey is the One Maize Tooth Seed from which sprouts forth his son Jun Junajpu known as Jun Ajaw Itzamnaaj in the Classic Period who is nourished with water by Yax Bʼalam who pours this sacred sustenance from Grandmotherʼs qʼebʼal-tinaja-war jug while his twin brother Jun Ajaw gives his Father a hand up as Father sprouting out from a Skull-Seed-Head of Jun Nal Yeey spoken of as Xpiyakok known as who ws sown there within the tortoise shell earth.

Grandfather Xpiyakok ʼHe who comes forth from the Tortoise Shell carapace of the Earthʼ this archetypal name that is reproduced alongside multiple images of the Maize Deity being provided for and sustained by grandsons through his son who sprouts from his skull-seed-head as  he sprouts out of the underworld through his kʼexel or replacement who is his son. The Maize Deity has been decapitated as Jun Junajpu is decapitated and it is in the skull head seed or gourd head seed where his soul had been captured and kept captive by the Lords of Death.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
It is from within his ʼskull-seed-headʼ that will the Maize Deity will come back to life once he is given proper ʼadornment-adorationʼ and ʼworship-ritual sacrificeʼ from which he receives his sacred sustenance and remembrance to feed he who needs to be fed: the Maize Deity who contains the spark-kʼas or life-kʼaslem within him that will ignite the fire that will return his power to him so that he comes to rule the Face of the Earth again as Noble Lord and Ruler with power of rule and authority bestowed upon him by his being presented with his signs and symbols of investiture and entitlement as a Noble Lord.

This is the direction we are moving; and fast. So one last time for Xpiyakok so you will never forget the essence of this Maize Deity who is always present in this Ancestral Account as being the One who is dead from the very beginning of this storyʼs being told

Xpiyakok then is the name of the Grandfather of the Maize People that complements the archetypal image and mythic idea of Xpiyakok, Xpeyakok the Maize Deity who comes forth from the Tortoise Shell Earth-Kok  to form the name Xpiyakok: X-he that pe-comes or sprouts ya-out of; kok-tortoise shell earth. He is thus a Merchant Lord who bears his maize and cacao in his ʼkok or kakaxtleʼ to deliver it to those who must be fed throughout the great Mesoamerican Civilization.

There are painted and sculpted  images of Xpiyakok as Jun Ixim or One Maize also spoken of a Jun Nal Eey of the Classic Period being helped out of the Tortoise Shell Earth-Kok by his Grandsons Jun Ajaw, Yax Bʼalam. But it is because this Maize Deity comes forth from himself it has traditional been difficult to delineate who is the Grandfather, Father, Son, and Grandson. So if one thinks of all of them being the Maize Deity who takes different forms of himself then the images are better understood as a Maya Cross that comes forth out of the skull-seed of Jun Nal Yeey to rise up as Jun Ixim of Jun Junajpu to then separate off to the left as Junajpu or Jun Ajaw and to the right as Ixbʼalamkej or Yax Bʼalam.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
In the famous Resurrection Plate of the Boston Art Museum we see this image with Jun Ajaw-Junajpu acting out the gesture of ʼgiving a handʼ to his Father while Yax Bʼalam pours water from the qʼebʼal-tinaja of his Grandmother and/or Mother over the parched countenance of the dried-up Old Man who struggles to come back to life from the skull-seed within which his soul is held captive by the Lords of Death. This water falls to feed the seed the hand rises up to help the First Father of Maize sprout forth-tzuq pa-shoot forth from there inside the Tortoise Shell of the Face of the Earth or Turtle Shell Earth: Kok.

Nevertheless, it is the all-important skull-seed of the Grandfather Jun Nal Yeey who embodies the One Maize Skull Tooth Seed which is sown as the origin of his lineage; the lineage of the Maize People: Ixim Winaq.

And so it was that Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej ʼleft themselves plantedʼ as a remembrance of themselves and their passage through ordeals of life-death-rebirth on the Face of the Earth as the direct descendants of the First Father of the Maize People.

Before they can plant anything they need to ʼput order to the cosmosʼ as any Cultural Hero must do so these Boys begin their ordering of the Sky-Earth by taking down Wuqubʼ Kaqix as their Ancient Animal Adversary is their Chief Bird Enemy to place him in the Northern Quadrant of the Night Sky as the Bigger Dipper as Chimalmat becomes the Little Dipper.

These Boys headed out each shouldering a blowgun and so it is they avenge the deaths of the Four Hundred Boys who become the Four Hundred Sons of the Southern Quadrant of the Night Sky where the Pillars and Crossbeams of their Kabʼal or Initiation Hut form the Southern Cross and False Cross of their Kabʼal or Initiation Hut.

The Four Hundred Boys or  Omuchʼ Kʼajolabʼ will enter the Night Sky so that when the Boys become the Sun and the Moon the Four Hundred Boys become the great abundance of stars in the Southern Sky as in the Nahua mythos with Centzon Huitz Nahua.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Meanwhile the Boys have been busy transforming Sipakna as the Maker of Mountains into the Mountain Meʼawan in the West; they transform his brother Kabʼraqan into the Dawning Mountain Saqiribʼal in the East.

They then place their arrogant and prideful; greedy and jealous half brothers Jun Bʼatzʼ, Jun Chowen in the treetops of the forest as Spider Monkeys at which point the Boys, the Sons are no longer needed as hunters to hunt for the Monkey Boys sustenance.  At which point Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej pick up their family hoe and axe to set them to work clearing the forest to plant the seed where the forest once was.

This is why I made this quick summary to illustrate the idea that these Boys, these Engendered Sons are those who were brought into the world to sow the sacred seed of the sacred sustenance that is maize. But before that can happen they must be transformed completely so that they can transform the Sky-Earth; Lake-Sea; Kaj-Ulew; Cho-Palo completely.

They have accomplished that impossible goal by surviving the Houses of Xibʼalbʼa to then defeat and destroy the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa. And to think they had no idea what was theirs to do in life. So let us take a moment for a bit of remembrance and recollection to place us firmly here at the end of this Epic Maya Myth of Maize.

When the Boys, the Sons vanquish the Monkey Twins like they vanquished the Xibʼalbʼan Twins Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame they return to what is their Fathers. Yes, these Boys, these Sons just want to ʼknow the face of the Fathers Jun Junajpu, Wuqubʼ Junajpu. In the Maya World onesʼ Uncle is oneʼs Father as it should be in this World and as it is in this World where Uncles are Fathers.

And so it was that when the Boys find out what is not theirs in life which is not sowing and tending la Milpa they find what is theirs in life. And what that is, is the ballgame equipo hanging in the rafters of their Grandmothers home which is their Fathersʼ house.

So to repeat, now the time has come for the Boys carry out their destiny by doing what is theirs in life and what is theirs is not sowing maize.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Before they can sow this sacred seed they must finish the work of theirs as Cultural Heroes which is to prepare it for the Dawning of the Sun of the Age of the Maize People.

Before this cosmic work of ordering the cosmos of the Maize People these Boys they cannot yet seed and sow the maize that will sprout and grow as the sacred sustenance from which the First Fathers of the Kʼicheʼ Maya can be formed and shaped in the hands of the Former and the Shaper; Tzʼaqol, Bʼitol who is about to return to this mythic narrative.

Before the Boys can find their Fathers in the Underworld of Xibʼalbʼa they, the Boys, must do what their Fatherʼs could not do. The Engendered Sons of the Dead and Disappeared Fathers were required to overcome the Nightly Ordeals in the many Houses of Xibʼalbʼa with their many tests and many trials; trials and tests that are complemented with Daytime Matches of the Competition of Serious Play that is an Intimidating and Dangerous War on the Ballcourt-Battlefield of the Pusbʼal Chaaj of Xibʼalbʼa where the name of the game is sacrifice on the Sacrificial Ballcourt of Ballcourt Sacrifice.

Once they make their way through this Initiatory Ordeal of Sleepless Nights and Stressful Days they have become ʼotherʼ than who they were before. The Boys sacrifice the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa just as they sacrificed all their other rivals and now finally they are who then have come to be the Entitled Sons who were Engendered Sons who proved themselves through ritual sacrifice of their uninitiated selves to become Noble Lords who will now enter upon the celestial thrones that await them. Their great suffering and profound sacrifice has made them who they have come to be: Nobles who are Wise Warriors capable of guiding and protecting the People of their Pueblo.

The Boys have arrived for they are well on their way to finally meeting with their Fathers beside the Sacred Ballcourt of Ritual Sacrifice where as Father and Son they will come together to experience atonement as the Boys see the Face of their Fathers again to realize the truth of their death, dying, and disappearance.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
The Boys will ʼadornʼ the skull and bones of their Fathersʼ through ritual adornment and the humble veneration experienced through their worship of those who gave them life. And in this way they are able to release their Fathersʼ souls from pain and suffering; torment and torture experienced in their soulsʼ being captured there beneath Pusbʼal Chaaj.

Once the soul and spirit of the Ancestral Fathers are released the Eternal Return of the Infinite Lifecycle of Maize and the Maize People is allowed to live the Divine Life that will begin now unimpeded by the Lords of Death; Lords of Xibʼalbʼaʼ who now are dead and gone. The Boys, the Sons, the Hero Twins Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej are not only free but empowered to sow the sacred seeds of the sacred sustenance of the Ixim Winaq. We have arrived at the Sowing of the main mythic metaphor of the Popol Wuj known as the Sowing and the Dawning. The Dawning lies just a little bit farther up the road. Yet we have arrived to where we set out for on the very first page of this Translation and Interpretation. We have arrived just as this Translator-Interpreter has arrived after overcoming infinite trials, tests, and ordeals as a Mother-Father of the Ancient Word in search of finding closure and completion in this lifetime lived with the Maya of the Western Highlands of Guatemala.

The Death and Remembrance of Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej

Here then is the remembrance of how they died; here then is the remembrance of those named Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

Here then is the ancestral account of their death: the death of JunAjPubʼ, XBʼalamKiej.

We will remember them by telling of their death and departure; the death and departure of Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.  This then was when they received orders from the Heart of the Sky; when they received instructions from Ukʼuʼx Kaj to then carry those instructions out just as they were given by the One there known as Heart of the Sky.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Their death is what we shall tell of next in this ancient ancestral account, in this sacred remembrance of all that they were counseled to do; for all they were counseled to do; they did. The instructions they were given where the instructions they brought to completion; for these two were those that did what they were given to do.

They endured all that they were made to endure; the torments they were made to go through were just tests to make them stronger; just as the ordeals they were made to survive simply showed the superiority of their ancestral nature and genius; for their nature that was their character was the nature that was the character of Nawal Winaq.

These Boys knew the pain and suffering of sacrifice just as they knew the happiness and contentment of play and laughter. This is what made them Nawinaq in every way.

They did not die because of the trials of Xibʼalbʼa. Nor were they defeated by the many devouring beasts that existed there in its Houses of trials, tests, and ordeal:  the Houses of Xibʼalbʼa. Their death was of their knowing; the way they died was of their own genius and this is what we shall tell of here.

So then it was that they sent for two Midmost-Seers-Nikʼwachinel-Diviners who saw into the depths of everything that came into existence through being and becoming; these were those who were the Two Seers-Ilol that saw all that there was to see and be seen.

Their names were: Xuluʼ, Pakʼam. They were Great Sages-Etaʼmanel-Great Knowers.

Xuluʼ, Pakʼam are those who go down, to go down; and, those who go up to go up; Xulu-to go down; Pakʼam to go up; xuluxik, pakʼapik; those who descend into Xibʼalbʼa; those who ascend into the Sky; those who go down into the Canyon Country, those who go up into the Mountain Places; those who go down into the Lowland Cave Palaces. And so it is that they descend and ascend Xuluxik, Pakʼapik as Descender and Ascender: Xulu, Pakʼam.

These are those known a Nawal Winaq: the Magical Transforming People. Xuluʼ, Pakʼam are those who go up into the Mountain Forest to look out from the Temple Top Mountain Altars; like Saqiribʼal, Place of the Dawn known as Relebʼal Qʼij: Coming Out Place of the Sun.

body:
Descender, Ascender; Xuluʼ, Pakʼam they know the ways the lifecycle of beings and their passage through life, death, and rebirth.

Xuluʼ, Pakʼam are known as nikʼwachinel because they ʼseeʼ into the center in order to enter the ʼcenterʼ of that which they have been called to divine in the future by seeing the past and present. The Sons, the Boys, Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej have called on them with whom they wish to celebrate council in order to ask their advice and give their instruction that comes from the Heart of the Sky-Ukʼuʼx Kaj Jun Raqan.

The Boys have summoned them to ask for their assistance in matters of Life, Death, and Rebirth. Nikʼwachinel Mid-most Seers are also known as Ilol which means Seers and what they see is what they divine; and what they divine is what will come to be; but they are also called on to give advice and counsel such as the advice that will be asked of them by Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame regarding the death and burial of the bodies of the Boys, the Twins so they do not come back to life.

The Hero Twins are way ahead of their rivals, the Lords of Death, and get to the Seers in time to tell them what they must say to the Lords of Xibʼalbʼaʼ when they call upon Xuluʼ, Pakʼam for advice as what must be done with the Boys once they are dead, for it was Xuluʼ, Pakʼam who were Great Seers who were Great Knowers; for they were those who were known to be Great Sages who saw all there was to see in order to know all there was to know.

This is what the Young Men said when they spoke with Ancient Old Couple of Seers in the Road:

“If those of Xibʼalbʼa should ask you why we are not yet dead; why we have not been defeated; why we have not failed a single test, a single trial of theirs; or why their wild animals have not devoured us, then it is you who might just answer them in this way; with these words,” said the Sons.

“This then is the ʼsignʼ we carry in our heart: it is the sacrificial stone oven-chojim abʼaj-that is the place of our death,” said the Boys to Xulu, Pakʼam.

“Havenʼt those of Xibʼalbʼa gathered together to end our days? The truth is that we are not yet dead nor shall we die,” said Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej.

body:
“These then are the instructions that we shall leave with you; instructions that you will then leave with them. For this is what you will say when they come to question you about our death; when they ask you about what to do with us, once we burn ourselves up to finish ourselves off in the sacrificial fire of the stone oven of sacrifice: chojim abʼaj.”

“What will you say, you-Ix Xulu, you-Ix Pakʼam when they ask you: ʼWouldnʼt it be good if we throw their bones down there in the canyon? Wouldnʼt that be good?ʼ” said the Boys.

“ʼNo, no that would be no good since they might just come back to life,ʼ is how you should answer them.”

“ʼWouldnʼt it be good if we were to just hang them in a tree?ʼ They might just ask of you then.”

“ʼThat would just be no good, since you will surely see them again,ʼ you might just say.”

“When they say then for the third time: ʼthis is what would be good to do: shouldnʼt we just throw their bones in the river?ʼ”

“If they should say that then, then this is what you should say: ʼThat would be a good death for them! And better yet if you grind their bones on a grinding stone; like the way one grinds maize; one by one you should grind their bones; on a grinding stone you should grind their bones.ʼ”

“ʼThen throw them in the water; just sprinkle them along the river; spread their ground bones along the footpath of the river water; there in the running water of the stream is where you must scatter their bones for this is the way of the rivers, streams, rivulets, and springs; this is the way of the water as it runs down the mountainside when the footpaths of the water-raqan ya first coursed their way down the small mountain; the great mountain,” they said then.

body:
“ʼJust sprinkle their ground bones alongside the stream where the water from the spring falls-chi ri qaj kʼwaʼ on the way down through the Small Mountains; on its way down through the Big Mountains,ʼ” this is what you should say when they ask for your counsel; when they come to you to question you about our death asking you for your advice; asking you for your instructions,” said the two of them-the Boys-when they indicated just what to do; this was when the two of them-the Sons-gave them-the Ancient Old Ancestors-their instructions there on the Road.

This is what you might say to them, “This is our counsel, shown here to you; let this be an indication of the direction to be taken by you, One Death, Seven Death; these are just our instructions that we give to you here,” said XJunajpu, Xbʼalamkej.

XJunajpu, Xbʼalamkej

This is what was said by the Older Boys; the Young Men named here as XJunAjPu; Xbʼalamkej; Little Ancestral Blowgun Boy; Little Jaguar Deer. This is what was indicated by these two Grandsons when they gave their Elders, the Mid-Most Seers; Xulu, Pakʼam their instructions that were to be given as counsel upon their dying; at the time of their death; the advice given as to the way of their burial when they came to celebrate council with the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa: the Death Lords; the Lords of Death: Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame; One Death, Seven Death as they named so are they known by all as the Death Lords of Xibʼalbʼa.

For it was the Boys, the Sons XJunAjPu, Ixbʼalamkej who knew the mind of Ukʼuʼx Kaj and it was because they knew the mind of Jun Raqan that they knew they were going to die; so this then was when they took leave of Xulu, Pakʼam on their way to their ritual sacrifice and death in the sacrificial fire of the great stone oven of sacrifice: nima chojim abʼaj.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
They knew their death; they knew it well; they knew it when they left them their instructions while taking leave of Xulu, Pakʼam; they knew of their departure, they were advised of its arrival; the Boys were given counsel; they knew of their death and disappearance; it was clear to them; they could see it; they knew of their dying for they saw the way of their sacrificial death. Ta xepixabʼik, xketamaj kikamik.

This then was when those of Xibʼalbʼa made their great stone oven to make the sweet drink; this is the kind of stone fireplace-chojibʼal-oven that Xibʼalbʼa made.

They used the really big leaves; these were the big leaves they used: nimaʼq xaq, the big leaves they used to ignite a big burn ablaze-nimaʼq xaq-to set a great fire to burning there in the stone oven of the sweet drink, the bitter drink known as: nima chojim abʼaj kiʼ.

Nimaʼq Xaq

There is some sort of double entendre and word-play going on with the Big Leaves-Nimaʼq Xaq they use to build their sacrificial stone oven where they ʼsetʼ a great fire ablaze to create a Big Burn-Nimaʼq Xaqʼ in this fire place chojibʼal where the traditional sweet drink-ki is drunk when the performance of ritual sacrifice takes place. This is the sweet drink-kiʼ of the big maguey leaves-kiʼ from which comes the alcoholic beverage known as Kiʼ. I am the first to admit this is another one of those places in the Ojer Tzij that I know I am incapable of writing some sort of definitive translation; yet, I am more than content to venture an alternative reading of this most ʼbeguilingʼ passage that no doubt is placed here to ignite our mythic imagination.

body:
Mesoamerican People and their Pueblo made alcoholic beverages just as they are spoken about here in the making of these ceremonial stone ovens where the text tells  us those of Xibʼalbʼa are preparing to become ritually inebriated at the time of their sacrifice of XJunajpu, XBʼalamKej. Mesoamerican people drank alcohol during the ritual performance of sacrifice otherwise drink alcohol and becoming intoxicated outside of the ceremonial intoxication was a religious and cultural offense that was punishable by physical punishment and even sacrifice if this practice persisted.

So do realize the Maya are not getting drunk all the time but they do drink in ritual ways; ways that are  indicated here in this passage   Here then is an alternative translation of the passage: Are kabʼan ri nima chojim abʼaj, kʼeje ri chojibʼal ki xkibʼan Xibʼalbʼa, Nimaʼq Xaq xkikojo. A passage one is left wondering if the Nimaʼq Xaq are indeed Big Leaves of Agave used to make their sweet drink-ki that was a bitter drink-ki because why are they using big leaves here at all?

Perhaps it is in context of some cultural context we no longer understand or simply because I as a translators like the other translators are clueless when it comes to understanding the depths of Kʼicheʼ Maya religion prior to the Castilian Conquest and Colonization.

Perhaps it is because the text is not talking about leaves-xaq at all but the setting a big fire ablaze-nimaʼq xaq xkikojo or is it the placing of a big fire-nimaʼq xaq to make a big burn-xaq that is to say to make a great fire in the stone oven. because what is certain something else is going on here that past translators simply want to fly right over on their way to a making a translation more concerned with North American cultural equivalents instead of seek to understand the ritual performance of ceremony and their subtleties that are reflected in the Original Maya Kʼicheʼ text of the Popol Wuj.

body:
So then they made their great stone oven of sacrifice; the fireplace carved out beneath the earth, this was the dugout oven-chojibʼal that those of Xibʼalbʼa made; it was in here that they set a great fire ablaze-nimaʼq xaq xkikojo; this was the kind of stone oven that those of Xibʼalbʼa made their sweet drink-Kiʼ-bitter drink in which ʼbig leaves-nimaʼq xaqʼ were used; big leaves of agave known by their name: Kiʼ.

The Messengers arrived to accompany the Boys and so it was that the Boys accompanied the arriving Messengers of Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame.

They came for the Boys; they came to show them the way to the Great Stone Oven-Nima Chojim Abʼaj of Xibʼalbʼa, this is what the Messengers said to the Boys when they said what the Lords sent them to say.

This then is what they said: “You are to say to them: ʼKepetoq! Come along then! We have come to show you what we are cooking up in the great stone oven,ʼ say the Lords to say to you; you, the Two Sons-Ix Kaʼibʼ Kʼajolab” said the Messengers.

“Utz bʼa la, very well indeed,” said the Boys.

Quickly, they went walking so that quickly they arrived beside the round stone circle that formed the stone oven-chuchiʼ choj.

And there it was that the Noble Lords of Xibʼalbʼa hoped to tempt them with a little game.

“Letʼs jump over our sweet-drink that sits cooking in the oven; just four times each, back and forth, each one of us, in turn, you oh Boys-Ix Kʼajolabʼ,” they were told then by Jun Kame.

“You canʼt pull that one on us, donʼt we know our death, you oh Noble Lords-Ix AjAwabʼ?  Watch this!-Chiwila na!”  They said!

Then, they paired off face to face to then take hold of one-an-other by the hands; and then, the two of them dove ʼhead-firstʼ into the sacrificial fire of the stone oven: e pu jupujuj ta xebʼek pa choj. There in the fire the two of them died.

Pu Jupujuj
