source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Amazing, astounding, astonishing expression of the idea that the ʼbicameral brainʼ with its ʼtwo lobesʼ that act in complementary ways as ʼMasterʼ and ʼEmissaryʼ who twin one another as ʼDivinityʼ and ʼHumanityʼ that communicate with one another to fulfill our destiny here on the Face of the Earth. Once again the question of duality or twinship is suggested here as we prepare to leave the Coming Out Place of the Sun or Relebʼal Qʼij after each Pueblo ʼreceivingʼ their Kabʼawil.

To then begin the divine life by walking off into the Sacred Landscape to be guided and protect by the Kabʼawil who will give each ʼgroupʼ their language with which to speak among one another.

Destinies will be found and ways of life will form into traditions as the land these people come to live will shape their traditions that are created by the dreams of divinity being dreamed by humanity. In this sense humanity learns vast knowledge while sleeping with hopes of dreaming; dreaming that is induced by ingesting tea made from the bark of Tzʼite.

Dreams that are dreamed by Kabʼawil to form and shape their divine imagination in order to bring forth the forming and shaping of creation here on the Face of the Earth. Here where the ʼdream is dreamed-onʼ in miraculous sorts of divine ways that connect humanity and divinity through dreaming; where dreaming forms the bridge across which humanity crosses over into the divine; and where divinity crosses over into the human. If in fact those distinction need be made.

Popol Wuj speaks to us in ways we are just learning to decipher which is all the more reason to move through it slowly in order that it might better reveal the essence, character, nature-kʼojeʼik-soul, and spirit of the natural and cultural history of the Maya-Nahua-Pipil Mesoamerican World.

One saw many sorts of people from where one was standing there at the edge of the Sea; there under the Sky; there on the Horizon at the Coming-out place of the Sun-pa Relebʼal Qʼij.

There were the Mountain People-Juyubʼal Winaq-the kind one had never seen the likes of before.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
They had no homes; no place to live;  just on the Small Mountains; just on the Big Mountains did they wander about as they wandered along.

“As if they were crazy folk,” is what was said of them.

“This was when they belittled the Mountain People; this was when they mocked the Mountain People for they had no ancestral ways of their own,” as it was said of them; those who were known as the Mountain People: Juyubʼal Winaq.

It was there that they saw the Dawn: Relebʼal Qʼij. It was there that they saw the Dawning of the Sun in that one place when it finally did arrive; in that one place  just one language was spoken by them at the Coming Out Place of the Sun: Relebʼal Qʼij.

“They had yet to invoke the ʼwood-stone; che-abʼajʼ that were the limestone stelae when they remembered what was said by Tzʼaqol, Bʼitol, Ukʼuʼx Kaj, Ukʼuʼx Ulew,” they said.

ʼCheʼ-Abʼaj-Stelae-Tree-Stonesʼ

There, at that place, they did not yet invoke wood-stone steleas; they did not invoke the sacred effigies of deities carved out of wood; they did not call upon nor pray to images of deities sculpted in stone. They didnʼt do that there; the invocation of ʼtree-stonesʼ or ʼstelaeʼ was not done by them there. For this was before they did all of that.

Back then they did not carve the ʼtree-stonesʼ known as the ʼche-abʼajʼ that are the sculpted ʼtree-stoneʼ spoken of today as limestone sculptures that are fine stone sculptures worked ʼas ifʼ they were the kind of stone sculptures known as ʼche-abʼaj or wooden-stoneʼ sculptures.

For truly this ʼtree-stoneʼ that was known as cheʼ abʼajʼ was a ʼwooden stoneʼ that was a stone one could carve and sculpted ʼas ifʼ its essence were of a wooden character.  These ʼcheʼ abʼajʼ are limestone stelae found throughout the Lowlands of the Ancient Maya World. They are fine refined carvings of relatively soft limestone; carvings that are carved and sculpted ʼas ifʼ their essence were of hard-wood when in fact they are of soft-stone. This is what these ʼcheʼ abʼajʼ are when speaking of limestone stelae of the Ancient Maya: ʼCheʼ-Abʼaj-Stelae-Tree-Stonesʼ.

body:
Gift us Our Way, Gift us Our Word; Chayaʼ taj qetal, qatzijel

Give us Our Tradition, Give us Our Truth; Chayaʼ taj qetal, qatzijel

Give us Our Track, Give us Our Trace; Chayaʼ taj qetal, qatzijel

Give us Our Daughters, Give us Our Sons; Chayaʼ taj qetal, qatzijel

Give us Our Replacements; Give us Our Descendants;

Give us Our Sign; Give us Our Symbol; Chayaʼ taj qetal, qatzijel

Give us an Example; Give us a Message; Chayaʼ taj qetal, qatzijel

Chi Bʼe Qʼij, chi Bʼe Saq!

For as long as the Sun Shines;

For as long as Day Breaks;

Chi Bʼe Qʼij, chi Bʼe Saq!

For as long as the Sun Dawns!

For as long as the Dawn Comes!

Raqan Qʼij, Raqan Saq!

Footpath of the Sun, Footpath of the Dawn!

May the Sowing of Maize Come to be!

May the Seeding of Milpa Come to be!

Ta Chawaxoq! To the Sowing of the Seed!

Ta Saqiroq! To the Dawning of the Sun!

May the Sun Dawn a New Day! Ta Saqiroq!

May the Dawn Come to Brighten Our Way! Ta Saqiroq!

Place us upon Many Resplendent Roads!

Kʼi ta Raxal Bʼe; Kʼi ta Raxal Jok!

Place us upon Many Verdant Roads!

Place us upon Many Green Paths!

Kʼi ta Raxal Bʼe! Kʼi ta Raxal Jok!

Place us on Many Jade Green Paths!

Place us on Many Emerald Green Roads!

May there be Precious Peaceful Valleys-Liʼanik Saq!

May there be Perfect Flat Plains-Liʼanik Saq!

May there be Peaceful Pueblos; Tranquil Nations-Liʼanik Amaqʼ taj!

May there be the Calm, Quiet Life-Liʼanik Saq!

May there be Calm People in Quiet Pueblos-Liʼanik Amaqʼ taj

May there be the Fine Life, the Good Life-Utzilaj Saq

May there be Fine People, Kind Pueblos-Utzilaj Amaqʼ taj

May there be Sweet Life, Sweet Existence-Utzilaj Kʼaslem-Winaqirem

May there be the Good Life, Fine Existence-Utzilaj Kʼaslem-Winaqirem.

May you bestow upon us that which is Ours that comes from Yours!

May you bestowed upon us all that is Ours; We, who are Yours!

You Who are those who are known and named:

At Juraqan,

Chʼipi Kaqulja,

Raxa Kaqulja,

Chʼipi Nanawak,

Raxa Nanawak,

Wok,

Junajpu,

Tepew,

Qʼukumatz,

Alom,

Kʼajolom,

Xpiyakok,

Ixmuqane,

Ratiʼt Qʼij,

Ratiʼt Saq

Ta Chawaxoq!

Ta Saqaroq!

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
And so they prayed in a reverent way, when they raised their gaze to meet the Day face-to-face; when they came to greet the Day, there at Dawn, at the Coming Out Place of the Sun.

This was when they invoked the ancestral names, just watching and waiting for the Dawn to rise up at the Coming Out Place of the Sun: Relebʼal Qʼij.

They were there just watching; just waiting for the Morning Star to Rise; for the Morning Star to Dawn; Sun Bearer-Ikʼoqʼij; Great Star-Nim Chʼumil-Bearer of Sun; Great Star Birther of the Sun; Messenger Light the Great Vault of the Sky; Messenger Light of the Great Bowl of the Earth; Footpath and Guide of the Sun; Footpath and Guide of the Dawn; Pathfinder of the Formed People; Pathfinder of the Shaped People.

Kilawachin Nima Chʼumil, Chalaxik Qʼij; Tzijol re Upa Kaj; Upa Ulew; Ubʼinibʼal Winaq Tzʼaq; Winaq Bʼit; Kʼamol Bʼey Winaq Tzʼaq; Winaq Bʼit.

Great Star there to Open the Way for the Birth of the Sun; Sacred Ember; Ancient One; Bright Burner Blazing Bright; Sacred Spark, Sparkler; Divine Flash, Flickerer; Flame, Flare of Fire; Dawning Light of the Vault of Sky; Burning Blaze Messenger of the Womb of Sky; Burning Blaze Messenger of the Womb of Earth; Star Seed of the Sowing; Sun Sprout of the Dawning; Footpath, Guide of the Formed People; Footpath, Guide of the Shaped People;  Pathfinder of the Formed People; Trailblazer of the Shaped People; Ubʼinibʼal Winaq Tzʼaq; Winaq Bʼit; Kʼamol Bʼey Winaq Tzʼaq; Winaq Bʼit.

As it was said, as it was spoken then by them:

Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ,

Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ,

Majukʼutaj,

Ikʼi Bʼalam

“Let us wait then for its Dawning!” they said.

“Qoyobʼej na uSaqirik!” Xechaʼ.

They were Great Knowers-E Nimaʼq Etaʼmanel-Great was their Knowing.

They were Great Thinkers-E Naʼonel-Great was their Genius.

They were those who gave sacrifice with great reverence-E AjKʼixibʼ.

They were those who humbled themselves with great humility-E Aj Nim.

This is how they were known, as they were spoken of by all those who were assembled there: Waiting before the Dawn.

There were no wooden effigies; there were no stone effigies to watch-over Our First Mother-Fathers-e QaNabʼe Chuch-Qajaw.

body:
There were no limestone stelae-maja bʼi kʼu ja bʼioq ʼcheʼ abʼaj-there were no ʼtree stoneʼ to be spoken of to shield and shelter Our First Mother-Fathers-e QaNabʼe Chuch-Qajaw.

Which is to say there were yet to be carved the finely formed ʼlimestone stelaeʼ of the Ancient Ones to preserve and protect Our First Mother-Fathers-e QaNabʼe Chuch-Qajaw.

Their hearts just tired there: Waiting for the Dawn!

Alternative Translations

Their hearts just tired there while watching; while waiting for the Dawn. Their solemn souls drew dreary in the dark before the Dawn; their hearts grew weary; their vision became bleary from the tedious and tiresome watching and waiting for the Sun.

Fearful and fretful were they now from their wearisome watching and worrisome waiting in the shadowy shades of night and its dim darkness that enveloped them there before the impending Dawn; there at the Coming Out Place of the Sun.

Their wearisome worrisome care and concern began to exhaust their heartʼs resolve to stay vigilant as it wore down their soulʼs deep desire to stay alert and awake as they watched for the sign to the Great Starʼs arrival; as a signal of the Sunʼs appearance at the Coming Out Place of the Sun where they remained fast and firm while Watching and Waiting for the Dawn.

Their hearts just tired there: Waiting for the Dawn!

They had all tired there waiting for the Dawning of the Sun.

By then there were many Pueblos who were there; many people were there who were present including the Yaki Winaq-Méxica People-Méxica Pueblo; those known as AjKʼixbʼ; those known as AjKʼajbʼ.

AjKʼixb AjKʼajbʼ Yaki Winaq

So the original text tells us almost nothing so I will explain. This AjKʼajbʼ are those who are known as penitent punishers who punished-kʼajbʼ themselves through self-sacrifice and others through ritual sacrifice-kʼajbʼ-by bleeding themselves with the razor-sharp-edge of their Obsidian Blade. They use the Obsidian Blade to draw blood by ʼlettingʼ blood by causing blood to bleed through the performance of blood sacrifice; these are those known as AjKʼajbʼ.

body:
The Yaki Winaq are those of Maguey Spine-AjKʼixbʼ who are always paired together with Obsidian Blade Sacrifice-AjKʼajbʼ and now they are bound together with the Yaki Winaq who are those that specialize in blood sacrifice as is suggested here with the naming of their names as Yaki Winaq who are AjKʼixbʼ who are AjKʼajbʼ and it is they who are Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ; Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ; Majukʼutaj; Ikʼi Bʼalam. Confusing right? Well it gets worse because they receive their Kabʼawil: Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz, Nikʼaj Taqʼaj who they will end up hiding on mountains and in ravines with multiple names. So get ready for more ʼnaming of the namesʼ which is a play that will not end to the very last name is named with the very last name named at the end of this recitation of Popol Wuj. Letʼs go! Jo junam jo!

They, AjKʼixbʼ were always paired together with AjKʼajbʼ and now they are bound together with the Yaki Winaq who were those of the ritual sacrifice that was blood sacrifice as is named here in the naming of their names: Yaki Winaq; AjKʼixbʼ; AjKʼajbʼ and it is they who are Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ; Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ; Majukʼutaj; Ikʼi Bʼalam.

It was they who were there watching and waiting in the dark at the Relebʼal Qʼij: the Coming Out Place of the Sun.

“Xa Joʼ! Letʼs go! Let us search, in order to find, the One who will provide us with guidance and protection.  Let us find the One who will talk to us; the One who will listen to us in order to bind and bond with us; to connect and communicate with us to dictate and direct us on our way; to protect and provide for us on our way. Let us find the One who must be found because the way it is now we have no One to celebrate council with in order to provide us with sound advice and good counsel. For truly we need someone with whom we can gather together our thoughts to know what we must do next in order to know where we must go next. We need a Kabʼawil who will talk to us and walk with us so that we never lose our way. This is who we must look for in order to find so that we will have Jun-One to guide and protect us.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Because the way it is now we have no One-Jun to lead us like a Kabʼawil can lead us; we have no one to provide us with protection like a Kabʼawil can provide us with protection; we have no one to guide us like a Kabʼawil can guide us like a Kabʼawil can guide us with their guidance; guidance and protection that we need right away!” said those named: Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ; Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ; Majukʼutaj; Ikʼi Bʼalam.

Let us just take up the burden of bearing our Kabʼawil day after day to accompany us in order to show us the way by leaving us signs on our path while providing us with opportunity and protection wherever we pass!

Just the way we are now there is nobody here to protect us; nobody here to guide us! Letʼs go, let us search for, in order to find our Kabʼawil who will guide and protect us!” said those whose names are:

Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ;

Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ;

Majukʼutaj;

Ikʼi Bʼalam

They heard of  the ʼOne Citadelʼ known as ʼJun Tinamitʼ that was spoken of as a City of Sustenance, so it was there, in that direction, that they went in quest of their new way of existence; they took up their walking staffs to begin their long and difficult journey!

This is the name of that sacred place Juyubʼ Waʼ-Mountain of Sustenance; Juyubʼ Waʼ-Sustenance Mountain. So that is where they went, those known and named:

Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ

Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ

Majukʼutaj

Ikʼi Bʼalam

They went there with the Tamubʼ and Ilokabʼ when they went to place known as Tulan Tzuy-Wa, Wuqubʼ Pek, Wuqubʼ Siwan. This was the name of the Citadel City; Tinamit as these mythic cities were spoken of as Tulan; Ancient Ancestral Place of Abundance in the Bountiful Reeds of Plenty; Tzuy-Wa Place of the Gourd Head-Skull Head also translated as Place of the Gourd Head of Sustenance, Place of Skull Head of Sustenance.

Sustenance Mountain; Place of Abundance;

Gourd Head; Gourd of Sustenance:

Juyubʼ Wa Tulan Tzuy Wa

The Meaning of Ancient Ancestral Names

body:
For it must be remembered that ʼwaʼ means both ʼfoodʼ and ʼheadʼ and ʼhereʼ in a world where knowledge is said to be taken in from the ʼfoodʼ one eats and imbibes right here; right where one is; not ʼthereʼ where on isnʼt. Especially when talking about prepared food that is seen as sacred sustenance because of the vast amount of preparation that goes into creating sustenance from hard kernels of maize cooked in lime, cleaned, then ground, to be cooked again as atole or our one drink of maize made from one kind of ground maize known as jukʼi and any other of the many drinks of maize including with cacao: qʼatuj.

Or when maize is formed and shaped into tamalitos-subʼ or tortilla-lej both of which that are ʼwaʼ best eaten right here wa or waral or wawe. This is in the Maya-Olmeca-Xicalanca-Nonohualca cultural inheritance in which maize was first drank as maize porridge that was drank or taken from a skull-jolom gourd-tzel-tzuy-aqʼabʼalʼ or guacal or jícaro known as a calabash gourd that was seen to be the very head-wa of the Maize Deity-Jun Ixim or Jun Junajpu or Jun Ajaw or Jun Ajpu whose skull-jolom was seen as a gourd-tzuy that was a head-wa. You get the idea of the transforming head of transforming sustenance and the transubstantiation of maize as sacred sustenance into the body of formed and shaped being who are people that are persons who are human beings who see themselves formed and shaped from the maize they eat as wa to become the flesh of their bodies also wa or tyoʼjil.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
So once again we are back with the mythic metaphor of Jun Junajpuʼs skull hanging in the tree of sustenance beside the ballcourt. This is a story developed over thousands of years of Mesoamerican working and living with maize. It is also a story that was transformed through its movement through many villages, town, small and great walled cities of the Mesoamerica Maize and Cacao Growing Empire. So then let us transform it here in a profound way. What then was the essence of the ʼspittleʼ of Jun Junajpu if not ʼground maizeʼ that comes forth as the ʼessenceʼ that is the ʼtransforming essenceʼ of the maize people who drank their sacred sustenance from gourds so that the essence of maize was taken in as the truth essence of the maize people.

This Primordial Mountain Place;

Now we have arrived at the Primordial Mountain Top of Chi Pixabʼ

In this way the Popol Wujʼs  mythic metaphors and mythic words transform into mythic images that like the primordial mist that envelops our imagination at the very beginning of the telling of the Popol Wuj changes and transforms through the spoken world of myth to become the Primordial Mountain that is said to ʼsprout forthʼ from the Primordial Water-Sky. This Primordial Mountain that is brought forth through the invocation of the word: Ulew! Earth then comes forth as this Mountain that rises out of the Mist to climb up into the Sky.

This Primordial Mountain changes and transforms through the incantation of the Ancient Word to become the Mountains of Sipakna and Kabʼraqan; that change and transform to become the Primordial Mountain where Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej live with their Mother IxKikʼ and Grandmother IxMuqane.

This Primordial Mountain is where the Boys, the Sons go every day shouldering their  blowguns to hunt sustenance for the Elder, Older Brothers changes as it transforms to become the Primordial Mountain where these Artisan Twins are changed and transformed into the  Monkey Twins Jun Bʼatz, Jun Chowen who are changed and transformed to end up swinging up and away into the Trees as Kʼoy or Spider Monkey into which they have been changed and transformed through the playing of their song Junajpu Kʼoy.

body:
This Primordial Mountain of change and transformation becomes the Primordial Mountain of Bent Over; Broken Oven Cane of Maize which is none other than Sustenance Mountain; Harvest Mountain known as Meʼawan. Meʼawan changes and transforms into  Pan Paxil, Pan Kayala by simply naming their names to then change and transform into Mountains of Maize that provide the Maize known as Saqijal, Qʼanajal that is changed and transformed by IxMuqane into maize dough or Tziya with which to  form and shape the First Four Fathers.

This Primordial Mountain of Maize Meʼawan changes and transforms to become the Primordial Mountain known as Sajribʼal where the First Dawn of the Kʼicheʼ Maya is experienced by the Kʼiche Lineages. And on goes this sacred story of this Original Mountain Place of Origin that will change and transform to  become the Primordial Mountain Place known as Jaqawitz where the Original Abode of the Original Settlement the Original Mountain Place of the First Four Fathers. This One Primordial Mountain changes and transforms as the Imaginal Realm formed and shaped by the mythic imagination that takes form through the Ancient Word while taking shape through the Ancestral Account of Popol Wuj.

It is through the Nawal essence of this mythic narrative that bring forth change and transformation so that the Primordial Mountain Top of Jaqawitz become the refuge of the First Four Fathers who change and  transform into the Sacrificial Priest known as the AjKʼixbʼ AjKajbʼ who change and transform into the Noble Lords and Rulers of the Kʼicheʼ People; Kʼicheʼ Pueblo who have changed and transformed as the First Four Father who have changed and transformed into Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ; Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ; Majukʼutaj; Ikʼi Bʼalam who are changed and transformed by their Kabʼawil Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz, and Nikʼaj Taqʼaj  each of which lives upon their own Primordial Mountain.

body:
Tulan is the Sacred City where the Noble Lords journey in a sacred way to receive their Kabʼawil; their Kabʼawil that will be bestowed upon the Noble Lords as a People; as a Pueblo; Noble Lords who embody the People; who embody the Pueblo; Noble Lords who are Ajaw Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ; Ajaw Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ; Ajaw Majukʼutaj; Ajaw Ikʼi Bʼalam; Noble Lords who walk in a sacred way to Tulan to be given their Divinity; their Divinity that is their Destiny.

Tzuy Wa Wuqubʼ Pek, Wuqubʼ Siwan

This is why I make this short interjection to say, “we are moving to a new sacred space with a new narrative of a Mesoamerican World where Sustenance Mountain is found at the Heart of the Sky-Earth as the Splendid City-Sacred City; the Mythic City known as Tulan Zuywa or Tolan Tzuy Wa Wuqubʼ Pek, Wuqubʼ Siwan:  Place of the Reeds and Rushes of the Ancient Ancestral Gourd Head People of the Seven Caves, Seven Canyons; known in the Nahua-Nahuatl Tradition as Tula-Tollan Tzuy-Wa Chicomoztoc.

This is the Ancient Ancestral Place of the Original Gourd Head People known as the Olmeca-Xicalanca of the Gulf Coast where the Ancient Ones of the Age of the Gourd Headed People once existed as those who are a remembrance of the Ancestral Origins of the Maize People.

body:
These Ancestral People, the Gourd Head People; Tzuy Wa are those who lived in the abundance of the Reeds and Rushes of the Primordial Lakeshore Villages of Mesoamerica but it is also the remembrance of the First People of the Caves, First People of the Canyons. It is they who came forth to be transformed by their pilgrimage of transformation that is the pilgrimage of initiation to Tulan Tzuy Wa where the uninitiated Wild People; Mountain People who are the Cave People, Canyon People will become entitled Noble Lords who will be given the power of rule and authority by the Great Lord; Nima Ajaw Tepew Quetzalcoatl of Tolan who will bestow ʼfireʼ that is ʼpower-qʼaqʼal upon these wild uninitiated Mountain People by bequeathing them emblem of power as well as signs, symbols, and insignia of investitures that will grant them power and status as they confer noble entitlement upon them with their new names of nobility and the position of power borne out from these newly minted names and positions of power and nobility.

Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej leave their mountain clothed in rags; dressed in rags, wrapped in rags as poor orphan boys to pass through the Houses of Xibʼalbʼa  and after playing many ballgames to finally be given the opportunity to show the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa how truly gifted they are as well trained performers of magic and dancers of dances. We need only use our mythic imagination to realize how once story tells the other in a world where these stories were lived out by Young Men and Young Women who became the Mother-Fathers of their Ancestral Lineages. Isnʼt this the greatest understanding of how living myth once functioned as that Ancestral Account that formed and shaped an Indigenous People by being performed as a Long Performance while being lived out as a Way of Life?

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This is the story we are stepping into here as we take up the road with First Four Fathers of the Kʼicheʼ who like the ʼMountain Peopleʼ and ʼCanyon Peopleʼ seek to transform their status and position on the Face of the Earth by becoming members of the Empire of Lord Quetzalcoatl known as Tulan Tzuy-Wa. This cultural context is taken for granted in the Popol Wuj by ancestral scribes who are Scribal Lords of their Lineages and known as Chuch-Qajaw Ojer Tzij; Mother-Fathers of the Ancient Word; Ancestral Account who assumes everyone knew the grandeur of this Kingdom of Quetzalcoatl at Chichen Itza in the Yucatan or Cholula-Chollan; Tula-Tollan in Puebla or Mayapan in Yucatan or Cozumel or Teotihuacan or Tenochtitlan; all of these Sacred Cities existed at the Center of the Word; Heart of the Sky-Earth. And it was to them that Young Noble Lords walked in acts of initiation to receive their emblems and insignia of Noble Investiture. This is the story told here.

The Noble Lords arrived there at Tulan; Ancient Ancestral Place of Reeds. Innumerable quantities of People arrived there; so vast were the quantities of People who arrived there that there was no way to count them all.

They came walking in great multitudes, yet they were given their Deities in perfect order. And so they; the People who were embodied by their Lords received their Kabʼawil in perfect order; the Lords received their Kabʼawil with great satisfaction.

The first were Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ; Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ; Majukʼutaj; Ikʼi Bʼalam, their hearts were made content with their Deity; truly pleased were they with their Kabʼawil.

“This is what we are looking for here. Have we not just found them!” they said as they spoke.  “Are qatzukum waʼ. Mixqariqo!” xechaʼ.

The first one to come forth was Tojil, that is the name of the Deity; this is the name of the Kabʼawil that was carried away on the back of Bʼalam Kiʼtze; Tojil was just carried on the back of Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ slung with a tumpline over the crown of his head so they walked together back to back; the One carried by the other as sacred burden; the One being carried was Tojil; Tojil was the One who was there to guide and protect his bearer; Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ carried Tojil; Tojil was borne away as sacred cargo spoken of as a burden; as a cargo that hung down his bearerʼs back in its ʼcarrying frame-ukok; tortoise shellʼ so that Tojil was borne across the back of Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ.

Jun patan, jun ejqan xekel ukok riqaxik rumal Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ.

The next Kabʼawil to come forward was Awilix; Awilix was the name of the next Kabʼawil that Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ carried hung by his tumpline-patan-slung down his back; the back and tumpline of Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ known as Jaguar Night; Jaguar Lord of the Night; Jaguar Lord of the North; Jaguar Lord of the Dark.

Jaqawitz came next; Jaqawitz was the name of the Kabʼawil that Majukʼutaj bore as his burden that he came to carry away upon his back with his merchantʼs tumpline; Jaqawitz is the Kabʼawil of Majukʼutaj; Majukʼutaj is the Bearer of Jaqawitz.

Majukʼutaj-Invisible One-Jaqawitz-Trickster Mountain-Trickster Deity

Majukʼutaj is the Invisible One who was Just Not There; No Sign off Him to be seen as the Pantera Negra-Black Panther of the Black Shadow Darkness of Night he was the Invisible Lord of the West where the Sun disappears at the end of the day to enter the dark of night in the direction of the Setting Sun.

Majukʼutaj is another aspect of Ukʼuʼx Juyubʼ or Tepeyollotl which is the Heart of the Mountain where the wisdom of the wilderness is offended by human being destroying the wilderness. Thus the Black Jaguar lives with a perpetual primordial hunger and vengeance that calls for the devouring of human hearts; hearts of human who grow maize on cleared off mountains-Saqawitz. This devouring of human hearts is a reciprocal pay-back for the Ixim Winaq destroying the Mountain Abode of the Kabʼawil known as the Heart of the Mountain or Tepeyollotl.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Majukʼutaj is a Lord of Deception and Disruption who instigates conflict and conflict leading to war like the Lords of the Underworld Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame.  Majukʼutaj known as Not One Is Here is a trickster Jaguar Lord of the West thus of Night suggesting a Black Panther who walks as the Invisible One; the Night Wind; the One Not There that is There in the Dark of Night as Jaguars always are and often are not like Majukʼutaj the perfect embodiment of Tezcatlipoca as Tepeyollotl-Heart of the Mountain. His darkness suggests divination through the use of the Obsidian Mirror of Tezcatlipoca.

Jaqawitz in the name of his deity as well as the Mountain-Top he will come to settle where war will break out as might be expected through this Deity Jaqawitz who is carried by Majukʼutaj who bear the aspect of the chaos created by war and conflict.

This seems almost prophetic despite my never understanding this aspect of these two together as Majukʼutaj bears Jaqawitz who transforms into a Mountain that transforms into multiple names of the mountain Jaqawitz; Jakawitz; Saqawitz; Kaqawitz; Qʼaqʼawitz which one would expect from the chaos of conflict made in the dark of night which is the essence or nawal of Jaqawitz and Majukʼutaj.

Nikʼaj Taqʼaj was the name of the Kabʼawil that Ikʼi Bʼalam carried as his burden. And so it was that Ikʼi Bʼalam bore Nikʼaj Taqʼaj on his back like the other Noble Lords bore their cargo that was their sacred burden.

Nikʼaj Taqʼaj means in the Middle of the Coastal Plain of the South Coast of Guatemala; this is the Southern Quadrant where great plenty is found thus the name Ikʼi Bʼalam or Many Jaguars is a fine association with Nikʼaj Taqʼaj where great quantities of Maize or Aj was once grown by the Maya who grew two crops of maize in one year because of the vast amount of heat and rain on the South Coast known as Taqʼaj or the Great Plain.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This Noble Lord may well have taken up residence in the very Center-Nikʼaj Taqʼaj of the South Pacific Coast where many settlement are found beside rivers that run all year long out of the Highlands to water the cacao and rubber plantations that grew next to indigo and cotton plantation where iguanas were found everywhere above the Pacific Coast estuaries where shellfish produced murex dye as well as great quantities of protein rich sea foods-crab, shrimp, minnows, fish, langoustine- to be dried in the villages in the Middle of the Coastal Plains to be carried up into the Highland Markets.

The other companions of the Kʼicheʼ Pueblos were there too and they received their Kabʼawil just the same as the Kʼicheʼ Winaq, it was just Tojil who was the Kabʼawil of the Tamubʼ.

Tojil was the name of the deity of the Tamub; and so it was that Tojil was adopted by the Grandfathers and Fathers; Mam, Qajaw of the Lords of the Tamubʼ as we know them today.

The third to receive Tojil were the Ilokabʼ for it was just they who were the bearers of the sacred burden that was Tojil; their Kabʼawil; their Deity; their Divinity.

So these are just the three names of the Kʼicheʼ who never separated from one another because they all worshipped a single deity: Just One Deity Tojil is his name; Xa Jun Kabʼawil Tojil ubʼi.

Tojil for the Kʼiche; Tojil for the Tamub; Tojil for the Ilokab; it was just One Kabʼawil for the Three of them; One Deity for them all; One Divinity for all of them. Tojil chi Kʼiche; Tojil chi Tamub; Tojil chi Ilokab; xa Jun ubʼiʼ uKabʼawil qe.

This is the reason the three groups of Kʼicheʼ never separated from one another; they remained bound together as they remained bound to Tojil as their Kabʼawil.

These three Kabʼawil were truly of a potent essence-nimaʼq kikʼojeʼik; they were of a powerful nature-nimaʼq kikʼojeʼik; they were of a strong character-nimaʼq kikʼojeʼik: Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz.

And then it was the other Pueblos, the other People who entered there at Tulan Tzuy Wa, Wuqubʼ Pek, Wuqubʼ Siwan.

Rabʼinalebʼ: Achi speaking People

Qʼaqʼchekelebʼ; Kaqchikel speaking People

Aj Tzʼikina Ja: the Bird House People, Tzʼutujil speaking People

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Yaki Winaq: the Méxica People of Mexico; Nahua People speaking the Nahuatl Language; Méxica as they are known and named today.

It was there that the language of the Pueblos changed; it was there that their speech became different from one another. No longer could they understand one another well after they left Tulan.

It was there that they separated from one another: some of them headed off into the Coming Out Place of the Sun-Relebʼal Qʼij but many more came over here, this way.

Only with animal skins did they cover themselves; just in animal pelts did they bundle themselves up; they had no fine cloth; they had no fine woven textiles; they had no fine clothing to clothe their bodies; no proper woven clothe did they have to dress themselves up in; they just used animal skins to adorn themselves; to embellish themselves they just wore animal pelts.

They were poor orphans-e mebʼa, they had nothing of their own, yet they were just First Born Ancestral People-Nawal Winaq-Ancient Magicians, Magical Transforming People was their essence, they were just Nawal Winaq when they came away from Tulan Suywa; Tulan Tzuywa, Wuqubʼ Pek, Wuqubʼ Siwan as it is called in the Ancient Word, Ancestral Language: Ojer Tzij.

Tzuy Wa-Gourd Head; Tzuy-Wa-Sustenance drank from a Gourd; Wuqubʼ Pek-Seven Caves, Seven Outcrops; Wuqubʼ Siwan-Seven Canyons; Seven Ravine

They were many, those who walked together to arrive at Tulan: Place Thick with the Ancient Ancestral Reeds; Place Thick with the Abundance of the Ancient Ancestral Origins; Ancestral Lakeshore Place of the Primordial Reeds and Rushes.

And so it was they who arrived at Tulan but they had no fire; they arrived there with no power; they had no authority; no burning embers did they have to keep them warm.

Just those of Tojil alone were there; Tojil, their divinity; Tojil the deity of the Peoples; Tojil the divinity of the Tribes; Tojil the divinity of the Pueblos-Tojil uKabʼawil Amaqʼ.

He was the first to cause fire to sprout forth; he was the first to bring fire forth by causing fire to sprout forth from his sandal but they did not see him to be the first to have created fire: nabʼe xwinaqir uqʼaqʼ.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Tojil was the one who created fire, the power of the Tribes; the power of the Pueblo that was the fire of the People; that was the fire-power-qʼaqʼ of the Pueblo, of the Tribes: Amaqʼ.

It was not revealed as to how his fire was made to sprout forth; it was not seen how itʼs being born came about. For their fire was already burning when Balam Kiʼtzeʼ, Balam Aqʼabʼ saw it.

“¡Aqaroq; Por Dios; Ayayayay! Our fire hasnʼt come out; our fire hasnʼt come forth. Surely we will die from the cold!” they said when they spoke there with Tojil.

So then it was Tojil who spoke to them: “Donʼt worry, donʼt think on this anymore. There is that which is yours. The ʼfireʼ that they speak of will be lost,” said Tojil when he spoke to them; those who were there were the Tribes; the Pueblos of People: Amaqʼ.

“Is it not you who are our Kabʼawil; is it in true that it is you who are our Divine One; are you not the true one, our Divinity?”

“You who are our Kabʼawil; you the one who maintains us; you the one who sustains us, you our Kabʼawil who nourishes us, you who nurtures us as our Divinity; you our Deity; At Qa Kabʼawil?” they said in gratitude to him; in thankfulness to their deity; in gratefulness to their divinity: At Tojil Qa Kabʼawil.

“Utz bʼa la! Very well then! Truly, I am your Kabʼawil! Ta chuxoq! So be it! I am your Noble Lord; I, your Noble Ruler! So be it! Ta chuxoq!” he said to them; he said to those who were the AjKʼixbʼ; AjKʼajbʼ of the Kabʼawil.

“Utz bʼa la! Very well then! Truly, I am your Kabʼawil; I am your Earth Lord-Kabʼawil-Seer on Two Sides; Seer of the Near and Far; Seer of the Far and Near! Lord Two who Sees All, Knows All; the Full One; the Complete One; the Perfect One; the Even One; the One of Perfect Balance and Strength: Kabʼawil! Ta chuxoq! So be it! I am your Noble Lord; I, your Noble Ruler! So be it! Ta chuxoq!” he said to them; he said to those who were the AjKʼixbʼ; AjKʼajbʼ of the Kabʼawil.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
The AjKʼixb; the sacrificial priests of maguey thorns and stingray spines who passed their thorns, who passed their spines through their skin to then take their twisted grass of sacrifice to thread it through their elbows as sacred twine as a punishing form of self-sacrifice as it was once done in ancient times when they performed this sacrificial practice.

AjKʼajb;  these were the sacrificial priests of the obsidian-blades and twisted grass who used the twisted grass as sacred twine that they pulled slowly through their skin to collect their sacrificial blood as their most painful punishing penitent practice to then burn the ʼtwisted grassʼ as an ancestral way to pay for the transgression of themselves and their people by showing obedience and humility; surrender and submission to their Kabʼawil through their performance of these ritual forms of sacrifice that shaped the relationship of debt and subservience of Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ; Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ; Majukʼutaj; Ikʼi Bʼalam to their Kabʼawil: Tojil; Awilix; Jaqawitz; Nikʼaj Taqʼaj.

These were those who were they that chose to give their blood as sacrificial offerings in a most painful and punishing penitent way. These sacrificial priests performed rituals of sacrifice with thorns and spines-AjKʼixbʼ of Tojil; they were those who were sacrificial priests who were penitent priests who punished themselves in penitential ways; ways that gave them their names: AjKʼajbʼ of Tojil.

Thus Tojil spoke to them; he spoke to his sacrificial priests, his providers of sacred sustenance, his sustainers of his fire which was his power-qʼaqʼal-his strength so that in return he would provide them with his warmth and sustain them with his heat in the form of divine nurturance and divine embrace that made the Tribes; the Pueblos; Amaqʼ so very content.

It was just because of Tojil that the Tribes-Amaqʼ-the Pueblos were pleased and satisfied. They were made content; they were pleased with the warmth that came forth from their burning, blazing fire.

Amaqʼ-Mountain Tribe-Mountain Pueblo

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
The Pueblos known as Amaqʼ were formed from the Tribes that Tojil made content by gifting them their heat by bestowing upon them their flames; their embers, their warmth that came from their warm nurturing heat; their burning coals of charcoal that burned as perpetual sacrifice in their sacrificial braziers; they were made content from the warmth that radiated from the eternal release of heat from the red hot embers of their burning, blazing ritual fire; qʼaqʼal that burnt as blazed in their braziers of sacrifice as the essence of Tojil who burnt as the fire and flames of their Father, the Sun, whose warm embrace of the Face of the Earth nurtured the People of the Pueblo as it nourished their Maize and Cacao.

So then it was that a great rain began to fall there where the fire of the Tribes burned, their fires continued to burn just as the hail continued to fall; and, as it fell upon those who were there it soon became certain that they were no longer able to keep their fire burning; the fire that had kept them warm; the fire that kept them dry no longer could be kept alive and so they no longer received the warm embrace of the heat of their warm, hot fires with their burning hot embers to keep them warm; to keep them dry; to keep them health and alive.

Thick hail fell and as it fell it fell over the Tribes; and, as the hail fell so did their fires begin to fail; and as the hail fell, it fell over the tribes huddled there together against the cold.

And so it was that their fires were put out by the Tojil-the Storm; all were drenched by the downpour;  left wet, soaked by the rain, the hail-saqboch-the hail that fell on the Tribes; the hail that battered the People; the hail the froze the Pueblo: ri Amaqʼ.

No longer did the flame of their fire come forth; no longer was there any fire, no heat, no warmth among them there; no longer was there contentment among the People of the Tribes; no longer were the hearts sweet of those who were of the Pueblos; ri Amaqʼ who were those of Tojil.

body:
So this then was when they went to ask for their fire; when they went to ask for their fire, again. It was Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ who went before their Kabʼawil to ask for their fire that was the power-qʼaqʼal of Tojil: “You, oh Tojil, truly, we will be finished off by the freezing cold!” they said then to Tojil.

“Utz-Fine, donʼt be afraid, have no fear!” said Tojil who was there to guide the People and protect the Pueblo; Winaq, Amaqʼ the People, the Pueblo who would find no contentment without the warmth of his fire; the fire of Tojil that was his great power.

Immediately he drilled fire there; Tojil drilled fire by spinning in his sandal; once again, just like that, immediately they were given their fire to keep warm.  Content again were they there with their fire, those known and named:

Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ,

Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ,

Majukʼutaj,

Ikʼi Bʼalam

Little by little they warmed themselves; once again they were made content-xekikot chik; their hearts made sweet; kiʼ kikʼux.

But then once again the fire of the Tribes was put out; once again they were just finished off by the cold. This then was when the Pueblos of Mountain People who were there from the many different Mountain Tribes of Mountain People arrived before the First Four Fathers  to ask for fire for those whose blazing flames and burning embers had been ʼput outʼ. Those First Four Fathers who the Pueblos went to asked for fire were those whose names were:

Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ,

Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ,

Majukʼutaj,

Ikʼi Bʼalam

For the Pueblos could no longer bear the freezing cold from the falling hail. They were just shaking, they were just shivering; no longer was there a spark of life left within them; their legs just began to quiver, to shiver; their arms just began to shake, to quake. They were just done in by the cold; finished off by the freezing cold!

“We feel no shame coming before you here to ask for our fire. For we must ask you perhaps for a bit more fire; maybe a small load of burning coals, embers nothing more?” they said upon their arrival.

body:
But they were not well received; they were not given a seat upon which to be attended. And so the Tribes felt cursed, they felt great affliction there in their hearts; and so they cursed those who they came to ask for a ʼloadʼ of burning embers; a load they were not given; embers they did not receive.

And so it was that realized their speech was different; their language had changed; their language and its speech it was no longer the same; the speech of those with the names were those with the languages no longer the same as:

Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ;

Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ;

Majukʼutaj;

Ikʼi Bʼalam

“Ay! Aqaroq! We lost our language, where has our speech gone?”

“What have we done? We are lost!”

“Where were we tricked?”

“How were we deceived?”

“We were of just one language when we went walking as one to Tulan!”

“Just one place of birth was our place of origin; just one single place was our place of ʼsprouting forthʼ into existence-qatzʼuqibʼal-our place of origin.”

“Just One-Xa Jun was our place of origin-qawinaqiribʼal-just one was our place of creation; our place of becoming the people who people; who populated our place of origin.”

“Xa Jun qachʼabʼal ta xojpe chilaʼ Tulan; xa pu jun qatzʼuqibʼal, qawinaqiribʼal”

Xa pu jun qatzʼuqibʼal, qawinaqiribʼal; Just One Place of Our Origin; Our Place of Sprouting Forth; Our Place Peopling; Our Place of Populating Our Place of Origin.

Just One Place of Our Sprouting Forth-Qatzʼuqibʼal; Our Place of Creation;-Qawinaqiribʼal;  Our Place of Formation-Qatzʼuqibʼal;  Our Place of Germination-Qatzʼuqibʼal

Our One Place of Peopling-Qawinaqiribʼal; Our One Place of Populating-Qawinaqiribʼal

Just One Place of Our Origin-Qatzʼuqibʼal; Our Place of Germination; Qatzʼuqibʼal

Our Place of Creation-Qawinaqiribʼal; Our Place of Sprouting Out; Qawinaqiribʼal

body:
ʼJust One-Xa Jun rich line of mythic metaphor to speak to us of a people whoʼs place of origin is known to them as ʼour place of sprouting forth or tzʼuqibʼal known as their place of origin-Pu that is their place of peopling forth as a people-winaq who people forth-winaqiribʼal at their place of peopling forth that is their place of origin; that is their place of creation. These are people who populate their Mountain Places and Canyon Country as a People of a Pueblo who perceive themselves as sprouting tendrils-uwi, unaq-from a hard kernel or pit of a seed.

You know this but here it comes again after being invoked in the first pages of this Ancestral Account of the Sprouting Forth of the Trees and Vines to People Forth as the Population of Animal People. Now we are speaking of People of Pueblos. We have evolved just as we have remained very much the same by keeping the metaphors of the People of Maize who Sprout Forth in the Milpa like never before yet there is more; much more.

There is more because this exceedingly subtle yet extraordinarily ingenious one single line stated above that ʼevenʼ makes a play on ʼPuʼ that literally signifies ʼandʼ yet is meant to play on Tulan-Pu-Tolan as the Place of Ancestral Place of Origin; the Original Place of Maize Sprouting Forth that is ʼjust-xaʼ the Place of the Origin; Place of Creation of the Mesoamerican Civilization; PU being the Ancient Ancestral Place Thick with Reed and Rushes: Pu.

This is the Place of Origins that story-tellers may have once used their storytelling ʼinflectionʼ to ʼinflectʼ the vowel sound to change the Pu to Po thus creating the sound that provide the word Moon-Po-Ikʼ  and whatever meaning was desired from the context of the story being told. So realize Pu can easily sound like Po so that the Mother of Jun Ajpu who we know as Ixkikʼ may have given birth to her sons on the mountainside by them sprouting forth as Jun AjPo; or he the Original Ancestral Son of the Moon.

body:
There is no end to the ecstatic play that prayer-makers and story-tellers are capable of in Maya Languages which a fantastic reason to our changing our teaching of them from the linguistic language paradigm to the mythopoetic philological paradigm. Many more students would learn to speak the language while being thrilled by the experience of language transformation that one becomes involved by approaching Maya Language through Mythopoetic instead of Linguistic which literally kills the soul of language. And I should know because I studied Maya Languages through the life sucking death dealing language paradigm of linguistic which kills the excitement of language learning.

Pu  is the ancestral place of origin that is known and named as the ʼorigin place of sprouting forth-tzʼuqibʼalʼ which it their ancestral home that is the ʼplace of peopling forth-winaqiribʼalʼ to go out into the world searching for a ʼlivable mountainʼ upon which to  then multiple and grow to then divide and separate to find another ʼlivable mountain place to multiply and growʼ until, alas, they could no longer ʼevenʼ  speak to one another much less understand one anotherʼs needs.

The divine Oneness of this People is now ʼonly-xa-justʼ nostalgic longing because they are quickly dividing against one-an-other instead of acting like Junajpu, Ixbʼalamkej who work and play in perfect twinship in a complementary collaborative twinning and winning relationship.

“Tzʼuq pa awex-the milpa has sprouted out” is as common as any saying there is when speaking of the milpa. This line provides us with a deep sense of Maya metaphor of human life being that of the life of maize; the life of maize that sprouts forth at the beginning of the Kʼicheʼ Kingdom and its life sprouting out to then begin separating and dividing into ʼTribes or Pueblos or Amaqʼʼ that become antagonistic of one another.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
It is important to comprehend in order to value how they suffer the loss of their Original Unity as One People with One Language yet with No Kabʼawil. This is paradox they once lived in. Whereas their remembrance of their primordial unity of language takes us back to the very origins of the Kʼicheʼ Maya Scribes myth-making in which the Former, Shaper want to form and shape beings that speak a single language with which they can ʼname the namesʼ of their Former, Shaper; Bear, Begetterʼ.

This primordial perfection of One People; One Language is something they once experienced in their nostalgic recollection of Tulan when they spoke one language at the beginning when they first arrived there and lived as one people at the moment of their ʼcreation-winaqirikʼ that was their moment of origin of their ʼsprouting forth which was a sprouting outʼ to then sprout out into the world and then separate out to then divide into different Tribes with different Kabʼawil.

These Kabʼawil poke different languages to develop different ways of living expressed by different traditions that formed different truths that are spoken in language spoken by the Kabʼawil who teach their People to speak. The Kabʼawil teach their People to speak  by providing their Prayer-making Invocations; Invocations that are made to the Kabʼawil themselves through their Priests and Priestess who invoke their Kabʼawil through the enchantments that come from the Kabʼawil that are direct to the Kabʼawil through the voice and sacred speech of their Day-keepers and Prayer-makers.

These Day-keepers and Prayer-makers become the Kabʼawil to who they direct their petitionary prayers and pleas as well as the counting and keeping of the Days of their Deities-Kabʼawil in order to communicate to their Kabʼawil Deities through the divine language that is spoken through the incantations and enchantments of their Priests and Priestesses who speak the language of their Kabʼawil that comes ʼthroughʼ them as a means of remembrance that is a means of enchantment that is a means of communication through which the Divine Ancestors connected to their Kabʼawil through the language of prayer as a divine form of enchantment.

body:
This is important to understand: the Kabʼawil speak to themselves through their voice that comes up and out of their Day-keepers and Prayer-makers who become the Kabʼawil who they are given to provide for and sustain in exchange for the guidance and protection of the Kabʼawil.

This must be understood for the reader to understand how the Kʼicheʼ Maya learn the Maya Kʼicheʼ Language through Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz, and Nikʼaj Taqʼaj who enter into those who are their Priests and Priestesses who hear the ʼvoiceʼ of their Kabʼawil that comes up and out of them as the Day-Keepers and Prayer-Makers of Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz, and Nikʼaj Taqʼaj.

This is how the different Tribes develop different languages and dialects within languages. It was all a matter of the Kabʼawil of each ʼGroupʼ speaking through their Care-takers and Guardians in slightly different ways over the decades the language were formed through prayer and shaped through exchange.

This was a world in which the Divine Ancestors became their Kabʼawil just as the Kabʼawil became the Divine Ancestors who went to Tulan Tzuy-Wa in search of finding a Deity who would guide and protect them in exchange for those Tribes-Amaqʼ  providing sacred sustenance for their Kabʼawil by sustaining them with Sacred Sustenance in the form of ʼSelf-Sacrificeʼ or in the shape of ʼHuman Sacrificeʼ but it will be one or the other that will determine the ʼTraditionsʼ and ʼTruthsʼ of each and every Pueblo of People known here as the Tribes-Amaqʼ. It will be the Prayer-makers and Day-keepers who will intone that language through their many divine forms of enchantment. Let us move on after making this important idea understood.

“This is just no good. What we have done is simply no good!” said then all the Tribes there under the trees, under the vines-xe cheʼ, xe kʼaʼm.

Then a Person; a Being appeared; Jun Winaq appeared before the presence of:

Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ,

Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ,

Majukʼutaj,

Ikʼi Bʼalam

This person who appeared that was the Messenger of Xibʼalbʼa said:

body:
“Truly, since this is your Deity, your Divinity, your Kabʼawil; the One that you looked for that you must provide and sustain is the replacement of the memory of your Former and your Shaper. Truly, your Kabʼawil who is Tojil is the replacement or substitute for your Former; for your Shaper who formed and shaped you. For your Kabʼawil named and known as Tojil is the replacement of the memory that you have of your Former and of your Shaper: ukʼexwach natbʼal re Tzʼaqol iwe, Bʼitol iwe.

So do not give Fire to the Tribes until they give that which is due to Tojil. Donʼt accept what they, the Tribes, wish to give Tojil; but instead ask Tojil what it is that belongs to him. It depend on Tojil to say what he wants to receive in exchange for the Fire he is willing to give to them,” said he of Xibʼalbʼa.

His winged appearance looked just like that of a winged bat; Kʼo uxikʼ kʼeje uxikʼ Sotz.

“I am the Messenger of the Former of you. I am the Messenger of the Shaper of you. In Samajel Tzʼaqol iwe; Bʼitol iwe,” said the Worker who was the Messenger of Xibʼalbʼa; usamajel Xibʼalbʼa.

Chinese Box; Maya Puzzles; Messages within Message; Names within Names

We have stepped into what I would call a very nawal text of changing and transforming mythic figures in which Tzʼaqol, Bʼitol are spoken of as Xpiyakok, Ixmuqane who referred to as Alom, Kʼajolom whom are said to be Tojil. Whereas the ʼMessengerʼ of Xibʼalbʼa who was a group of Four Owls is now a Bat who is said to be the Worker of Xibʼalbʼa because Tzʼaqol, Bʼitol must have died and become the Ancestral Dead thus one of those of Xibʼalbʼa where the Lords of Death reside in the Underworld of Xibʼalbʼa.

It is confusing unless one understands it to be a riddle meant to baffle and bewilder the uninitiated. Because all of the sudden  the Former and the Shaper known as Tzʼaqol, Bʼitol want their memoryʼs replacement or ukʼexwach natbʼal who is Tojil to receive what it is that will ʼprovide for him in order to sustain himʼ for the power of life that the fire he is willing to give them. What is going on?

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
The Maya Scribes of the Popol Wuj are masters of forming and shaping these ʼChinese Boxʼ that are ʼMaya Puzzlesʼ known as riddles of Tzuy-Wa that comes hand in hand with the Naming the Names and relaying messages within message within message as they place names within names.

This placing one mythic idea or mythic figure inside the other is ʼserious playʼ that always seems to make a perfect fit out of multiple layers of mythic reality founded in ancestral ages with their different mythic figures that transform into one-an-other in a Nawal Cosmos that seems to enjoy this play with the ever-changing faces of the many mythic characters that come from the many changing faces of the multiple mythic ages. What is important to understand is that the Trickster Lord Tojil has brought Jun Kame, Wuqubʼ Kame back to life as One Death, Seven Death come back into existence as the Kabʼawil known and named: Tojil!

And Tojil wants what the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa wanted which is why they sent a Bat Messenger up and out of Xibʼalbʼa in the name of Tzʼaqol, Bʼitol to say: ʼWe want what we hunger for most; we want what satisfies our appetite; we want our sacred sustenance; we want what provides for us: Human Sacrifice!

Upon hearing this they who were the Kabʼawil were made content; their hearts grew larger; their hearts grew strong those Kabʼawil that were named Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz. They were made content by what the Messenger of Xibʼalbʼa said to them; when he said what he said to them, the Kabʼawil: Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz…

Just like that the Messenger of Xibʼalbʼa disappeared before them; they watched him disappear without seeing where he went, he just disappeared.

Messenger of Xibʼalbʼa

He was there and then he wasnʼt; the Messenger, the Worker, he of Xibʼalbʼa disappeared into thin air. Now he is; now he isnʼt; then he was; then he wasnʼt. They saw not where he was or where he wasnʼt; for they knew not where he went or where was because what they saw was that he simply wasnʼt; they just knew he no longer was there where he was, because where he was, was where he now just wasnʼt; this One from Xibʼalbʼa simply disappeared; to appear again where he wasnʼt.

body:
“We donʼt want your silver, we donʼt want your precious metal,” said Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ.

“So what is it then that you might want from us; what is it that we might ask you to tell us what it is that you might want from us,” asked the Tribes; ri Amaqʼ; the Pueblos.

“Utz bʼa la, very well, very well, we will ask this of Tojil, then we will let you know!” they said then-xeʼuchaʼxik chik.

So then they asked Tojil: “What is it that the Tribes might give you, Tojil? What might they give you, Tojil; what might they give to you those who come to ask you for fire, oh Tojil; what then might they give you for you to give them fire?”

“The Pueblos; the Tribes; ri Amaqʼ they want to know what you want from them in exchange for your fire; your fire that you will give them; those People of the Pueblos; the Tribes. What is it that you want from them who are those who come here asking for your fire?”

The ones who asked Tojil what he wanted from the Pueblos; the Tribes were those who were known; were those who were named:

Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ,

Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ,

Majukʼutaj,

Ikʼi Bʼalam

“Utz bʼa la! Could it be that they let me suckle them their below their chest on the left? Could it be that they might offer up their ribcage to me so that I might just suckle them there beneath their armpit?” asked Tojil.

“Would they not allow me to embrace their hearts, I who am Tojil?”

“If they donʼt want to do this for me then I donʼt want to give them their fire,” says Tojil,ʼ you shall say to them.

“Utz bʼa la! Ma chikaj kituʼnik xeʼ kitolokʼ, xeʼ pu kimeskel? ʼMa karaj on kikʼux kinkiqʼaluj, ri in Tojil? Ta ma kʼu chiraj, ma kʼu chinyaʼ kiqʼaqʼ,ʼ kachaʼ Tojil, kixchaʼ chike.

ʼKa tikʼal na kʼut, mana kamik taj xkituʼnik xe kitolokʼ, kimeskelʼ kachaʼ chiwech,” Kixchaʼ. Tojil: he of the Debt; Toj-he of the Torch; Tojil-he of the Payment of Debt with Fire

“This is yet to be, it is not time for this to happen; it is not yet time that they should give up the side of their ribcage, there under their armpit; tell them, tell them you were told to tell them this when you speak with them again,” he said to Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj, Ikʼi Bʼalam.

body:
Right away they passed along his word; utzij; the good word of Tojil; utzij Tojil; the word that was the news that was sent from Tojil to the Tribes; who were the People of the Pueblos; ri Amaqʼ.

This was when he sent his word with those who were his AjKʼixbʼ who were those who practiced sacrifice with the AjKajbʼ who were those who would provide the Kabʼawil with sacred sustenance for the fire that was the power he provided those who sustained him in a reciprocal relationship that was formed and shaped to function with a perfect sort of precious perfection.

“Utz bʼa la! Very well! Very well indeed then! Let them be suckled by Tojil, let them embrace him as theirs!” this is what they said when they were made to endure the full authority of the word; the word of Tojil.

This is when they concurred with the word; when they agree to the will and the way of Tojil. They didnʼt give it a second thought, they just immediately said: “Utz!”

Then they took up the fire given to them, they just gathered it up to warm themselves; they warmed themselves with the fire of Tojil, the warmth of Tojilʼs fire warmed the Tribes, the strength of Tojilʼs fire was enough to heat the Tribes, the Pueblos: ri Amaqʼ.

But there was a group of them who just stole away the fire among the smoke, these were they who were known as the Sotzʼila Ja, those who are known and named the Bat House People. Chamalkan-Beautiful Serpent-was the name of their Kabʼawil; the Kabʼawil of the Kaqchikeleb known as Chamalkan.

Their divinity who went by the name Chamalkan was the Kabʼawil of the People, of the Pueblo known  as  the  Qʼaqʼchikelebʼ whose image of their lineage is a Bat-Sotzʼ. The Nawal of the Kaqchikelebʼ or Qʼaqʼchikelebʼ was just that of a Winged-Bat-xa Sotzʼ uwachibʼal: just a Bat was its image; the image of the lineage of the Bat Pueblo, the Bat People; ri Sotzʼil Amaqʼ; ri Sotzʼil Winaq.

body:
When they moved through the smoke they moved through so, so suave; they just flew right through so, so smoothly, through the smoke they moved as they flew right through carrying the fire with them as they glided by so slyly; just like smoke they moved when they took up the fire and stole it away like smoke.

The Qʼaqʼchikelebʼ or Kaqchikelebʼ did not ask for the fire nor did they give themselves up in defeat in exchange for the fire of Tojil. They just took up the fire there amongst the smoke; up out of the smoke they gathered up their fire there; they just stole it away: the fire of Tojil was whisked away by the Bat-Sotzʼ who was the Nagual of the Kaqchikelebʼ who just hung there beside the door to swoop down through the smoke to swipe their fire to float away in the smoke; they were just like smoke those Bats of the Qʼaqʼchikelebʼ; those Warriors of the Fire-Spears; those Warrior People; spoken of as the Red Spears Come Out.

But the other Pueblos, the other Amaqʼ, the other Tribes were defeated when they gave themselves up to have their hearts suckled from beneath their rib-cage; there below their armpit; there where their heart beat within the cage of their ribs.

This then is the suckling that Tojil spoke of when he spoke to the Tribes-ri Amaqʼ who were the Pueblos of the Mountain People when they came to be sacrificed before him. This was when their hearts were torn out from just below their armpits, there in-between their ribs is where those of the Obsidian Blade-AjKajbʼ tore out the beating heart of the Tribes, of the Amaqʼ, of the Pueblos to then suckle the blood that came to rest there in the chest that formed the nest of the Hummingbird on the Left known as Huitzilopochtli who suckled what was his ʼon the Leftʼ there ʼto the Southʼ where the ʼblood gatheredʼ to be suckled to sustain Tojil with his sacred most sustenance: the heart and blood; the blood and heart of ritual sacrifice. Tojil reapportioned sacrifice through disrupting the fire to then take what his appetite desired.

body:
This was yet to be done; this heart sacrifice had not yet begun. It was only divined by Tojil; when he saw that it was he who would take power; qʼaqʼal and sovereignty; tepewal over the Pueblos; Amaqʼ through those known and named:

Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ,

Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ,

Majukʼutaj,

Ikʼi Bʼalam

It was from there that they came, when they came away from Tulan Tzuy-Wa. When they were there in Tulan Tzuy-Wa they didnʼt eat anything, they ate nothing so that as One they fasted together while keeping their eyes on the horizon where the Sun rose at the Coming Out Place of the Dawn.

They waited for the Sun to rise at Dawn just ʼstayingʼ their vision on the Coming Out Place of the Sun; Relebʼal Qʼiij. They took turns watching as they waited for the whitening brightness of Dawn-Saqirik-of the brightening whiteness of the Sun as it rose up and out of the Coming Out Place of the Sun at Dawn.

They took turns watching for the rising of the Great Star-Ikʼoqʼij-known as the Bearer of the Sun; the Sun Bearer as is named the Morning Star; Ikʼoqʼij. For Ikʼoqʼij is the One Great Star that rises out of East; when it comes out of the House of Dawn just before the Sun: Qʼij to bear the Sun as the Old Man; Rilaj Tat to then begin walking with him as his burden borne on his back as the Old Man who must be carried up into the Sky to then walk with his precious cargo in his carrying frame; kok to bear his sacred burden across the Face of the Earth on the Sacred Path of the Sun.

This bright shining Star shows itself there in the dark of Night as a shimmering sign of the impending arrival of Dawn; right there where the Sun will be born rises the Morning Star that sprouts up and out of the horizon as the brilliant, benevolent bearer of Time; the radiant resplendent carrier of the Sun-Raxa Ikʼoqʼij.

body:
This is where they held their vision; towards the East where the Sun rose at Dawn; this was when they were there in Tulan Tzuy-Wa that is its name; the place from where their Deities came; the place from where they received their Kabʼawil to bear them up in the carrying-frames; kok to then carry them on their back just as Venus carries the Sun; just the same so that the Divine Ancestors bore the burden of their Kabʼawil as Venus carried the Sun; so that the First Four Fathers:

Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ,

Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ,

Majukʼutaj,

Ikʼi Bʼalam carried Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz, Nikʼaj Taqʼaj.

It wasnʼt ʼhereʼ where they received their power; kiqʼaqʼal and authority to rule; kajawarem; it was ʼthereʼ where they received their sovereign rulership; ʼthereʼ in the Kʼicheʼ; ʼthereʼ in the place from where; from wince they had once come.

It was ʼthereʼ where ʼtheyʼ were defeated and subjugated; they, the Big Tribes; Nima Amaqʼ; they, the Small Tribes; Chʼuti Amaqʼ when they were sacrificed before Tojil; when they were made to give their blood; when they were made to be sacrificed for their ʼgathered blood, coagulated bloodʼ when they sacrificed them on their sides; when they sacrificed them through the ribs of their chest as it is said; when they sacrificed them there under their armpits; when they, the People of the Pueblos were sacrificed before their Kabʼawil: Tojil.

This was when those of the Pueblo; Amaqʼ were sacrificed by the Providers-Tzuqul; the Sustainers-Kʼool; when those of the Tribes-Amaqʼ were given up as gifts sacrifice to provide for their Kabʼawil; when the day came when the Pueblos-Amaqʼ were sacrificed as sacred sustenance to sustain their Kabʼawil; the sacred sustenance that was given to provide for and sustain their Kabʼawil: Tojil.

Straight from Tulan came their power; kiqʼaqʼal; directly from Tulan came their power to rule; kajawarem over all the other Tribes; all the different Pueblos; all of the many Amaqʼ so that it was seen that their right to conquer and rule over others came straight from Tulan; Tulan is from where their power came.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
And so it was and would always be that their power of rulership; kajawarem; their power of warriorship; kiqʼaqʼal was received there in Tulan, to be taken with them when they left Tulan to return to their Mountain Places of Origin.

Qʼaqʼal and Tepewal

This is when we come to passages when qʼaqʼal and tepewal come to mean power and authority or strength and majesty or rule and authority; all of which will be the power and authority given to Kʼicheʼ Warlords and War Captains who will go off to conquer and subject the Mountain People and Canyon Country to the power and majesty of the Noble Lord of Tollan Tzuy-Wa: Nakxitl Qʼuqʼkumatz known as Sovereign Lord Quetzalcoatl; the Noble Lord Sovereign Plumed Serpent.

Qʼaqʼal and tepewal translated as ʼpowerʼ and ʼrule and authorityʼ are going to be vastly important in the last third of the Popol Wuj. Qʼaqʼal is translated as ʼfireʼ but it is really the ʼburning embers of burning charcoalʼ. So qʼaqʼal that is translated as ʼfireʼ and spoken of as ʼfire and powerʼ were once imagined by the Maya as the burning embers of charcoal-qʼaqʼal that burned as divine fire and sacred embers to consume the sacred sustenance of the human heart burnt on the sacrificial pyre devoured by the Kabʼawil to satisfy their divine appetite and its insatiable hunger for human hearts and human blood to feed those that must be fed.

Remember IxKikʼ and the Lords of Xibʼalbʼa saying: ʼgo ahead and stir up the burning embers of our fires so we can ʼthrow-downʼ the heart of IxKikʼ to smell how it burnsʼ when her heart burnt so sweetly there on the those burning embers that were stirred up in the sacrificial brazier of ritual sacrifice! This is where the power-qʼaqʼal deceive the Lords by blinding the Lords as trickster deities often do to cause disruption in order to transform the what things are done and who gets what when comes to divvying up the sacrificial offering when it comes to the apportionment of sacred sustenance that becomes a reapportionment of sweet smelling gifts of sacrifice.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Great knowledge came to them in the Dark of Night; in the Darkness genius came to them.  Great insight, great understanding came to them in the Dark of Night-chi qʼequmal; in the Darkness they found their genius, their insight.

Great wisdom came to them through the sacrificial ordeal they went through there in the Dark Darkness before the Dawn-chi Aqʼabʼal where they watched and waited at the Coming Out Place of the Sun.

This is the divine place and the sacred time when and where the ritual practitioner experiences the relief of the return of the light and warmth of the Sun; the sensation of renewal and rebirth of life in the warmth and in the light after staying focused on the horizon through the ʼedgyʼ Darkness of Night-Aqʼabʼal and ʼthresholdʼ dark before the Dawn-Aqʼabʼal while all the while praying out loud to articulate the needs of their People and their Pueblo to fill the mountain air and ears of their Kabʼawil  with their petitionary prayers while all the while making certain to maintain ritual vision and ceremonial  focus on the Coming Out Place of the Sun-Relebʼal Qʼij-Place of the Dawn: Saqiribʼal.

So then they came away from there; they just pulled themselves up and left there; leaving behind that place known as the Coming Out Place of the Sun-chi Relebʼal Qʼij; the House of Dawn; the Coming Up Place of the Sun; there in the East: Tulan is its name.

“This here is not our home, letʼs just get going to see where we can go to establish ourselves over there, let us see where we can settle down,” said Tojil.

Truly, it was he-Tojil-who spoke with them, those known and named:

Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ,

Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ,

Majukʼutaj,

Ikʼi Bʼalam

“Upon leaving show your gratitude; upon departing leave your thanks; just give of yourself! This then is when you must bleed your ears. This then is when you must sow thorns in your elbows! Perform your sacrifice! This is the way to show your gratitude there before your Kabʼawil!” said Tojil their Kabʼawil.

“Utz bʼa la!” they said upon taking leave of the place they came to know: Tulan, Tzuy-Wa. This is the place they pulled themselves up and out of to begin their journey of return back to where they had come.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Then they bled their ears. They drew blood from their ears when they wept in their song. This is when they came away from Tulan; when they left Tulan weeping as they sang their song of departure; when they sang their song upon abandoning the East at their leaving Tulan.

Truly their hearts cried out when they came away from there; when they pulled themselves up; when they left Tulan; when they abandoned Tulan.

“¡Aqʼaroq! Ayyyayayayay! This is not the place we will watch for the Sunrise. When the Sun is born to shine its light upon the Face of the Earth,” they cried out as they called out to one and all.

So then they came away from there; just sleeping alongside the road did they come away from there. And so it was that a few remained where they slept beside the road, a few stayed where they slept; they did not continue on.

Other Tribes rose-up and began moving again, always with their eyes set upon the place of the dawning Sun at the Dawn of the day where the Star shines as a sign at the place where it rise there before the coming forth of the Sun; before the sprouting out of the Sun

They just came walking along with their eyes set on the horizon; always with their vision seeking the Star that shines as the sign of the Sun.

This was the remembrance of the ʼDawnʼ in their hearts, in their memory, when they left the Coming Out Place of the Sun; Relebʼal Qʼij when they left the East, when they came away walking from Tulan.

Together as ʼOneʼ they passed upon the place there known as Nim Xol-the Great Hollow, the Great Opening as they call it today beside the place known as Karchaj.

And then they arrived atop One Mountain Jun Juyubʼ. There is where all of the Kʼicheʼ People; Kʼecheʼ Winaq gathered together with the other Tribes-Amaqʼ.

This is the place where they celebrated council with one another. This is the place where they gave advice and provided counsel while giving instructions to one another. The name of the mountain today is Chi Pixabʼ: Place of Council; Council Place; Place of Counsel.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Chi Pixab, Council Place is the name of the mountain where they came together to name one another at Chi Pixabʼ known as Place of Council; Place of Counsel; this is where they took leave of one another.

This is where they acknowledged one another as Kʼecheʼ Amaqʼ which is to say the Kʼicheʼ Pueblo; Kʼicheʼ People; Kʼicheʼ Winaq; Kʼicheʼ Pueblo; Kʼicheʼ Amaqʼ.

“In waʼ, in Kʼicheʼ Winaq!

I am here; I am of the Kʼicheʼ People;

I am here who stands before you; I am a member of the Kʼicheʼ People;

I who am here before you stands as a member of the Many Trees People; Kʼicheʼ Winaq: In waʼ, in Kʼicheʼ Winaq!

I who am here; am here as a member of the Kʼicheʼ People.”

“And you there, you who are Tamubʼ; Tamubʼ the name of those who are known as the People of the Trunk. Tamubʼ is the name youʼve been named to name the Trunk People, the Pueblo Tamubʼ is who you are,” was what the Tamubʼ were told.

And then it was said, “Ilokʼabʼ, At Ilokʼabʼ, this shall be your name, you the ʼHoney Huntersʼʼ those ʼPeople of Visionʼ as you are spoken of to become the People, the Pueblo you now are: Ilokʼabʼ Winaq!

May that these three branches of the Kʼicheʼ lineages never be lost, for our word is just one-xa junam qatzij-just one and the same shall be our word, our truth, our tradition-xa junam qatzij,” they said when they placed names upon one another.

Then they named the Qʼaqʼchekelebʼ and so the Kaqchikelebʼ is the name they were given.

And just like them the Rabʼinalebʼ is the name they were named and who the Rabʼinalebʼ came to be.

These names of the Tribes-Amaqʼ; these names of Pueblos are used today; they are not lost on us today. These are the names the Pueblos; the names of the Pueblos that the People of the Pueblos continue to used to name themselves when they name their names today.

And then there is the Aj Tzʼikina Ja; the Bird House People; Bird House Pueblo and that continues to be their name today: Aj Tzʼikina Ja.

These then are the names that they the Pueblos-Amaqʼ; the People-Winaq named one another. This was when they named each other; when they named each otherʼs names as Kʼicheʼ Winaq; Kʼicheʼ Amaqʼ.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Are kʼu kibʼi, ri xkibʼij chi kibʼil kibʼ. This is how they were named; they named each other by name.

There was the place where they wished to go in order to arrive so they could await the Dawn. It was there in that place that they wanted to get to so that upon their arrival they could watch for the return of the Star that bore up the Sun in his tumpline to carry him up into the Sky.

So they went walking to this place to watch for the Coming Out of the Star-Chʼumil; known as the First One before the Sun-Nabʼe chuwach Qʼij; the First before the Sun; the One coming up before the Birth of the Sun-Qʼij.

“There is the place we came from when we divided up to split apart from one another when we abandoned Tulan,” they said to each other; kibʼil kibʼ.

Tormented were their hearts; sorrowful were their souls for the great suffering they experienced for all they had gone through with one another there.

They ate nothing; nothing was eaten by them there; no sustenance was taken by any of them.

They just inhaled the smell of the point of their walking stick; they just breathed in the tips of the walking sticks to take in their scent to give them the feeling they had eaten.

And so it was that they ate nothing while they walked along the way from where they came walking on their long walk from Tulan.

It is not clear as how they crossed the Sea-pa Palo. They crossed the sea as if there were no sea to cross; that is the way they crossed the sea; they just crossed over upon the rocks. For there were just stones; there were just rocks lined-up in a row on the sand where they crossed over the Sea when they crossed over the Sea walking.

And so this then is the naming of this place: Line of Ordered Stones-Cholochik Abʼaj-Ordered Line of Stones and Pulled-Up Sand-Bʼoqotajinaq Sanayebʼ-Raised-Up Sand. These are the names of the places where they crossed-over the Sea. The waters were separated there where they crossed on their way.
