source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
“In this way you will defeat the Pueblos; in that way you will subjugate the People so you can nourish and nurture us in order that we might be better able to nourish and nurture you!”

“In this way you will be able to bring their blood; their sacrificial blood that is their live essence given to us as their sacrifice to us; just bring them to us as our sacred sustenance. You will bear them before us as sacred tribute, for it is they the Pueblo, they the Tribes, the Amaqʼ who promised to be brought before us so they can embrace us, for now they pertain to us; for now they are ours! And what is ours is most certainly yours that it may be ours!” said: Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz; los Tojiles.

They appeared to be Young Men when one looked upon them, when one burnt sacrificial offerings before them. So then began the hunt for the brood of birds and the descendants of deer.

And so it was the search for offerings was initiated by the AjKʼixibʼ, AjKʼajbʼ: the sacrificial priests as they are named for those who gather blood with Maguey Spines and Obsidian Blades. These were ritual objects, maguey spine and obsidian blades that were the emblems of their divine office; the divine burden they bore;  their sacred cargo to carry on behalf of their People in favor of their Kabʼawil; their ancestral obligation to provide  sacrifice to feed those who must be fed: provider, sustainer; nourisher, nurturer; feeder, maintainer.

When the hunters who provided sacrifice found the birds and deer they then immediately brought the blood of the deer and blood of the birds as sacrificial offerings that they placed in the mouths of the stones Tojil, Awilix.

When the blood was drank by the Kabʼawil the stones immediately began talking with the AjKʼixbʼ, AjKʼajbʼ who had arrived with them there; when they went to provide burnt offerings of sacrifice to their deities, to their Kabʼawil in the places they were left to be sustained with these drops of blood that the Kabʼawil received as a gift taken as a precious gift that was so very dear to those Images of Stone: Abʼajil.

Sacred Deer Bundle-KʼuʼKej

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
The original text ʼseemsʼ to willfully create confusion as to where the Stone Statues of the Kabʼawil actually are because if the AjKʼixbʼ, AjKʼajbʼ must go to visit the Kabʼawil to place blood in the mouths of Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz then Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, and Majukʼutaj are all in different places.

Since they left their Kabʼawil in different places such as the Great Forest where there is a Hidden Canyon in amongst its wild animals is found the hidden Hiding Place of Awilix. Then there is Tojil who was place in Kunabʼal Tojil in the Mountain Place of the Medicine of Tojil which was found in the Great Forest of Pa Tojil; and, Kaqajawitz of the Mountain Jaqawitz where stands the Red House of Sacrifice on top of the mountain Chuwi Juyubʼ of  Jaqawitz.

So all of the sudden Sacred Bundles are made from the Deer Skins as Envoltorio Sagrado: Sacred Bundles: KʼuʼKej. So the nawal essence of each of the stones of the Kabʼawil are now up on top of the mountain of Jaqawitz that is known as Chuwi Juyubʼ just as it is known today. The stones just taste the blood and that is enough to fill the up satisfying their appetite for fresh hunted blood while one assumes the meat of the birds and deer goes to feed the growing Nation; growing Tribe of the First Mother-Fathers.

So does this mean they are all together up there atop Chuwi Juyubʼ Jaqawitz. The text never clarifies this and since is myth and myth often allows our imagination to create order out of  the creative confusion crafted and created by the Nawales of these Good-looking Young Men who are Talking Stones that speak through the  Nawal Essence bundled in the Deer Skin Pisom Qʼaqʼal Sacred Bundles enabling the Kabʼawil to  move about in order  to come in and out of focus like breath on a mirror. On this mythic mountain upon which the hunters will hunt to provide and sustain those who will sustain them with the rain they need to feed their milpa of the productive People of the prolific Pueblos.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
They did the same thing before the Sacred Deer Bundle-KʼuʼKej-when they provided for them; when they sustained them with burnt offerings of pine tree resin-qʼol; when they burnt pericón flower-iyaʼ and jolom okox-skull of mushroom  as sacred sustenance upon their sacred fires right there on top of the mountain-Chuwi Juyubʼ before their Kʼuʼ Kej: the Sacred Deer Skin Bundles of the Kabʼawil.

There was a Sacred Deerskin Bundle-KʼuʼKej-for each one of them that was carried up to the top of the mountain: Chuwi Juyubʼ

There was nobody home during the day because they were out walking about on the mountain.

They just ate the larva of large round bees-ral wonon, the larva of black wasps-ral sitaʼl, and the larva of little black wasp-ral aqaj; this was their sustenance, the sustenance of those known as AjKʼixibʼ, AjKajbʼ.

Xa ral Wonon, Xa ral Sitaʼl, Xa ral Aqaj

Just the larva of large round bees; just the larva of black wasps; just the larva of small black wasp this is what they searched for; for this is what they ate; their Sacred Sustenance. Oh how massively suggestive line telling of sacred sustenance is so very, very big; so very, very genius in the way our beloved Maya Scribes just tuck it away in this hidden hideaway of simply naming the names of the Larva of the Big Round Bees; Larva of the Tiny Black Wasps; Larva of the Black Metallic Wasp; Xa ral wonon, xa ral sitaʼl, xa ral aqaj.

This then is when metaphorical mythic words alone can act as the hideaway hiding place as the sacred sustenance of the AjKʼixibʼ, AjKajbʼ. And if it is their sustenance then what will be the relationship between the AjKʼixbʼ, AjKajbʼ and the Wonon, Sitaʼl, and Aqaj; Big Round Bees, Black Metallic Wasps, and Little Black Wasps? What then is that I ask?

This is what they were out searching for on the mountainside. This was not good food; this was not good drink.

Nor was the path to and from their homes well marked, nor was it very clear where they came from or where they had left their women behind during the day while they were out hunting with their deerskins-mawi qʼalaj kʼo wi kanoq kixoqila.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Meanwhile the Tribes grew thick with offspring; each one, each Tribe gathered together to settle themselves where they wished to establish themselves on the mountain; this is where they settled in groups; and this is where those groups grew and grew.

Each gathering of people, each group of the Pueblos walked the paths of their own making and those paths of theirs made it quite clear where these people walked about on the mountainside. Their paths, the paths of the Pueblosʼ were clear as could be and just as easy to see; so, it was easy to see where they came from and just as easy to see where they went walking there on the mountain.

However, with regard to those known as Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj,  Ikʼi Bʼalam it was not clear where they were;  nor where they went; nor when they would return from where they had gone and when they would come;  this was not clear; not clear at all.

So that is when they saw the People of the Pueblos pass by on their mountain trails; when they saw them pass by on their tracks; upon their traces; when they passed on their mountain paths that came and went to where they made their way coming and going on their paths that passed their on their mountain.

This is when they-the hunters with deer skins-began calling out from the summits and ridges; just yapping, just yammering like coyotes; just calling, just crying like foxes; imitating the grumbling growl of puma; but it was the deep throated bawling of the jaguar that did it; that is what did it; that is what hid them from the people walking along in the shadows of the mountain roads.

“It is just a coyote howling, just a fox crying, just a puma calling, just a jaguar bawling,” said those of the Tribes; the people of the Pueblo as they passed by looking up and down then around and around to then quickly look back behind.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
It was just as if they were not people; it was as if they were not human in the minds of the many members of the Tribes, of the Pueblos. They just did it to deceive the people; they willfully wanted to trick them; they intentionally wished to deceive the people of the Pueblos; they didnʼt want the Pueblo to think they were people; they wanted them to think that were wild animals that were there on the mountain; not people; definitely not people.

They knew exactly what they were doing; they knew what they had to do; so this is what they decided to do.

They didnʼt want to cause the people fear by doing what they did. They knew what they wanted by imitating the intimidating deep growl of the Puma; the bawling bellow of the Jaguar and its hair-raising sneering snarl.

When they saw a person all alone or two people walking along the road they just wanted to disappear them. That is what they wanted to do; they just wanted to make them disappear.

Every day when they returned home to their wives they just brought back the larva of Big Round Bees-ral Wonon; the larva of Black Metallic Wasps-ral Sitaʼl; the larva of Little Black Wasps-ral aqaj.

That is what they brought home with them when they returned home every day with their sustenance. And this is what they provided their wives with as sustenance to feed them with their food that we come to protect them when they time of reckoning came for the Mountain Tribes and those known as los Tojiles: Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz.

Every day when they went before the presence of they spoke to themselves in their heart, in their soul; when they spoke to themselves in silence; when they spoke:

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
“So these ones Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz; to these ones we only give them offerings of blood; we offer them the blood of deer and the blood of birds. Wouldnʼt it be better if we were to pierce our own ears?  We should bleed our own elbows before our Kabʼawil to ask that they make us hard, tough to endure hardship. We should bleed ourselves to ask that we might develop strength and endurance to withstand pain and suffering; we should ask them for more vigor and vitality so that we can better overcome adversity. This is what we must ask of Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz,” this is what they said to one another when they had a heart to heart talk with one another in silence.

“Who will be the ones that will be given the sacred burden that is the divine obligation of performing sacrifice on those of the Pueblo who will be offered-up when the time comes to sacrifice those of the Pueblo? Could it be that we ourselves just sacrifice them one by one?” They asked themselves when they spoke to one another on their way to see los Tojiles.

So this then was when they went before their presence; the presence of Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz. And there it was that they pierced their ears with maguey thorns; they pierced their elbows before their Kabʼawil to offer them their blood as sacred sustenance to provide and sustain their Kabʼawil.

They poured the divine drink; xkiwaquj of the Kabʼawil into the mouths of their stone images, but truly they were no longer these stone effigies were no longer of stone, each one of them transformed into a Young Man: Kʼajolabʼ.

And so it came to pass that the Kabʼawil were made content with the blood that was sacrificed to them by the AjKʼixibʼ, AjKajbʼ; for truly the Kʼabʼawil were satisfied like never before; for truly happy and content were los Tojiles.

Then a sign came telling them what they should do: “You should defeat them because their defeat is your deliverance. This comes from Tulan; this comes from decisions made in Tulan when you carried us away from there.” This is just what the Kʼajolabʼ gave them as a sign; when the Young Men; Nawales of the Kabʼawil gave them with counsel.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This is what they the AjKʼixibʼ, AjKajbʼ were told there by their Kabʼawil when they spoke to them about the Pueblo and the great many People that the Pueblo had become; the great many People that now made-up the Pueblo.

This was when a ʼsignʼ was given telling them what to do: “You must defeat them now because their destruction is your deliverance. This comes from Tulan; this comes from decisions made in Tulan when you received us to then bear us away as your sacred burden.”

This is just what the Young Men; Kʼajolabʼ gave them as directions to follow that signaled what the AjKʼixbʼ, AjKajbʼ must do when the Young Men;  Kʼajolabʼ told them what they must do; when the Nawales of the Kabʼawil gave them their instructions that told them what was to be done next.

This was when they spoke of the Pueblo and how they offered their breast and their blood to be suckled by Tojil there at Place of Trembling; Pa Silisibʼ when fire was given in exchange for the blood that now would fall as rain; a great flood of sacrificial blood offered as sacred sustenance to Tojil along with Awilix, Jaqawitz.

This then is the beginning of the theft of the People of the Pueblos; this then is the origin of the stealing away of the Tribes; the Mountain Tribes; the Mountain People; the People of the Pueblos who were those of the Mountain Places; the Canyon Country.

This then is our telling of the ancient ancestral account of the theft and disappearance of those known as the People, Winaq; the Pueblo, Amaqʼ who were stolen away to be sacrificed by Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj, Ikʼi Bʼalam; known as los Tojiles.

And so it was that it began; and what began was the death of the Tribes; that is what began; the hunting down of the People; Winaq of the Pueblo; Amaqʼ by those known as Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj, Ikʼi Bʼalam.

It was they who just-xa grabbed those who walked by themselves, or those who walked in pairs; in this way no one could see that they, the People of the Pueblo, were being disappeared by being stolen away on the mountainside.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Immediately they took them to be sacrificed before Tojil, Awilix. They would sprinkle their blood on the trail, before sending their heads rolling down the road for the people to find.

And so the Pueblo; the Tribe; ri Amaqʼ would say: “It was just a Jaguar; it was just Jun Bʼalam that ate them,” this is what they said because of the footprints of the Jaguar that they made; los Tojiles made the paw prints in the road, on the trail, in the dust, in the mud.

They never showed themselves; they never revealed themselves as the nagual of the Jaguar Lords of the Mountain; Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ naguales of Tojil, Awilix.

It wasnʼt long before there was a great number of people that they stole away; and it wasnʼt until much later that the Pueblo; Amaqʼ felt they were losing people; at first they didnʼt notice a thing.

“Surely it must be Tojil, Awilix who entered here among us; letʼs just look for the AjKʼixb; letʼs just search for the Sacrificial Priests of the Maguey Spine.  Letʼs just search for the AjKajbʼ; letʼs just look for the Sacrificial Priests of the Obsidian Blade.

We will find them there when they are home to then follow their footprints!” they said then when they gathered together on the mountain.

So this is when the Pueblos celebrated council together to begin following the traces of their footprints that led to the tracks they made with their footsteps that showed the way to the footpath that was the trail of the  AjKʼixibʼ, AjKʼajb but these tracks and traces of their trails were not clear, not clear at all.

Xa raqan Kej, xa raqan Bʼalam chikilo-Just the hoof-prints of Deer, just the paw-prints of Jaguar is all they could see, these were the only signs left there to be seen: Deer, Jaguar; Kej,  Bʼalam.

They couldnʼt see any prints of the thieves; they couldnʼt find any sign of anything, anywhere. The first tracks were of the four-footed ones, just four-footed hoof prints were there, this was just to confuse them; hoof prints, deer tracks  were everywhere; they could not find their way because of the great plenty of tracks and great many traces on and off the trail.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Their trail could not be made out; the trail of the AjKʼixibʼ, AjKʼajbʼ could not be seen or found, neither here nor there;  just hoof prints of deer were all there were as they tried to find their way up on the mountain only to end up lost following tracks that went nowhere.

Their paths were not clear, they just rose-up like clouds-sutzʼ; they just rose-up to suddenly appear as dark black rain-qʼeqʼal jabʼ of a great rainstorm known as a temporal; like hurricane rain where they there; those tracks that that traced on the land that end up as rain falling from the Heart of the Sky.

This is what became of them who transformed into what they willed; these Nawal Winaq were quite content changing and transforming into whatever they wanted to become as they became the transforming ways of the water that fell from the sky to as rain that inundated the earth.

They just appeared to be mud-xoqʼol; they just rose-up to fall back down as mist-mutzmul; as rain-jabʼ; as mist rain-mutzmul jabʼ which was like mixed rain of drizzle and fog.

Nothing was clear, for truly these were those that were Nawal Ancestors; true transforming being more than just magicians; they were Kabʼawil that looked like Young Men; Kʼajolabʼ when their Nawal took this form to be formed and transformed into People; People who were not like those of the Pueblo; not like those kinds of people at all.

This is what the Pueblo saw before them as they searched the Face of the Earth for their tracks, their footprints; but nothing was there to be seen; nothing was there to be heard, so that nothing was found no matter where they searched.

The People of the Pueblo lost heart, they lost heart looking for them; they tired of searching all about; they became distraught, distressed from their hunting them down only to lose their trail right when it looked as if they were about to find them out; but they did not find them out; it was not like that because those who they searched for so long and hard were nowhere to be found; because absolutely not one was there: maj jun kʼo taj chʼila; Majukʼotaj!

body:
It was just their great powers transformation; the nawal powers of transformation of  those known as Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz who now revealed their ancestral ways of being and becoming whatever it was they needed to be; their character, their nature, their essence of existence was known as ukʼojeʼik of their existence, and what that was and what that meant was that they were Nawal Winaq.

For a long time this is how the lived up there atop of the mountain; there on the mountaintop place known as Above the Mountain-Chuwi Juyubʼ-On Top of the Mountain. There on the edge of the Pueblo-Amaqʼ is where they sacrificed them; them, those, the People of the Pueblo.

This is how the stealing away of the people came about there beside the Pueblo of the Mountain People. This then was when they selected them before capturing them by the side of the road to then carry them away to where they were sacrificed before their Kabʼawil: Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz.

This they did while keeping their own children safe and protected up there above, on top of their mountain: Chuwi Juyubʼ. This they did along with their women; they did this as best they could; and this they did quite well.

There was a river there. It was there in the river where they bathed; it was only there beside the river that they ʼshowedʼ themselves when they went to the river to bathe; when they went there where they bathed by the side of the river.

They called this place Chi Ratinibʼal Tojil or ʼBeside the Bathing Place of Tojilʼ; this is how the bathing place of Tojil was named.

The three of them; the Three Young Men went there every day at the end of the day to bathe in the place known as Chi Ratinibʼal Tojil. Bathing in this place was the way the Three Young Men ended their day beside the river; which is to say the Young Men went down to their bathing place beside the river where they went to bath day after day at Chi Ratinibʼal Tojil.

Many times the People of the Pueblo saw the three of them there in the river, Jaʼ; in the water, Jaʼ; in the river water, Jaʼ.

body:
The People of the Pueblo saw them beside the river bathing in the water when they went to the river to bathe at the end of the day. But as soon as they were seen they disappeared; instantly the Three Young Men vanished into the air when they were seen there bathing in the river.

This was when news came as to the whereabouts of Bʼalam Kitzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj, Ikʼi Bʼalam.

That was when the Pueblo gathered together their thoughts in council to design a plan with which to finish them off.  The People of the Pueblo gathered together to figure out how they would defeat Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz known by all as: los Tojiles.

It was they who were spoken of and talked about in Council before the Pueblos, before the Tribes; Amaqʼ as the AjKʼixbʼ, AjKʼajbʼ who were those who the Pueblo now discussed to find a way to defeat them.

It was they who were contemplated when the People of the Pueblo took council with one another in order to find a solution to the AjKʼixbʼ, AjKʼajbʼ who were those that captured and sacrificed their daughters and sons who they were finishing off.

They pulled everyone together; they gathered everyone together in order to unite with one another; they sent a message to summons the Pueblo. There wasnʼt one group; nor were there two groups that were left behind. All of them assembled with one another as they called themselves together in a great Council of the Pueblos; all the Pueblos were gathered together to find a way to defeat the AjKʼixbʼ, AjKʼajbʼ.

This was when they brought forth their ideas as one Pueblo that spoke about those known as the AjKʼixbʼ, AjKʼajbʼ who gave sacrifice to Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz.

Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz: Los Tojiles

Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj, Ikʼi Bʼalam

These three Kabʼawil were those known as Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz. These were those three that took the appearance of Kʼajolabʼ to look like Young Men so that they walked like Young Men yet those Young Men were just the nawal of their stones-xa unawal ri abʼaj; the nawal of Stone Images; Abʼajil of the Kabʼawil is what they were.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Those Kabʼawil were those that were carried on the backs of the First Four Fathers Bʼalam Kitzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj, Ikʼi Bʼalam when they came away from Tulan Tzuy-Wa as the AjKʼixbʼ, AjKʼajbʼ bearing the stone images of their Kabʼawil: Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz, Nikʼaj Taqʼaj. Who was who it was difficult to say since they were nawal transforms of one-an-other that were difficult to keep apart.

These sacred stones carried from Tulan Tzuy-Wa were the embodiment of these three divinities, the three Kabʼawil who the Sun turned to stone but now were transformed back into their  Nawal; the living form, the living shape of  Three Young Men, and it was they who were known as those of Tojil: los Tojiles.

This then is what they said when they asked one another what should be done next:

“Would it be so very difficult for us, the Pueblos, to defeat the Kaweq People who are the Kʼecheʼ Winaq? Because of them our daughters, our sons are being finished off; it is not clear how they ʼdisappearʼ our people; but it is clear they do ʼdisappearʼ our people. It is also clear that their ʼstealing awayʼ of our children goes on all the time; it never stops, never. So be it! Let us find a way to end the ʼlosing and lossʼ of our daughters and our sons: our children; our descendants!”

“So be it! If the powers of Tojil-Awilix-Jaqawitz are so great then we shall accept Tojil as our Kabʼawil; our Deity; our Divinity. We must capture them then if they are to become our Kabʼawil to whom we shall give sacrifice!”

“We shouldnʼt let them finish us off. After all, do we not constitute a great multitude? Meanwhile the Kaweq are relatively few in number, really, they are not so very many,” they said, when they took council with one another; those of the Pueblo when they celebrated council together as one Pueblo.

There were a few who were there who spoke directly to the People of the Pueblo gathered there, and this is what they said:

body:
“Who has seen them bathing there on the banks of the river every day? If those are Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz; it would be best to finish them off first. Then we can turn to defeating the others, the AjKʼixbʼ, AjKʼajbʼ; those who give sacrifice with maguey spines and obsidian blades;  those that perform sacrifice as they are spoken of before the Pueblo.”

So then immediately there were others who spoke: “How are we to defeat them?”

To which they replied: “This should be the way that we defeat them: since they appear to be Young Men when one sees them beside the river, we should send them Two Maidens; the maidens sent to them must be good-looking, handsome maidens; they must be real beauties, these maidens that we send them there where they bathe must be attractive, enchanting Young Women.”

“Utz bʼa la! Very well then! Let us look among our daughters for two fine maidens who are willing and able to do that which is asked of them.”

Truly beautiful, sharp-looking-chaʼom-fine-looking, handsome Young Women did they find.

Truly divine, radiant-saqloqʼoj-resplendent Young Maidens did they find; those who were precious-utzilaj-perfect Young Maidens who were willing to do what was asked of them to do; as indeed these Young Women were willing and able to do what was theirs to do for the good of their Pueblo and its ancient ancestral linage.

These Young Women were prepared to complete this most tricky mission that their Fathers-Qajaw-Lords called upon them to complete for their People; for their Pueblo who need their help to defeat these Three Young Men.

This was when they, the Lords gave their instructions to these Young Women; their Older Daughters; the Older Daughters of the Lords; and this is what they said:

“You must go then, precious daughters of ours! You must go down to the river to wash these blankets! And if you should see those Three Young Men who the Pueblo has spoken about then greet them with your words; if you should see these Three Handsome Young Men then undress yourself before them.”

body:
“And if their desire should call them to you then let your natural charms enchant the so that you might overcome them; once you have done all you can do to seduce and entice them then possess them with your beguiling ways so that you might come to defeat them.”

“And if they were to say: ʼwe would like to come to youʼ it would be good for you to say, ʼUtz bʼa la! Fine indeed! Come then to us,ʼ you shall say,” said Lords who were the Fathers of the Daughters of the Lords.

“And if they should ask: ʼWhere do you come from? Who then are you the daughters of, you, you who are Young Maidens?”

“Perhaps you shall say: ʼAre we not Daughters of the Lords?ʼ this is perhaps what you shall say,” they were told.

“You should bring us a ʼsignʼ from them. Whatever it is that they might give you as a ʼsignʼ of their desire for you; to have you, to possess you, then it is best that you ʼgive yourselvesʼ to them.”

“And if you do not give yourselves to them then we will have no other choice than to end your days. Our hearts will only be satisfied when you bring back a ʼsignʼ that is a ʼsymbolʼ of your union with these beautiful Young Men who bathe beside the river at Chi Ratinibʼal Tojil. This ʼsignʼ will satisfy our hearts that they came to you there; a ʼsignʼ of their defeat,” they said.

This then is what they said; those who were the Lords of the Pueblo who instructed the Two Young Women, the Two Precious Maidens; truly resplendent were these beguiling Young Women; truly radiant were  these enchanting Daughters of the Lords; these powerful and potent Young Women of the People; truly enchanting Young Maidens of the Pueblo.

There were two of them, these are their names:  IxTaj is the name of the first of the two maidens known as ʼShe of Desireʼ since ʼTajʼ is to ʼdesireʼ.

IxPuch is the name of the second maiden known as ʼyouthful young womanʼ these were their names because of their beguiling powers of youthful enchantment and attractive desire.

It was just the two who were chosen, IxTaj, IxPuch are their names. They were sent to the river to the Bathing Place of Tojil known as Ratinibʼal Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz.

body:
This was just the genius of the Pueblo, just their thinking; just their planning; just their imagination that found the idea to send the maidens-qʼapoja there to speak with the Three Young Men that bathed beside the river every day at the end of the day.

IxTaj is the name of one maiden who one might imagine as ʼShe of Desireʼ; and, the second maiden chosen was IxPuchʼ ʼYoung Woman, Precious Maidenʼ from the Nahuatl IxPochtli, “Young Woman, Precious Maiden” these were the names of the two Daughters of the Lords: IxTaj, IxPuch or Ixtaj, Ixpuch.

And so then it was that they started out walking to the river attractively attired, desirously dressed, enchantingly adorned. For truly magnificent were these two Noble Young Women who were sent to the bathing place of the Tojil.

They appeared to be going down to the river with their wash-kichʼajon-where the Three Young Men were seen bathing. Contented were their Fathers, the Noble Lords-AjAwabʼ-Sovereign Rulers, who sent their two dutiful, devoted daughters to do what was asked of them.

When the Two Maidens arrived by the side of the river, they went straight to washing their wash. They made themselves naked just as the two of them were instructed to do by those who gave them their instructions as Noble Lords of the Pueblo.

They were kneeling by the riverside, the two of them bent over their washing stones-e chakachaxinaq chuwach taq abʼaj-just kneeling over their washing stones working as women work washing their wash on their washing stones.

This is how they were seen when the Three Young Men arrived beside the river; those who are known and named as: Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz.

They arrived there at the riverʼs shore without taking notice of the Two Young Women that were washing their wash on their washing stones.

And so it was that these Two Maidens were made to feel shame when the Three Tojiles arrived there beside the river without taking notice of them washing.

The desire of the Tojiles was not awakened by the Two Maidens who were immediately asked: “From where then have you come?”

body:
Before they could answer the first another question was made: “What is it that you want that you should come here alongside our river?” they were asked.

“We were sent by our Fathers, the Lords who told us: ʼGo then to where the Tojiles bathe to see if you can talk with them; to speak with them.ʼ This is what we were told by our Fathers who sent us this way,” responded the Two Maidens.

“They instructed us when they said: ʼReturn with a sign that you have spoken with them, so that we may see it is true they you came to know them!”

“Just bring us a sign of their word, if you should come to know their face in order to speak with them, there beside the river, beside the water where they bathe.ʼ This is what we were told,” said the Two Maidens when they spoke with those with whom they were sent to speak with; those who they spoke with.

What the Lords of the Pueblo wanted was that the Two Maidens would tempt the Nawal nature of the Tojiles.

So then they spoke, those Good-looking Boys, those Three Beautiful Young Men known as Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz they spoke with the Maiden; they spoke with the Young Women when they turned to talk to IxTaj; She of Desire and  IxPuch; She the Lively Young Woman; those who were truly enchanting Young Maidens as they are known as they were named  Kaʼibʼ Utzilaj Taq Qʼapojibʼ; Kaʼibʼ Saqilaj taq Qʼapojibʼ; Kaʼibʼ Saqloqʼoj chi Qʼapojibʼ: Two Beautiful Precious Maidens; Two Perfect Beloved Maidens; Two Resplendent Divine Maidens.

“Very well, you shall go with the ʼsignʼ of our speaking together; we will send you with a ʼsignʼ of our conversing with one another. Wait so that we might prepare something for you to deliver to your Lords-AjAwabʼ-your Fathers,” they were told there beside the river where they spoke, where they came to know one another, those young attractive beauties who were there with Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz.

This is when the AjKʼixbʼ, AjKʼajbʼ took council with one another seeking to find a solution to their problem. How could they leave a ʼsignʼ of their speaking together with the Two Maidens?

Then the Nawales spoke to: Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj, Ikʼi Bʼalam:

body:
“Paint three blankets-Pintan tres lienzos-Kixtzʼibʼanoq oxibʼ kʼul-Paint Three Cotton Mantas with signs of your nawal essence-ikʼojeik-the essential nature of your being so that these Painted Pictures might arrive there with the Lords of the Pueblo. They must be given to the maidens so they, the Two Maidens can pass them on to the Noble Lords of the Pueblos who ask these who are Daughters of the Lords to bring them a ʼsignʼ of their ʼknowing our face; knowing our fruitʼ they said. Paint them so they can return with the Two Young Women, the Two Maidens, those who have arrived here to wash their wash on their washing stones beside the river. Give them to them,” said the Nawales to Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj; said the Three Young Men; said Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz; said los Tojiles to Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj.

It was then when each One of the Three painted the image of their Nawal Nature, their Natural Essence by painting images of their Nawal Presence on the blankets they used as mantels or cotton mantas for painting lienzos or canvases.

The first to paint was Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ: Jaguar-Bʼalam was his Nawal Essence, so the image of a Bʼalam is what he painted on the lienzo of his lineage: Jaguar.

Then Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ painted: Eagle-Kʼot was his nature, Eagle-Kʼot was his Nawal Essence, and so he painted an image of an Eagle-Kʼot on his blanket-kʼu, the lienzo he painted for the Lords of the Pueblo.

Then was painted the lienzo of Majukʼutaj: just a swarm of Round Black Bees-Jumaj Wonon; just a swarm of Black Wasps-Jumaj Sitaʼl was his Nawal Essence; so this was the image that he painted on the lienzo of Majukʼutaj.

When all three Lords were finished painting the images of their Nawal Nature; Nawal Essence on their blankets they folded them up ʼjust soʼ that the three lienzos were ready and prepared to be sent to the Lords of the Pueblo.

This was when they were delivered to the Two Maidens IxTaj, IxPuch as they are named and it was they who went directly back to deliver them to those who sent them to bring back as a sign; as a symbol of their washing of the Lordsʼ blankets beside the river.

body:
So then the Two Maidens were spoken to by Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz; Los Tojiles who said the Two Maidens

“ʼHere is proof of our speaking with one another!ʼ This is what you must say when you come before the Lords of the Pueblos, your Fathers, so that perhaps you will say: ʼTruly they spoke with us, the ones known as los Tojiles, it is they who spoke with usʼ you are to say to them. ʼHere is the proof that we bring to you,ʼ say to them. ʼBlanket your bodies so that you just cover yourselves with the blankets we painted for you-Chikikʼuj kʼu ri kʼul chiyaʼ chike.ʼ” is what was said to the Two Maidens when they were given the painted images; when they were given their instructions; when they were give the painted lienzos to give to the Lords as a ʼsignʼ of their speaking with the Three Young Men.

The maidens returned straight-away carrying the lienzos upon which the nawal images of the Tojiles were painted. When they arrived, immediately the hearts of the Lords-AjAwabʼ-Rulers were made content. They hung the blankets over their arms; over their arms they hung the painted lienzos that had been commissioned to be brought back to the Lords; the Fathers of the Maidens-ri Qʼapojibʼ.

“Did you not see the Three Tojiles?” they were asked.

“Yes, we saw them!” answered IxTaj, IxPuchʼ.

“Utz bʼa la! Very well, very well indeed! What then did they give you as a ʼsignʼ of your speaking to them in order to know their faces, if what you say is true?” asked the Lord Rulers of the Pueblo.

The drawings on the blankets, the paintings on the lienzos were just proof of the Two Maidensʼ knowing the faces of the Young Men; the Young Men from whom the Ajawabʼ had asked for a ʼsignʼ of their having known one another when they came ʼto know each otherʼs Face-Ruwach; to know each otherʼs Fruit-Ruwachʼ as it is said, as it is known; this speaking of one knowing another ʼface to face.ʼ

This was when the maidens brought forth the blankets upon which were painted the images of the Nawal Essence of each of the Lords that were painted upon each of the lienzos; each of the blankets.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
The first blanket was a painted lienzo filled with a ʼprowlʼ of Jaguar; another was painted with a ʼflockʼ of Eagles; and, the last was a painting of a ʼswarmʼ round black bees, and a ʼcloudʼ of wasps, all of which were painted on the lienzos.

They were absolutely enchanting to gaze upon, enthralling indeed were they, the painted drawings of the jaguars, eagles, and swarms of bees and clouds of wasps.

So then it was that they felt a longing for the lienzos; they felt as certain sense of desire to feel the painted images on the blankets. They could not help but wish to blanket themselves with them; to envelop their bodies with the nawal images left as signs by the Tojiles.

So that is what they did; one by one they wrapped themselves in the lienzos of the Tojiles when they blanketed themselves with their natural essence; with the nawal nature of the First Four Fathers.

The Jaguars didnʼt do anything at all; it was the first painting to be placed over the back of the first of the Lord; that was the first lienzo with which they blanketed the Lords of the Pueblo.

Then the next Lord of the Mountain Pueblos placed the painting of the Eagle upon his back. This was the second of the three painted blankets; it was painted with Eagles.

The second Lord, the second Father was blanketed with the image of the Flock of Eagles on his back; immediately he was captivated by the magical embrace of the painted lienzo as if he were one with the Eagles.

Utterly enchanted was the Lord who began circling around the others flying while flocking with the Eagles as they circled about the Sky.

Then, the Third Lord-Rox Ajaw-Third Father blanketed himself in the third lienzo; third painting that he now wore upon his back. This was a precise painting of a swarm of bees; a perfect rendition of a cloud of wasps that immediately began stinging his flesh the moment he covered himself with this bewitched blanket that became a swarm of bees and a cloud of wasps.

Excruciating, unbearable were the stings and the bites of this most deadly enemy who took revenge on the Lord; the Lord began to cry out in pain because of the biting bees and stinging wasps.

body:
They were just images painted upon a blanket, painted upon a lienzo that was the exact replica-kʼexuwach of the nawal of Majukʼutaj, the third painting: rox tzʼibʼ.

This was the defeat of them; the third image was the cause of their defeat.  Immediately the Two Maidens were punished by the AjAwab: the Lords of the Pueblos.

IxTaj, IxPuch the two of them were immediately punished by the Lords, these Two Maidens were scolded for doing exactly what they were told to do.

“What kind of paintings are these that you have brought to us here? Where did you go to bring those back? IxKʼaxtokʼ you Tricksters,” yelled the Lords.

This was when the Two Maidens were summoned before the Lord Rulers of the Pueblos; Ajawal Amaqʼ to be reprimanded for what they were commanded to do as the Daughters of the Lords.

But those who were defeated were those of the Pueblo who wished only defeat for the Tojiles; but it wasnʼt like that because it was the Tojiles who defeated them; the Lords of the Pueblos. What they wanted was to possess the Tojiles by their being possessed by the irresistible Young Maidens: IxTaj, IxPuch.

They want to incite their desire; they wanted to inflame their knee-scrapping lust, joxol chʼek to be seen as ʼfornicatorsʼ in the hearts of the Pueblo.

And so it was that the Two Maidens were sent to bring about their defeat and demise; the Young Women were sent to provoke the downfall and destruction of the Tojiles.

But it wasnʼt like that; the Pueblo did not do what they set out to do; they did not defeat the Nawal Winaq; they did not bring down los Tojiles; nor did they humiliate those known and named: Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj.

No, no, not los Tojiles.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Enough was enough; the Pueblos have sent their Beautiful Daughters first to diminish and demean the integrity and dignity of the Noble Lords of Tulan Tzuy-Wa who are no animals driven by their ʼbase most instinctsʼ no, no, not los Tojiles. The will not be seduced by beautiful irresistible maidens who work naked over their washing stones; the most erotic image of the Traditional Maya World: a world where it continues to be forbidden for men to watch women working at their grinding stones, washing stones, and weaving because of the motion generated in the hips and shoulders of the woman. So imagine what this text is suggesting in brave kinds of bold ways.

The Young Women are sent to the Bathing Place of Tojil where the Young Men bath everyday where the Two Maidens arrive with hopes of ʼstealing away their heat of their conquest by stealing away the fire of their loins with their feminine powers to be used now as ʼweapons of the weakʼ to enchant and enthrall, bewilder and beguile these handsome Young Men with these Young Womenʼs ʼheat-fire-power-potencyʼ of the seductive enchantresses; ancestral temptresses who are the Daughters of the Lords. Young Women were used to create and maintain powerful alliances between the fertile cacao groves of the Pacific and the fecund milpas of maize of the Highlands.

Their knee-scrapping-joxbʼal trickery did not succeed; it was just the deception of the Lords of the Pueblo that ended in their being deceived by stinging wasps and biting bees; it was just the flawed thinking and the wrong-doing of the Lords of the Pueblo that ended in disaster for the Lords who sent their Daughters to do that which was the divine office and sacred obligation of warriors. The Daughters who allow themselves to be deceived by los Tojiles who wish to deceive the Lords of the Pueblos who sought to deceive the Three Young Man who are the Nawales of los Tojiles which just another name and another ʼfeelʼ for those Kabʼawil known to us as Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz who are shamanic deception as nawal transformation incarnate.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
To keep this Sacred Narrative straight requires rites of passage that are rites of initiation to open the way for those called to ʼenter the word, enter the wayʼ of the Saq Bʼey; Sacred Path; Precious Road; Perfect Path of the Divine Ancestors that leads to being and becoming Day-keepers; AjQʼijabʼ Divinatory Priests and Priestesses who guided and protect their People of their Pueblo through the connection and communication they maintain through ʼjust sacrifice, just ancestral magic; xa pus, xa nawalʼ to form and shape the sacred relationship of sacrifice and petition to obtain what is needed to survive in live through the power and authority of the rule and command of these very same Deities; these very same Kabʼawil named here.

It was just the nawal genius of the Tojiles that brought about the great reversal to bring about the disgrace and degradation of the Lords of the Pueblo. It was all because of their deep need to destroy the Tojiles that the Pueblos did what they did. Now they would need to contemplate what it was that they would do next. And so it was that they gathered together to celebrate council once again to think upon what it would take to finish off the Tojiles there on the Mountain of the Mountain People of the Mountain Pueblos.

Pueblo of Warriors;

Pueblo of Killers;

Pueblo of Assassins: Amaqʼ Kamisanel

This then was when the entire Pueblo took council together; to think it through; xenaʼojin to find what it was they needed to do.

“How much longer must we put up with this? Truly, their nature, their condition, their way of being is now quite powerful; they have become a powerful Pueblo of powerful People. So be it! Ta chuxoq!”

So this is what they said then when they gathered together their thoughts, kinaʼoj; when they brought forth their ideas, kinaʼoj; their genius, kinaʼoj; their imagination, kinaʼoj; their knowing of knowledge, kinaʼoj.

“We should just invade them there where they live and then kill them all! Let us arm ourselves with our arrows and our shields; chi chʼabʼ, chi pokobʼ to then climb up to where they are and finish them off, one and all! Are we not many; are we not more than they?”

body:
“May there remain neither one nor two of them once we finish!” they cried out there below the mountain where those of the Pueblo gathered together in council; when those who were the Mountain People celebrated council with one another below the Mountain Top; Chuwi Juyubʼ of Jaqawitz.

And so it was that they armed all the many People who were gathered there from all the Many Pueblos; all of those who gathered together as one great Pueblo, a great quantity of Warrior-Killers gathered together there when the many People of the many Pueblos armed themselves with arrows and shields. This is when they became a great Pueblo of Warrior-Killers: Amaqʼ e Kamisanel.

Meanwhile it was they the First Four Fathers who were gathered together there atop the mountain Chuwi Juyubʼ Jaqawitz, those known as:

Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ,

Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ,

Majukʼutaj,

Ikʼi Bʼalam

They were there in their citadel mountain fortress Jaqawitz; Jaqawitz is the name of the mountain upon which the Lords were settled together along with their children; their children who they moved up to the top to protect; their children who were made to ascend the mountain to defend the mountain that the place named: Above the Mountain-Chuwi Juyubʼ.

Chuwi Juyubʼ is the mountain top of Jaqawitz had been placed by Majukʼutaj in the Red Temple of Sacrifice Mountain Top Temple House on this place known also as Kaqajawitz that the Kabʼawil had conquered and made their own, the place that all  of them now called home.

They werenʼt many people on top of Jaqawitz, certainly not like the great multitude of people gathered together by the Pueblos.

Just a little part of the mountain top did they occupy; just a small part of the mountain summit did they enclose themselves behind a palisade wall of wood known as a kʼoxtun.

This is where they decided to fight to the death the great multitude of warrior-kamisanel-assassins; the killers who now gathered together as a great invading force of the Pueblos that were there below arming each of the warrior people with a bow and shield.

body:
All those there on Jaqawitz gathered together there up on top of the mountain were they were gathering together in one great council together after the entire Pueblo had been called there by summons; xepoponik, xetaqo kibʼ konojel.

Here then is when all the Pueblos; the Tribes assembled there to arm; to adorn themselves with bow; with arrow; with shield; chi skobʼ; chi chʼabʼ; chi pokobʼ; in nahuatl:  tlahuitolli; mitl; chimalli.

Waʼe kʼute kimolowik kibʼ konojel Amaqʼ e kawutal chik chi chʼab, chi pokobʼ konojel.

Jaqawitz; Kabʼawil of Majukʼutaj; Mountain Top Place of Majukʼutaj

Jaqawitz; ʼOpenʼ Mountain from where to ʼseeʼ the Dawn

Jaqʼawitz; Smashed Open Sacred Pots Mountain

Saqawitz; Cleared-off, Cleaned-off Mountain

Qʼaqʼawitz; Fire Mountain

Kaqajawitz; Red House Mountain of Sacrifice

This cleared off mountain known as Saqawitz with its Red Temple on top giving the mountain the name Kaqajawitz becomes the place known as Jaqawitz. This is where Jaqawitz the Kabʼawil Majukʼutaj was left when Jaqawitz was hidden there on the ʼcleared-offʼ mountain top named Saqawitz.

Jaqawitz is the name of the Kabʼawil that Majukʼutaj bears on his back as his sacred burden. His sacred burden Jaqawitz transforms this mountain of the Red House Temple Nima Kaqja or Kaqaja giving the name of the mountain Red Temple House Mountain is Kaqajawitz.

This is the mountain top we are told is an open, cleared-off mountain known as Saqawitz; that will become Jaqawitz that will be known for the magical war that takes place here where ʼgreat big tamale cooking pots-kukʼubʼ these great pots of sacred sustenance are fitted with tops to cover them that will be ʼbroken open-jaqʼaʼ  to be ʼopened-jaqaʼ the Kukʼubʼ or Sacred Pots in order not to break the sacred pots and by doing so the secret weapon of Jaqawitz will be released as the Animal Transforms or Naguales of Jaqawitz in the form and shape of  big round bees and black wasps known as wonon and sitaʼl.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
This is the magic transforming mountain of the Kʼicheʼ Winaq; Kʼicheʼ Amaqʼ who will establish themselves here on top of the mountain also known as Chuwi Juyubʼ or Atop the Mountain because of the Kabʼawil  known as Jaqawitz is hidden here in the open by Majukʼutaj-ʼNot One is Hereʼ or ʼNothing to be Seenʼ or the ʼInvisible Oneʼ. Who ʼseeminglyʼ uses his powers of invisibility to hide his Kabʼawil in the open beside the temple walls-chi tzʼaq that is suggested when the Kabʼawil tell their ʼBearersʼ that they need to find hiding places for them so they are not taken captive by finding a place: Chi Tzʼaq which is beside a Temple Wall.

To recap and reiterate this all in a very Mesoamerican Way by repeating that which has been repeated to avoid confusion:

Majukʼutaj is guided by counsel given to him at chi Pixabʼ to leave his Kabʼawil Jaqawitz ʼon top of a One Big Red Temple House-chuwi Jun Nima Kaqa Ja upon the Mountain of the Red House Temple of Sacrifice known as Kaqaja the Red Temple House on top of this open, cleared off, cleaned off mountain, Saqawitz giving it the name Kaqajawitz. So that Jaqawitz the Kabʼawil is left out in the ʼopenʼ on Jaqawitz, Saqawitz, Kaqawitz, Kaqajawitz, Qʼaqʼawitz; Qʼaqʼawitz because there is a war here where things heat up and the power-qʼaqʼal of the Kʼicheʼ Warriors is put to the test.

This is an example of infinite and exhausting shamanic play on this first citadel where the Kʼicheʼ will come to establish themselves after the  magical battle takes place where the Kʼicheʼ are guided and protected by their Kabʼawil from Tollan Tzuy-Wa showing their magical superiority as Deities of Conquest and Colonization over the Mountain People, Mountain Pueblos. The power-qʼaqʼal of the Kʼicheʼ as magical Warlords and War Captains and Pueblo of Warriors with powerful  Women Warrior begins here at: Qʼaqʼawitz.

Covered in immense quantities of silver adornment were those stunningly embellished Warlords as well as their War Captains and Warriors.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Truly resplendent was the grandeur of their adornment, their embellishment; astounding, astonishing was the appearance of the Warriors; dazzling was the awesome appearance of all the many Lords; and, the great multitude of Vassals and Subjects gathered together armed for battle on the mountain top of Chuwi Juyubʼ Jaqawitz.

And so it was that those who were gathered to do battle were all well armed and well adorned for the struggle that lay before them.

This was it they were ready and prepared with their bows, arrows, and shields; silver ornaments and feather headdresses as Warlords and Warriors of the Mountain Pueblos has always armed and adorned themselves to live or die in a flowery war to the death.

It was they, the brilliantly adorned warriors, who spoke rousing words to one another to inflame their hearts; just as they roared glowingly of their own warrior prowess; how one was greater than the next; for truly they boasted of the fearsome feats they would accomplish and those of their comrades in arms as if they were truly seasoned warriors; as if they were expert assassins; trained killers; celebrated soldiers.

But in the end it was all the same; just as their self-glorification was all for nothing because in the end they all became the very same as one-an-other; as the names they were named was the exact same as this one and the other.

Because in the end all of them joined together as one to form a great mass of war captives; as they became a great multitude of prisoners of war; for at the end of the day it was they who became captured warriors who were warriors that had been captured.

But they did not think of this when they boasted of their courage in combat; their valor in war; their bravery in battle as they bragged about the enemy they would capture; as the bragged about all the warriors they would kill above on that Ancient Mountain Place; Original Mountain Place known as Above the Mountain; Chuwi Juyubʼ that was an Open Mountain Top known as Jaqawitz.

This is how they spoke before the battle of Jaqawitz when the leaders of the Pueblos spoke to all those gathered beneath the mountain:

body:
“And as for this Tojil; the one with power; he is truly divine for he is a Kabʼawil, and if it is he who we shall come to worship then we shall have to take him captive first.  So let us capture him now,” they cried out; as they rallied together as One Pueblo that made their presence known with their thunderous roar that made the Sky to shudder and the Earth to shake; ecstatic were the Warriors and their Warlords who were now properly prepared for battle; armed and adorned for war.

But this was something Tojil already knew; just as they who were ʼthoseʼ of Tojil knew the nawal ways of their Kabʼawil Tojil; those who were they that were known and named as:

Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ,

Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ,

Majukʼutaj

They heard it all; they heard them their below when the invasion of their mountain was planned; for they did not sleep; nor did they rest their on top of Jaqawitz ever since the warriors armed themselves with arrows and shields.

This was when the warriors rose-up together in the night; perhaps they would invade in the dark, perhaps they would attack out of the shadows under the cover darkness in a nighttime assault.

This is what they thought; this is what they imagined; this is what they knew; those who knew the ways of the enemy that surrounded them now from all side; they knew it all because they saw it all through the thoughts and vision; knowing and knowledge given to them as the instructions of Tojil their Kabʼawil.

They now knew what they knew they would do which was what Tojil instructed them to do. So that when the battle finally came this was what they came to do.

Meanwhile the Pueblos did what their thinking led them to do; which is what they did when it came time for them to do what they had planned together to gather together in the night to invade the mountaintop under cover of darkness.

And this is just how their thoughts guided them as they did everything possible to prepare for their invasion of the mountain top in the dark of night; and so the Pueblos decided as One that it was in the nighttime darkness that they would rise-up and attack the Mountain Top; Chuwi Juyubʼ of los Tojiles and all those who were theirs that lived there now.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
The Pueblos would march on their enemy at night in the dark; in the night they would climb the mountain to attack the poorly protected mountain top. This is how they prepared for their invasion of Jaqawitz, the mountain top citadel of Tojil, the Kabʼawil of those known as those of Tojil: ri Tojil.

And so it was that the Pueblos began their invasion, the resplendently adorned warriors rose-up in the dark of night to begin their steep climb.

They left but they did not arrive; only in the road did they sleep; the many Warriors-AjLabʼal-Guerreros just fell into a deep sleep, right there in the road; and so they were defeated once again by:

Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ,

Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ,

Majukʼutaj.

It was just in one place on the road that they fell into a deep asleep. They didnʼt feel a thing when all of them were finished off by the sleep that left them sleeping in the road.

So then they began pulling their hair; they pulled the hair of their eyebrows; they pulled the hair on their beards; they unfastened the silver adornments bound around their necks; they did the same with their headdress and necklaces. They untied their embellishments as the warriors and warlords slept in the road.

It was from the silver clutches of their noble-staves that they took away all their precious metal, all their silver, all their copper, all their gold as they lay there in the dust sound asleep not feeling a thing as they were picked clean of all that was theirs.

They did this to punish them; they did this to teach them a lesson; they did this to humiliate them by showing them the superiority of the Kʼecheʼ Winaq-Kʼicheʼ People.

As soon as they woke, they grabbed for their headdress-yachwach-penachos and the precious silver ornaments that adorned the clutches, the grasps of their noble staves, those sublime symbols of noble rule; those emblems of divine sovereignty; those insignia of superiority of Noble Lords and their divine right and authority to subjugate and enslave others.

body:
“Who has plucked us clean? Who is pulling our hair like this, making fools of us; us the Noble Lords of the Pueblos? Where could they have come from? Those who rob us of our precious adornment, our silver, our precious metal ornaments that manifests our power, our rule, our authority?  Who are they? From where have they come?” asked the Guerreros-AjLabʼal-the Warriors.

The very same warriors who had planned their perfect invasion of Jaqawitz with so much confidence were now left wondering just who they had come to conquer, kill, and take captive up on top of this mountain they decided to invade in the dark of night with a great deal of preparation and skill.

“Could it be the same ones, the same tricksters-kʼaxtokʼ, who steal away our people without ever beings seen? Is that who has fallen upon us here in the road; in the dark; in the night; in the road in the dark of the night? Could it be they who have stolen away all that we wore as our adornment as well as our arrows and shields that we carried as the warriors we are? Is that who took everything that was ours as we slept in the road?”

“This just-xa canʼt be; this just-xa cannot end this way. It is just-xa no good that we should become frightened of them who took all that we wore to become fearful of them just because they left us without eyelashes and eyebrows; should it be that we become intimidated of them without even knowing who they are or where they come from!”

“There are many ways to invade their citadel to see our silver ornaments again; there are many ways to take back what is ours! We shall do as they have done!” said those of the Tribes; the Pueblos; ri Amaqʼ; but it was just them making words; it was only they who were making up lies. Xawi xere bʼanoj tzij konojel; tzʼaqol tzij xkibʼan na.

Meanwhile, great confidence rose-up in the hearts of the AjKʼixibʼ, AjKʼajbʼ the sacrificial priests, those of the maguey spine, those of the obsidian blade who were there on top of the mountain; the mountain of Jaqawitz.

body:
That ʼopen mountainʼ, that ʼcleared off mountainʼ, that ʼflat-topped mountainʼ where the ʼred temple of sacrificeʼ stood as a remembrance of the ancient ancestral past where the First Four Fathers now prepared for the worst on this sacred mountain of ancestral sacrifice on its red temple steps of its red altar of sacrifice that stood in the Red House of Sacrifice on top of the Mountain of Sacrifice: Kaqa Ja Witz-Jaqawitz-Saqawitz-Jaqʼawitz.

It was just their insight, imagination, and intelligence that gave them their ideas that told them what they needed to know, and so they made their plans in order to know what to do next:

Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ,

Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ,

Majukʼutaj,

Ikʼi Bʼalam

This was when they came to know all that they knew, those named:

Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ,

Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ,

Majukʼutaj,

Ikʼi Bʼalam

They would build a palisade: kʼoxtun. The kʼoxtun was built out of split board planks and pointed stakes, it surrounded their mountain-top citadel-tenamit to form and shape this now completely enclosed walled fortress that protected its People; the wooden palisade that encircled its Pueblo.

The palisade they would build was a defensive wall surrounding their mountain-top fortress that stood as the citadel-tenamit of Jaqawitz; the palisade wall they built was known as a kʼoxtun: they built their palisade out of ʼpalitos-chut-stakesʼ and that is where the word palisade-impalisada defined as: muro de fortaleza de tablas y estacas puntiagudas; a fortress wall of timber planks and sharpened wooden spikes to form the pointed pikes placed in palisade walls.

Then they made wooden men-poy that were carved and sculpted as wooden works of worked wood that looked just exactly as one would imagine puppet people whittled from wood would look as wooden works of wood.

This was because of the superior craftsmanship of their carvers and shapers, sculptors and scrapers who carved as they crafted these wooden warriors of whittled works of wood that stood as wooden men who would become wooden soldiers once they were carved and crafted as wooden warriors that were wooden works of wood that looked as good as their makers, modelers, and molders wished they would.

body:
Next they lined them up; they lined up the decoy soldiers and wooden warriors; they lined-up those who were formed and shaped from wood to then place them right next to one another along the palisade wall.

And so it was that they left these wooden works of worked wood all lined-up in a row along the wooden barricade of the kʼoxtun of this tinamit that was now a perfectly enclosed mountain-top citadel; an encircled fortress; a sound and secure summit stronghold complete with wooden soldiers who were looked just like wooden warriors one and all.

Once the wooden men were perfectly aligned along the protective palisade wall they armed them with the shields and arrows found amongst the sleeping warriors who had slept so well through the dark of night right there on the mountain road.

When those of Jaqawitz were finally finished decorating their decorated decoys; those decorated decoys were left looking like finely adorned and ornamented soldiers who appeared to be well armed and highly disciplined fearsome looking soldiers; truly terrifying warriors meant to intimidate all those who looked upon them from down below; down there beneath from where they now stood silent and stock still; as silent and still as one would expect a highly disciplined arrangement of warriors should stand silent and still because they were trained so that they would stand silent and still like these wooden warriors now stood silent and still just as they could stand silent and still because they were formed and shaped from wood that by its very nature of its existence and condition of being was of a nawal essence of being silent and still.

For these works of wood were now being observed from below by the ʼeyesʼ of the Pueblo that were the ʼspiesʼ of the Pueblo who saw the many warriors preparing for war high up on Jaqawitz as little by little they lined themselves up along the palisade wall to remain standing there silent and still.

They were strikingly attired to appear stunningly attractive with their traditional headdresses-yachwach similar, if not the same, as the sort crafted by the Young Men of the Pueblo; those yachwach of the ballplayers.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
Those yachwach or feathered headdresses were set-off by shiny silver trimmings and trapping that embellished their highly ornamented heads.

These wooden men who were now standing in a perfectly straight line along the fortress wall of kʼoxtun looked and acted just like the resplendent warriors they appeared to be; well armed soldiers with shields and arrows for all to see ready for battle and imminent victory.

Those who formed and shaped these beguiling works of deceptive enchantment bestowed upon them spectacular necklaces that glinted and glimmered as they glistened in the early morning light; light that shined as swept across the mountain top and valley below as the first shimmering, shinning rays of daylight known as saqnatanoj.

The precious metal adornment that the Wooden Warriors wore and the jade necklace that hung around their necks were taken from those who slept so very well in the middle of the road down below the mountain above.

The same precious metal that los Tojiles had lifted from those who now looked upon all that once was theirs that dressed and adorned the Wooden Warriors who stood silent and still on the palisade wall of Jaqawitz.

The Warriors of the Pueblos looked upon all that was theirs that now embellished the recently formed soldiers who were shaped from recently carved wood who stood there as silent as they stood there still in straight, straight line of well-armed warriors each with a bow, a quiver of arrows, and a shield to parry any arrow or blow that came from those who now coming up from down below.

Behind the palisade wall; the kʼoxtun wall of Jaqawitz alongside Tojil safe and protected were the women and children who had multiplied and grown to become many, many descendants of the First Mother-Fathers of the First Lineages of Kʼicheʼ Kingdom known and named:

Kaqa Palama Ja; Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ

Chomi Ja; Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ

Tzʼununi Ja; Majukʼutaj

Kaqixa Ja; Ikʼi Bʼalam

This then was when those of Jaqawitz revealed what was on their heart before asking for their final counsel; a bit of advice; and, some reassurance from their Kabʼawil, Tojil; when they revealed what hung heavy on their hearts.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
And this is when they went before Tojil to ask him of their destiny; to consult his knowledge of what will happen to them:

“Could it be that they kill us; could it be that they defeat us?” This is what they asked their Kabʼawil Tojil.

Will We Die?

And so they opened their hearts as they lay bare their souls before Tojil. Were they going to die; would they be defeated after having come so far; after walking for so long; after struggling so hard? Were they to die; were they to be defeated after finding solutions to the endless problems they confronted on the way?

The question asked of their Kabʼawil is the question all People of Pueblos must ask before a decisive battle in a definitive war: Will we die; will we be defeated; or, will we live and survive to defeat those who came to kill and defeat us?  The Kabʼawil is to console the hearts of his People to encourage their Pueblos by heartening their souls.

It had been their Kabʼawil Tojil from Tulan Tzuy-Was who guided and protected them ever since they received him as their Kabʼawil in that sacred citadel; distant city so very, very, far away from where they were now: surrounded by an enemy that vastly outnumbered; an enemy driven by vengeance rooted in the sacrifice of their own daughters and sons; an enemy driven by a vengeance that comes from being utterly humiliated by being preyed upon in the most degrading and demeaning ways: the sacrifice of oneʼs descendants; oneʼs replacements; the very fruit of oneʼs branches that comes from the trunk of the tree of oneʼs origins. Surely, they are going to die; surely they will be defeated.

Yes, it was clear, their enemy, all the many Pueblos that now surrounded them on all sides with infinite numbers of warriors was ready to kill them and more than willing to defeat them, los Tojiles. Come what may the Pueblos of Mountain People were going to finish them off on the mountain top of Jaqawitz. This then would be the last day, the final day of life for those who were the First Four Fathers; First Four Mothers and all of their many Daughters and Sons who were going to be killed and defeated on Jaqawitz.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
If this was the way it was going to be then so be it! What else could they do other than put their faith in Tojil who had guided and protected them every step of the way.

Tojil did not hesitate when Tojil spoke to all of those who were there held up on top of the mountain of Jaqawitz; there on the cleared-off summit of Jaqawitz in their enclosed citadel known and named Jaqawitz where the Noble Lord Jaqawitz readied himself with all the other Lords to defend their now completely sealed off and surrounded citadel known as Jaqawitz.

If they were going to be killed; if they were going to be defeated; if they going to be finished off then they thought it only proper to ask their Kabʼawil who had guided and protected them all this way.

They just wanted to know; if Tojil could tell them so; then so be it! So they asked and this is what he said; this is what Tojil had to say when he spoke to his People; when he gave counsel to his Pueblo.

This then is when Tojil spoke to them in order to tell them what he knew. This was when he celebrated council with them; those who were his People; his Pueblo there on Jaqawitz:

“Mixbʼisonik! Donʼt be sad! Mixbʼisonik!”

“Mixbʼisonik! Donʼt be worried! Mixbʼisonik!”

“In kʼolik! I am here! In kʼolik!”

“Mixibʼij iwib! Fear not; you need not be afraid! Mixibʼij iwib!”

“Itʼs going to be alright; just donʼt you frighten yourself!” There is something that is yours that you are going to use against them.”

“So be fearless, donʼt be afraid! Mixibʼij iwib!”

And so Tojil spoke to them and as he spoke to them he gave them their instructions when he gave them their counsel; when he left his word of a Kabʼawil with those known as: Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj, Ikʼi Bʼalam.

This was when they were given their nawal weapon: swarms of bees, clouds of wasps. The First Fathers gathered together and then went as one to gather the Bees and Wasps together.

body:
It was then that all of them started back together to bring the Bees and Wasps back as they were counseled to do by Tojil their Kabʼawil who told them just what to do as their guide and protector who guided and protected him as the Noble Lords had always wished to find a Kabʼawil like Tojil who did all he came to do for them, the First Four Fathers of the Kʼicheʼ Winaq; Kʼiche Amaq.

The four of them brought back those that were; just Big Round Black Bees; just Black Metallic Wasp; xa Wonon, xa Sitaʼl.

Right away they-Bʼalam Kiʼtzeʼ, Bʼalam Aqʼabʼ, Majukʼutaj, Ikʼi Bʼalam-gathered the Bees and Wasps and placed them into Four Great Big Pots-Kajibʼ Nimaq Kukʼubʼ-Cuatro Grandes Tinajones.

Spoken of as Kukubʼ that were great big terracotta clay pots used for cooking Maize Tamales or Wa-Cuatro Grandes Tinajones-Kajibʼ Nimaq Kukʼubʼ once upon a time known as ʼGod Potsʼ by a past generation of interpreter-translators.

Then they carried the four great big pots filled with swarms of bees; clouds of wasps back to within the palisade walls; kʼoxtun of their citadel; they carried the four big clay pots; ri Kajibʼ Nimaq Kukubʼ to set them in four very perfect places around the edge of their mountain-top citadel, their walled and well-protected stronghold.

It was in the four great big pots; los cuatro grandes tinajones; kajibʼ nimaq kukʼub that they kept the bees and wasps enclosed, they kept them captive to be left waiting in the four perfectly picked places that were there beside the four entrances to the citadel settlement there on the Mountain Top; Chuwi Juyubʼ.

These Bees and those Wasps were the nawal weapon; nawal ally the First Four Fathers would wield against the angry and aggressive attack of the Warriors and Warlords of the People;  of the  Pueblos who were there below making plans of their own as they surrounded in order to encircle and enclose those of Chuwi Juyub;  Jaqawitz. Those of Chuwi Juyubʼ were they women and children of the First Mother-Fathers of the Original Kʼicheʼ Pueblo.

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
It was they who were now completely enveloped by a swarm of warriors and a cloud of killers with their arrows-chi chabʼ, their shields-chi pokobʼ that they held together in a great mass of assassin-warriors who were coming up from down below to take back what was taken from them not so very long ago.

Kukub; Sacred Pots

Wonon; Big Round Bees

Sitaʼl; Metallic Black Wasps

Remember how the Two Maidens who were both powerful and potent attractive temptations were not successful at seducing the Three Young Men; los Tojiles. They had not succeeded in their purpose and its intention to ʼsteal the fire that burned in the loinsʼ of the Three Young Men. Their deception ended in reversal as the nawal power of transformation of los Tojiles transformed into the trickster magic of Majukʼutaj-the Invisible One.

Majukʼutaj drew Swarms of Bees and Clouds of Wasps in order to send the ʼinvisible enemyʼ in the form and shape of his nagual; his animal transform that came to life as a swarm of warriors; as a cloud of enemies who erupted from the painting; out of the lienzo that Majukʼutaj was commissioned to paint by los Nawales on behalf of the Two Maidens as requested from their Fathers; the Noble Lords of the Pueblo.

The Swarm of Bees-Jumaj Wonon; Cloud of Wasps-Jumaj Sitaʼl were made to bite and sting the ʼenemy on all sidesʼ in an all out attack on the Fathers of the Daughters of the Noble Lords of the Pueblo who were stung and bit by the Big Round Bees and Metallic Black Wasps; Bees and Wasps-Wonon and Sitaʼl.

Best we remember their names; Wonon, Sitaʼl-Bees, Wasps to memorize them by heart. Best and better yet to provide a place for them to nest around the house inviting them in as allies and protectors of the Sitio; guardians of the Compound; Watchers, Sentinels, Sentries of the home and garden in town and out of town in the countryside since Wonon, Sitaʼl are remembrances of the Divine Ancestors and Kabʼawil; these are Nawal Animal Transforms or Naguales to be enveloped and embraced as the beloved protectors of People of Nature in a world where not all naguales are jaguar, puma, eagle, hummingbirds, and hawks: not at all!

source: Popol Wuj: Translation and Interpretation, Vincent James Stanzione (Grove Press manuscript, October 24-27 2025)
body:
As a matter of fact there is a hive of Little Black Stingless Bees Melipona beecheii or Aqaj began building their hive when I began investigating all of the different varieties of bees and wasps during this Translation and Interpretation of the Ancient Word. They are an auspicious gift of the Forest in which I live providing me with happiness in contentment as we reciprocate by providing them a peaceful and protected place to live. The Maya live with bees and wasps who are understood as Kʼexuwach Ojer Winaq thus gratefully received to work around the house and gardens; groves and fields pollinating flowers and making honey. What is best they act as guardians and protectors of the household!

Those of the Pueblo watched those of Tojil at a distance and so it was that those who were they who were there on the Mountain Top were being spied upon by those who were secretly watching them from down below Chuwi Juyubʼ by the Messenger Warriors of the Pueblo-Samajel Amaqʼ-who were sent to Jaqawitz as Spies of the Pueblos; Amaqʼ to watch everything that los Tojiles and his People did there atop the Mountain; Chuwi Juyubʼ.

“There are not so very many of them there,” they said then-los de abajo-those from below.

This was only because the spies could only see the wooden-men; the adorned wooden-men who were seen by the spies moving back and forth all along the watchtower wall of the kʼoxtun.

They could see the fearsome appearances of the ornamented warriors on the palisade wall moving with their bow; moving with their arrows; moving with their shields as they appeared to be moving there along the kʼoxtun with its watchtower where the wooden warriors seemed now to be moving all along its wall that the spies saw so very well from where they were down below.

They looked like real warriors; they looked just like real killers there on the palisade wall; there behind the wooden fortification of the palisade-kʼoxtun theyʼd formed and shaped just a short time ago.
